On the Track of Unknown Animals (Heuvelmans, 1958)
==================================================
The founding text of cryptozoology: Heuvelmans' worldwide survey of unknown and out-of-place animals in seven parts and nineteen chapters — from the orang-pendek and the yeti to sea serpents and the mammoth of the taiga — in Richard Garnett's 1958 English translation, public domain. Scan via Internet Archive.

BERNARD HEUVELMANS


With an Introduction by
GERALD DURRELL


$7.50


At the beginning of the nineteenth century
Georges Cuvier, the “Father of Palaeon-
tology,”’ categorically stated that there was
little hope that any large animals were still
unknown. Since then have been discovered
the largest species of bear and gorilla, a white
rhinoceros, the pygmy elephant and hippo-
potamus, the bizarre okapi and the fabulous-
looking Komodo dragon, and dozens of other
large and unusual animals. Yet official zoo-
logy is still apt to repeat Cuvier’s dictum.
Dr Heuvelmans thinks otherwise, and with an
immense wealth of reference, ranging through
scientific literature in many languages from
classical writers to obscure monographs in
East Indian journals, examines the evidence
about the animals which may yet be found
and are still unknown to science. When na-
tives’ and hunters’
reports
of mysterious
animals and palaeontologists’ descriptions of
fossil species now thought to be extinct begin
to converge, may it not be that, like the
Coelacanth, the animal is not extinct after


_ all?


The creatures examined range from animals
like the spotted lion of Kenya and the Queens-
land marsupial tiger, which are unsensational
enough to be almost admitted in the official
catalogue of zoology, to the more mysterious
but equally well-documented
abominable
snowman and other lesser known ape-men
that have been reported in south-east Asia.
The author traces the history of the moa, the
giant sloth and the mammoth, all of which
were contemporary with man and are now
known to have survived until much later than
was at first thought, and argues that it is not
impossible that they may still exist. He shows
the close and fascinating similarity between
various animals such as the agogwe and the
kongamato which are firmly believed in by
many natives although they seem so strange
and terrifying as to be barely credible, with
the indisputable palaeontological discoveries
of such fossils as the Australopithecus, a tiny
ape-man, and even the Pterodacty]l.


The drawings of the animals on the cover are by
Monique Watteau. More information about them
will be found on pages 32, 112, 129, 193, 214
257» 303) 314, 413 and 474.

Introduction


WHEN I was asked to write this introduction I agreed to do so with
somewhat mixed feelings, as for a number of years I had been collecting
material to write just such a book myself. However, after reading Dr
Bernard Heuvelmans’s book, my feeling of chagrin vanished, for I


realised that the amount of information I had collected and the amount


of research I had done were infinitesimal compared to his efforts.


Nowadays, to say you believe that in some parts of the world there
may be quite large animals unknown to science is tantamount to admit-
ting that you are slightly weak-minded. Come back from a remote
part of the world and report that you have seen something which does
not fit in with any category of known animal from that area, and you are
branded immediately as a drunkard or a liar—or preferably both. It
seems to me a very odd attitude to adopt, when you consider the vast
areas of the world that, although they may be adequately mapped, are
inhabited by only a scattered handful of people, most of whom have


little knowledge of, and little interest in, the local natural history. I am
referring now, of course, to what are laughably called “reliable sources
of information,” i.e. white officials on the spot. The indigenous in-
habitants are well known to be most unreliable, since they have spent
their whole lives on the spot and know most of the local countryside
intimately. The fact that the officials on the spot have generally very


little time for observing the animal life around them, and are in most


cases uninterested in natural history is, I think, one of the strongest
arguments in favour of finding unknown species.


I remember once in West Africa, after I had spent three or four
months there collecting animals for zoos, I had my collection housed
in a large marquee, and a local official paid me a visit to see the animals.
I had at that time some 250 different kinds, and as I led him from cage


to cage he became more and more amazed.


“I have spent twenty-five years on the coast,” he said to me, “and
I thought I knew it pretty well, but I have never seen any of these
things before. Are they all exceedingly rare?”


B
17


INTRODUCTION


Of course, the majority of the animals were not rare; some of them had
been caught in fact within a couple of hundred yards of this official’s
bungalow. As he had never taken the trouble to look for them, he had
never seen the creatures that inhabited his backyard in such quantities.


To say, therefore, that such a thing as a Nandi bear or an abominable
snowman cannot possibly exist is an extraordinary attitude, and you feel
that the people who adopt this argument would, on being presented
with a hand-tame abominable snowman in a wrought-iron cage, remark
—like the Irishman on seeing the giraffe for the first time—“I don’t
believe it.”


In the last 150 years an astonishing number of large animals have
come to light in the most odd places: the pygmy hippo, for example, in
Liberia; and the okapi. This latter animal, incidentally, was known
only as an extinct relative of the giraffe until it was discovered living and
breeding in the Congo forests. In more recent years there was the dis-
covery of the Congo peacock; the Indo-Chinese forest-ox; the Komodo
dragon; and the king cheetah. This latter is, perhaps, the most surpris-
ing, since it was found in Rhodesia almost within a stone’s throw of the
capital of Salisbury, in an area that had been so well traversed by big-
game hunters and zoologists that you would have thought nothing as
large as this could have remained undiscovered so long. Most of these
animals were known first from native reports about them, and, of course,
in many cases the reports were disbelieved, since, as everyone knows,
primitive tribesmen all over the world spend their spare time making
up stories about animals in order to confuse and delude European
zoologists.


It is curious how little faith is placed in a native report. The fact that,
in the case of large predatory animals, the reports will naturally be
highly coloured and exaggerated is surely no reason for dismissing them
out of hand. When I was collecting in the Cameroons once, I obtained
some rather unusual forest tortoises and lavished upon them all the
foods that are normally beloved of the tortoise family: fruit, succulent
leaves and occasional pieces of meat. To my extreme annoyance the
tortoises refused to touch any of this food and grew thinner and thinner,
An elderly native hunter one day, watching me trying to persuade the
reptiles to eat, informed me, with ill-concealed amusement, that I was
giving them the wrong thing. He went off into the forest and after some
time returned carrying a calabash full of small white forest mushrooms.
Before my disbelieving eyes he scattered these in front of the tortoises,
and they fell upon them with avidity. Now, had he informed me that


18


INTRODUCTION


these creatures ate forest mushrooms, I would, I regret to admit, have
dismissed it as just another native tale.


So the argument of the sceptics runs: native reports are unreliable,
and in any case the country is so well traversed that how could any large
unknown species escape observation.
Of all the parts of the world
where you would think this argument held good you could hardly pick
two better places than Bermuda and New Zealand. You would imagine
by now that both would have been pretty thoroughly explored and
worked over by zoologists and ornithologists, and yet since the end of


the war two supposedly extinct species have been rediscovered, in


Bermuda the cahow and in New Zealand the Notornis. When you think


that these birds have been living and breeding in little pockets, as it


were, under the very eyes of competent observers for so long without


discovery, it is surely not straining credibility too far to imagine that in


the vast, sparsely inhabited, or completely uninhabited areas of the


world, such as the Congo forests, the great swamps of Africa, the Matto


Grosso, the thick evergreen forest of Patagonia, or on the huge shining


ramparts of the Himalayas, there may be found animals unknown to


science.


Take the unfortunate, long-suffering sea-serpent as an example.’ So
much scorn and ridicule has been poured on the heads of those who
stated in the past that they had seen curious monsters in the sea, that
nowadays if one hauled itself ashore on Brighton beach during August
Bank holiday, you would probably have difficulty in obtaining twelve
witnesses who would be willing to come forward and risk the storm of
disbelief that would descend upon them. Why, the experts would cry,
don’t we see them more often if there are such things? Why have their
dead bodies never been washed up on shore? Of course, the reason we
don’t see them more often should become reasonably obvious to anyone
who takes the trouble to glance inside a school atlas and work out the
proportion of the world that is covered by sea, and the proportion of


the sea that is covered by regular shipping routes. As regards the sea-


serpent’s corpse, one could point out that round the land masses of the


world there is a fairly extensive shore-line, and most of it so sparsely


inhabited that a couple of dozen sperm-whales could lie and rot in the


sun without even being noticed. I wonder what proportion of people


(even interested naturalists), who have spent all their lives in Africa,


have seen the corpse of an elephant that has died from natural causes?


1 The sea-serpent, with other unknown marine animals, will be dealt with in
a separate work.


19


INTRODUCTION


But the chief argument against the sea-serpents appears to be that if they
do exist they must of necessity be a form of “prehistoric monster.” Why
everyone should consider this so impossible, I have yet to discover. The
crocodile and the tortoise have come down to us almost unchanged
through millions of years. The tuatara, of New Zealand, is a living


fossil, as also is the okapi. And it is difficult to deny the prehistoric
qualities of the Coelacanth.


Of course, the scientists want positive proof of the existence of these
“mythical” creatures in the shape of skins and skulls, but they would
make much better use of their energies in looking for them, rather
than wasting their time desperately trying to disprove the few bits of
evidence we have. It would be more to the point if they tried to obtain
an abominable snowman rather than trying to prove that he does not


exist by the curious argument that his enormous footprints are created
by a leaping monkey the size of a dog.


Up to now most zoologists have treated the whole subject of sea-
serpents, abominable snowmen and similar creatures as something that


is not quite nice. It is as though they feel there were some gigantic
conspiracy afoot to undermine their ideas of what does and what does
not exist in the world. This attitude has made it extremely difficult to
get at the facts behind reports of these alleged creatures. Whether they


exist or not, it was essential for someone to collect all the reports and


sift them through for publication. If the animals do exist and are
discovered, this book will prove a valuable piece of research. If, on the
other hand, it is proved that they do nor exist, the book loses none of its
value, for it becomes an important contribution to zoological mythology.


In this book Dr Bernard Heuvelmans has marshalled an astonishing
parade of unknown animals, and he has done so with great skill and


scientific detachment, resisting the temptation to sensationalise.
To
anyone who is interested in animal life it will provide a spur, making him


feel he should leave immediately on the trail of one of these strange
creatures. In these days of high-speed travel the world has become a
rather drab place from an explorer’s point of view, so it is nice to think
that in the few remaining inaccessible parts of the globe there may
be animals unknown to science, awaiting discovery. It is pleasant to
imagine that the grandeur of the Himalayas shelters an abominable
snowman, or that in the swamps of Africa there may be scaly monsters
sporting in the waters, as their ancestors did millions of years ago, but it
is to be hoped that they occasionally allow themselves to be discovered,
if only to confound the sceptics.
GERALD DURRELL

Acknowledgments


THIS English edition is in many respects better than the original
French edition published in 1955. It has been brought up to date and
many errors and inexactitudes corrected; moreover, while much sub-


sidiary matter has been abridged by the translator, a vast amount of


unpublished material has been added. Some important chapters have


been rewritten and several new illustrations have been included.


I am deeply grateful to the large number of people who, by giving me
information which has often been invaluable, have helped me to compile
my dossiers, particularly: Excellentissima Senhora Anna Isabel de Sa
Leitdo Teixeira of Rio de Janeiro; Professor A. Ledoux of the Faculty
of Science at Toulouse; Dr Serge Frechkop and Dr André Capart of
the Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences; Professor Paul Bonnivair,
Honorary Inspector-General of Agriculture in the Belgian Congo; M.
Lucien Blancou, Chief Game-Inspector of the French Colonies; Pro-
fessor N. Boeff of the Faculty of Biology and the Zoological Garden at


Sofia; M. Georges Sandrart, formerly the Resident in Ruanda-Urundi;
the late Dr Walter Tamm, Director of the Hospital at Soerabaya;
M. H. Dumont, French Consul at Bombay; M. Henri Pitaud, Director
of the Sociedad de Estudios Franco-Paraguayos of Asuncion; Count
Guy de Germiny of Florence; Count Christoph Vojkffy of Schloss Zeil,
Wiirttemberg; M. Pierre Srinati of Geneva; M. Robert Kirch of Spiez;
M. Jean Delaborde, formerly Chief Paymaster of the French Navy;
Colonel Alex Godart, late of the Belgian Congo Police; Commandant
Imbard, of the Territory of the Ouargla Oases in Algeria; M. Henry
Thétard, Founder of the Colonial Zoo at Vincennes; Dr Sam Thomas
of London; Maitre Marcel Bouquet of Casablanca; M. Morel, the
chemist at Rosendaél; Sefior Léo Bottenwieser of Buenos Aires, M.
Jacques Blanchard of Paris, M. C. A. Loverdo of Athens; M. Pol Caput
of Bordeaux; M. Cyrille de Neubourg and Charles H. Dewisme, the


writers; and finally Mr Richard Garnett, the author of the present


translation, who has proved to be not only a translator, but also a


most diligent and valuable collaborator.

ACKNOWLEDGMENTS


I should like to thank in advance any readers in Britain and America
—which have given so many travellers, explorers, naturalists and
scholars to the world—who can help me to complete my dossiers, either
with their own evidence or by pointing out published material that I
have overlooked.


I should like to take the opportunity of thanking those distinguished
figures in the world of Natural History who have encouraged me in my
researches into animals as yet undescribed by science, particularly
Professor Roger Heim of the National Museum of Natural History in
Paris and President of the International Union for the Conservation of
Nature and Natural Resources, Professor Edouard Bourdelle, also of


the Paris Museum, and Dr Maurice Burton, late of the British Museum
(Natural History).


I must also acknowledge my debt to those who have gone before me


‘fon the track of unknown animals,” in particular Philip H. Gosse, the
Victorian naturalist, Willy Ley, Frank W. Lane, Dr Ingo Krumbiegel,
and especially Ivan T. Sanderson, some of whose writings gave me the
idea of this book.


Finally I should like to thank those who have given me permission to

CHAPTER ONE


There are Lost Worlds Everywhere


I think it is arrogant from a scientific point of
view to deny the existence of things one does not
Know. I am not one of those scientists—respect-
able ones at that—who decree from their studies
that the surprising stories of seeing unknown
giant animals are mere fables.
I maintain that
the world still hides numerous species of giant
and monstrous animals.


LORENZ HAGENBECK,
director
of Hamburg
Zoo, to a journalist.


Even to-day there are in every part of the world
inaccessible areas where there certainly exist wild
creatures unknown to naturalists.


JOSEPH DELMONT, the great animal-catcher.


MosrT zoologists are sceptical about the possibilities of discovering new
species of large animals, and some of them do not, with legitimate
scientific scepticism, keep an open mind until the species is proved to


exist, but categorically deny that it can possibly do so until they have
been forcibly proved wrong. Their obstinacy is based on three pro-
positions: the world has now been completely explored; no new animals
have been discovered for a long time—at least not since the okapi; and
many of the animals alleged to exist are fossil species and therefore long
extinct. All three propositions are fallacies, as I hope to show in the first


three chapters of this book.


Since this is the official attitude it is hardly surprising that the man in


the street is contemptuous of the stories of unknown animals, often


circumstantial and from reliable sources, so often and so summarily


reported in the Press. Small wonder too that journalists are apt to treat


the subject with facetious irony. And all too often their suspicions are


justified.


25


THE GREAT DAYS OF ZOOLOGY ARE NOT DONE


In 1950 a photographic agency circulated a picture of a huge beast
stranded on a beach near Suez, which according to the caption was a
“mystery Sea-monster.” The creature in the photograph seemed to be
a big whale with large curved tusks, but to the informed eye there was no
doubt that it was an ordinary whale whose jaw-bones had been pushed
out of its jaw by an accident: it had probably hit a mine or a ship’s
screw.


Just before the war, a number of newspapers and magazines an-
nounced that a living ape-man, called Azzo, had been discovered in
North Africa, and published a photograph of him. Actually he was a
poor microcephalous idiot, one of those cretins with a stunted skull that
one sometimes finds among freaks in fair-grounds.


But a few bloomers of this kind do not mean that all reports of un-
known animals are untrustworthy. Because one has been taken in by a


liar there is no reason to disbelieve honest men. Yet this is what the
public and the journalists do. And often this has disastrous results. The
Press made such a laughing-stock of the Loch Ness monster, even
though most of the local inhabitants had good reason for believing in it,


that no scientific commission has ever dared to tackle the problem of
what may be one of the most exciting zoological discoveries of the
century.
All because of the pernicious official attitude, based upon
three fallacies.


The world is by no means thoroughly explored. It is true that we
know almost all of its geography, there are no more large islands or
continents to be discovered. But because a country is on the map it
does not mean that we know all about its inhabitants. There are still
more things in heaven and earth than are dreamt of in Horatio’s
philosophy.


Let us begin with the most unknown but least hopeful continent,
Antarctica.
It covers 5 million square miles, the area of the United
States and Western Europe put together, and even after the Inter-
national Geophysical Year is over I doubt if more than half of it will
have been explored. Of course it is the most inhospitable country in the
world, and boasts no known terrestrial mammals, The only amphibious
ones, the seals, rarely venture far from the coast, nor do the penguins,
petrels, gulls and skuas, which are all sea-birds. There is little hope of
finding unknown mammals or birds in the middle of Antarctica, but
there is a faint chance. During Admiral Byrd’s great 1947 expedition
to explore the continent, some of his airmen flying over Wilkes Land
near the Knox Coast found an area the size of a small county, quite


26


THERE ARE LOST WORLDS EVERYWHERE


free of snow and ice, 5 miles inland and 110 miles from the open sea.
Bunger’s Oasis, as it was named after David Bunger, who was the first


to see it, was visited by helicopters and found to be scattered with


small pools of salt water, full of seaweed of different colours. No doubt


Antarctica holds other surprises.1


Greenland is hardly any better known. The central and northern
parts have never been trodden by the foot of white man. But all this
country has frequently been flown over by low-flying aircraft, from
which you can clearly see seals lying in the sun and polar bears which


are sometimes found 500 miles inland.
On this white background
everything stands out like a flea on a white sheet. This is why Paul-


Emile Victor, the great French polar explorer, writes: “Perhaps one


day hitherto unknown species of animals will be discovered in these


regions.
But it should be understood that they will only be small


animals, like insects for instance.”


Africa is infinitely better explored, but holds more promise for the


naturalist. Although none of it is utterly unknown, except for a few
patches in the middle of the Kalahari Desert, and thus there are few of
those intriguing white blanks left on the map, much of it has been
mapped but not explored. The geographer has only to take a series of
geodesic bearings, often from mountains a long way off, to follow the
course of rivers by canoe or along their banks and to fill in the gaps with


aerial photographs. The naturalist’s work often begins where the geo-
grapher leaves off, and the use of aerial photography gives the illusion
that the world is much better known than it is. For there is not the
least hope of finding out from an aerial photograph of forests or steppes
of tall grass and bush what animals live there, even if they are as large


as an elephant or a rhinoceros. There is even less if they are aquatic
animals like the hippopotamus, the manatee and most of the large


reptiles.


The likeliest country to contain large unknown animals is the great
equatorial rain-forest in which six of the most important zoological

discoveries of the present century have been made. The American
naturalist Herbert Lang writes of it:


Whoever penetrated here was, so to speak, “‘on the wing,” and wings
beat doubly fast across these inhospitable regions.
The numerous
sportsmen who had visited nearly all parts in Africa found no attraction
in these forests.
Indeed, the many pale, haggard faces that emerged
from the western half of equatorial Africa were no incentive for
pleasure-seeking people. The immensity of the wilderness is appalling;
for over eighteen hundred miles without a break it stretches more than
half-way across the continent, from the coast of Guinea to the Ruwen-
zori. In spite of tropical luxuriance, it is one of the most dismal spots
on the face of the globe, for the torrid sun burns above miles of leafy
expanse, and the unflagging heat of about one hundred degrees day and
night renders the moist atmosphere unbearable. Over the whole area
storms of tropical violence thunder and rage almost daily.
Here
natives have become cannibals, and the graves of thousands of white
men are merely a remembrance of where youthful energy and adven-
tures came to a sudden end.


Other little-known areas in tropical Africa are the mountainous parts
of Kenya and Katanga and the areas of swamp or scattered lakes which
might shelter large unknown animals; that is to say the Rhodesian lakes,


the Addar marshes, which cover 1,500 square miles, or those of the
Bahr-el-Ghazal, a tributary of the White Nile in Sudan, which are even
more vast and some parts of which have never been crossed.


In Asia the Arabian desert of Dahana is, according to the geographer
Maurette, ‘‘the least explored in the world.
It is infinitely less well-
known than the poles.” But this arid and sterile tomb of ancient


civilisations is chiefly of interest to the archaeologist. There is more for
the naturalist in the foothills of the Himalayas and the valleys in the
north and south-east of this great mountain range and in the vast
Siberian coniferous forest, the taiga. In 1955 Soviet geographers were
surprised to discover that whole ranges of mountains in the Kolyma and
Indiguirka areas, the general shape of which was supposed to be known,
actually stretched in quite unexpected directions. Where mountains
can so long remain unknown, there is good hope for the naturalist.


Zoologists have far from exhausted the wealth of the tropical jungle
in such supposedly known lands as India, Burma, the Moi country in
Indo-China, Malaya, central Borneo and Sumatra. Nothing whatever is
known about the mountainous centre of New Guinea except that
various tribes, many of them pygmies, still live there in the Stone Age.
In 1938 the American naturalist Richard Archbold accidentally dis-

covered in the western part of the island an excellently irrigated valley
inhabited by 60,000 people. And in June 1954 patrol aircraft found
quite unknown tribes in valleys in the south-west. Their population
was estimated at 100,000, a third of the number of Papuans already
known.


Most of the interior of Australia is covered with deserts of sand, salt
and thorny bush. Even the least inhospitable parts are steppes of tall
grass scattered with stunted shrubs. Hardly anybody goes there except


a few prospectors, who come back with tales of animals so fantastic that


they are usually thought to be drunken visions. But anything can hap-


pen in a continent where there are ranges of mountains which have


never been seen except from an aeroplane.


The continent that holds the most mysteries is certainly South
America. There are dozens of blank spots on the map. On the more
accurate surveys the Amazon basin is as full of holes as a Gruyére
cheese. Bertrand Flornoy, who has spent much of his life exploring this
country, calls it “a vast night of trees which stretches for two million
square miles.” Four centuries of exploration have not got to the bottom
of it, because, as Flornoy says:


The virgin forest constantly opposes man’s efforts with its irresistible
power which transforms all decay into new life in a matter of hours. A
path is no sooner opened than the jungle wipes it out. And, if you fly
over the Amazonian forest, towns like Belem and Manaos in Brazil and
Iquitos in Peru look like clearings. As to the clearings in which the
Indians live, they are invisible.


Besides the heart of the Matto Grosso, a large part of Colombia is
unknown, at least in practice, and so is the hinterland of Venezuela and
Guiana and a large chunk of the Cordillera of the Andes. The wooded
part of Patagonia is far from being thoroughly explored.


There is one part of South America which is of special interest, since


it is a perfect example of an almost inaccessible nature reserve. It lies


in that corner of Venezuela which includes the sources of the Orinoco.


There, among the almost impenetrable jungle of the Gran Sabana, rise


the mesas, vast limestone plateaux cut off from the rest of the world by


sheer cliffs between 3,000 and 10,000 feet high. Some of these mesas are


almost 20 miles long, great islands of thick vegetation about which often


nothing is known. On those which have been explored rodents have


been found that are unknown in the local forests but recall those of the


Venezuelan Andes hundreds of miles to the west. In any case these


29


THE GREAT DAYS OF ZOOLOGY ARE NOT DONE


plateaux are not easy to reach. In 1937 Jimmy Angel tried to land his
aircraft on the top of the Auyan Tepui mesa (or Devil’s Mountain) but
crashed in a swamp not far from the edge of the cliff. Even so, he was
able to explore only a few hundred yards from the site of the crash, for
the mesas are split by a network of deep crevasses. It was on this same
mesa that Jimmy Angel recently discovered a waterfall fifteen times
higher than Niagara. From the sheer 5,000-foot wall of Auyan Tepui
gigantic columns of water fall 3,200 feet. As the top of the waterfall was
usually hidden in clouds, the Taurepan Indians long ago told the
conquistadors that there were terrible waterfalls that fell directly from
the sky. Naturally they were not believed.


This may give some idea how little we know of the Venezuelan Gran
Sabana. If the highest waterfall in the world should have remained so
long unnoticed, how can we be sure that this country does not still
conceal some unknown animals, even quite large ones? I do not suggest
that we can hope to emulate Professor Challenger’s success in Conan
Doyle’s famous precursor of science fiction, The Lost World, when he
found on a similar plateau all the enormous reptiles from all parts of the
world in the Mesozoic era and even some ape-men.! But it is absurd to


insist that there can be mo unknown animals in such little-known
country.


In any case, animals of a past age do not need to be imprisoned on a
small island or on the top of a mesa to be preserved from destruction by
their subsequent competitors. A continent or large island will do as well.
Australia is the marsupials’ “lost world” ;
Madagascar the lemurs’; and
New Zealand that of the rhynchocephalous reptiles and a once-flourish-
ing empire of birds. Even on continents a particular habitat, unsuitable


for most other creatures, can provide a very safe retreat for the species


that have managed to adapt themselves to it.


But in fact for the zoologist the whole world is terra incognita, and
not only for the ichthyologist who may bring up a new species every
time he hauls in his net. On land there is still hope of finding many
new species—especially of small animals.

The entomologist can make a scientific discovery by exploring his
own garden. Nor need those concerned with other small freshwater or
land invertebrates go far afield. In deep wells, caves and underground
streams they can be sure of new and interesting finds. Cave-explorers
bring so many new and unknown forms of life to the surface that a whole
new branch of science has been formed to record and study their


discoveries.


But if we are content with small things [writes Dr Maurice Burton],
insects, spiders and the like, there is no need to search the inaccessible
places; we may quite easily find new forms on our doorstep.


The entomologist has the largest haul, which is hardly surprising,
since three-quarters of a million kinds of known animals belong to the
troublesome insect empire. On the average 5,000 new species or sub~
species of insects are described each year.
Discoveries of new land
vertebrates—which are what we are concerned with here—are obviously

These figures imply that since the beginning of this century an


average of about 15 reptiles or amphibians, 220 mammals and 400 birds


have been described each year. Of course this does not mean that they


were all really new and hitherto unknown.
It is a pet foible of many


zoologists to create new species and sub-species on the strength of barely


perceptible differences, often by arbitrary divisions of known forms. All


the same, we can reckon that one in ten of these descriptions refers to a


clearly distinct species. Therefore each year the catalogue includes some

40 birds and 20 mammals that were hitherto unknown. The former are
usually small song-birds, the latter little rodents or bats or even small
marsupials or insectivores. Reptiles and amphibians are much rarer and
almost an exception: there are no more than one or two a year.


As soon as you set about looking for large animals the area of the
world to be searched becomes much smaller, and is generally restricted
to the places I have detailed above. All the same, we should not forget
that even without Antarctica, the regions that are little known or quite
unexplored amount to no less than one tenth of the land surface of the
globe.


Anyone who has travelled will agree that even in the supposedly
best-known parts of the world there are less accessible areas where
unknown animals might hide. In the Swiss, Bavarian and Austrian
Alps a sort of stumpy “lizard” at least 2 to 3 feet long has frequently

Naturally some of the legends about the Tatzelwurm are suspect. It


is said to be able to jump 2 or 3 yards, to be oddly aggressive for a lizard,


to attack and wound cattle, and even to be venomous—so venomous that


“its breath alone can kill you.”’ But not all of these superstitions are so


exaggerated. In 1908 a professional hunter, in whom A. von Draseno-


vitch had complete confidence, told this Austrian Privy Councillor that


he had met the beast near Murau in Steiermark some 5,000 feet up. It


looked like a monstrous worm 18 inches long and 3 inches thick, but

with four very short legs. Knowing its reputation, the hunter prudently
drew his knife before approaching. As soon as he came close the beast
flew in his face; he replied with his knife, but the blade would hardly
penetrate its leathery skin. The “worm” made half a dozen attacks
before it retreated into a crack in the rock to nurse its wounds. Despite
the hunter’s persistent attempts he could not make it come out or even.
find it again.


Although the stories about the Tatzelwurm are so common and so
similar, many people have doubted its existence.
One of the most
frequent versions is that it is a stray otter; and indeed this animal could
make fairly long jumps and hiss like a snake (or like a cat, for that
matter). Another suggestion, made by the Swiss naturalist Revilliod,


is that it is a mangy badger that has lost its fur. But those who had seen
the beast, many of whom knew the local fauna well, insisted that they
were not such fools as to mistake an otter or a bald badger for a
Tatzelwurm.


Other sceptics have asserted that the legend will not hold water, since


lizards are never venomous. This may be true as a rule, but there are
two exceptions: the Gila monster of Texas and Arizona (Heloderma
suspectum) and the Mexican escorpidén (H. horridum). These big lizards,


3. The Mexican escorpién (Heloderma horridum).


which may reach a length of 2 feet 6 inches, well deserve all their names,


for on their lower jaw they have a whole row of venomous fangs. When
they bite they bury their hooked teeth in so deep it is impossible to
make them let go. But though it is very painful to be bitten by one, it is
not fatal for man.


They are squat, with a short, thick tail and fit the Tatzelwurm’s des-


cription so well that Jakob Nicolussi, an Austrian schoolmaster, went so


34


THERE ARE LOST WORLDS EVERYWHERE


far as to baptise it Heloderma europaeum. He was too hasty, for the
beast’s identity is far from being definitely established.


On the other hand, the Tarzelwurm’s venom may well be merely a
myth invented by the popular mind. There will be many instances in


this book where people have tried to justify their fear of the unknown
by pretending that a creature they rarely see is more terrifying than it


really is. A correspondent of mine, Robert Kirch of Spiez in the


Bernese Oberland, thinks that the Tatzelwurm may be a kind of large


slow-worm, adding: “As to its terrible and dangerous character, it


would seem merely that it is not so gentle as the slow-worm, that it


doesn’t like being tormented, and defends itself when it is attacked.”


The slow-worm or blind-worm—or glass-snake as it is called in
America—is of course neither a worm nor a snake, but a legless lizard.
This tendency towards leglessness is noticeable in several families of
burrowing lizards. Thus the skinks have legs so small that they barely
touch the ground, and the two-legged worm-lizard of Mexico (Bipes
caniculatus) has no hind-legs at all. This makes the statement that the
Stollenwurm has only the two legs in front at once seem much less
fantastic—indeed it helps to vouch for the animal. For how should the
peasants in the Swiss mountains, who have certainly never heard of the
Mexican worm-lizard, know that lizards may in fact have only two legs?


The worm-lizard is quite as stumpy as the Tatzelwurm, and so are
certain skinks, such as the Australian Tiligua rugosa. Nor are skinks
found only in distant countries; there is one species, Chalcides striatus,


that is 2 feet long and lives in the French maritime Alps, which are
an extension of the Tatzelwurm’s habitat. Even the Tatzelwurm’s size
would not be extraordinary; in south-eastern Europe there is a giant
slow-worm (Ophisaurus apodus) called sheltopusik in Russian, which
reaches a length of 4 feet.
It is not at all unlikely that there may
be a large skink in the Swiss and Austrian Alps; and it would provide


a most matter-of-fact explanation for the persistent Alpine legend.


According to an Austrian schoolmaster, who met one in 1929 while
exploring a cave on the Tempelmauer, the Tatzelwurm is not a reptile
but an amphibian. His account is as follows:


Well-equipped, I started out on a spring morning (near the end of
April 1929) and after a short climb I reached the top of the Tempel-
mauer.
After a short rest between the cliffs I started to look for the
entrance to the cave. Suddenly I saw a snake-like animal sprawled on
the damp rotting foliage that covered the ground.
Its skin was almost
white, not covered with scales but smooth. Its head was flat and two very


35


THE GREAT DAYS OF ZOOLOGY ARE NOT DONE


short feet on the fore-part of the body were visible. It did not move
but kept staring at me with its remarkably large eyes. I know every one
of our animals at first glance and knew that I faced the one that is un-
known to science, the tatzelwurm.
Excited, joyful, but at the same
time somewhat fearful, I tried to grab the animal but I was too late.
With the agility of a lizard the animal disappeared in a hole and all my
efforts to find it were in vain. I am certain that it was not my imagina-
tion that let me see the animal but that I observed with a clear head.


“My” tatzelwurm did not have large claws but short and atrophied-
looking feet; his length did not exceed 4o or 45 centimetres (16-18
inches). Most probably the tatzelwurm is a rare variety of salamander
living in moist caves and coming only rarely to the light of day.


Here I should mention that in the south of the United States there


is a species of salamander (Siren lacertina) which has fore-legs only and
may reach a length of 3 feet. It can survive long dry periods by burrow-
ing in the mud and coming out only after the first rains. Might it not
be for the same reason that the Tatzelwurm is most likely to be seen in
the first storm after a long drought?


Towards the end of 1934 a Swiss photographer called Balkin claimed


to have photographed a Tatzelwurm by accident. He was out taking
photographs of views around Meiringen and saw what he thought was
a very photogenic fallen rotten stump. Just as he pressed the shutter to
photograph it, the stump began to move and proved to be a large and
very hostile lizard. He took to his heels, and when he developed his film
found that he had a picture of a quite unknown animal (see photograph
facing page 40). It looks remarkably like a head-on view of Fig. 1, even


to the markings on the head and the projecting teeth.
It could be a
genuine photograph, but it looks more like a photograph ofa model of the
beast in Fig. 1 than a living animal. At all events the Berliner Illustrirte
Zeitung published it twice and financed a systematic search for the
creature. The winter soon put a stop to this project. In the spring the
beast was no longer news, and the search was shelved indefinitely.


Whether the Tazzelwurm is a European species of Heloderma, an
enormous skink, a giant salamander or some completely new animal,
there is little doubt that it exists. Even in a country every corner of
which is known, not all the fauna is known to science. It will bea long
time before all the world is really thoroughly explored. Many zoological
surprises await us. And those who have listened to the tales and rumours
which are current in various parts of the world, and which I shall re-
count here, will spare themselves a lot of trouble, for they will know
where to look.


36


THERE ARE LOST WORLDS EVERYWHERE


I think it safe to prophesy that it is in the most remote places that the
strangest creatures will be found, creatures ill-adapted to the struggle
for existence which have taken refuge in inhospitable and almost im-
penetrable country, creatures which are relics of once-flourishing groups
which have been driven there by newer and more successful species. If
there is any chance of finding really extraordinary animals on the earth,


it will be in those very places where we have not looked—not exactly


“lost worlds,” but in those worlds almost all over the earth, which we
have not yet found or not thoroughly searched.

CHAPTER TWO


Cuvier’s Rash Dictum


You must not say that this cannot be, or that that
is contrary to nature.
You do not know what
Nature is, or what she can do; and nobody knows,
not even Sir Roderick Murchison, or Professor
Owen, or Professor Sedgwick, or Professor Hux-

Grove... They are very wise men; and you
must listen respectfully to all they say: but even
if they should say, which I am sure they never
would, ‘““That cannot exist. That is contrary to
nature,’’ you must wait a little and see; for per-
haps even they may be wrong.


CHARLES KINGSLEY, The Water-Babies.


Moke than a century ago, in 1812, Baron Georges Cuvier was rash
enough to pronounce that “there is little hope of discovering new
species of large quadrupeds.”” The living fauna of the world was well
enough known for him. The animals even of such newly explored lands


as America and Australia had been numbered and described. Naturalists
should now concentrate on extinct animals, remains of which were being
disinterred in such quantities. Zoology was out of fashion, palaeonto-
logy, the new science which Cuvier had fathered, was all the rage.


This pronouncement, like others of his, would not have mattered had
he not been such a despot. Brilliant anatomist though he was, the ill-


effects of his tyranny are still felt, and reactionary scientists still repeat


his dictum, though it has been disproved over and over again.


In 1819 Cuvier had not long uttered his words when his pupil Diard
sent him a drawing from India of a white-backed tapir saying:


When I first saw the tapir—of which I send you a picture—at
Barrackpore, I was astonished that such a large animal should still be
unknown, especially as I had seen at the Asiatic Society the head of a
similar animal which Governor Farquhar had sent there on 2 April
1806, saying that the tapir was as common in the Indian forests as the
elephant and the rhinoceros.
38


4. White-backed tapir.


Actually the tapir had been known to the Chinese and Japanese since
time immemorial, but whether Cuvier knew of the oriental descriptions
—which is most unlikely—or not, he scorned all popular legends and


beliefs of simple people. Indeed, he even distrusted all travellers’ tales.
Hence it was that he was still maintaining that the tapir was a specifically
American animal, after Wahlfeldt mentioned a little black-and-white
“rhinoceros” that looked very much like a tapir in Sumatra in 1772.
Marsden had described it less equivocally in the same island in 1783.
Sir Stamford Raffles had learnt about it in 1805, and Farquhar had shot
one near Malacca and described it to the Asiatic Society in 1816.


But when Cuvier received Diard’s letter and drawing he swallowed


his scepticism for once and hastened to publish an official description,
but he was too late. Someone else had beaten him to it.


The Indian tapir was only the first of a long series of large animals
which were gradually discovered. I cannot hope to list them all here,
but will confine myself to the most striking examples: animals which
were quite new or could not easily remain undetected.


Three primates deservedly open the list. In 1820 Anselme Gaétan
Desmarest, the French mammalogist, announced the existence of a
monkey (in the narrowest sense) big enough to be called an ape: the
black or Celebesean ape (Cynopithecus niger), which is really a sort of
would-be baboon with a very prominent snout. A year later Sir Stam-


ford Raffles described the largest of all the gibbons, the siamang of


Sumatra, which required a genus of its own (Symphalangus syndactylus) ;


it stands more than 3 feet high on its hind-legs. And in 1835 the German

(Theropithecus gelada) in the rocky mountains of southern Abyssinia.
When it stands up on its hind-legs this ““dog-headed” monkey which
does not have a dog’s head—its nostrils are not at the end of its nose!—
may be as tall as a man, even though its legs are much shorter.

It was the first of many living fossils to be found in the great
equatorial rain-forest.

But “R. Owen” had said otherwise. And he was Professor Sir Richard
Owen, the greatest British palaeontologist, a fervent disciple of Cuvier
and as brilliant an anatomist as his master, but none the less intolerant,
prejudiced and sceptical. He was a man who could deny evidence when


it was before his eyes, and, unfortunately, like Cuvier’s, his word was
taken as gospel.


Around 1870 a young pygmy hippopotamus, which weighed barely
30 pounds, was sent to the Dublin Zoo, where it lived for several weeks.
Twenty years later Johannes Biittikofer, curator of the Rijksmuseum at
Leyden, came back from two long visits to Liberia with much informa-
tion about the pygmy hippopotamus’s habits and even several skulls and
skeletons in a rather poor state.


At the beginning of the twentieth century there were at least a score
of specimens—many very fragmentary, it is trtue—in museums in various
parts of the world. Yet many naturalists still thought Choeropsis was
more or less mythical, some alleging it was just a young hippopotamus,
others that it was an individual freak. A few more daring than the rest
supposed that it was a small variety of the ordinary hippopotamus.
There was even one natural history museum in which a badly mounted
specimen was classified with the fossils—an original way of denying that
the creature was extant!


Eventually, of course, its existence was established so that no one
could deny it, but not for many years. For the moment let us leave the
poor beast temporarily buried alive, and proceed to other discoveries.


The last century also had its own “‘abominable snowman,” or rather
“abominable man-of-the-woods,” a terrible hairy giant that according


to travellers’ tales lived in the Guinea jungles. There were the same sort
of rumours about it as are now current about the Himalayan yeti, which


is said to be as strong as ten men, to be able to stun a yak with its fist, to
strangle men and to carry off children but look after them well. The
rumours about the African “man-of-the-woods” seem to go back to
the fifth century before Christ, when the Carthaginian navigator Hanno
fought and killed “hairy savages” on his famous journey. The inter-
preters called them gorillas. This incident occurred in a rather unlikely
place, so it has been said that these gorillas could not have been gorillas,
yet it is strange that their name should be so like that still used to de-


scribe the large ape in some dialects, for instance n’giya in Eveia and
n’gila in Bakoueli.


For a long time there was a great confusion between the gorilla and

When B. H. Hodgson was exploring Tibet and the neighbouring

hours in thickets of rhododendron and dwarf bamboo, emerging to

Schomburgk’s deer (Rucervus schomburgki), which was described by
Blyth in 1863, is remarkable not only for its curiously forked antlers
which may boast as many as 20 points, but also because it has never
been seen in its natural habitat in Siam by a single white man. All that


is known about it has been learnt from rare specimens captured by the
Siamese or born in captivity. There is indeed little hope that any
European will ever see it in its natural state, for it is quite likely that it
has been extinct for several years.


The same fate awaits many animals known only from rumours and
legends, which makes one all the more impatient with those who
obstinately refuse to listen to evidence of this kind.


Occasionally an intelligent naturalist with his ears open has been
able to save a species. When the French missionary Father Armand
David crossed eastern Asia between 1865 and 1869, he not only recorded


a great number of new plants but also discovered three new kinds of
large mammals. Had he not been incurably curious there would be no
mi-lus alive today.


When he was in Pekin in 1865 he heard that sacred animals were kept
in the Nan Hai-tzu Imperial Park several i south of the city. His
curiosity was aroused, but he knew that entry to the park was strictly
forbidden; so he eluded the Tartar guard by climbing the 45-mile wall
that encircled the park and protected it from curious eyes. He was most
excited by what he saw. Besides the animals that he knew well, there


was a large herd—some 120 head—of deer so strange that the Chinese


called them sze-pu-hsiang or “like none of the four.” This meant that


they were “not like a deer,” “not like a cow,” “not like a horse” and


“not like a goat”; presumably because they resembled each of these


four animals, but only in a few particulars, having the general anatomy


and antlers of a deer, a tail as long as a cow’s but ending in a hank of


horsehair like a horse’s, and large spreading hooves like a goat’s. For-


tunately the beast also went by the less cumbrous name of mi-lu.

On Chinese vases and silk-paintings you can sometimes see a sort of

which no European naturalist dreamt could exist, was Father David’s

The crested rat (Lophiomys imhausi) is certainly the most conspicuous
of rodents. It may reach a length of 16 inches and its body is covered
with a coat of long black and white hairs, which stand up to make a
striking crest along its spine. Yet this creature, which lives among the
rocks in the mountains of East Africa, was not discovered until 1867,
when it was immediately described by Alphonse Milne-Edwards, who
was then having a remarkable run of luck. This rodent was so unusual
that a whole new family had to be created to accommodate it.


Six years later another no less extraordinary rodent came to light and


also added another family to this order. It was the Dinomys branickit,
often known by its native name of pacarana. This beast looks like a
marmot, and so is much less striking than the crested rat, but it is
nearly 2 feet long—the size of a fox-terrier. Yet, though it is one of the
largest rodents in the world, it was not known until 1873, and then not
particularly well. Professor Walter Henricks Hodge of the University
of Massachusetts, one of the greatest experts on the pacarana, writes:


This giant rodent is at home in the region of mountain rain forests
in the eastern Andes from Peru to central Colombia. For many years
the Pacarana was known only from the original specimen that was


captured in 1873 as it wandered about in a hacienda building at the


hamlet of Vitoc, Peru, at the headwaters of the Perené River just east


across the Andes from Lima. Until 1904 the species remained out of


scientific headlines, but in that year two living Pacaranas were seen in


Pard from the upper Rio Purus in Brazil. In 1922 a series of specimens


was obtained from the forested Andean area to the east of Lima 3 and,


finally, in 1925 the New York Zoological Garden obtained a living


specimen for exhibition.

In 1872 and 1878 Sir Victor Brooke christened two African gazelles.
The first, Grant’s gazelle (Gazella granti), was merely a new species, but
the second, Waller’s gazelle (Litocranius walleri), belonged to a quite
new genus. It is a most unusual-looking beast with a neck as long as its
body—a sort of giraffe-gazelle. It is confined to Somaliland and British
East Africa. The natives call it gerenuk and have known it since time
immemorial, and it appears in Egyptian bas-reliefs dating from the


sixth century B.c.

or primitive art as a source of information. Had they studied Egyptian
murals more carefully they would not only have noticed the gerenuk,
but also a zebra with particularly narrow and numerous stripes. The
Scottish explorer James Augustus Grant—after whom the gazelle was
named—claimed to have seen one of these zebras in Abyssinia in 1860,
but the experts were still sceptical.

In 1882, however, Menelik I, Emperor of Abyssinia, gave the French
President, Jules Grévy, a zebra which exactly fitted Grant’s description.
When it was brought to France and desposited in the Jardin des Plantes
everyone could see that it was a new species, which was larger than the
other zebras and had a different pattern on its coat. The poor brute
was worn out by its long journey and had a fit and died several days
after its arrival. All the same, Oustalet was able to add another new
large quadruped (Dolichohippus grevyi) to the world’s fauna.


At about the same time the news reached Europe that the Russian
explorer Nikolai Mikhailovitch Przewalski, the first to explore Central
Asia, had discovered a species of wild horse in Dzungaria in Western
Mongolia. Actually, though he was a cavalry officer, Przewalski had
taken it for an ass, for it had a large head and relatively short legs. I. S.
Poliakoff, who published the first description of it in 1881, needed all
his patience to convince him that it was really a horse, a horse (Equus
przewalskii) which immortalised a name all too difficult to remember
correctly.
It is the only living example of a truly wild horse—and
not a descendant of tame horses that have gone wild, like those in
America. The very last specimen of the only other surviving wild horse,
the tarpan (Equus gmelini) of the Polish forests and southern Russian
steppes, died in the Ukraine at Christmas 1879. Hence the special
importance of Colonel Przewalski’s discovery. In 1955 Street alleged
that Przewalski’s horse had disappeared in its wild state, but in the same
year the Soviet zoologist Professor Bannikov estimated the number in a
wild herd at some 40 individuals. There are small herds in zoos at
Munich and Prague which breed and have thus been able to supply
other zoos. Whipsnade received a pair in 1954.


In 1891 Oldfield Thomas christened another large quadruped, the
dibatag antelope (Ammodorcas clarket), commonly called Clarke’s gazelle
because it was discovered in Somaliland by W. H. Clarke.


Here I wish to add a large bird to the list. You may object that no
bird, however big, can be a large quadruped, and that Cuvier never
suggested that there was little hope of finding new species of large birds.
True, but this was certainly because he thought there was no hope at all.
There are no more conspicuous creatures than birds. Their ability to
fly away at the first alarm means that they do not have to hide so much


as mammals. For the same reason they can wear brilliantly-coloured
plumage without suffering for it. Certainly it is very rarely that a large
and quite unknown bird is discovered.

been known to exceed 5 feet 11 inches. An old male with its arms

But the greatest sensation of the 1900s was the okapi. As Dr Maurice
Burton has said: one can have no idea today of “the romance surround-
ing the discovery of the Okapi, nor of the excitement caused in natural
history circles, first by the vague reports of its presence, and later by its


actual finding.”


The first evidence of the okapi’s existence was extremely slender, and
consisted of no more than three lines in H. M. Stanley’s In Darkest
Africa, published in 1860. In his linguistic notes he remarks of the
Wambutti pygmies in the Ituri forests of the Congo:


The Wambutti knew a donkey and called it ‘‘atti.”” —They say that they
sometimes catch them in pits. What they can find to eat is a wonder.
They eat leaves.


There was no reason to doubt Stanley’s statement, journalist though
he was, but no one had ever heard of wild asses in the Belgian Congo.
The only Equidae known there were zebras, but these specifically run-
ning beasts never lived in forests, certainly not in the thick jungle
inhabited by the shy pygmies. So the experts were sceptical.


All the same, Sir Harry Johnston, then Governor of Uganda, was
intrigued by Stanley’s remarks and decided to gather more information
about the ati on his visits to the Congo. He had an unusually good
opportunity at the end of 1899, when he saved a party of pygmies from
being carried off by a German showman to be exhibited as curiosities at
the 1900 Paris Exhibition. They were his guests in Uganda for several
months until he could take them back to their native forests. Meanwhile
they became firm friends and Sir Harry was able to question them
through an interpreter about the horse-like animal which lived in their
forests.


They at once understood what I meant; and pointing to a zebra-skin
and a live mule, they informed me that the creature in question, which
was called OKapPI, was like a mule with zebra stripes on it.


Okapi or o-apt is evidently the name that Stanley mistook for arti.
When Sir Harry arrived in Fort Mbeni in the Congo Free State, he
questioned the Belgian officers stationed there and learnt that though

CUVIER’S RASH DICTUM


they had never seen the animal alive, their native troops hunted it in the
forest and killed it with spears. They brought back the meat to add to
the fort’s provisions and cut up the skin into strips to make belts and
bandoliers. One of the officers said that there should be a new skin
somewhere in the fort, but Sir Harry was bitterly disappointed to find


that it had already been cut into pieces, and hé was able to salvage only


two of them.


On 21 August 1900 he wrote a memorable letter to Dr Sclater of the
Zoological Society of London telling of this partial success of his in-
vestigations. He said that the precious strips of skin would be sent off


at once and that the Belgian officers had promised to get him a complete
skin and send it to him in Uganda.


All this time [Sir Harry remarks] I was convinced that I was on the
track of a species of horse; and therefore when the natives showed the
tracks of a cloven-footed animal like the eland, and told us these were
the foot-prints of the okapi, I disbelieved them, and imagined that we
were merely following a forest-eland.


Sir Harry was very wrong to disbelieve the natives. Had Dr Sclater
known that the beast had cloven hooves he would have been saved from
making a bloomer. When he received the strips of skin he hastily
christened the beast Equus johnstoni, though he cautiously added a
question mark after the generic name Equus.


Meanwhile Karl Eriksson, a Swedish officer in the Belgian service,
sent Sir Harry a whole skin of an okapi and two skulls. The skin and
one of the skulls had come from a young male. Gradually a picture of
the beast was built up from the pygmies’ descriptions and the anatomi-
cal specimens.
It was an odd animal—reminiscent of those mythical
monsters made up of bits from different creatures.
It was as big as a
medium-sized horse, a little like a giant antelope in shape, but without


visible horns; on the other hand it had a long tongue like’an anteater’s


and ears as big if not bigger than a donkey’s; its thighs and hindquarters


were covered with stripes. Because of this last detail alone it had been


taken for a new species of zebra. Actually, as Sir Harry wrote:


Upon receiving this skin, I saw at once what the okapi was—namely,
a close relation of the giraffe.


The shape of the skull, the structure of the teeth, the ruminant’s
cloven hoof are all evidence that it is a sort of short-necked giraffe, a


creature related to its long-extinct ancestors, a cousin, no doubt, of the

Helladotherium whose remains Albert Gaudry had disinterred from
Miocene deposits in Greece.


Sir Harry sent his new trophies to Professor Ray Lankester in London
suggesting that it should be called Helladotherium tigrinum. But Lan-
kester was better versed in comparative anatomy, and came to the
conclusion that the okapi was closer to the giraffe than to the Hellado-
therium, almost half-way between the two, and that it deserved a genus
of its own no less than Sir Harry deserved the credit for discovering it.
He therefore named it Okapia johnstoni.


It was soon noticed that, unlike the quite hornless Helladotherium
but like the giraffe, the male okapi had little miniature horns hidden
under the skin, making a bump on the forehead.
It undoubtedly
belongs to a vast group of primitive Giraffidae (such as the Hellado-
therium, Samotherium, Palaeotragus, Sivatherium and so on) which
flourished in Africa and Asia in the Miocene and even more in the
Pliocene.


As soon as the okapi’s existence—which most people had doubted—
was firmly established, everyone began trying to prove that it had been
known for thousands of years. Archaeologists and Egyptologists kept
thinking they had found its features in Neolithic rock-carvings in the
Sahara and on predynastic Egyptian painted vases or bas-reliefs dating
from the Pharaohs. Sometimes there is indeed a striking resemblance.

When Sir Harry Johnston came home from Uganda he met Stanley
in England. Naturally they discussed the new animal they had both
helped to discover. Stanley told him that he thought that the okapi was


only one of the many animals that would eventually be discovered in the


tropical rain-forest and said that he had seen a huge hog 6 feet long and


some antelopes of a quite unknown type.


After the harvest of new species reaped by zoologists during the last
few decades the atmosphere was optimistic. The okapi had shown that
the natives’ tales could be trusted, and people took an eager interest in
the rumours which had been current for a quarter of a century about a


sort of monstrous wild boar in the Ituri forests. This senge was said to
be a fierce beast as black as the night and as big as a rhinoceros—or, at


least, as a little rhinoceros. Stanley’s evidence lent weight to this legend.


In 1904 Captain R. Meinertzhagen of the British East Africa Rifles
happened to acquire a skin of the beast. It had come from the forests
around Mount Kenya and was unfortunately in a poor condition. A


little later the same officer obtained a skull of the same animal, which


this time had been shot in the forests bordering Lake Victoria. This
enabled Oldfield Thomas to give a scientific description of this par-


ticular senge and christen it Hylochoerus meinertzhagent, or “‘Meinertz-
hagen’s forest-hog.”


It is true that it was nowhere near the size of a rhinoceros—even a
small one; all the same it was the largest of wild boars, since it may reach


a height of 4 feet at the shoulder and a length of over 8 feet. It is also
the blackest boar ever seen and its tusks are long and massive.

This monster was no sooner added to the zoological catalogue than a
similar-looking beast was rumoured to live in the other end of the equa-


torial forest. The up-country natives in Liberia claimed that a large
black pig called nigbve lived in the forests of this area. As early as 1668
Dr Dapper had noted in his compilation, Naukeurige Beschryvinge der
Afrikaensche gewesten van Egypten, that in the Greyn Kust, or Pepper


Coast, which is now Liberia,


There are two sorts of swine, the red called Cowja, which are the size
of our own, and the black called Couja Quinta which are much larger
and more dangerous; for they have teeth so sharp that they break every-
thing they bite as if they were so many axes.


The Couja is evidently the red river-hog (Potamochoerus porcus). As


to the black pig, some suggested that it was not a giant forest-hog at all,
but one of those pygmy hippopotami reported from the same area so
long before.1 To which it was objected that the migbve was a forest
animal, whereas the hippopotamus was by definition aquatic, and the
pygmy hippopotamus’s survival had by no means been established.


Carl Hagenbeck, the great German animal-dealer, decided to get


to the bottom of the confusion and sent his agent, Hans Schomburgk,
out to Liberia in 1909. The expedition got off to a bad start. The
natives insisted that the migbve was such a very fierce beast, with teeth
sharp enough to cut a man in two, that they stoutly refused to help
Schomburgk, whom they thought was mad to want to capture such a
monster. Nevertheless he eventually managed to persuade them, and on
13 June 1911, after months of searching, he came upon the creature


10 yards away in the forest. It was a shiny black and did look like a big
pig, but it was obviously related to a hippopotamus. Unfortunately
Schomburgk—who was the first white man to see a pygmy hippopota-
mus in its natural surroundings—had no means ready to catch it and
had scruples about shooting an animal which was thought to be extinct
and was certainly very rare.


Back in Monrovia no one believed his story: the migbve was a mere
superstition, or at best a legend based on a long-extinct animal. Schom-
burgk could do nothing. The rainy season was setting in, and he had to
return to Hamburg empty-handed. But now he knew he was not hunting
amyth, and by Christmas 1912 he was in Liberia again. This time he was
luckier, On 28 February 1913, having made sure that the species was

much less rare than he had thought, he shot the first specimen. The

teeth looked unpleasant it was actually much easier to tame than an
ordinary hippopotamus. Besides being smaller it was much less heavy


in outline, had smaller jaws in proportion and was blacker and shinier.


Moreover it was a forest animal which went into the water only occa-

genus, Choeropsis, since the word Hippopotamus, or “river-horse,”’ does


not describe its anatomy or its habits. The name “pygmy hippopota-

Five months later Hans Schomburgk confounded the sceptics by
bringing back five live pygmy hippopotami to Hamburg. These little
beasts weighed one-tenth of the weight of a true hippopotamus. An
adult male was no more than 2 feet 6 inches high and 5 feet 10 inches
long.


It is little over half a century since the largest of the bears and the
largest of the apes were discovered and the largest rhinoceros was found


to exist in a country where it had been quite unknown. The largest of
the lizards was not discovered until 1912, when an airman made a forced
landing on Komodo, an island 20 miles long by 12 miles wide between
Sumbawa and Flores in the Lesser Sundas in the Malay archipelago.
The only men who lived there were convicts deported by the Rajah of
Sumbawa. The airman came back with a tale that he had met fierce
and monstrous dragons, at least 12 feet long, which according to the
inhabitants ate pigs, goats and deer and even attacked horses. Needless


to say nobody believed a word of his story.


But soon afterwards the existence of these giant reptiles was confirmed
by Major P. A. Ouwens, curator of the Botanical Gardens at Buitenzorg.
He had been corresponding with J. K. H. van Steyn van Hensbroek,
the Civil Administrator of Flores, about them since December 1910.
The islanders had told this official that around Laboean Badjo, on their
own territory, and on the neighbouring island of Komodo, there was


a boeaja darat, or “land crocodile.” Van Steyn was interested, and pro-
mised to find out more about the beast and even obtain a specimen at


the first opportunity. When his duties took him to Komodo he learnt


from Kock and Aldegon, stationed on the island with the pearl-fishing


fleet, that the lizards were sometimes over 20 feet long. Aldegon boasted


61


THE GREAT DAYS OF ZOOLOGY ARE NOT DONE


that he had killed several of this size. But fishermen are proverbially
unreliable judges of size.


Van Steyn was more modest. During his stay he obtained the skin of


a specimen 7 feet long and sent it with a photograph to Major Ouwens,
saying that he would try to catch a bigger one, but it would not be easy,
since the natives were terribly afraid of its teeth and its thrashing tail.


The Zoological Museum at Buitenzorg sent a Malay animal-catcher


to van Steyn, who had the bad luck to be posted to Timor, so he missed
the first successful capture. Rajah Ritara lent his hunters and dogs to
the animal-catcher, who managed to bring back four specimens alive,
the largest being 9 feet 6 inches and 7 feet 8 inches long. A little later,
according to van Steyn, a Sergeant Beker shot one 12 feet long.


Major Ouwens at once recognised that these monstrous prehistoric-
looking lizards were a giant species of monitor lizard. He described it
under the name of Varanus komodoensis in the Bulletin of the Buitenzorg
Botanical Gardens.


When the Komodo dragon was better known it was found that it
was only rarely dangerous to man. All the same it is a fearsome-looking
beast which certainly kills and eats buffaloes, wild pigs and deer. It is
now to be seen in several zoos, where you have only to watch at feeding
time to witness its extraordinary gluttony, which may perhaps explain
why, although Komodo means “‘rat island,” there is not a single rat
there now.


Later it was found that the dragon also lived on the small islands of
Rintja and Padar at the eastern-end of Flores, and that the Bima archives
had expressly mentioned its existence in 1840, when the Rajah of
Sumbawa had taken steps to protect the monster from extinction.

freshwater dolphin of a quite unknown genus was discovered in Lake
Tung-Ting, 650 miles from the mouth of the Yangtze Kiang. It was

Meanwhile there were plenty of zoological discoveries still to come
from Africa. In 1908 Lydekker described a new species of spiral-horned
antelope from Abyssinia, the mountain nyala (Strepsiceros buxtont).
More interesting from our point of view were the pygmy gorilla and
pygmy chimpanzee.


The American zoologist Daniel Giraud Elliot described the pygmy
gorilla in his monumental three-volume monograph on the primates in
1913. His description of Pseudogorilla mayema is based solely on a few
skeletons and skins from the delta of the Ncomi and the Rembo near the
mouth of the Ogowe south of Fernan Vaz. Even its appearance is still


little known.
Its coat is dark grey, except on the head and shoulders,
where it is a slightly reddish chestnut. The male rarely exceeds 4 feet
6 inches—the height of a female -chimpanzee—while the two sub-
species of large gorilla may be as high as 6 feet and 6 feet 6 inches.


After forty years we are still waiting for further and more detailed
news of this “pygmy giant ape,” which apparently has never been seen


alive except by the hunters who provided the skins and skeletons, no
doubt by shooting the beast the moment they saw it. Yet, strange to


say, the existence of this species about which we know so little has never
been doubted, although the pygmy elephant, which is much better
known, has been so bitterly disputed that I have had to treat it as an
unknown animal in a later chapter in this book.


The pygmy chimpanzee was discovered in a museum, of all places!
In 1925 Ernst Schwartz examined the skins and skeletons sent to the
Congo Museum at Tervueren in Belgium from the country between the


left bank of the River Congo and its tributary, the Kasai, he realised
that there must be a new and quite distinct variety of chimpanzee. The
pygmy species is thinner, its limbs are slenderer; its bones are all more


delicate (the skeleton weighs only half of that of the ordinary chimpan-


zee, Pan troglodytes) and it is shorter by 15 per cent. Its face and ears


are quite black from birth, except around the mouth—like a music-hall


coon—while the other chimpanzees are born light and darken with age.


Later the pygmy chimpanzee was observed in its native forest, and
Professor Urbain of the Vincennes Museum and Zoo brought a live
specimen from the French Congo, on the right bank of the river.
Though every care was taken it lived only for a year, from 1939 to 1940,

in the Vincennes Zoo. A few specimens can now be seen in the zoo at

Another no less sensational discovery was made in the same way—
and in the very same museum. It is true that the animal was not one of
the large quadrupeds with which we have been refuting Cuvier, but
merely a bird the size of a pheasant. However, since it also comes from
the equatorial forests of Africa, still so full of surprises, and since the
discovery of a quite unknown genus of bird is almost unheard of, the


story deserves to be told here.


In 1909, while Schomburgk was on the pygmy hippopotamus’s track
in Liberia, an expedition was organised by the New York Zoological
Society in order to bring back a live okapi to the Bronx Zoo: Herbert
Lang and his young disciple Dr James P. Chapin took part in it. The
attempt failed. But they did not return quite empty-handed. When
Lang and Chapin got home they found that the tall native head-dresses
they had brought back from Avakubi as curiosities included two reddish
feathers striped with black, which none of the experts could identify.


The problem remained unsolved until 1936, when Chapin happened


to recognise some similar feathers on two stuffed birds, thrown out
among the lumber in the Tervueren Museum. At first he did not believe


his eyes, especially as one of the birds was labelled “‘Pavo cristatus,
juvenile, imported.” All the same he had no difficulty in proving that


it was not a common peacock, but a hitherto unknown genus of Congo
peacock which he named Afropavo congensis and described in the Revue
de Zoologie et de Botanique Africaines for November 1936. It was the


first unknown genus of bird discovered for more than 40 years.


Chapin could not wait to capture a living specimen. On 19 June 1937
he flew to Stanleyville in the Belgian Congo, where he found that the
news of his discovery had gone before him and no less than eight speci-
mens had been shot and were waiting for him. He was astonished to
learn from the natives in the forests of the Ituri (the site of so many
discoveries) that though the Congo peacock had a restricted habitat it
was very common in the vast stretch of country between the Ituri and
the Sankuru.


This was the sixth species of largish animal to be discovered in the
equatorial rain-forests of Africa in less than 50 years, and it was not the
last. In 1919 Glover Allen discovered near a stream in the darkest part
of the Ituri forest a genet of aquatic habits which lives on fish. It is the
size of a domestic cat with a splendid chestnut coat, marked with white

even kept a young specimen, given him by the natives, for several days,
but it died for lack of proper food. The black-and-white “bear” was on
the point of being considered an extinct species when two sons of Presi-
dent Teddy Roosevelt—Colonel Theodore Roosevelt and his brother
Kermit—saw one dozing in the top of a hollow pine-tree. A salvo of
shots pitched the poor brute into its last sleep, and its stuffed skin was
soon being admired in the Field Museum at Chicago.

This did not prevent further slaughter. Dr Ernst Schaefer shot one

that Alphonse Milne-Edwards had been quite right in thinking that
the bei-shung was not a bear but closely related to the panda and
also ate bamboo shoots. So it came to be called the giant panda—a
name still unfamiliar to the public—with odd results. When William
Harkness announced to the Press that he was off to Szechwan to catch
a giant panda and bring it back alive, the teleprinter-operator misunder-

going to China in quest of a “giant panther”—and another unknown
animal was born!


In 1936 Floyd T. Smith succeeded in catching the first giant panda


alive, but it died at Singapore. That same year Harkness died suddenly
in Shanghai before he had a chance to catch his panda. But his widow
was determined to carry on his task and set off on the panda’s track in
1937. She knew next to nothing about the animal, and still less about
China, and for months she searched the jungle with extraordinary


pertinacity. She had the luck she deserved, and, where the most ex-
perienced explorers had failed for 70 years, she succeeded. One day she
found a baby panda in a hollow tree. It was crying as if its heart was


fit to break.
She picked up this child of her husband’s dreams and
nursed it in her arms.
It survived a delirious welcome to the United


States, but in the Brooksfield Zoo at Chicago it swallowed a branch too
gluttonously and died in March 1938. The second time Mrs Harkness
was luckier. She brought back another female giant panda, called Mei-
mei, who settled happily in her new home.


Soon there were toy pandas in the nursery and pandas in the comic


strips, but for the zoologist the problem had only begun, for no one
knew how this apparent carnivore which ate nothing but bamboo-shoots
should be classified.
Eventually the great American expert William
King Gregory, agreeing with Alphonse Milne-Edwards’s opinion, put


it in the Procyonidae along with the raccoons, the coatis, the kinkajou
and various other purely American animals. Dr Frechkop has since
suggested that the pandas and the kinkajou alone should form a family
of Ailuridae
of their own, which would fall between the bears and the

Other writers have gone on classing the giant panda with the
bears, and the recent serological work by Leone and Wiens supports
their view. Perhaps Father David was right after all in thinking he had
brought back the skin of a bear.
