THB MAN-FACED ANIMALS OF SOUTH-EAST ASIA


In 1927 there were new rumours about the orang pendek in southern
Sumatra. One day a tiger trap was found sprung, but the animal which
had sprung it escaped without being seen. To judge by the tracks left
in the vicinity it must have been an orang pendek.


But on the trap [writes Dr Dammerman] some hair and traces of
blood were found; only the discovery was not made at once, but a few
days after the animal had escaped. The blood and the hair were ex-
amined; it was impossible to obtain any positive results with regard to
the hair, but the blood pointed faintly to human origin. However we
may not accept for a fact that the blood found came from the escaped
animal: it is quite possible that it came from some native who had
injured himself while handling the trap.


Dr Dammerman’s comments puzzle me. Why was it “impossible
to obtain any positive results with regard to the hair”? The analysis of
hair is an advanced science which gives very precise indications about
the nature of the animal. It should at least have been possible to say
what animal could not have left the hair. To know, for instance, that it
was neither a bear nor an ape would be infinitely precious. Note also
the subtlety of the phrase “the blood pointed faintly to human origin.”
The analysis of the blood must have shown that it was either of human
or of animal origin. But that it could “faintly point” to a human origin
passes understanding. Does it mean that the creature from which the
blood came was almost
aman? Or that Dr Dammerman could not bring
himself to admit the human characteristics of the orang pendek in ques-
tion? This is what his suggestion of “some native” lends one to believe.


It is clear that the analysts have not been able to identify either the
hairs or the blood with those of any known creature.


On 22 May 1932 it looked as if the mystery would at last be solved.
The West Sumatran newspaper, the Deli Courant, announced that it
had received a despatch from O. J. Rookmaker in Pasir-Pengojaran in
the south of the island saying that the Rajah of Rokan had surprised two
orang pendek, one of them a baby. He had fired at them and had brought
back the body of the smaller one.


Actually the news was incorrect, for the Rajah had not done the deed
himself, though in 1912 he and a friend had seen four orang pendek
looking for bamboo shoots 15 yards away. They agreed with the usual
description and were the size of a child of 12 or 13. The Dutch settlers
had not heard of this incident until 1931, when similar accounts were
reported by people prospecting for rattan and rubber. They had


124


ORANG PENDEK, THE APE~MAN OF SUMATRA


begged the Rajah to do all he could to capture the beast. A large reward
was offered to anyone who succeeded; and in May 1932 four natives of
Rokan had decided to organise an expedition to bring back one of these
jabbering men, dead or alive. According to their story they had sud-
denly come upon an orang letjo in the River Rokan Kiri. It was some
60 yards away, collecting small shellfish on a half-submerged tree-


trunk, and looked more human than ape-like. They had fired at it all the


same and wounded it in the arm, whereupon it had dropped a pale object,


a baby Jetjo which had been mortally wounded by the same bullet that


had hit its mother.


A few days after its first despatch, the Deli Courant published a more
detailed report: the new-born Jetjo was 164 inches high and seemed very
human in its anatomy.
Its skin was bare, the hair on its head was an
even grey. It was sent to the Zoological Museum at Buitenzorg to be
examined. On 9 June more details were published in the Deli Courant
together with a photograph. The creature’s arms were rather short;
and it could not therefore be an anthropoid ape. On the other hand it
could not be new-born, for its teeth were well-developed. It seemed as
if a surviving specimen of a “Missing Link” had at last been discovered.


But a few days later the results of Dr Dammerman’s examination of
the young “ape-man” were published. The whole thing was a colossal
hoax. The supposed baby was merely an ordinary lotong (Trachy-
pithecus), a sort of langur, which had been shaved all over except on the
top of its head. To complete its appearance, its nose had even been
stretched with a piece of wood, its cheek-bones had been crushed and its
canine teeth filed to a point.


There was nothing new about such hoaxes in Sumatra. Marco Polo
had exposed them seven centuries before, when pedlars selling curiosi-
ties from the Far East to Western travellers asked a high price for the
mummified bodies of “little men” which they said came from the


Indies.


It should be known that what is reported respecting the dried bodies
of diminutive human creatures or pigmies, brought from India, is an


idle tale, such pretended men being manufactured in this island in the


following manner.
The country produces a species of monkey, of a


tolerable size, and having a countenance resembling that of a man.
Those persons who make it their business to catch them, shave off the


hair, leaving it only about the chin and those other parts where it


naturally grows on the human body. They then dry and preserve them


with camphor and other drugs, and having prepared them in such a
mode that they have exactly the appearance of little men, they put them


125


THE MAN-FACED ANIMALS OF SOUTH-EAST ASIA


into wooden boxes, and sell them to trading ‘people, who carry them to
all parts of the world. But this is merely an imposition, the practice
being such as we have described; and neither in India, nor in any other
country, however wild (and little known) have pigmies been found of a
form so diminutive as these exhibit.


Annoyed at being taken in by the same trick that had been played on
innocent travellers in the Middle Ages, the world of science has ever
since remained obstinately silent about the orang pendek, and shelved it
with the unicorn and the phoenix.


But is this logical? The fact that a forger of genius painted “Ver-
meers” which took in experts of the highest repute does not mean that
the great Dutch painter never existed or that he did not paint his own
pictures,


It is quite possible that the problem of the orang pendek may even
have already been solved. Last March several newspapers published the
following despatch which clearly seems to refer to the mysterious beast
in question, though it has been given another name:


FIRST CAPTURE OF A “‘SINDAI’’ (ANTHROPOID APE) IN SUMATRA


Jakarta: The Indonesian authorities announce the capture of a
sindai in the jungle in South Sumatra. The sindai is an anthropoid
ape which is known to exist (the Dutch once offered a reward of 5,000
florins to anybody who could produce one) but no specimen has ever
been captured.


The animal caught is a female, about 4 feet high, very hairy and with
very long nails. It will be taken to Palembang.


Unfortunately a revolution broke out in Sumatra soon after this news
was announced, and so far I have been unable to discover anything more
about this sensational capture. It may of course be yet another hoax,
perhaps even a code message to the rebels to rise! Who knows?

CHAPTER SIX


The Not So Abominable Snowman


There was exactly the very Print of a Foot, Toes,

DANIEL DEFOE, Robinson Crusoe.


AFTER his sixth attempt on Everest, Eric Shipton was exploring the
neighbouring Gauri Sankar range with Michael Ward and the Sherpa
Sen Tensing. At four o’clock in the afternoon of 8 November 1951 they
found a very clear trail of enormous human-looking feet in the powdery
snow on the south-western slopes of Menlung-tse. They followed this
strange trail for about a mile until they lost it in a moraine of ice. Being
unable to follow the mysterious creature any farther, they took photo-
graphs of its footprints.


Roughly oval in shape, they seemed to have been made by human
feet—but feet more than a foot long. Shipton remarks that they were
“slightly longer and a good deal broader than those made by our large
mountain boots.” A man on this scale would stand about 8 feet high.
The big toe was clearly visible, slightly separated from the rest, but
there seemed to be only three other toes. Of course it was possible that
two toes might be held so close together that they left only a single
print in the snow. ‘Where the tracks crossed a crevasse,” Shipton goes
on, “one could see quite clearly where the creature had jumped and
used its toes to secure purchase on the snow on the other side.”


Ever since 1899, when explorers still had to disguise themselves as


pilgrims or itinerant merchants in order to enter Tibet, strange rumours


had been reaching the West about the giants that lived in the icy heights


of the Himalaya. In that year appeared Major L. A. Waddell’s Among


127


THE MAN-FACED ANIMALS OF SOUTH-EAST ASIA


the Himalayas, in which he tells how in 1889 he found large footprints in
the snow leading up towards the high peaks in the north-east of Sikkim.


These were alleged to be the trail of the hairy wild men who are
believed to live amongst the eternal snows, along with the mythical
white lions, whose roar is reputed to be heard during storms. The
belief in these creatures is universal among Tibetans.


During the first attempt to climb the North Face of Everest in 1921
the rumours became more detailed. On the way from Kharta to the pass


at Lhapka-la, Colonel Howard-Bury and his companions saw dark
spots moving over the snow in the far distance—there were living crea-
tures in these almost inaccessible heights well above the snow line.
Then, on 22 September 1921, when they reached the place, about 23,000
feet up, where they had seen them, they found enormous footprints—
more than three times as big, they said, as normal human footprints.
The leader of the expedition attributed them to a large stray grey wolf,
but the Tibetan porters thought otherwise. To them there was no
doubt that these were footprints of the metoh kangmi or “‘abominable
snowman.” They trembled with fear as they gave an alarming account
of the creature.


From the native reports, which agree in the main, one can compile
the following description of the monster. The snowman is a huge
creature, half man, half beast; it lives in caves high and inaccessible in
the mountains. The skin of its face is white; the body is covered with a
thick coat of dark hair. Its arms, like those of the anthropoid apes, reach
down to its knees, but its face looks rather more human. Its thick legs


are bowed; its toes turn inwards—some even say they turn backwards.
It
is very muscular and can uproot trees and lift up boulders of remark-
able size. The female can be recognised by her long breasts which she
throws over her shoulders when she runs.


These monsters are said usually to feed on yaks’ meat and snow-
worms. Sometimes, when driven by hunger, they come down into the
valleys, carry off people and devour them gluttonously. They are so
savage that in time of famine the females will occasionally eat their
mates. Naturally there are few details of their habits, for those who see
them from close rarely live to tell the tale. But you can escape from
the abominable snowman by rushing down a snowy slope as hard as you
can go; if it tries to follow you, its hair falls into its eyes and it cannot


see. Some say that abominable snowmen are the wandering spirits of
women who have died a violent death and that they are not dangerous
if they are not provoked.

These legends are found for thousands of miles all over the Himalayan
range, from the Karakoram to northern Burma, in Tibet, Nepal, Sikkim,
Bhutan and Assam, and the creatures have many different names in
different countries.

the snowman is known as tok or “‘mouth-man.”


As one might expect, most naturalists dismissed the legend of the
abominable snowman with its ludicrous details. But uneducated Tibe-
tans or Nepalese were not the only people to spread this story. Some
decades ago an Englishman called Hugh Knight on his way to Tibet
reported that. he met a creature whose description agreed with the
legendary monster. In order to let his mount get its breath he halted in
a sort of amphitheatre surrounded on all sides by mountains capped in
snow. Suddenly he heard a sound of stones rolling down a slope and
turned his head. Some 30 yards away a sort of large blond gorilla was
standing up on its bow legs. When it realised that it had been seen it
made off, running sometimes on its hind-legs and sometimes on all-
fours. But the most astonishing part of Knight’s description is that with
one muscular arm the creature was holding a bow and arrow!


Be that as it may, Knight is not the only educated man to tell of such
an astonishing encounter. In 1925 a Fellow of the Royal Geographical
Society called N. A. Tombazi reported a no less startling story in his
Account of a Photographic Expedition to the Southern Glaciers of Kang-
chenjunga in the Sikkim Himalaya. About 9 miles from the Zemu


glacier, at an altitude of some 15,000 feet, he noticed his porters waving
and pointing at an object lower down.


The intense glare and brightness of the snow prevented me from
seeing anything for the first few seconds; but I soon spotted the “‘ob-
ject”? referred to, about two to three hundred yards away down the
valley to the East of our camp. Unquestionably, the figure in outline
was exactly like a human being, walking upright and stopping occasion-

ally to uproot or pull at some dwarf rhododendron bushes. It showed

- serub and was lost to view.


Such a fleeting glimpse, unfortunately, did not allow me to set the

six to seven inches long by four inches wide at the broadest part of the
foot. The marks of five distinct toes and of the instep were perfectly
clear, but the trace of the heel was indistinct, and the little that could be
seen of it appeared to narrow down to a point. I counted fifteen such
footprints at regular intervals ranging from one-and-a-half to two feet.
The prints were undoubtedly of a biped, the order of the spoor having
no characteristics whatever of any imaginable quadruped.
Dense

on my return journey, I gathered that no man had gone in the direction
of Jongri since the beginning of the year.


When the news reached Darjeeling, the press, as usual, headed their
comments with captions of ““Wild Man,”’ ““Snow-Man,”’ and the like,
seen near Kangchenjunga by an “‘Italian’’ traveller...


When I asked the opinion of the Sirdar and the coolies they naturally
trotted out fantastic legends of ‘““Kangchenjunga-demons.”’ Without in
the least believing in these delicious fairy-tales myself, notwithstanding
the plausible yarns told by the natives, and the references I have come
across in many books, I am still at a loss to express any definite opinion
on the subject. However, I can only reiterate with a sufficient degree of
certainty that the silhouette of the mysterious being was unmistakeably
identical with the outline of a human figure. I personally rejoice in
particularly acute vision and am sufficiently familiar with the appear-
ances of mountain fauna to be able to distinguish a bear, monkey,
snow-leopard, ostrich, kiwi (if you like) —and even a man. I am also
somewhat versed in the simple analysis of spoor, and can unhesitatingly
state that the prints were those of no wild animal common to the Sikkim
Himalaya.


Tombazi goes on to suggest his own theory, somewhat tentatively,
since it does not agree with the shape of the footprints, which were too
broad in proportion to their length to be a man’s:


I conjecture then that this “wild man” may be either a solitary or else
a member of an isolated community of pious Buddhist ascetics, who

have renounced the world and sought their God in the utter desolation

The explanation often put forward that the snowman is a sadhu, one
of those Hindu hermits who do in fact live at altitudes up to 15,000

Unquestionably the strangest account we have of the abominable
snowman is that given by Jean Marqués-Riviére in L’Inde Secréte et sa
Magie. It comes from an Indian pilgrim, that is to say a well-educated
person who could be expected to know several languages and often be

His description therefore deserves to be quoted in full,
strange though it is:


Yes, there is a race of giant men, who are neither monkeys nor bears,
and who live in certain forests in Nepal. I have met witnesses who have
seen them from afar and have heard them talking in an unknown
language; I -have seen them myself once...
.


When I was going to certain Tibetan monasteries on the northern
frontier of Nepal, some Nepalese friends told me one day that foot-
prints of the snowman had been seen and that a small armed expedition
was going off in that direction. I joined them; for eight days we walked
through jungle ten feet high. . .
. At last, one day, we heard in the still-
ness of noon, a continual rumbling sound: the place was wild and
desolate. The snow sparkled above us, and crumbling rocks, huge trees
and imposing waterfalls formed a splendid landscape.
At first we
thought it was a far-off avalanche; but to an attentive ear the continual
rumbling had.a certain rhythm. We thought that a tribe of aborigines
was somewhere near and decided to go and question them...


Suddenly, as we were approaching the place from which we supposed
the noise came, one of us noticed some footprints in the moist and clayey
ground we were walking on; in front of us the tracks of enormous naked
feet about two feet long disappeared in irregular lines. A gust of terror
shook the little party. ‘“Snowmen!’’ they cried, and fled, forgetting
that they had come to look for them. In the end we found that there
were three of us willing to go on; we told ourselves that after all these
creatures could not be more savage than tigers and wild elephants; we
had survived those, so we should be able to survive these.


We went forward cautiously; the noise grew louder. Suddenly one
of us made a sign to stop and look. In front of us, in a natural circle of
high rocks, among the huge hunks of broken stone, an extraordinary
spectacle met our eyes: some ten giant ape-men, ten to twelve feet high,


132


THE NOT SO ABOMINABLE SNOWMAN


were gathered in a ring. One of them was beating a primitive tom-tom
made of a hollow tree-trunk.
The man’s strength must have been
terrific to judge by the noise he was making. The others swayed silently
in time with the tom-tom.
It was some religious ceremony, no doubt,
for their solemn manner and attitude showed that they were performing
a magic rite. Their bodies were covered with hair and their faces were
half-way between a gorilla’s and a man’s. But there was nothing of the
animal about their attitude, and the one that was beating the tom-tom


stood quite upright like a human being. They were quite naked, in


spite of the bitter cold in this desolate region, and a strange sadness


could be seen on their frightful faces.


We looked for a long time at these representatives of an unknown
race that fled from man. Where did they come from? What were they?
There was no tribe of men in this neighbourhood, and they were only
known in these areas by the huge footprints that they left in the snow
and the muddy clay. How did they live? What did they eat? The men
and women that they sometimes carried off had never come back to
tell us.


It is more than likely that this story is a little embroidered and poeti-
cised in the oriental tradition of narrative, but this does not mean that


it is a complete invention.


Inevitably most of the descriptions of the snowman come from very
simple people: peasants and porters, who are terrified of it. The guides
who accompany travellers threaten to turn back when fresh prints of
bare feet are found. Frank Smythe tells how during the 1930 Kang-
chenjunga expedition the noise made by a yak bursting in unexpec-
tedly set his porters in a real panic; they thought they were being at-
tacked by snowmen. When he learnt the actual cause of the commo-


tion, one of the Sherpas called Nemu told Smythe that he had several
times seen “bad manshi,” as he called them in pidgin-English, with his
own eyes. He said that they were huge white men covered with thick


fur. A Miss MacDonald of Kalimpong also told Smythe how, when she


was passing through a defile at a great height on a journey to Tibet, she


heard a terrifying roar, unlike any animal’s cry that she had ever heard.


Her porters were panic-stricken; they dropped their loads and left her


there alone. According to the numerous witnesses who have described


the snowman’s cry—some even trying to imitate it—it is a “loud yelp-


ing,” often compared to the sad sound of “the mewing of a sea-gull,”


but of course much louder.


Western explorers had no way of verifying the snowman’s existence
except by studying the strange tracks of bare feet in the high snows.

After Smythe’s mistake, many other Himalayan explorers found
strange footprints in the snow at unusually high altitudes. Among them
was a correspondent of The Times who signed himself “‘Balu.” In 1937

any sign of overlap,” he remarks, “‘as would be the case with a four-

snowman, unhesitatingly recognised a bear’s trail which they found in
a valley several days later. They could not have mistaken the two.


In the same year, John Hunt discovered footprints in the Zemu Gap.
Then in 1938, H. W. Tilman found them in the same place during a
new attempt on Everest.

The snowman became news: Prince Peter of Greece, who was en-

For some time one of these snowmen—which were actually large
monkeys—had been in the habit of coming in the night and drinking

visitor, the villagers prepared for it a bucket full of fermented liquor.
The brute came, drank as usual, and eventually collapsed, dead-drunk.
The men found it in the morning and lashed it firmly to a pole. When
it sobered up it recovered not only its senses, but also all its strength;

In 1953, when the successful Everest expedition was at Thyangboche,
Sir John Hunt took the opportunity of making inquiries about the -yeri
among the lamas at the monastery which lies some 15 miles south-west
of the mountain at a height of 14,000 feet. He learnt from the second

above their settlement, and did not think there was anything mysterious
about them. The last time they had seen one, in November 1949, it came
out of a large clump of rhododendrons and played for some time in the
snow no more than 200 yards away. “It was,” Sir John reports, “a
largish animal, five feet or more in height, covered with greyish-brown


hair, It went mainly upright and occasionally dropped on all fours: it
was also seen to scratch itself monkey fashion.”” The monks made a
shindy with trumpets and cymbals, which soon drove the intruder back

Actually this lama’s report merely confirms the main details of Sen
Tensing’s; for he was present on this occasion with several other
Sherpas.


The yetis were not welcome among the mountain people. Several
miles away, on the northern slopes of the mountains, in Tibet, a party
of snowmen made themselves thoroughly unpleasant by stealing crops,
smashing outbuildings, fouling linen left out to dry and tearing the
roofs off houses. Like the people in Prince Peter of Greece’s story, the
villagers put out bowls of chang (a sort of beer) near their dwellings.
When they found the beasts sleeping off their liquor they slaughtered
them without mercy. This massacre may seem a little improbable in a
country where Buddhism teaches men to respect all forms of life. But
the story also relates that after this outbreak the authorities took strict
measures to prevent anyone in future from maltreating these simple if
savage brutes.

This was how the snowman’s dossier stood at the end of 1953. On
the whole it was treated with utter disbelief. When I tried to talk
seriously about the creature to a fellow-scientist he gave me an old-
fashioned look and asked whether I believed in Father Christmas. But
the footprints in the snow could not be imaginary. How did science
explain them?


Colonel Howard-Bury, as we have seen, attributed them to a grey
wolf and Ronald Kaulback, though with some reservations, to a snow-
leopard. Neither hypothesis in fact accords with the shape of the foot-
prints. But in 1937, other and better supported explanations were put
forward in The Times, the best arena in the world for passionate and
learned controversy.


Guy Dollman of the British Museum (Natural History) believed
in most of the natives’ descriptions and pointed out that in the Himalaya

there were two species of monkeys of reasonable size. One was the
Himalayan langur (Semmnopithecus schistaceus) a stout quadrumane
closely related to the hanuman, the sacred monkey of India (Semnopithe-


cus entellus): it had been recorded in Tibet up to an altitude of 13,000


feet. It had a tougher constitution and longer and fleecier fur than the
common species. The other was Roxellana’s snub-nosed langur (Rhino-

pithecus roxellanae) which the Chinese called the snow-monkey. It was
a primate of much heavier build than the langur, with thick fur and a
comically snub nose which made its face look very human. These
monkeys were very rare and then still unknown in captivity; there were
only a few stuffed specimens in museums. Thus it would be rather
surprising to come upon a wild one.


The size of these creatures does not of course agree with the tradi-
tional description of the snowman, for the largest hardly ever exceed
4 feet 6 inches in height when standing on their hind legs. Moreover,
the langur’s area of distribution does not reach the places where the
snowman’s footprints are usually found: the snub-nosed monkey is
found in country to the north-east of the Himalayan range, eastern
Tibet and western China, whereas it is on the south-western slopes that
we seem to hear most about the snowman.


All the same, most zoologists favoured the monkey theory when Eric
Shipton brought back his famous photographs. They were supported
by no less an authority than Dr T. C. S. Morrison-Scott, of the Mam-
mals Section of the British Museum (Natural History), and went so
far as to specify the race of langurs the pseudo-monster belonged to.


It was a Presbytis [alias Semnopithecus] entellus achilles, they said, a
langur which may stand as much as 5-feet high: the type specimen
of this sub-species came from a place 12,000 feet up and some 50
miles north-west of Katmandu in Nepal. It was a graceful quadrumane,
mainly fawn in colour with a black face and silvery head and neck. Its
description, these zoologists maintained, agreed fairly well with that
given by Sen Tensing, Shipton’s guide.


Against this theory it was shrewdly objected that the footprints of a
langur with long toes were not in the least like those in Shipton’s photo-
graphs made by a large solid foot with short toes, and in any case an
animal with feet no more than 9 inches long could not leave footprints
13 inches long. This latter objection was ingeniously evaded by an
argument which a newspaper put thus:


The colossal dimensions of the footprints_are no doubt to be ex-
plained by the fact that they are made in the night in fresh snow and in
the day-time they melt in the snow and increase in size. When night
comes the footprints freeze again, retaining their shape so well that it
is easy to attribute them to a race of giants.


Unfortunately, a few lines above, the same newspaper rashly observed
that “the footprints are so far apart that it is impossible that they could
have been made by a human being.” A little thought should-have made


142


THE NOT SO ABOMINABLE SNOWMAN


it obvious that if a small animal’s footprints were enlarged by the snow
melting the length of its stride would appear to decrease, the prints
might even merge.


Oliver Jones, Curator of Mammals at the London Zoo, put forward
a very ingenious theory in an attempt to explain how a small langur
could have left giant footprints.
His view was that the footprints
Shipton photographed had been made by all four feet at once. As it
bounded across the snow the langur first put down its two hands side


by side and then its hind feet, also held close together, immediately


behind them. This would produce a string of large bilobate footprints.


This explanation seemed to be confirmed by W. W. Wood, a South
African who had spent some time in Kashmir. In 1944, when on a trip
in the mountains at Liddarwat near Srinagar with Major Kirkland and
Captain John B. Maggs, he saw a monkey which he took for an abomin-
able snowman. He wrote to Country Life:


We were somewhere near the timber line—about 13,000 feet—when
we saw a large animal bounding towards us down the snow-covered
khud on the opposite side of the river. Its gait appeared to me to be
that of a monkey in a hurry, with all four paws off the ground together.
Maggs’ recollection is that its rear legs were longer than the forelegs and
its running not very different from that of a rabbit...


The animal came up the mountain side, crossed our path and then
sat down, monkey fashion, among the boulders to look at us. It obviously
found us as strange as we did it... . It was tawny in colour, with a
fringe round its face, was about the size of a man and had a long tail
with a tuft on the end, like a lion. Maggs thought that its tail was more
bushy than that of a lion and its coat of longish hair—reddish brown in
colour—rather like that of a bear. The Kashmiris said that it was
bandar (monkey).


This strange creature was certainly neither bear nor langur. Can it,
wandering alone at these altitudes, have been abominable snowman?


To which the editor replied:


Despite our correspondent’s assertion to the contrary, the creature
was almost certainly a langur, for he gives a good description of Semno-
pithecus entellus ajax, a species of langur that lives at high altitudes
among the head waters of the Indus drainage basin and is often found
above the snow line. Admittedly this langur measures only about 30


inches head and body, but size is notoriously hard to judge in the


mountains.?


1 This is very true, and one may as well underestimate the size as exaggerate


it. Thus the yeti could easily be larger than the 5 feet 10 inches to 6 feet 6 inches
which some witnesses have reported. The huge size of its footprints would seem


to show that it is.

THE MAN-FACED ANIMALS OF SOUTH-EAST ASIA


All the same Wood’s description of the monkey’s strange progress in


leaps and bounds corroborates Oliver Jones’s theory. The snag is that


some of Shipton’s prints are too clear to have been made by four feet
merged into one. You can distinctly see the general outline of the foot
and the details of most of the toes. Moreover if you look clearly at the
photograph of the trail you can see that the footprints alternate to


left and right. This is proof that the animal is walking, for why the devil
should an animal jump alternately to left and to right with absolute
regularity? And a monkey like a langur would have left marks in the
snow with its tail.


The footprints so often found in the snow were not made by a mon-
key, at least not by a tailed monkey standing hardly 4 feet 6 inches high.
But this does not mean that no one has ever mistaken a tall Himalayan
langur or a snub-nosed monkey for the legendary snowman.
This is
what Wood probably did and what Sen Tensing was thought to have


done; but he did not; for it is unlike a man who knew the mountains so
well not to recognise a monkey with which he must have been familiar.
Nor was he the only person to think that the animal in question was a
yeti; several other Sherpas and monks from the Thyangboche monastery
were there and confirmed his opinion.


The party who maintained the yeti was a bear were in a stronger
position, especially after Frank Smythe’s mistake. According to their
champion, Reginald I. Pocock, the creature responsible for the giant
footprints could only be the red bear (Ursus arctos isabellinus), a local
Tibetan species of the European brown bear. This bear, which rarely
exceeds 6 feet 6 inches in height, could easily leave footprints 13 inches
long, and what is more they would be astonishingly like a man’s. Like
the rest of the plantigrades, it sometimes stands on its hind-legs. If it
were surprised in that position might it not give rise to the legends of
hairy giants? And if some natives were attacked and eaten by an old
male that had turned carnivorous (being often enough starving in coun-
try so poor in food) it would substantiate the rumours of ogres with a


taste for human flesh.


This argument was firmly supported, among others by G. S. Cans-
dale, Superintendent of the London Zoo, and there were many good
arguments in its favour. What, one might reasonably ask, could an
entirely vegetarian monkey—a specialised leaf-eater like the langur—
find to eat at an altitude of 19,000 to 23,000 feet? For these monkeys
have never been reported above 13,000 feet—that is, above the tree line

THE NOT SO ABOMINABLE SNOWMAN


—and this height is very exceptional. Major R. W. C. Hingston of the
Indian Medical Service, who took part in the tragic attempt on Everest
in 1924 and has collected much information about Himalayan fauna and


flora, tells us that the plant Parnassius is sometimes found at 18,000


feet, but higher up all vegetable life seems to have disappeared. Never-


theless the 1952 Swiss expedition found traces of vegetation up to 21,000


feet. Vegetarian animals never go above this limit, except on rare occa-


sions when driven to take refuge there. Certain rodents do so, for in-


stance the pika or Everest mouse-hare (Ochotona wollastoni), a large


tailless “rat,” actually related to the hares, which is common up to 17,400


feet, but may stray as high as 20,000 feet. In the rocky country between


the tree line and the perpetual snow there are also: wild boar; musk-


deer; wild yaks; goat-antelopes like the serow and goral (Naemorhedus);


the takin (Budorcas), a strange “‘ox-goat” related to-them; the chiru


(Pantholops), a gazelle-goat; such true goats as the Kemas tahr (Hemi-


tragus) and the markhor (Capra falconeri); and the bharal or blue sheep


(Pseudois). Certain species of agamid lizards of the genera Phrynoce-


phalus and Leiolepis are often found on Everest above 16,000 feet. The


Daily Mail expedition confirmed this in 1954. “In fact,” the leader


wrote, “we have found that wild life abounds as high as we have been


able to climb—that is, certainly to 20,000 ft.”” Above 20,000 feet there


seem to be only birds, but of many kinds. Climbers say that there are


choughs above 26,000 feet and near the highest summits. While carni-


vores, such as snow-leopards, leopard-cats, wolves and Tibetan foxes,


manage to live at 13,000 to 20,000 feet or even higher by coming down


every day (or almost every day) to hunt for food at a lower altitude,


vegetarians could not possibly live at such a height, for they cannot sur-


vive on large but irregular meals: they have to feed or chew the cud for


most of the day.


For bears the problem of food does not arise the whole year round.
During the bad season they leave off feeding and become lethargic and
sluggish. Thus there is no theoretical reason why some species of bear
should not spend the cold months of the year at high altitudes where it


would be absolutely safe from attack. And it is at the beginning and at


the end of the hibernation season that footprints are usually found at


unusual heights. The snowman generally leaves its tracks in autumn


snows.

Every single mark is made by two footprints superimposed, and

would never fit into one another perfectly). They are clearly outlined in

Shipton has

was no “sign of overlap, as would be the case with a four-footed beast.”
So if the animal was a bear, it was a bear that walked on its hind-legs.


It is indeed true that bears occasionally adopt an upright gait when they


are inquisitive or threatening; but I do not think they would ever do so
for several hundred yards or that they could even manage it if they
tried—especially on such sloping ground. Shipton followed the yezz’s
track for about a mile.


It seems much wiser and more honest to adopt Sir John Graham
Kerr’s opinion. The Emeritus Professor of Zoology at Glasgow Univer-
sity replied to these hasty theories by acknowledging his ignorance; and
admitting that, as far as he could judge, the footprints belonged to no
animal known to zoologists.


If the species is unknown, one may still ask which zoological group
of animals the yeti is most likely to belong to. The only plantigrade
bipeds are man and those tree-dwellers the gibbon and the indris—all
primates. Could the yeti be a large anthropoid ape as yet unknown?


There are two points against this hypothesis.
Firstly, that all the
anthropoids have an opposable big toe—like a thumb—clearly separated
from the other toes, indeed almost at right angles to them when the foot


is put on the ground. But in the snowman’s footprint the big toe is
almost as close to the other toes as a man’s. Secondly, the anthropoids


are usually quadrupeds. This is particularly noticeable in the gorilla,
which soon grows too heavy to live in trees. The orang-utan seems to
stand more upright, but this is just because its arms are so long that
even when they are on the ground it can stand erect. It uses them like
crutches. The gibbon uses its long arms in an original way, like a tight-
rope-walker’s balancing rod, when walking on its hind-legs. They would
both walk like quadrupeds with their bodies horizontal if their arms were
not too long. Unlike man, the anthropoid apes are not built to walk on

their hind-legs. Their skull does not sit upright with the centre of its

Nevertheless it is not impossible for anthropoid apes to walk on their
hind-legs, even if they find it hard going. With patience it is possible to
train a chimpanzee to walk some distance on its hind-legs. Certain
climates may even naturally encourage such a gait, or so it would seem
from the evidence of Dr Sydney W. Britton, Professor of Anthropology


at the University of Virginia. Snow had fallen, and he was curious to


see how a chimpanzee that had arrived from Africa during the previous
year would react to a phenomenon so utterly new to it. He did not
expect it to walk erect in the snow, but to his surprise it stood up after
the first few steps and went on walking in the same position. The
American anthropologist thought that this showed that snow had played


a vital part in man’s evolution into a biped. Be that as it may, his
evidence undoubtedly throws light on the problem of the snowman: it
shows that in the Himalayan snows an ape could easily have learnt to
walk on its hind-legs in an attempt to reduce to a minimum its painful
contact with the ice beneath the snow. The “human” formation of this

trees would, like him, have retained truly plantigrade feet. It is easy
to see how if a line of apes evolved in increasing size they would very

hardly suitable for a giant species (this, according to Urbain and Dekey-

probably has already reached it). A giant ape would have a better chance


of surviving in open country, and being relatively ill-armed for the

mountains would be its ideal habitat, and there the snow would en-


courage it to become a biped. Thus, in theory at least, a race of giant


apes, with primitive plantigrade feet and a tendency to stand on their


hind-legs, could have arisen in the mountain snows.


So, in the end, had we not better humbly accept the evidence of those
who describe the snowman as a giant ape, a sort of hairy ogre? Most
people may reply that giants have never existed, but have merely arisen
in popular imagination, and that science has never found the least trace
of their existence. This view might have been defensible a dozen years
ago, but not today.


In 1934 Ralph von Koenigswald, a young Dutch geologist and
palaeontologist, who later contributed so much to our knowledge of the
Pithecanthropus (the famous Java ape-man), was wandering about the
streets of Hong Kong looking for curiosities. He went into an old-
fashioned Chinese chemist’s shop. It was not so much a dispensary as


a junk-shop where magical drugs were compounded of such diverse
ingredients as rhinoceros-horn and the intestines of flying lizards, and
he vaguely hoped to pick up something odd or even interesting. He had
come to China to study its fauna, and among this junk one sometimes
came upon stuffed specimens of rare animals, dried insects, shells or
even pieces of fossils sold as lung tchih (dragon’s teeth) or lung koo
(dragon’s bones). On the counter he noticed a jar full of teeth of all
sorts and picked up a handful. It was child’s play for him to recognise
what animal they belonged to, for teeth, especially those of mammals, are


like identity cards to an expert. Suddenly he stopped with a shiver, so


astounded, as he later recalled, that his hair actually stood on end. He


held in his hand a tooth that looked to be human—he could tell that it


was a third lower molar—but a tooth far larger than any man or ape had

Was it man or ape? It is hard to say; for the teeth of men and the

that Gigantanthropus, or ‘giant man,” would be a more suitable name.


A considerable difference in size between creatures belonging to the
same zoological order usually involves numerous variations in the details
of their anatomy. The distinction between ape and man here seems
premature. Perhaps it is even meaningless. After all, we have many
more relics of the Pithecanthropus than a handful of teeth, yet scientists


still cannot agree whether to call it man or ape. It is therefore more

Von Koenigswald’s discoveries about giants did not end there. After

were only three-quarters of the size. The creature to which they be-

very satisfactorily from a study of these fragments. It did not have such

its huge jaws, which contrasted oddly with its relatively small cranium.


It is not therefore surprising to find that this huge-jawed creature had a


crest along the top of its skull like that to be seen on old male gorillas,


for these crests are closely linked to the muscular strength of the jaw,
the terminal tendons of which are attached to the parietal bones near the
top of the skull.

Therefore until there is proof to the contrary it seems more reasonable

not still be called a giant?


Finally Weinert reported in 1950 the discovery made by Dr Kohl-
Larsen in Tanganyika in 1939, but not published or studied owing to
the war. Twenty-five miles north of Lake Eyasi this German doctor
found in upper Quatenary deposits the remains of a palate, nasal
bones and jaws of a giant primate. As the molars were comparable in


size to the Meganthropus’s molars, Weinert considered it as an African
cousin of the Java giant and called it Meganthropus africanus. All the
same I think it much more likely that it is more closely related to the
Paranthropus, a fellow-African, than to the Indonesian Meganthropus.


The discovery of authentic remains of prehistoric giants has revived
a very old riddle, which has always puzzled the learned. It concerns this
passage from Genesis:


And it came to pass, when men began to multiply on the face of the
earth, and daughters were born unto them, that the sons of God saw
the daughters of men that they were fair; and they took them wives of
all which they chose.


155


THE MAN-FACED ANIMALS OF SOUTH-EAST ASIA


And the Lord said, My spirit shall not always strive with man, for
that he also is flesh: yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years.


There were giants in the earth in those days; and also after that, when
the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men, and they bare
children to them, the same became mighty men which were of old, men
of renown.


It is not really surprising that the ancient Jews should have thought
that giants, or nefilim as they called them, were the offspring of women
and the strange “sons of God” who seem so incongruous in the sacred
books of a monotheistic religion. For primitive people it is a natural
step from greatness in size to greatness in spirit; and this change con-
tributes to the distorted interpretations which historic events undergo in
the course of thousands of years.


The point for us about Moses’s text is that the oldest chronicles report
that man lived on earth at the same time as a race of man-like giants.
The Pentateuch is not the only work of antiquity to mention the exist-
ence of giants. According to Brahmin mythology a whole hegemony of
giants preceded the advent of the primitive red race which founded the
present human civilisation on the southern continent. This version is
very widespread and has been believed all over the world since time
immemorial. And stories of giants—usually man-eaters—are found in
the folk-lore of all the peoples on earth. They are always considered as
man’s worst enemy and all the purest heroes of legend have a victory
over some giant or other to their credit. Ulysses blinding Polyphemus’s
one eye, Sinbad the Sailor following his example, Odin and Ymer, David
and Goliath, the battle of the Hottentot warriors and the great Haitsi-
Aibab, ““He-who-hurls-to-the-ground,” the stories of gigantic bogy-men


that are told in America from Peru to the country of the Eskimos, the


fear of Asourikes in Siam, of Assouras in India and Aessouri in Mongolia,
the processional giants that are part of the folk-lore of so many towns in
Europe (Gog in London, Druon Antigon in Antwerp, Gayant at Douai
and so on), are not all these fables based on the memory of battles
which our ancestors actually fought with giants more than twice their
size?


Sceptics have never failed to counter these legends with the complete
absence of tangible remains. Where were the bones of these giants?
At first they were improvised. Empedocles found fossil elephant-bones
in Sicily and was misled by the single hole formed by the joined nasal
fossae into thinking it was a Cyclops. In the Middle Ages a surgeon
called Mazurier went all round France with a Mastodon’s skeleton


156


lied
bind)
ttl


THE NOT SO ABOMINABLE SNOWMAN


found in the Dauphiné which he said was that of Teutobochus, King of
the Apes. As comparative anatomy progressed and palaeontology was
born, scientists soon exploded these errors. They remained obstinately
against the giants, until quite suddenly official science came to provide
arguments for those who believed in the truth of legend and biblical


infallibility.


Von Koenigswald’s and Broom’s giants would have left an indelible
mark in the memory of ancient man. These huge brutes, not yet entirely
graduated from bestiality, must have made life hard for our ancestors.
Weidenreich and von Koenigswald would have it that we are their
direct descendants, but this is as absurd as to suppose that a Diplodocus
could have given birth to the small lizards of today.


Quite apart from the question of size, there is no reason for thinking
that these creatures had human intelligence. No doubt they were no
more than clumsy and monstrous sketches for man which were swept
aside just because they were so ill-adapted. Perhaps the gorilla and
orang-utan may even owe the fact that they have not been totally
exterminated to cunning greater or at least equal to that of these
giant primates. The offspring of the sons of God and the daughters
of men must have been very stupid, to be dethroned by puny little
men.


No doubt these stupid or too peaceable great brutes, weary of always
being beaten by man, gradually fell back into country where their
adversary could not reach them. For giant apes, still agile but no longer
able to live in trees, mountains were evidently the most suitable habitat
and safest refuge. For the Gigantopithecus which used to live in China,
the high Himalaya was the obvious shelter.
There, out of reach
of their enemies, they could have survived until today, just as their
contemporaries have survived in the marshy forests of Borneo and
Sumatra.
This theory, which is utterly hypothetical, provides the
only entirely acceptable explanation of the mystery of the abominable
snowman.


Similarly, if we suppose that the Meganthropus of the Sunda Islands
had also taken to the mountains—especially those of Sumatra—it would


also explain the mystery of the giants in that island. For rumours very


similar to the Himalayan ones are reported there, and human-looking


footprints with an unusually large big toe have been found in the


mud. These prints were enormous: about 2 feet long by 8 inches wide.
A native who claimed to have seen an orang gadang (big man), which was


supposed to have made the footprints, put its height at 10 feet; it was

I had already related the legends of Himalayan ogres to von Koenig-
swald’s discoveries for some time when in December 1951 the first
photographs of clear footprints of the snowman were published. I took
the opportunity to write a series of articles on unknown animals which
appeared in Sciences et Avenir (Paris) in the following January, March,
May and August. In the issue of May 1952 I published the gist of what
I have written above, and put forward for the first time my view that the
snowman was a giant and biped anthropoid no doubt closely related to
the Gigantopithecus.
At this time scientific opinion almost unani-
mously rejected the idea that the snowman was an unknown animal.
Apart from Sir John Graham Kerr, who gave the yeti the benefit of the
doubt, all the zoologists who expressed an opinion tried to identify it
with some known animal and were not sparing in their sarcasm of those
who put any faith in the Himalayan legend. Nobody took much notice
of me.


But little by little opinion began to change as the conquerors of
Everest brought back the same persistent rumours, Sherpas gave more


detailed accounts, a lama claimed to have examined the mummified
remains of what he called “‘big monkeys,” and Sir John Hunt himself
declared after his interview with the second senior lama at Thyang-
boche: “There is an interesting problem for an enterprising party to
investigate.”
;


By the end of 1953 scepticism was breaking down, and scientists
in several countries thought that it was possible that the Himalayan
giant might exist and be a new and unknown species. The Daily Mail
decided to send an expedition to look for the abominable snowman.
When this news was announced a Pole called Slavomir Rawicz, who had


settled in the Midlands and married an Englishwoman, came out with a
strange account which was taken down by Ronald Downing, a Daily
Mail reporter, and printed in that newspaper. Subsequently Rawicz’s


entire story was published under the title of The Long Walk. Eastern


travellers have been very sceptical of this tale, and Rawicz offers not the

At the beginning of 1941 Rawicz was sent as a political prisoner to
Soviet Labour Camp No. 402 in Siberia, some 200 miles north-west of
Irkutsk and Lake Baikal. One day seven prisoners managed to elude
their guards’ vigilance and escape. Then began the long walk. They
covered more than 2,000 miles on foot in country where nature was even
more hostile than man. They crossed Mongolia, Sinkiang and Tibet,
and in June 1942 the four survivors, indescribably thin and exhausted,
were taken in by Indian soldiers.


In May 1942 there were still five of them and they were near the
frontier of Sikkim and Bhutan in the narrow Chumbi valley which
leads from Tibet into the Indian plains. When they saw two black dots
moving over the snow in the distance they hurried towards them, in the
hope of catching some creature they could eat. But when they reached
an overhanging rock about 100 yards from the two creatures and 12 feet
above them, they saw their hopes were vain.


They were massive creatures, nearly 8 feet tall and standing erect.
They were shuffling around on a snow-covered shelf which formed part
of the obvious route for us to continue our descent. Armed as we were
with only one knife and one axe the whole five of us together would have
stood no chance against them.


We thought perhaps they would go away if we waited.
It was
obvious that the pair had seen us. They looked at us and were quite
indifferent. They certainly were not frightened of us.


I wanted to climb down the rock and get a little closer but my com-
panions refused to join me. So we just sat there, our legs dangling over
the edge of the rock, and watched them.


For two hours we watched them. One of the party said that if we
waited long enough we should be bound to see them descend on all
fours. But they never did. They moved around quietly on their hind
legs with an almost comical swinging motion.


As a regular officer in the Polish Army in 1939 I was specially trained
in assessing distances and heights for setting gun sights. I have not the
slightest doubt that they were at least 7 feet high, but probably nearer
8 feet. One was slightly smaller than the other, and we decided they
must be male and female.


Their faces I could not see in detail, but the heads were squarish and
the ears must lie close to the skull because there was no projection from
the silhouette against the snow. The shoulders sloped sharply down to
a powerful chest and long arms, the wrists of which reached the knees.

Seen in profile, the back of the head was a straight line from the

Prussian.”


I tried to decide what they were and the nearest I could get was
an idea of a cross between a big bear and an orang-outang type of
ape.


P The nearest I can get to describing their colour is a rusty camel.
They were covered with a long loose straight hair, which, in the light,
seemed to have a greyish tinge, but the bodies seemed to be covered
also with a very short reddish fur.


They were doing nothing but move around slowly together and
occasionally just standing and looking about them, like people admiring
the view. So eventually we had to move off in another and more diffi-
cult direction.


On the way down the little party found half-blurred footprints of these
creatures. They were more or less oval in shape and were about 20
inches long by 8 inches wide at their widest point. The change of route
was fatal for one of the Poles: he slipped off a narrow ledge of rock and
crashed to his death.


If we accept this story, what can we deduce from it? Firstly, that the
animals were certainly not bears, for bears never stand on their hind-
legs for long and, when they do, their front-legs are too short to come
down anywhere near their knees. Moreover their ears stand up on
the top of their heads and would certainly have been visible in their
silhouettes against the snow. And they do not have particularly power-


ful chests. The only bear-like feature is their short and presumably
thick fur. Everything else points to an anthropoid—which might well
have adapted its coat to suit the climate.


The Prussian neck is most interesting. Old gorillas also have a thick-
ened nape like a stiff-necked and muscular soldier. And it is clear that


this effect would be exaggerated in an anthropoid which had become a
permanent biped in order to save its precious hands from painful con-


tact with the frozen ground. Most monkeys have a very concave nape of
the neck as a result of holding up their heads when walking on all four


legs. This makes them look a little hunchbacked. The yeti’s remarkably
straight neck no doubt implies that it is a biped of very long standing—
which would confirm the deductions I have already made from its
primitive plantigrade foot, with no marked sign of having derived from


a tree-dweller. May not the snowman, unlike all the primates but man,
have by-passed this stage? Yet the long arms seem to imply that once it
swung from branches like the larger anthropoids.
Perhaps the yeri
developed into a giant so soon that its life in trees had not entirely left

its mark upon it before it had to take to the ground. This may be why


its big toe is so slightly separated from the smaller ones.


On the other hand, the yezi’s long arms could be not a sign of a past


life in trees but a necessary consequence of being a biped. A man’s skull


sits upright with the centre of its base resting on the spinal column,
which is curved in the small of the back so as to stand erect; very straight


legs complete the tall but perfectly vertical structure. A monkey, as I


have already remarked, is very ill-balanced when it stands on its hind-


legs, and is obliged to use its arms as crutches or as balancing rods.


Perhaps the yeri’s ancestors used their long arms as balancing rods be-


fore they learnt to walk quite upright like man.


Being a long-standing biped would have a much more important
effect on the Himalayan giant than merely giving it a stiff neck. In the
evolution of mammals and in their individual growth there is a very
clear opposition between the development of the occipital part of the
skull which contains the brain and the facial part which includes the
jaws. An upright position allows the brain to develop freely on the end
of the spine rather like a flower on its stalk, while the jaws are confined
and inhibited by its growth. But when the body is horizontal, as in
quadrupeds, the brain is compressed between the spine and the facial


part; the jaws, on the other hand, can lengthen into a snout. In other
words, it is impossible to have the large spherical brain that goes with
higher intelligence at the same time as a beast’s snout; and the prepon-
derance of the one over the other is related to the angle of the body.
Thus monkeys, which use their hands to climb in trees and tend to be
in a half-upright position, are half-way between man—a complete biped
—and the quadrupeds with their horizontal bodies. Those monkeys—
baboons and the like—which have given up living in trees and become
quadrupeds have much longer muzzles than the others and are known


as Cynocephala or dog-headed monkeys. The Asian anthropoids—the
gibbon and the orang-utan—unlike the African apes which often walk
on the ground, live almost exclusively in trees.
They are expert


trapezists and have developed such long arms that when they come
down to the ground they are still as vertical as when they are swinging


from branch to branch. Their upright position ought logically to have


favoured the growth of their brains and inhibited that of their jaws.
This is what one finds, but it is not very noticeable, because they have


retained, from having once been quadrupeds, a very backwards position


of the occipital condyles, which form the articulation between the skull


and the spinal column. Therefore, unlike man’s, their skull does no¢

161


THE MAN-FACED ANIMALS OF SOUTH-EAST ASIA


sit in equilibrium on the top of the spine, but is as it were stuck on in
front of the body. They have in fact taken the wrong road towards
standing upright. Nevertheless the orang-utan and the gibbon have
higher, rounder foreheads than their African cousins, and their jaws,


after growing forwards, have begun to grow downwards as a result of the
change in angle of their bodies. This is most striking in the orang-utan,
the most different from the other apes of the two, which once it is adult
has a thick and heavy jaw, as well-developed in height and breadth as in


length.


The yeti’s evolution must have run in the same direction as the orang-
utan’s, but, having become a biped much sooner, the downward growth
of the jaw would have started at an earlier stage. Consequently one
would expect to find not only a much higher forehead and very slight
prognathism, but also considerable development in the depth and
breadth of the jaws. Comparing this with the only giant primate of
which we have a more or less complete skull, the Swartkrans Paran-
thropus (see reconstruction facing page 136), we find that its face is
rather flat, and the development of the jaws, considerable though it is,


is almost entirely in depth and thickness, hence the impressive size of
the molars. Ifthe snowman is closely related to the Gigantopithecus,


as I believe it is, Professor Broom is right in thinking the Asian giant
primates are not of a size proportionate to their teeth. According to his
calculations the Gigantopithecus must have stood between 8 and 10 feet
high, which, according to most witnesses, is about the height of the yert
and agrees with the size of its footprints. Thus it is legitimate to
consider equating the two creatures.


If the snowman, then, like his African cousin the Paranthropus, had


a remarkably over-developed masticatory apparatus, without any marked
prognathism, he would have exceptionally powerful jaw-muscles and


like him would have a considerable sagittal crest on the top of his already
high skull, comparable to the crest of an old male gorilla.


This conclusion, reached by a priori argument and comparison with
various known species, not only agrees with the Sherpas’ accounts that
the yeti has a pointed or conical head, but is also confirmed most strik-
ingly by the discoveries of the Daily Mail expedition.


The expedition set off from Katmandu in January 1954. Including
the Nepalese porters it consisted of some 300 men. Besides a veteran
mountaineer John A. Jackson, the adventurous reporter Ralph Izzard,

Charles Stonor had already set off in December 1953 on a reconnais-

piece of ground sparsely covered with bushes.
It was the first yeri
Pasang had seen. According to him it was the size and build of a small
man.
Its head, its body and its thighs were covered with long hair.


Its face and chest looked less hairy and there were no long hairs on the
legs below the knees. The colour of the fur was “‘both dark and light”
and the chest was reddish. It walked nearly as upright as a man and
bent down occasionally to grub in the ground for roots. When it

did it go on all fours. As all the villagers insisted that Pasang was speak-

To which the Sherpa replied with disarming logic:

Let me digress a moment to clear the philological problem of the


snowman’s many names out of the way. Prince Peter of Greece, who
knows the Himalaya well, was the first to explain what teh meant. “It


is, I believe, a rather vague colloquial term for ‘brown bear’ (spelt dred


and pronounced ¢(r)e).”” He added that in the Kalimpong area where he


was living mi-go (wild man) was the usual Tibetan name for the snow-


man.
A really thorough philological study of the problem was published in


1955 by an Indian scholar Sri Swami Pranavananda in the Journal of the
Bombay Natural History Society. He confirmed that tre (with the r so


softly pronounced as to be almost inaudible, thus making it te or teh)


was indeed the name for the brown bear. He explained that there were


three bears known to the Tibetans: the black bear which they called


tom, the brown bear called te, and the mi-te or “‘man-bear” (from mi,


“‘man,” and te, “‘bear’’) so called because it walked on its hind-feet like


aman. Pranavananda asserted that this is certainly the red bear, adding:


‘Since the mi-te walks sometimes on all fours and sometimes on hind-


legs only, it is but natural that the tracks of footprints are sometimes seen


in pairs and sometimes in single files.”


He went on to say that the name of metoh kangmi (from metoh or
meteh, “‘abominable,” kang, “snow” and mi, “‘man’’) was an unjustifiable
conjunction of different names for the red bear: mi-te (man-bear) and
kang-mi (snowman), the former having been misunderstood and mis-
translated. The term mi-go usually translated as “wild man” according


to this Indian scholar actually meant “‘beast that walks like man” and
was the name for the snowman in Tibetan provinces of Amdo and Kham
(which are now part of China) and was also used by the Tibetans on the
Indian frontier with Kham. As for yeh-te (yi-te, yih-dah or yeh-da) it
was a quite mythical creature “with the throat as thin as a needle and
stomach as big as a mountain, hence a glutton.”


Sri Swami Pranavananda’s article was welcomed by the sceptics.
Newspapers reported that the legend of the abominable snowman had
been exploded once and for all. And the distinguished anthropologist
William L. Strauss, Jr., of Johns Hopkins University repeated the Indian


scholar’s conclusions in Science with evident satisfaction.


Actually Pranavananda would have done better to have stuck to the


165


THE MAN-FACED ANIMALS OF SOUTH-EAST ASIA


linguistic side of the problem, for his zoological conclusions are quite
absurd. There are only two known species of bear in the high Himalaya:
the black or collared bear (Selenarctos thibetanus) and the local variety of
brown bear known as the red bear (Ursus arctos isabellinus). It is true
that in Tibet and Kansu there is another variety of brown bear called
the blue bear (Ursus arctos pruinosus), but it does not spread as far as the
Himalaya. So if the mi-teh is a third bear, even more mysterious than
Graham Greene’s Third Man, in these great mountains, it must be an
unknown species. And if this third bear really walks on its hind-feet as
often as its name implies, and does so for miles at a time as its tracks
show, it is a truly extraordinary bear, much more extraordinary to the
zoologist than a large biped ape.


From Pranavananda’s article we can conclude that the people who


live in the Himalaya know a creature which they call mi-teh, probably
because it resembles both bear and man; no doubt it is the same beast
which in some areas is called mi-go because it walks like a man, and in
others kangmi because it sometimes leaves tracks in the snowfields;


lastly it is often nicknamed yeh-te, a word originally meaning an all-
devouring demon, just as we sometimes call an actual but particularly
savage and voracious beast a monster.


If Pranavananda has really unmasked the snowman he has revealed


that it has a much more agreeable face: it was originally called abomin-
able in error and unjustly maligned ever since.


Continuing his reconnaissance Stonor finally found some tracks of
the yeti 14,000 feet up near Namche Bazar. They were the human-
looking footprints so often seen by travellers, but smaller than any
reported before: the average length was Io inches, the maximum width
5 inches and across the heel 3 inches. Stonor was much encouraged.


““My own view,” he wrote, “is that we are concerned with some quite
unknown and extremely interesting beast.”


When the main body of the expedition had arrived and were split into

were soon found. Jackson and Jeeves went up the Khumbu glacier and
discovered one two or three days old which had undoubtedly been made
by a biped. The prints were ro to 11 inches long by § to 6 inches wide.

Meanwhile members of the expedition also found occasional heaps of

a quantity of mouse-hare fur; a quantity of mouse-hare bones (approx.

The outer surface is now largely bare and the skin fairly smooth: but
it was quite clearly covered with hair in its original state and is still
minutely pitted all over with hair bases. A fair proportion of hair still
remains. The hair is foxy-red in general colour, barred with blackish-
brown. The individual hairs are a very few inches in length and are
extremely stiff and bristle-like.
It is impossible to say if there were
formerly hairs of greater length. From what is presumably the forehead
the hair slopes backward, and slightly downwards along the sides, much
as in man: while at the back of the head it slopes almost vertically down-
wards. This is quite noticeable and I think it to be the natural con-
formation.


An extraordinary feature is a crest or “keel’’ which runs from the
base of the forehead straight upwards over the crown and down the
back. It has a uniform width of almost exactly one inch. It is covered
with bristle-like hairs of the same colour as the rest, which are no more
than 1-25 in. in length and which slope inwards from each side so as
to meet in the centre and form a crest, which is thus triangular in cross-
section. In common with the rest of the hairs much of the crest is gone,
but it is distinctly marked as a slightly raised ridge in the skin.


When Dr Biswas, who was also a professional naturalist, examined
the Pangboche scalp soon afterwards he also categorically confirmed


Charles Stonor’s view that it could under no circumstances be false or


imitation. Only the ciné-cameraman Tom Stobart had doubts. ‘“Per-


sonally,” he said, “I would not rule out its being a ‘made article.’
When one considers the shrunken heads made in South America it is


by no means impossible. I should think that a boar would supply the


basic materials.” I shall discuss this question later.

When the expedition visited the Thyangboche monastery, the head


lama, with whom they had made friends, told them that there was a
second yeri’s scalp at the lamasery at Khumjung, 2} miles away. This
proved on examination to be the same size as the first, more battered
and with scantier fur. According to the tradition the two scalps had
come from a pair, the Pangboche one from a male and the Khumjung
one from a female.


Despite much bargaining the monks would not lend either of the
scalps to the expedition, but their friend Sanghi Lama got them a piece
of skin 3 inches long by 1} inches wide which he said had come from an
entire yeri’s skin that had long belonged to the village of Khumjung but
had recently disappeared in mysterious circumstances.


The expedition was subsequently able to examine a third yert’s scalp
in the temple at Namche Bazar, but it turned out to be merely a faked
version of the other two: it was made of pieces of hairy skin, identical
with that of the true scalps, but sewn together to form the same shape as
them. Doubtiess it had been made to satisfy Namche Bazar’s local
pride. Izzard suggests that “An impious thought is that possibly
the Namche Bazar scalp is the explanation of Khumjung’s missing
hide.”


Professor F. Wood Jones, the expert in comparative anatomy who
examined some hairs from the Pangboche scalp in London, said that he
was unable to determine what animal they came from. After comparing
them with those of an orang-utan and a black bear, he was convinced
that they were not those of an anthropoid ape nor of a bear, but thought
they might come from the shoulder of some coarse-haired hooved
animal, not from its head. In his opinion the hairs and the photographs
showed that it was not a true scalp, for he did not believe that any animal
would have a crest running from the base of the forehead right across
the top of the head and ending at the back of the neck.


The Daily Mail team were discouraged by this pronouncement. But
in fact one could hardly hope for an opinion more favourable to the
scalp’s authenticity. For it is clear enough that the scalp of a huge biped
anthropoid ape, a sort of animal as yet unheard of, would have to be
quite original in structure. One should not be in the least surprised to
find that it had a raised crest of standing hair. The ridge along the crest
of the scalp indicates that there was a bony sagittal crest beneath it, and


this, as I have shown, is what we should expect to find in a giant biped
primate closely related to the Gigantopithecus. The yeri must therefore
be like the Paranthropus, a primate with a heavy and powerful but not

very prominent jaw. This is also confirmed by such witnesses as
Tenzing’s father and the yak-herd Mingma, who were struck by the


size of its teeth. Clearly its very flat face and high forehead would give


it a remarkably human expression. This would be accentuated by its


crest, like a gorilla’s, which in some individuals, old males no doubt,


seems to be furnished with long hair looking like the hair on a man’s


head. Its biped gait would clinch the resemblance and justify the name


of snowman.


Thus the unusual shape of the alleged yeti scalps agrees better than
one could possibly have hoped with what I deduced the beast must be
on the evidence of its footprints alone. To make quite certain, I set
about trying to find out if it would be possible to make a fake scalp from
the shoulder of some hooved animal.


Let me explain at once that it would be by no means essential to use
the skin of a hump, like a camel’s or that of an Indian humped ox, to
produce a sort of conical mitre. Suitably moistened and stretched on a
mould any piece of flat skin could be made this shape. Nevertheless a
study of the skins of camels, various cattle, including the yak and the
Indian humped ox, and of wild boars, convinced me that the skin of the
shoulder or back of these animals could not have been used to make the
Pangboche and Khumjung scalps. There is no need even to refer to the
texture of the hair (which rules out creatures like the camel and yak
which have characteristically woolly coats) in order to settle the ques-


tion. In fact no quadruped’s back can provide a skin from which these
scalps could be faked, for the hair-tracts are arranged in quite a different
way. It would be utterly impossible. On a quadruped’s back the hairs


all point towards the hindquarters, parallel to the median line in what is
technically called “the primitive cranio-caudal stream”: and even if
there happened to be a tiny spiral hair whorl, on the top of the shoulder

THE MAN-FACED ANIMALS OF SOUTH-EAST ASIA


for instance, this would not alter the general direction of the hairs. On
the other hand, the hairs on the alleged snowman scalps begin parallel


to the median line on what is thought to be the forehead, soon turn at
right angles to it and remain at an angle until the nape of the neck where
they return to their original parallel direction. Since these scalps have


crests of standing hairs it is obviously impossible that they could be
made of the skin of any part of an animal’s body except the skull, the
nape of the neck and the back.


As a comparison I examined the skin on the heads of several large
apes, and found that the pattern of hair-tracts was much nearer to that
of the Pangboche and Khumjung relics. In the orang-utan the hairs
spread out in all directions from that part of the back of the head known


as the great fontanelle, like the hair-style affected by some monks, many
Amazonian Indians, the ancient Romans and Marlon Brando (early
period). They spread out on the sides of the head, but point forward on
the top of the head; and in this they are different. In the gorilla on the
other hand the hairs on the head are arranged like those on the alleged
scalps, even above the eye-sockets and on the forehead.


Incidentally I must contradict Charles Stonor when he says that the


first scalp was “astonishingly thick,” the actual thickness being 4 inch;
for I measured that of several gorilla-skins and found that they were
always around 4 inch (between 3 and 4 mm.).


The Pangboche and Khumjung scalps therefore offer all the guarantee
of their authenticity that one could wish. The fact that the people of
Namche Bazar did not succeed in making a fake which would pass as
the real article, even with the aid of similar skin, provides an additional
guarantee. I challenge those who have said that these scalps are fakes to
concoct one out of the shoulder of some hooved animal or indeed from
the skin of any animal they choose. The result may well be an attractive
fur cap, but I am certain that not even the most shortsighted of experts
would ever mistake it for a relic of the snowman.


Ever since the Daily Mail expedition the yeti has been in the news.
In May 1955 the French expedition on Makalu (a 27,190-foot peak 13
miles south-east of Everest) came upon several tracks; one of them, on
the Barun Col, had been made that very morning or late on the previous
evening. The Abbé P. Bordet, the team’s geologist, who photographed
the imprints, produced indisputable evidence that the beast was a biped:
even where the yeti had jumped down into the snow from a small wall
of rock there “were no tracks of its forefeet.”’

I have followed a yeti track for more than a kilometre [he writes], and
seen nearly 3,000 footprints. They are all of the same kind. They are
deep marks made by a foot somewhat resembling a human foot. The


sole of the foot is roughly elliptical and rounded underneath. In front


of it are the more or less circular marks of four toes (not five), the first


on the inside is larger than the rest and perhaps not quite so far for-


ward, the other three lie on the front edge of the sole of the foot and


very close to it. These toes are much larger than human toes. There


are no marks of claws. ...In the best imprints there are still little


ridges of snow dividing the toe-marks and showing that the toes are


slightly separated when the creature walks. The length of the foot-


prints is about 20 centimetres. ...


The animal walks with its feet almost parallel and only slightly
splayed.
Its stride was about 20 inches, a little less than my own on
this slippery ground....


The second track that I saw was that of an animal coming down to a
lake, no doubt to drink there. The prints were in a perfectly straight
line and the stride was much longer, sometimes as much as three feet.


All the same all these tracks were those of a biped which even in
difficult conditions had no need to use its front legs.


Professors Berlioz and Arambourg of the Paris Natural History
Museum, whom the Abbé Bordet consulted, admitted ‘‘there is no
known animal which leaves such footprints, and none which is a true
biped as this is.”” But they refused to draw any conclusions as to what it
might be. “Whether it is a kind of bear or ape,” Bordet concludes, “‘it
seems too soon to decide, our information being what it is at present.”
This opinion shows considerable ignorance of the problem and the
work that has been done on it. As I pointed out in 1952, one need only
look at a track to see if the big toe is on the inside or the outside to decide
whether it was made by a primate or a bear. Since the Abbé Bordet tells


us that “‘the first on the inside is larger than the rest,” the yet: cannot
possibly be a bear, even if it is an unknown biped species. Bordet also
points out, apropos of the yeri’s identity, the odd fact that:


The Indian map of the Himalaya marks the area round Everest as
the Mahalangur Himal (the mountains of the great monkeys). As no
monkey is known to live there this name may refer to the yeti, a charac-
teristic inhabitant in the natives’ eyes.

Mountaineering Association expedition to the Himalaya, Wing-Com-

fresh yeti tracks 12,375 feet up in the Kulti valley. They summoned
