photographed the track and sent a signal about it to the Air Ministry.
The official communiqué gives some interesting details.


There were many prints, each measuring about 12 inches by 6
inches, and indicating that the creature who made them was two-
legged, with five toes a quarter of an inch wide on each foot.


The prints were sunk 11 inches into the snow, compared with the
one-inch impression made by the R.A.F. mountaineers.


This shows that the creature which made such deep tracks must have
been several times as heavy as a man. (A gorilla, by the way, rarely
exceeds 40 stone.)


Less reliable than the Air Ministry communiqué is the agency report
published in January 1956 to the effect that a snowman had been caught
in a trap, killed with arrows and eaten by Naga head-hunters on the
frontier between Assam and China. The creature was reported to be


10 feet high, white as milk and with human features. Although the
incident itself is not improbable, the description of the beast killed
seems so fantastic that one is tempted to write the whole thing off as a
hoax. But this may be unjust, for a story told to a regional army officer
and passed on to a group of Indian journalists travelling in the frontier
area, must have been much altered in transmission especially if first told
in a dialect very difficult to understand. The Naga Angami which the
Naga speak, as R. B. McCabe has pointed out, is “‘still in a very primi-


tive stage of the agglutinating class,” and ‘peculiarly rich in intonation,”
although “for one Naga who clearly marks these tonal distinctions
twenty fail to do so.” It is easy to see what misunderstandings might
arise in a translation from such a language.


Professor René von Nebesky-Wojkowitz, who spent three years of
ethnographic research in Tibet and Sikkim from 1950 to 1953, tells
several stories about the abominable snowman in his admirably docu-
mented book. They agree very well with those that Izzard and his com-
panions heard in Nepal. He draws the following conclusions from the
evidence that he had obtained by questioning many witnesses:


It is a remarkable fact that the statements of Tibetans, Sherpas and
Lepchas concerning the Snowman’s appearance
largely coincide.
According to their description a warrant for the arrest of this most
“wanted” of all the inhabitants of the Himalayas would read as follows:
7 feet to 7 feet 6 inches tall when erect on his hind legs. Powerful body
covered with dark brown hair. Long arms.
Oval head running to a
point at the top, with apelike face. Face and head are only sparsely

covered with hair. He fears the light of a fire, and in spite of his great
strength is regarded by the less superstitious inhabitants of the Hima-
layas as a harmless creature that would attack a man only if wounded.


To this description, which confirms in every detail what we know
already, he adds some more interesting information about the crea-


ture’s habitat:


From what native hunters say the term “snowman”? is a misnomer,
since firstly it is not human and secondly it does not live in the zone of


snow.
Its habitat is rather the impenetrable thickets of the highest


tracts of Himalayan forest. During the day it sleeps in its lair, which it


does not leave until nightfall. Then its approach may be recognized by


the cracking of branches and its peculiar whistling call. In the forest


the migo moves on all fours or by swinging from tree to tree. But in the
open country it generally walks upright with an unsteady, rolling gait.
Why does the creature undertake what must certainly be extremely
wearisome expeditions into the inhospitable regions of snow? The


natives have what sounds a very credible explanation:
they say the
Snowman likes a saline moss which it finds on the rocks of the moraine


fields. While searching for this moss it leaves its characteristic tracks


on the snowfields. When it has satisfied its hunger for salt it returns to


the forest.


This suggests that—as I suspected—the snowman owes the accidental


fact that it is a biped to snow beneath its feet, and also that the places
where the creature and its footprints are usually seen are not its normal
habitat. If its desire for saline food is not the only cause that drives the
snowman to venture into open country, where it is more likely to be
seen, it is a strong enough reason to explain such journeys: moreover
they are strangely reminiscent of the long pilgrimages that elephants
sometimes make in search of saline soil.


In the spring of 1957 an American expedition led by a Texas oilman
called Tom Slick also searched for the snowman in eastern Nepal. Dur-
ing three months wandering among the Himalayan foothills the leader


collected much new data about the elusive animal. Not only did he


examine three sets of footprints, excrements and even hairs that had


come from yetis, but he also questioned some 15 Nepalese who


claimed to have seen the animal. From all this information he inferred


that the snowman must be a large ape like a gorilla or an orang-utan. It


had a pointed head and walked upright like a man. It was strong enough


to kill a yak with its bare hands, though it does not seem to eat these


animals. On the other hand when it happens to kill a man it eats his


175


THE MAN-FACED ANIMALS OF SOUTH-EAST ASIA


eyeballs, fingers and “other parts,” but has no special taste for human


flesh. Small rodents and bamboo shoots are its chief food.


Tom Slick’s most important contribution to the problem is, I think,
his belief that there are two kinds of yeris: one with blackish hair and
about 8 feet high, and the other reddish and smaller. This conclusion is
based on differences in the accounts he heard from the natives, on find-
ing two kinds of hair along the tracks and examining two kinds of foot-
prints. The largest, like those photographed by Shipton, were as much


as 13 inches long; the smaller are more like a medium-sized man’s.


This would explain the discrepancies that the reader cannot fail to
have noticed in this chapter. While some witnesses say the snowman is
a giant, all the Sherpas who have seen it say that it is smaller than a man


or about the same size. It is significant that all the reports which say
the yeti is a giant (Marqués-Riviére’s pilgrim, the lama Chemed Rigdzin
Dorje, Slavomir Rawicz and Professor von Nebesky-Wojkowitz’s
witnesses) come either from Tibet or from the very north of Sikkim


or Nepal, that is from very high places on the edge of these countries.
I should also mention that a teacher at Namche Bazar told Ralph Izzard


that there were two kinds of yetis. Since this man, who had recently


arrived from Darjeeling, was, according to Izzard, not “the most know-
ledgeable authority,” the reporter did not take his remarks very seriously
when ‘‘The larger lived ‘there,’ he said, pointing vaguely in the direction
of Mount Everest, and the smaller ‘there,’ waving equally vaguely in the
direction of the lower Dudh Kosi valley.”


This opinion was confirmed in 1957 by a Tibetan lama called Punya-
bayra, high priest of the monastery at Budnath, who spent four months
in the high mountains and brought back the surprising but valuable
information that the Tibetan mountain people knew three kinds of
snowmen: the nyalmo, the rimi and the rackshi bompo. The nyalmo are


real giants, between 13 and 16 feet high, with enormous conical heads.
They wander in parties among the eternal snows above 13,000 feet. In
such empty country it is hardly surprising that they should be carni-
vorous and even man-eating. The rimi are smaller, but still between
7 and 9 feet high. They live lower down between 10,000 and 13,000


feet, feeding on plants as well, and are thus omnivorous. Their favourite
place is the Barun Khola valley in eastern Nepal. The rackshi bompo are
about the size of a man.


What are we to make of these distinctions? Some may say that they
are the absurd supersitions one might expect a Tibetan lama to spread.
But we should not forget that he is an educated man with the rare


176


THE NOT SO ABOMINABLE SNOWMAN


privilege of questioning mountain people in the remotest parts of the
Himalaya in their own language. Punyabayra also offered to capture a
specimen of each kind of yeri if the Katmandu Government would help
him. This is evidence of his sincerity. Moreover his account agrees in


part at least with what we already know. The rackshi bompo must be the
Sherpas’ reddish yeh-teh or mi-teh which leaves the footprints 8 or 9
inches long that the Daily Mail expedition and the Abbé Bordet found


in such quantity. The rimi must be the large black snowman described


by Nebesky-Wojkowitz’s Tibetan and Sikkimese informants, and the


one whose mummified bodies Chemed Rigdzin Dorje saw in Tibet, and


which leaves footprints 12 to 13 inches long. It was in fact in the Barun


area or in eastern Nepal that Shipton and Slick found footprints of this


size. The nyalmo remind one of Marqués-Riviére’s pilgrim’s sad-faced


giants. Do they really exist, or are they just a myth? It is true that


J. R. O. Gent spoke of footprints 18 inches to 2 feet long, which logically


could only have been made by yetis even larger than the rim. But here


the evidence is far too slender for us to draw any satisfactory conclusions.


Possibly the myalmo are an invented addition based on the belief that


yetis increase in size the higher you go.


Meanwhile we can say that the existence of two kinds of yetis of dif-
ferent size and colour is well-established. No doubt they are different
geographic races of the same species. But it is also possible that they
may be merely the result of sexual dimorphism. Old male gorillas grow


so large that they can travel only on the ground, while the females still
climb trees. Thus the male yeti—stronger, more heavily built and con-
sequently better able to stand cold—might be the only one that could
venture into the higher parts of the mountains to hunt. Nor is it im-
possible that the small reddish yetis may be the young of the large black


ones.
In gibbons the colour may change completely with age, from
white with hardly a touch of grey at puberty to the deepest of blacks.
Here again the yetis may go up to greater heights as they become
tougher and stronger with age.


We can now even give a detailed description of the giant biped
anthropoid of the Himalaya, a shy survivor of the empire of giant
primates which once ruled a large part of the earth.


Only four giant ape-men are so far known to palaeontology: the
Chinese Gigantopithecus, of which we have only a few molars and a jaw-
bone more recently discovered in 1957, the Java Meganthropus, re-
presented by a fragment of jaw-bone with its teeth, the Tanganyika


M
177


THE MAN-FACED ANIMALS OF SOUTH-EAST ASIA


Meganthropus, consisting only of jaw and facial bones, and the South
African Paranthropus, of which several skulls and a biped’s pelvis have
been excavated. If I seek to relate the snowman to the Gigantopithecus


it is obviously for geographical reasons and because most reports of its
size agree with Dr Broom’s estimate of that of the Chinese giant.


It is high time that the snowman was also recognised by a scientific
name and since the palaeontology of giant primates is so slender, I
would give it a new name, Dinanthropoides nivalis,' or “terrible anthro-
poid of the snows.” If one day its teeth are examined and found to be
identical with those of the Gigantopithecus, its name will have to be
changed, according to the rule of priority, to Gigantopithecus nivalis, the
present species being no doubt quite distinct from the Pleistocene pri-
mate from Kwangsi. The layman may be surprised that one should give
an animal a scientific name on the mere evidence of some footprints and
a description of a scalp. In fact this procedure is not only universal in
palaeontology, but happens fairly often in zoology. The giant panda
and the wolf of the Andes were described merely from skins, the takahe
was first known only from a skeleton, the first description of the pygmy
hippopotamus was based ona
skull. And the first (mistaken) name given


to the okapi was based on shapeless strips of its skin which were taken
for those of some kind of zebra. Naturally the name Dinanthropoides


risks a similar mistake—firmly though I am convinced to the contrary
—but zoology cannot go on ignoring an animal which we know far more
about than many fossil species.


We have reason to believe that it is a large biped anthropoid ape, from
5 to 8 feet high according to its age, sex or geographic race, which lives
in the rocky area at the limit of the plant line on the slopes of the whole
Himalayan range. It has plantigrade feet, and the very conspicuous big


toe, unlike that of most monkeys, is not opposable to the other toes. It
walks with its body leaning slightly forward; its arms are fairly long and
reach down to its knees. It has a flat face, a high forehead, and the top
of its skull is shaped like the nose of a shell; its prognathism is slight,
but its thick jaws have developed considerably in height, hence the
disproportionate size of its molars. To this outsize masticatory appara-


tus are connected very powerful jaw-muscles. On the cranium there is
a sagittal crest which is revealed by a thickening of the scalp in the adult
male, at least, and the presence of upstanding hair. It is covered with

thick fur, which in the smaller specimens varies from fawn to dark
chestnut in different places with foxy-red glints, but the face, chest and
the lower legs are much less hairy. In the larger specimens the fur is an
even dark brown or almost black. It appears to be omnivorous: roots,
bamboo shoots, fruit, insects, lizards, birds, small rodents and occasion-


ally larger prey like yaks are all grist to its mill in such barren country.


Its cerebral capacity should be about equal or even greater than man’s.


But the development of the brain must have been affected by the strange


shape of the skull giving rise to mental qualities very different from those


in which man excels.


The position of this Dinanthropoid in the system of zoology is still
uncertain, as is that of the other giant primates, which to my mind do
not form a homogeneous group, but are the separate peaks of the evolu-
tion of different families of primates: the Paranthropus is the last stage
in the evolution of the Australopitheci into giants, the Meganthropus is


a giant Pithecanthropus. Just as the Pithecanthropus may be merely a
large biped descended from the gibbons, so the Dinanthropoid may
have evolved similarly, but on a parallel branch, from the orang-utan.
Gates and Remane consider that the Gigantopithecus is a giant of the
Ponginia, the family to which the orang-utan belongs.


Of course it is not until an actual specimen of the snowman is ex-
amined that my deductions can be checked and its provisional descrip-
tion completed. The Daily Mail expedition, alas, was unable to provide
one, although four columns of men carried out pincer movements over


a vast area, and Tom Slick had no better luck. The chances of success
seem to be seriously compromised for the future. Slick had no sooner
announced his intention of returning to the Himalaya in the autumn of
1958 and Punyabayra had also offered to capture a yeti when the Govern-
ment of Nepal announced that it required a fee of 5,000 rupees from
anyone wishing to look for the yeri. It strictly forbade anyone to kill


one except in self-defence.
The Nepalese were not allowed to give


information to strangers without permission from the Government,


which claimed a right in the creature, dead or alive, and even in any


photographs that might be taken.


This decree has not discouraged the enterprising. Now, in the spring
of 1958, no less than four expeditions, two American, one Scottish and
one Russian, are looking for the yeti, which has recently become news
in Russia.


Marxist diehards have often maintained that the snowman was a pure
invention, a pretext to enable Western expeditions to spy on the frontiers

of Nepal and Tibet. But in January 1958 a Soviet scientist, Dr Alex-
ander G. Pronin, announced that he had seen a galub-yavanna (or snow-
man) the previous August in the Baliand-Kiik valley in the Pamirs, thus
extending the animal’s area of distribution enormously. Dr Pronin, a
senior scientist of the Geographic Scientific Institute of Leningrad
University, was in the Pamirs leading the hydrological section of the
International Geophysical Year joint expedition of the Uzbek Academy
of Science and Leningrad University. It was on 10 August that he first
saw the snowman outlined against the top of a 1,500-foot cliff.


At first [he told Komsomolskaya Pravda] I thought it was a bear, but,
having collected myself, it became clear that this was no bear but a man-
like creature. It walked out of its cave for a distance of some 200 yards
and then disappeared beyond the edge of the cliff.


He had observed the creature for some five to eight minutes, and
three days later he saw it again at the same spot. He described it as “a
man-like creature walking on two feet in a slightly stooping manner and
wearing no clothes. Its thick-set body was covered with reddish-grey


hair, and it had long arms.”


Dr Pronin’s report was much criticised. Some asked why he had
waited so long before publishing his discovery. The meteorologists at
Glacier Fedchenko 2, in the area in question, were even more severe.
They had never seen any snowmen and said ““We do not believe Pronin’s
statement, and we think that a true scientist would not publish a dis-
covery until it had been verified several times.” Nevertheless they in-
tended to go and look for this non-existent beast at the earliest oppor-
tunity. Many first-rate Soviet scientists, the late zoologist P. Sushkin,
Professor N. Sirotinin of the Ukrainian Academy of Science, Professor
S. Obruchev of the U.S.S.R. Academy of Science and the greatest of


their zoologists, E. N. Pavlovsky, had, however, all come out on the side
of the snowman’s existence.


Soon after Dr Pronin’s announcement a Chinese ciné-cameraman
confirmed that there were snowmen in the Pamirs. In 1954 when he
was filming three colleagues on Mount Muztahl-Ata, 20,000 feet up, he
saw two of these creatures one morning. They were not very tall and
stooped slightly as they followed one another about half a mile ahead of
him.


Actually it is not absolutely necessary to examine a living yeti—nor


to kill a specimen, which would be needlessly cruel—to clear up the

In May 1957 the Katmandu Commoner revealed that a snowman’s

attacked in the middle of the night by a yeti which killed 31 of them.
The sole survivor gave the alarm and a patrol of 10 men armed to the
teeth were sent off to the place. They found the monster there, sleeping
off its meal after eating several of its victims. Ten guns were fired at it


at once, but a second salvo was needed to polish it off. The leader of the
patrol still kept the beast’s head as a trophy.


If an informed zoologist could examine a hand, or better still a skull,
he would be able to obtain most valuable information. Even so the
diehard sceptics would still suspect that these specimens were in a fossil


or sub-fossil state. General incredulity will not be overcome until we
can see a good photograph or film of a living yett.


The expedition which may one day bring back these trophies will be
able to benefit from the lessons of the Daily Mail team, who never suc-
ceeded in overtaking a yeti although their trails abounded. Each time
they lost track of the strange ape-man, which could move faster over a
terrain to which it was better suited and was no doubt more accustomed


to the lack of oxygen at those heights, while its pursuers had to stop for


breath more and more often. And, as Izzard remarked, “‘a party is as

The Surrealist Dinosaur of

Alice laughed. ‘““There’s no use trying,” she said:

LEwIs CARROLL, Through the Looking-Glass.


FEw newly married couples can boast of having met a dinosaur on their
honeymoons. Mr Charles Miller and his socialite bride decided to spend
theirs among the cannibals of New Guinea. Mummified heads and
braised babies eaten by expectant mothers were minor attractions of
this resort, compared with their encounter with a prehistoric monster
from the Mesozoic era. When they and their bodyguard of Javanese
head-hunters had climbed up the River Merauke and reached the
Sterren mountains, they discovered an unknown tribe, the Kirrirri,
between the virgin forest and the snowline. One day Mrs Leona Miller
saw a woman in the Kirrirri village breaking a coconut with a strange


tool which looked like a rhinoceros-horn or the end of an elephant’s
tusk. She was intrigued and told her husband, who found that there
were quite a few such tools in the village.


The tusks, if that is what they were, were composed of a substance
resembling horn, applied in cone-shaped layers like a nest of conical
paper drinking cups, gradually diminishing in size until the top one
came to a sharp point. The tusks were about eighteen inches in length
and about six inches through at the base. There was a small, cone-
shaped hollow in the bottom, but even so they must have weighed
about twenty pounds apiece.


When he asked Wroo, one of the village worthies, where these tusks
came from, he drew a sort of lizard in the sand. ‘‘It had a large neck, a
huge bulging, hump-backed body terminating in a long tail. At the end
of the tail, Wroo indicated, the horn fitted like a cap.” Thinking he had
misunderstood, Miller made him draw the picture again. This time the


185


THE LIVING FOSSILS OF OCEANIA


animal was more carefully depicted: its head was adorned with a broad
collar, and large triangular scales bristled on its spine. “Just as shown
on reconstructions of dinosaurs in the museum back home,” Miller
remarks. To show the length of the beast, Wroo made two marks in the
dust with his toe 30 feet apart. He stood back and considered the dis-
tance he had marked out. Then he added another 10 feet. So, according


to him, the animal was about 40 feet long.


Miller’s laughter having met only looks of stern reproof, he asked
where these monsters lived. Two or three days’ journey away, towards
the hills in the north-west, they replied by signs. The explorer, who
was also a camera-man and hoped for a sensational story, managed to
persuade several Kirrirri to lead him to the giant lizard’s lair. This was
not easy, for the natives were very afraid of these creatures, which they
called row in imitation of their cry, a cross between a roar and a snake’s


hiss. The expedition was fixed for the next day.


The first night, after having climbed all day up fairly steep slopes,
they reached an immense grassy plateau where they camped with their
native guides. At dawn they set off westwards along the edge of this


' plateau which became steeper and steeper until it was a cliff that fell
some 50 feet. When they reached the western end of the plateau, their
guides headed north; they seemed nervous and went more carefully.
At last they reached their goal and urged the explorers to lie flat in the
grass before looking over the edge of the cliff. Muller was surprised to


see a vast triangular marsh covering some 40 acres. It was wedged be-
tween the plateau that he was on, another similar one opposite, and the


side of the mountains, from which a small stream ran down into the
marsh. But he soon stopped admiring the view, for suddenly the reeds
began to move.


Miller was paralysed with terror at what he saw. When his wife
joined him, she saw in her turn and fell to the ground. Miller thought
she had fainted, but she was merely so terrified that she clutched at the


grass and dared not raise her head. Slowly Miller lifted his camera and
aimed it at the beast whose long neck rose among the reeds.


As if in obedience to my wishes, the colossal remnant of the age of
dinosaurs stalked across the swamp.
Once its tail lashed out of the
grass so far behind its head I thought it must be another beast. For one
brief second I saw the horny point. I heard it hiss—Roooow—Roooow—
Rooow.


When he started the camera running the row seemed to hear it whirr-

for it suddenly stopped, reared up on its hind legs, its small forelegs

Just then Miller was annoyed to realise that the monster was a fairly

Twice more the row reared up, giving me a good view of the bony

Then with a click my camera ran out just as the row slithered behind a
growth of dwarf eucalyptus.


What are we to make of this strange tale, more like a passage from
Conan Doyle’s Lost World than an incident in a travel book that pre-
tends to be true?


I must confess that I have quoted it here in such detail merely in
order to give a typical example of the sort of evidence that cannot pos-
sibly be accepted. I am not saying that “Cannibal” Miller, as he likes


to call himself, is an arrant liar, but he offers not the slightest guarantee
of his veracity.


There are many reasons for rejecting Mr Miller’s story. It is worth
stating them here to show what credit can be given to the other accounts
I have cited, which have all withstood a no less severe criticism.


What has happened to the horn from the end of the row’s tail? Did
Mr Miller bring it back (for the Kirrirri were supposed to have several
specimens) so that it could be examined by a palaeontologist? Not that
I have heard of—and it would have made some noise in the scientific


world. Although his book is lavishly illustrated, there is no picture of


this hunter’s trophy from a vanished age.


What happened to the film that Mr Miller brought back from Papua?
His book was published in London in 1950, and in it he more than once
describes showing parts of his film to British film magnates. But not a
word about what they thought of the dinosaur sequence. And even if
the creature merged into the background, since it was a quarter of a mile
away, and only looked like a lizard of indeterminate size moving through


grass, the scene would have been worth showing. Any zoologist would
have been able to draw valuable conclusions from enlargements of the


film.

Supposing the film had been completely spoilt and Mr Miller failed

be waived for a reputable zoologist or naturalist, but not for Mr Miller,

his row does not even resemble “the reconstructions of dinosaurs in the
museums back home.” It is an odd jumble of features from well-known
but very different animals. It has the long neck and interminable tail of
the huge Sauropoda (Brontosaurus and the other Diplodoci), the head
(without the horns) and the bony collar of Triceratops, and the body,
with its crest of triangular scales along the spine, of Stegosaurus
(except that this creature has a double row of scales). None of these
creatures has a horn on the end of its tail, though Stegosaurus has a
double row of them along the tail continuing the crest along its spine.


It is not a dinosaur. The row looks more as if some surrealists had
produced what they called an “exquisite corpse,” by playing their own
highbrow version of “‘heads, bodies and legs” with extinct animals. It
would be rash to assert that such an animal is impossible—zoology and
palaeontology are full of surprises—but the dinosaurs from which the
row has collected its features belong to two distinct and very different
groups: the Sauripelvians as far as the long neck and tail are concerned,


all the other details come from the Avipelvians. Moreover the Stego-
saurians are known only in the Cretaceous period in North America,
and it would be rather surprising to find that they had reached the south-
eastern tip of Asia, which seems never to have been joined to the North
American Continent.
It is also most unlikely that New Guinea was
ever invaded by large Sauropoda with long necks and tails.


Indeed, until there is proof to the contrary, the row looks damnably


like an ill-digested memory of a bad Science Fiction film made by a
producer ignorant of zoogeography.


No doubt, you may argue, New Guinea is so little explored that any-
thing is possible there. In fact it is just because this island, as big as
France and Italy together, is so little known that one must be particu-


larly cautious of accepting any unproved reports about it. For in this
paradise of head-hunters and cannibals there is hardly any chance of
other witnesses confirming a report made by a lone explorer. And so it


will remain until there are more expeditions to Papua and the settlers
establish peaceful relations with the natives in the very heart of the
largest of tropical islands.

So runs the Aborigines’ myth; and according to the

rainbow—which phenomenon, by the way, must be extremely rare in

coastal strip in the north-east. The aborigines who mostly live in the
dry interior could never have seen a diamond python or a rainbow
themselves. One can see how imaginary versions based on hearsay or
distorted by tradition could combine the two into a fantastic creature.

It is much easier to interpret the old Australian legend of thaballa,

with a flat round face and enormous round eyes. It lives in trees, where


it sometimes stands up on its hind-legs when it is threatened.
Its out-

After the American troops conquered the islands in 1898, guerilla

jungle; he wandered for hours and hours until he was utterly exhausted
and lay on the ground and slept. He awoke into a nightmare. A wood-

The tarsier certainly has more striking eyes than any other creature on
earth, and in the dark its enormous eyeballs shine with a bright yellow


light. It is easy to imagine the soldier waking among strange and sinister
noises to see one of these grinning little gnomes, that had come, full of
curiosity like the other primates, to have a look at the sleeping man.
Perhaps it even jumped on his throat. Dazed and bleary-eyed and per-
haps suffering from jungle fever, which oddly distorts one’s sense of
distance, he must have thought he was looking at a demon from Hell, a
demon that could vanish in a single bound.


Most people are bewildered, if not alarmed, the first time they see a


tarsier, for it really does look like a sprite. It is not surprising that the
naturalists called it “spectral” and that many people still believe it is a real
ghost. The only reason why it has not been identified with the yara-ma-
yha-who is that it is found only in the Malay archipelago: in Sumatra,
Borneo, the Celebes and some of the Philippines—never in Australia.

Tarsioids, of which the tarsier is the only remaining survivor, were
once very widespread. In the Eocene period at the beginning of the
Tertiary era these strange mannikins were found in the whole of North
America and in Europe. But, apart from species imported by man—the
dingo and the rats—and several bats which could have flown across the


sea, there are no wild mammals in Australia with placentas.


125 million years ago, in the middle of the Cretaceous period, the
marsupial mammals ruled the earth and were found over most of it.
Presumably Australia was then connected to the other continents and
accessible to land animals. At the very end of the Mesozoic era or at the
beginning of the Tertiary, Australia and New Guinea, still joined, were
cut off from the rest of the world. When the placentary mammals over-
ran the earth in their turn they had to stop short at the Wallace Line,
that invisible zoological frontier which runs between Bali and Lombok
and between Borneo and the Celebes. They could not reach New
Guinea or Australia, where the marsupials were able to develop in
peace until the arrival of man.


Thus it is unlikely, if not impossible, that there have ever been tar-


siers in Australia.
Small mammals might be carried across a narrow


strait of sea on a floating tree-trunk, and the tarsiers have in fact crossed
the Wallace Line and are found east of it in the Celebes. But that they
should have stowed away and made the perilous voyage, drifting across
the Timor Sea or through the Moluccas and the Banda Sea, is too


fantastic. They did not have a Kon-Tiki raft.


If there can never have been tarsiers in Australia, the legend of the
yara-ma-yha-who may throw some glimmer of light on the history of
the Australian people. John Mathew has suggested that men of Malay
race have infiltrated northern Australia at a relatively recent date. This
theory has been rejected, for it is in the north that the Aborigines are
particularly black and fuzzy-haired, and an invasion of Malays with fair


skin and straight hair would have diluted these features. But is it likely


that legends about tarsiers should have been handed down since the


Pre-Dravidian tribes came to Australia from the Celebes, Borneo or


Sumatra, an event usually put in the middle Pleistocene, at least 50,000


years ago? Most authors maintain that this invasion took place in a

series of waves as the Aborigines were driven out by the Malays. The

These creatures of aboriginal legend may seem strange, but it was

well-founded. So we should be less sceptical about those which are still
unexplained.


When, at the beginning of the seventeenth century, the brave seamen
sent out by the Dutch East India Company set about exploring the
eastern seas for spice islands, they several times set foot on what seemed


to be a very vast new land, which they loyally named New Holland.
There they said there lived an animal as large as a man, with head like


a deer and a long tail. It stood on its hind-legs like a bird and could hop


like a frog. In 1640 Captain Pelsart gave an accurate description of


it, only to be greeted with derision at the tall stories told by seamen.
In 1770 Captain James Cook landed in Trinity: Bay to repair the
Endeavour, which had been damaged on the Great Barrier Reef. On 9
July Sir Joseph Banks, the famous naturalist and patron of the sciences,
went off with one companion to look for game to replenish their rations.
In Cook’s words:


Going in pursuit of game, we saw four animals, two of which were
chased by Mr. Banks’s greyhound, but they greatly outstripped him in
speed, by leaping over the long thick grass, which incommoded the dog
in running. It was observed of the animals that they bounded forward
on two legs instead of running on four.


Later Cook learnt that this sort of giant jerboa was called kangaroo.1
His evidence had to be believed. But the world was in no hurry to do so.


It was twenty years before Dr George Shaw gave the kangaroo its Latin
name. Cook had overlooked its strangest feature: the pouch on the
female’s belly in which she carries her young. Marsupial pouches were
not new to zoologists. It had long been known that the opossum had a

In 1901, Dr W. E. Roth, in charge of native affairs in

similar pouch (though, as it was a quadruped, the opening was at the

they were so convinced that it was peculiar to the opossum that when
Seba described an “eastern philander” or cuscus, a pouched animal


that had been sent him from Amboina, Buffon thought that there had

Soon it was found that all the indigenous Australian mammals had
pouches. What was the rarest exception elsewhere was the rule here.
More surprises were to follow. In 1797 a settler in New South Wales
found an animal which he called an “aquatic mole.” Actually it was


more like an otter, but it had a duck’s webbed feet and, what was even


more extraordinary, a duck’s beak. When the first skin arrived in Lon-


don and was examined by the Zoological Society it was almost unani-


mously thought to be a fake, like the confected mummies that travellers


brought back from China. Nevertheless Dr George Shaw examined the


skin minutely and found no trace of glue or stitches. He announced that


the skin was genuine and in 1799 published the first scientific descrip-


tion calling it Platypus anatinus, or “‘the flat-footed animal with a duck’s


beak.” The skin was sent to the German zoologist, Blumenbach, then


considered the greatest authority on classification. He described the


animal in 1801 and gave it the name Ornithorhynchus paradoxus “the


paradoxical animal with a bird’s beak.” The name Platypus had to be


discarded, having been used in 1793 for a small beetle, and Ornithorhyn-


chus it has remained to this day.


It was one thing to give the strange animal a name, it was quite an-
other to classify it in the system of zoology. As it was covered with hair,
Shaw had no doubt that it was a mammal. But in which order did it
belong? Blumenbach put it in the Edentates, that rag-bag of unclassifi-
able mammals. Then in 1802 two more specimens, this time preserved
in alcohol, arrived in England. One of them was a female, and the zoo-


logists were astounded to find that this presumed mammal (or “animal
with teats”) hadn’t any teats at all! Moreover neither of them had a


separate anus and genital duct like the rest of the mammals, but a single


cloaca like the reptiles and birds. Yet they could not belong to either of


these classes since they were covered with fur, not scales or feathers. The


anatomist Everard Home therefore proposed to create a separate order


to include this duck-billed animal with another creature with a cloaca


which had been discovered in Australia in the meantime: the echidna,
a sort of porcupine whose long snout also looked like a beak. This was
done a year later when Etienne Geoffroy-Saint-Hilaire created the new


199


THE LIVING FOSSILS OF OCEANIA


order of monotremes or “animals with a single hole.” But he prudently
refrained from stating which class this order belonged to. Lamarck
more boldly wanted to create a completely new class, the Prototherians
or “first mammals.” For one could hardly include an animal without
teats among the true mammals, and a creature covered with fur could
not be a reptile.


Then news arrived from Australia that the platypus laid eggs, or so
Sir John Jamison wrote on 17 March 1817. This brought it even closer


to the birds and reptiles; it certainly could not be a true mammal. But
in 1824 the German scientist Meckel, examining the animal more care-


fully, found that it had mammary glands. They had not been noticed
before because they were very small except in the breeding season.


Impossible! argued Etienne Geoffroy-Saint-Hilaire and his son
Isidore, supported by Blumenbach. If the Monotremes lay eggs—and
they do lay eggs—they cannot have mammary glands. The glandular
formations must be musk-glands.


No, replied Meckel, they are true mammary glands. The mono-
tremes are true mammals and they are therefore certainly viviparous.
The legend that the platypus lays eggs is absurd.


And such eminent scientists as Cuvier, Oken and Blainville agreed
with him. There were others, like Richard Owen and Home, who subtly


sat on the fence and averred that perhaps they had mammary glands
and perhaps they did not, but as they seemed to belong both to the vivi-
parous mammals and the generally oviparous reptiles, they must be
ovo-viviparous—that is to say, they formed eggs which hatched inside
the body and so the young were born alive.


In 1829 Robert B. Grant claimed he had found four platypus eggs and
sent a very careful drawing of them to Europe. The triumph of the
Saint-Hilaire clan was short-lived when experts identified the eggs as
those of an Australian long-necked tortoise (Chelodina longicollis).


In 1832 Meckel, Cuvier and Co.’s victory seemed complete when an
Australian naturalist, Lieutenant Maule, established without a shadow
of a doubt that the glands on the platypus’s belly actually produced


milk. There was a small fly in the ointment, however: Maule had found
eggshells in the platypus’s burrow. But these eggs could have—indeed
they must have—come from some other animal.


Some thirty years later, on 21 September 1864, Dr Nicholson sent a
letter to Professor Owen in which he told how a platypus that a workman
had caught and put in a gin-crate laid two eggs during its first night in
captivity. The Professor was not convinced. He had stated once and

when on the same day in 1884 two naturalists—Dr W. H. Caldwell, who

Everybody had been wrong.
I have related the platypus’s history at such length in order to show
that an animal which all the scientists think impossible may actually


exist. The bunyip is not half so impossible as the platypus.


What is a bunyip? Not an easy question to answer. Nowadays the
Australians use it to mean a “bogey,” something at once frightening,
shadowy, imaginary and rather ludicrous. But to some men it is a flesh-
and-blood animal with a clearly-defined appearance and habits. Origin-
ally it was a native word meaning “devil,” “angel” or perhaps even
“sod”; for the totemistic religion of the Australian aborigines is so
different from our own that exact translation is impossible. It might,


I believe, derive from the word bunyil (or pundjel) which the Vic-


torian aborigines use to signify their Supreme Being. At all events it

The first report that Gilbert Whitley of the Australian Museum in-
cludes in his dossier of the bunyip comes from the French explorers in
the crew of the Géographe. In June 1801 Charles Bailly and his com-
panions made their way into the interior, having named a bay on the
southern tip of the west coast after their vessel. Suddenly they heard a


terrible roar, louder than a bull’s bellow, which seemed to come from
the reeds in the Swan River. They were terrified and took to their
heels, convinced that it was some great water-beast.
Later the ex-
plorer Hamilton Hume confirmed the existence of some such monster,
but at the other end of the continent. He said that in Lake Bathurst he
had seen an animal, which from his description must have been some


sort of manatee or hippopotamus. Five scientists of the Philosophical
Society of Australasia at once promised to pay all his expenses if he
managed to procure a skull, a skin or a skeleton of his unknown animal.
Hume never found one, but he had not invented the story, for many
similar tales at once began to come in from various places in Australia,
especially in the south-east. Thus Lieutenant W. H. Breton wrote of
Lake George, “‘It is pretended that a species of seal, or, as it was called,


a devil, has been seen in it.”


By the middle of the nineteenth century the legend of the bunyip was
well established. Everyone began to be interested in the beast, which
was soon saddled with anything mysterious that happened. In 1846 a
fragment of a skull was found on the banks of the Murrumbidgee, a
tributary of the Murray River.
It was sent to the naturalist W. S.
Macleay as the skull of a “true bunyip.” He identified it as the deformed


skull of a colt. But when Professor Richard Owen saw a drawing of it in
London he immediately decided that it was a calf’s. One of the experts
must be wrong. So the problem was not so puerile as they seemed to
imply. Quite possibly they were both wrong. We shall never know;
the specimen was deposited in the Australian Museum, but, as one
might expect of a bunyip, it has mysteriously disappeared.


In 1847 Governor Latrobe managed to get hold of copies of native
drawings of two kinds of bunyips from Victoria. He sent them to Tas-
mania, but, alas, they too seem to have vanished.


In 1848 one turned up in the Eumeralla River near Port Fairy in


Victoria. Those who had seen it said that it was a large brown animal

THE INCREDIBLE AUSTRALIAN BUNYIPS


with a head like a kangaroo. It had a long neck with a hairy mane, and


its mouth was enormous. When questioned about it, the natives said


that it had the strange power of drawing its victims irresistibly towards it


across the water.


In 1872 a strange and possibly similar animal was said to have been
seen in Lake Corangamite, Victoria. It came so close to a boat that the


terrified people on board dashed to the opposite gunwale and capsized
the vessel. It was said to be an “animal like a big retriever dog, with a
round head and hardly any ears.” Many people had also seen one in
Lake Burrumbeet near Ballarat.


The wee-waa which was seen more than once at this time and then
again a year later in a lagoon near Narrandera was also compared to a
retriever by those who saw it; but it was only half the size, and its body
was covered with long black hair, shining and as black as jet. It can
hardly have been a very fearsome apparition. In 1873, also, a creature
with a seal’s head was supposed to have been seen rising out of the water
near Dalby in Queensland. It had a-double but asymmetrical caudal


fin. In 1876 a hairy animal of unusual appearance turned up in Crystal
Brook in South Australia. A price was put on its head, but to no


effect. And reports went on coming in—from the Malmsbury reservoir,
Wagga Wagga, and many other places in Victoria and New South Wales
—and becoming more detailed. Most of them sounded like distorted
descriptions of a seal or a dugong.


But not all were as sober as those I have just quoted. The Rev. George
Toplin described the moolgewanke, or bunyip of Lake Alexandrina, as a
weird creature, half-man, half-fish, with hair like a sort of wig of reeds.
Unlike the sweet-voiced mermaids, this merman had a voice like the
rumble of a distant cannon; and unlike them it did not lure you to
destruction—it merely gave you rheumatism.


The tunatpan of the Port Phillip area was even more picturesque and


recalled the Eumeralla bunyip.


It was as big as a bullock, with an emu’s head and neck, a horse’s
mane and tail, and seal’s flippers, which laid turtle’s eggs in a platypus’
nest, and ate blackfellows when it was tired of a crayfish diet.


In 1886, horsemen fording the River Molonglo saw a creature,
“whitish in colour and about the size of a large dog. Its face was like
the face of a child.” All the same they had no qualms about throwing
stones at it and driving it away. The bunyip of the Tuckerbil swamp
near Leeton which was reported until the summer of 1929-30 takes
one into the realm of the marvellous.
It was described as “a two-

It was hardly surprising that it escaped its pursuers! But other reports
must have had more of a ring of truth, for in 1890.a team from the Mel-

Similar water-monsters have several times been reported in Tas-
manian lakes, outside the Australian continent. In the autumn of 1852
one of these big devils was seen in Lake Tiberias. It was between 4 feet
and 4 feet 6 inches long, had a bulldog’s head, and was covered with


_ shaggy black hair. It was seen at first in shallow water, giving a glimpse
of its crooked feet, but quickly disappeared into deeper water. No
doubt they were similar animals which were often seen in the Great
Lake. The length was always between 3 and 4 feet and the head was
round like a bulldog’s. Often they splashed water 6 to 10 feet into the


air. Between 1860 and 1870 there was no lack of reports about them in
the same terms. In 1863 someone was able to observe one for some
time and described it as a sort of sheepdog with two little fins, like small
wings. It moved at the considerable speed of about 30 miles per hour.
The dam at Waddamana and all the vicissitudes which the Great Lake
suffered for the Tasmanian hydro-electric schemes did not drive the
bunyips away, for they reappeared several times in 1932.


‘Apart from the most extravagant fabrications,” Whitley concludes


after reviewing the most consistent rumours, “‘we must be struck with
the comparative uniformity of bunyip description over a long period.”
Generally it is a large furry animal, the size of a dog and with a dog’s
head, but with very small or even invisible ears. It swims with fins and


lives in rivers, marshes and inland lakes.


This description reminds one irresistibly of a seal or a sea-lion; and
there are several genera of these animals in Australia and Tasmania:


seals (Hydrurga, Lobodon and Leptonychotes), sea-lions (Arctocephalus
and Zalophus) and even the great sea-elephant (Mirounga). But could
these sea animals reach inland waters? There is no reason why they
should not, for a species of seal exists which is never found in the sea:
the Calocephalus that lives in the lakes and inland seas of Asia, the
Caspian, the Aral Sea, Lake Baikal and Lake Oron. Moreover in Aus-


tralia seals and sea-lions are said sometimes to reach the drainage basin
of the Murray River and its tributary, the Darling. Dr Charles Fenner
mentions a seal killed at Conargo, on the Murrumbidgee in New South
Wales, 900 miles from the river’s mouth. A maned sea-lion was also
captured at the junction of the Kangaroo and Shoalhaven Rivers. A


204

sea-leopard was killed in the latter river in 1870. When it was cut open
an adult platypus was found in its stomach. As Whitley remarked,
“Surely a bunyip within a bunyip!”


Thus it seems well established that seals can travel long distances in
fresh water, and it is possible that they may go a short way over dry


land. Most of the reports about “‘water-devils” come from the south-


east of Australia, that is to say from the drainage basins of the only two


large rivers on that continent.


The sight of a seal or a sea-lion far inland would be very unusual, and


it is therefore hardly surprising that these strange animals should be
described as bunyips. It is worth recalling that when the Aborigines’


tales of specially formidable bunyips were investigated they turned out


to be merely Indian cattle (genus Bibos), which white settlers had im-
ported, and which had occasionally escaped and returned to a state of
nature. The sight of these huge and utterly unknown horned beasts


terrified the blackfellows.
They were quite unlike any indigenous
animal and thus well deserved to be called bunyips. Their bellowings
may account for some of the terrifying roars attributed to bunyips, but
not that heard by Bailly and his companions before these cattle had been
introduced into Western Australia. Whitley suggests that these dreadful


cries could have been made by seals or sea-elephants. Even if they were


a long way off their calls would have a terrifying effect in the lonely
western deserts. “*. . . in some parts in Western Australia,” he observes,
*T have known silence so utter that it was quite oppressive, and that the
sound of my solitary footsteps seemed, by contrast, to be a crunching
roar.”


The dreadful cries attributed to the bunyip in the south-east are more
likely to come from a much smaller but equally loud creature, the brown
bittern (Botaurus poiciloptilus), a bird whose booming voice has earned


it the name of “Murray Bull.”


It is, however, by no means certain that the legend of the water-
bunyip is based on stray seals and sea-lions. Many reports come from


places that these animals could not reach. Australian scientists have


therefore put forward much bolder theories to explain it.


The Bunyip [writes Whitley] has been thought to have been an
extinct marsupial otter-like animal, rumours of whose existence have
been handed down in aboriginal legends, the latter corrupted and con-
fused with crocodiles in the north of Australia and seals in the south.


Why “extinct”? The reports that have cropped up over a century
and a half speak of a living animal, not a ghost. There are marsupial
205


THE LIVING FOSSILS OF OCEANIA


equivalents of most types of placentary mammals: running, jumping,
climbing, tree-dwelling, gliding and burrowing types. “Nevertheless,”


as Jean Piveteau has remarked, “certain types of adaptation are missing ;
there are none truly aerial or truly aquatic.” Might not the bunyip be an
example of the missing aquatic type? In any case the insistence of some
zoologists that legends of unknown animals are based on extinct species
seems to be an idée fixe. Thus Dr Anderson, Director of the Australian
Museum, writes, “There may be aboriginal legends of the former
existence of the Diprotodon, which is commonly believed to have haunted
rivers, swamps and inland lakes.”’ But that is another story.


When. Mary Ellen Chase wrote Harvey, a play about a drunk whose
best friend is a rabbit 10 feet high that no one else can see, she must have
chosen this eponymous and invisible animal for its very improbability.
Yet there are plenty of people in Australia who claim to have seen crea-


tures not unlike Harvey. They were gold-prospectors who had pene-
trated into the vast sandy western desert and the waste of thorny scrub
in the central depression, which together are several times the area of
the British Isles. When they returned, exhausted and feverish, from
their gold-panning expeditions, they brought back ludicrous tales about
rabbits 10 feet long..Naturally there were hints that these monsters,


like Harvey himself and the pink elephants so beloved of humorists,
were a by-product of alcohol; for gold-mining is not an abstemious
trade.


But these stories recurred so insistently that in the end they aroused


the interest of some scientists, among them Ambrose Pratt, the great
Australian naturalist. He seriously asked whether these Brobdingnagian
rabbits might not be surviving specimens of the Diprotodon, a gigantic
wombat, as large as a rhinoceros, which once wandered the Nullarbor
Plain, before the increasing drought turned most of the continent into


a desert. The skulls that have been found of these giants of the marsu-


pial kingdom are as much as 3 feet long. There is no lack of information
about their anatomy, for more than a hundred more or less complete
skeletons were discovered in the Salt Lake at Callabonna.


This creature’s fat body reminds one more of a huge bear than of a


rabbit, but the same is not true of its head. Like the kangaroos, it has


a face very like a rabbit’s or a hare’s, with two conspicuously large in-


cisors in the upper jaw under a typical “‘hare-lip,”” hence the name of
Diprotodon (“with two teeth in front’’), a characteristic of the vegetarian
marsupials. As, according to several accounts, these harmless great


206


THE INCREDIBLE AUSTRALIAN BUNYIPS


beasts made off at top speed as soon as they met a man—who did like-
wise—the mistake is easily understandable. But, whether the Diproto-
don looked like a rabbit or not, could it have survived until today?


The climatic upheavals which have transformed the appearance of
Australia at a comparatively recent date are usually blamed for the
Diprotodon’s extinction. This placid vegetarian’s habits are supposed


to have been like-a tapir’s; it enjoyed a semi-aquatic habitat among the


lush vegetation which still covered the continent at the end of the last


Ice Age, between 12,000 and 30,000 years ago, until the ever-increas-


ing drought ate away the country like a leprosy.


No doubt the Diprotodon tried to survive in various oases, and, as
they dried up one by one, vast hordes of these brutes must have set off

to wander in search of new water-holes until they perished of thirst in
the sandy desert or died in herds most conveniently for the palaeonto-


logists. Thus in June 1953 Professor Ruben A. Stirton of the Univer-
sity of California returned to Adelaide from the dry north-west of
South Australia where he had found a Diprotodon graveyard con-


taining between 500 and 1,000 skeletons in a superb state of preserva-


tion. A vast herd of these poor beasts, dying of thirst, had apparently


ventured on to the hard crust where a lake had recently dried up to no


more than a few tempting pools. The crust gave way under their


weight and they gradually sank into the soft clay, which preserved their


skeletons from the weather. Some of them had their paws folded be-


neath them, as if they had met their death calmly welcoming the mois-


ture of their muddy grave.

How long can one say for certain that the Diprotodon survived?
According to more cautious estimates they must have been known and
probably hunted and eaten by the first blackfellows who came to Aus-


tralia. Among some aboriginal tribes legends are still current which
seem to refer fairly exactly to them. Professor John Walter Gregory is
firmly convinced that the central Australian aborigines’ mythical kadi-
kamara is based on knowledge of living Diprotodon. And in 1872 Dr
George Bennett, a palaeontologist of the Australian Museum, reported


that:


I have had a long conversation with ‘Charlie Pierce’, an aboriginal,
relative to these fossils; and he avers that they are those of an animal,
long extinct, known to the natives by the name Gyedarra. Tradition
among them has handed down the appearance and habits of the
animal for generations, but Charlie says he never paid much attention
to the descriptions that have been given to him, but imagines the
animal was as large as a heavy draught horse, walked on all fours the
same as any other four footed beast, eating grass, never went any dis-
tance back from the creeks to feed, and spent most of its time in the
water, chiefly in enormous holes excavated in the banks.
I told him he
must mean some other animal; but he spoke most positively, and
asserted that the bones we have been finding are those of the animal
he was speaking of, and that at one time the bones were very numerous
*
about the Gowrie water holes, where his forefathers had seen the
animals themselves sporting about. I again asked him if they did not
live on the leaves of trees, and his reply was that they were never
seen to feed on them, but always on grass, the same as a horse or
bullock.


Now van Gennep considers that an oral tradition cannot originate
more than two or three centuries ago, without being radically distorted
and transformed.
Thus even the boldest estimates, according to
which the Diprotodon still haunted the central plains hardly 2,000 or
3,000 years ago, would seem to be too cautious, and one should take
the more heed of prospectors’ tales of “giant rabbits.” For the drought
which certainly decimated the Diprotodon need not have exterminated
them entirely, any more than it has the other vegetarians—and the
carnivores that feed upon them—that are found in the continent. More-
over, Australia is by no means waterless: there are still lakes, marshes
and streams where the Diprotodon might find shelter as other animals
do.


All the same, the “giant rabbits” have, according to the prospectors’


tales, a habit that has made some zoologists pause before identifying
them as surviving Diprotodon. Witnesses have often stressed the extra-


208


THE INCREDIBLE AUSTRALIAN BUNYIPS


ordinary speed at which the “rabbits” made off—some even thought
that they literally vanished into dust. Indeed, these giants may have
been likened to rabbits because of their sudden flight as much as their
general appearance. Was Ambrose Pratt’s identification wrong? For it


is hard to imagine a heavy animal like the Diprotodon running like


lightning. Are not these “rabbits” more likely to be a gigantic form of


kangaroo, which can vanish in one jump? The larger species, like the


red kangaroo (Macropus rufus) and the grey kangaroo (Macropus


giganteus), which are almost as high as a man, can jump 30 feet in one


bound. And some reports have referred explicitly to “kangaroos 12 feet


high.”


The discovery of fossil remains of similar giants (Palaeorchestes) has
given added weight to these rumours, especially as it is well-established
that these animals lived recently. Even so, it is not impossible that the
rumours are based on encounters with much heavier and no less recent
animals like the Diprotodon. “Australians who hunt the water buffaloes
that now run wild in huge numbers in the north of their continent will


tell you that this great beast can literally vanish before your eyes even in
fairly open country,” Ivan T. Sanderson remarks—a cloud of dust, and
the beast has gone, disappeared, no doubt behind a convenient bush.
What is true of these cattle could clearly also apply to the Diprotodon,
of comparable size.


Whether it is a Diprotodon or not there is little doubt that an animal
of unusual size lives in the deserts of Western Australia, but what it is


still remains to be settled. Even the boldest naturalists hesitate to ven-
ture into this hostile country, remembering perhaps the tragic fate of
Dr Ludwig Leichhardt. He arrived in Australia in 1841 and imme-
diately went right across the whole continent to Fraser Island, cover-
ing some 2,500 miles.
He tirelessly carried out several other ex-
plorations, and his researches gradually led him to the belief that the
Diprotodon was not extinct. In 1847 he organised an expedition with


the secret hope of bringing’ one back alive. He set off enthusiastically


into the dry heart of the continent and it is known that he reached the


River Cogun on 3 April 1848. Nothing more was ever heard of him or


his companions. The trail of unknown animals sometimes leads to Hell.

To the zoologist Australia is indeed an upside-down country. While the
animals found there were strange, if not extraordinary—the marsupials,
and especially the monotremes, exceeded the scientists’ wildest hopes—
explorers and settlers constantly but vainly looked for familiar animals,


as if to reassure themselves that this bewildering place was somehow
normal.


Thus when that famous buccaneer, William Dampier, discovered a
bay on the west coast of Australia in August 1699 and named it Shark
Bay, he reported that it was inhabited by a quite imaginary hippopota-
mus. They had caught an 11-foot shark (hence the name of the bay):


Its Maw was like a Leather Sack, very thick, and so tough that a

Actually it was merely the head of a dugong, a large herbivorous
water-beast that ends in a mermaid-like tail and has a head vaguely like


a hippopotamus’s; the male has two bevelled tusk-like upper incisors,
larger than the rest and also reminiscent of that animal.


Thereafter explorers searched Australian waters for a non-existent
animal. It would have been most surprising to find a true hippopotamus
in the open sea, even though it is fond of brackish water. Settlers have
always been inclined to rediscover familiar animals in their new land
and name them after the species they knew at home. So Australia was

soon full of “native” rats and “native” mice—to say nothing of rabbits,

superficial connection with the real ones.


Crocodiles were also reported in places in Australia where there were
none. There are in fact two species of crocodile in Oceania: the double-
crested crocodile (Crocodylus porosus), a huge monster that may reach


a length of 22 feet, and Johnston’s crocodile (C. johnstoni). The first,


the only crocodile to enter the sea, is also found in the Indies and in


the Fiji Islands; the second is purely Australian. Both are found only in


the north. One would not expect to meet one in New South Wales.


But in November 1939 an engine-driver on the light railway to
Angourie beach in the north of that province was astonished to realise

that a log near which he had stopped his locomotive was actually a 15-

hurriedly started his engine and made off at full speed.


When he told his story several people remembered that they too had
seen a crocodile in the district. Then others recalled that several years


earlier a sick circus crocodile had been brought to Yamba. Did it really


die, as was said at the time? Sinister roars were heard at night. This


sort of thing could not go on; and politicians, ever anxious for glory,


helped the police to comb the district. They even went so far as to


dynamite suspicious holes in the ground, bagging a lot of snakes and


even a 5-foot goanna lizard which was exhibited for some time in a local


hotel. At last, the circus crocodile’s remains were exhumed, eliminating


it from the suspects once and for all.

Soon crocodile-hunting became a local attraction: even the Christmas

of goannas and four courting couples. The blackfellows began to whis-

place of the first excitement. People were careful to lock their doors
after dark.


Then tracks were discovered that looked as if they had been made by


a huge pigeon. Casts were taken and sent to the expert on herpetology


at the Australian Museum in Sydney. He recognised that, both in size
and shape, they agreed with a crocodile’s footprints. But as nothing
more was heard of the monster in the next few weeks the obsession
about it gradually dwindled and died. The roars heard in the district
were attributed to bitterns, and crocodile hunting was out of fashion.
But the footprints had been real enough—and must have been made by


a large reptile.


Was it really a crocodile? May it not have been an unknown species
of large lizard? Until quite recently Australia .was inhabited by a giant
monitor lizard (Varanus priscus) beside which the Komodo dragon would
have seemed quite small. It was 20 to 25 feet long, whereas I doubt if
the Komodo dragon ever reaches 12 feet. Such a monster could easily be
mistaken for a crocodile. And it would be much more likely to live near
the forests of New South Wales than would a crocodile.


The marsupial tiger is the most important of these apparently familiar
animals to be found in Australia. Its existence is no longer in doubt—
though it is still not officially recognised—but the first reports were
based on misinterpreted rumours.


In November 1642 Captain Abel Janszoon Tasman on board the
Heemskirk sighted land which he took to be the southern tip of New
Holland. He named it Van Diemen’s Land in honour of the Dutch
governor on whose orders he was seeking a southern sea-route between
America and the Orient. It was none of his business to explore new
lands, and he did not set foot on the island that was later to bear his
name;
but he sent his chief pilot, Francoy Jacobszoon, ashore with a
handful of men. They came back with some alarming tales. Besides
notches in trees which they thought had been made by giants they had
seen footprints with claws like a tiger’s.


There is no doubt that these had been made by a Tasmanian or
pouched wolf (Thylacinus cynocephalus), a sort of marsupial wolf, which,
by an odd chance, is striped like a tiger on the middle of the back, rump,


212


THE QUEENSLAND MARSUPIAL TIGER


thighs and tail. It has five toes on its fore-feet, the footprints of which
cannot therefore be confused with a dog’s or cat’s. It has only four toes
on its hind-feet like a dog or cat, but whereas they walk on their fingers,


it puts the whole sole of the foot on the ground, and so leaves a relatively


larger footprint. Hence the confusion with tigers.


Nevertheless Dutch explorers confirmed the presence of a tiger in
Australia half a century later. The administrators of the Dutch East
India Company at Batavia used to make reports on information collected
from pioneers’ log-books. Thus in an anonymous report dated 1705 and
quoted in Major’s Terra Australis, “snipe, a tiger and a large number of
black birds” are said to have been found in Australia. The birds are

In 1871 the first detailed report about an unknown cat in Queensland
was published in the Proceedings of the Zoological Society. It consisted
of a letter written on 2 August of that year to the famous zoologist
Sclater by Brinsley G. Sheridan, a Police Magistrate at Cardwell:


One evening strolling along a path close to the shore of Rockingham
Bay, a small terrier, my son’s companion, took a scent up from a piece
of scrub near the beach, and followed, barking furiously, towards the
coast-range westwards. My boy (thirteen years of age, but an old bush-
man, who would put half those described in novels to the blush)
followed and found in the long grass, about half a mile from the spot
the scent was first taken up, an animal described by himself as follows:—
“Tt was lying camped in the long grass and was as big as a native Dog;


its face was round like that of a Cat, it had a long tail, and its body was
striped from the ribs under the belly with yellow and black. My Dog
flew at it, but it could throw him. The animal then ran up a leaning
tree, and the Dog barked at it. It then got savage and rushed down the
tree at the Dog and then at me. I got frightened and came home.”’

Sheridan made inquiries and found that this was not the first time

Tracks of a sort of Tiger have been seen in Dalrymple’s Gap by

This letter did not fail to impress the Fellows of the Zoological Society

carnivore. A picture of a footprint was published with the letter in the
Proceedings of the Zoological Society. Scott also recalled that in 1864 a
bullock-driver said that he had met a tiger face to face in the area, but as
he was a notorious liar no one believed him. Perhaps, after all, he had
seen a similar animal.


Nonsense, wrote Gerald Krefft in another British scientific journal;
the bullock-driver was certainly a liar, and Scott’s footprint was an
ordinary dog’s! He was shocked that the Zoological Society should
waste its money publishing such stuff.


Meanwhile, on 5 June 1872, Scott sent another more detailed report
about this mythical cat from the Valley of Lagoons in Queensland.
Robert Johnstone, an officer of native police, who was in the scrub with

perched in a tree some 40 feet from the ground. When they approached

patches. Its head was quite round; they did not see its ears.
Its tail
was long and thick.


In 1895 there was serious alarm and a great deal of noise—at all events
in the Press—about a “tiger” at Tantanoola in South Australia. The
beast was hunted and finally shot.
Its dismembered carcase was ex-

Certainly there was plenty of talk of “tigers” at this time: one was

were seeing them everywhere, which naturally did not tend to make
young Sheridan’s story believed. But a shrewd observer would have

On another occasion the animal was even seen by a well-known

the head and body.


A Mr Endres of Mundubbera in Queensland caught one of these

large cat; very short head and neck; striped, but not right round.” It
was “‘very savage when caught.”


Ion Idriess, an Australian writer who spent his whole life in the wild
north-east of the continent, mainly in Coen, has written an account that
deserves to be quoted. He speaks of the mysterious creature as if it were
a very familiar beast.

Up here in York Peninsula we have a tiger-cat that stands as high as
a hefty, medium-sized dog. His body is lithe and sleek and beautifully
striped in black and grey. His pads are armed with lance-like claws of
great tearing strength. His ears are sharp and pricked, and his head is
shaped like that of a tiger. My introduction to this beauty was one day
when I heard a series of snarls from the long buffalo-grass skirting a
swamp. On peering through the grass I saw a full-grown kangaroo,
backed up against a tree, the flesh of one leg torn clean from the bone.
A streak of black and grey shot towards the ‘roo’s’ throat, then seemed


to twist in the air, and the kangaroo slid to earth with the entrails


literally torn out. In my surprise I incautiously rustled the grass, and


the great cat ceased the warm feast that he had promptly started upon,


stood perfectly still over his victim, and for ten seconds returned me


gaze for gaze. Then the skin wrinkled back from the nostrils, white


fangs gleamed, and a low growl issued from his throat. I went back-


wards and lost no time in getting out of the entangling grass.


It was not the only encounter.


The next brute I saw was dead, and beside him was my much-prized
-staghound, also dead. This dog had been trained from puppyhood in
tackling wild boars, and his strength and courage were known by all the
prospectors over the country.


This happened not far from the Alice River.


Among more recent reports I should mention P. B. Scougall and
G. de Tournoeur who were riding from Munna Creek to the little town
of Tiaro. Suddenly their horses shied.


We dismounted [they wrote to the Brisbane Courier] and were
startled to find the cause to be a large animal of the cat tribe, standing
about twenty yards away, astride of a very dead calf, glaring defiance at
us, and emitting what I can only describe as a growling whine. As far as
the gathering darkness and torrential rain allowed us to judge he was
nearly the size of a mastiff, of a dirty fawn colour, with a whitish belly,
and broad blackish stripes. The head was round, with rather prominent
lynxlike ears, but unlike that feline there were a tail reaching to the
ground and large pads. We threw a couple of stones at him, which only
made him crouch low, with ears laid flat, and emit a raspy snarl, vividly
reminiscent of the African leopard’s nocturnal ‘wood-sawing’
cry.


Beating an angry tattoo on the grass with his tail, he looked so ugly and


ready for a spring that we felt a bit ‘windy’; but on our making a rush
and cracking our stockwhips he bounded away to the bend of the


creek, when he turned back and growled at us.


Finally I should mention that the large striped cat has been known
by the Queensland aborigines since the earliest times.
It is not therefore surprising that the eminent zoologist E. Le G.

Troughton, Curator of the Department of Mammals in the Australian

Although there is some divergence concerning the size of the animal
and the disposition of the stripes, there seems some possibility that a
large striped marsupial-cat haunts the tangled forests of North Queens-

Nor would there be anything very odd about finding an Australian
animal that looked like a cat. That this “tiger” or (more modestly)
“tiger-cat” is a marsupial is very likely, since it lives in an almost ex-
clusively marsupial world. As I have already remarked, Australia has,
by a curious phenomenon of convergence, marsupials that resemble
most types of placentary mammals. Besides kangaroos, which take the
place of deer and antelopes, there are shrews (Marmosa), moles (Noto-


ryctes), mice (Sminthopsis), rats (the various potoroos), rabbits (Pera-
meles), squirrels (Petaurus), dormice (Cercaertes), jerboas (Antechinomys)
and even large rodents of the coypu type (the wombats); genets (Dasu-
ridae), wolves {Thylacinus), little bears (the Tasmanian devil or Sarco-
philus) and even lemurs (the koala and the cuscus).. Not long ago there
were large ungulates between tapirs and rhinoceroses (Diprotodon),
which may still not be quite extinct. It is also relevant that in South
America there was once a whole group of marsupials corresponding to
the larger carnivores of Africa and Asia: the Borhyaenidae. There was
even a “sabre-toothed tiger” among them, the Thylacosmilus. More-
-


over, in Australia there was until quite recently a sort of marsupial lion,
the Thylacoleo. It would be quite natural to find a smaller species of the
same group on the same continent.


This large striped animal which has been well described as “‘a cat just
growing into a tiger” is, of all the unknown animals dealt with in this
book, the one nearest to being officially admitted by science. Although
there is neither skeleton nor skin of it in any museum in the world, the
“striped marsupial cat” of Northern Queensland was included in a
standard work on Australian fauna in 1926 on the strength of the field
observations which I have quoted from its text. The authors, A. S.
Le Souef and H. Burrell, put forward a very subtle argument that the
animal is a marsupial.


Although there is nothing to indicate directly to what order this
animal belongs, we believe it to be a marsupial, from the fact that it
apparently cannot live in competition with the dingo. It inhabits the
only country that the wild dog cannot penetrate.


218


THE QUEENSLAND MARSUPIAL TIGER


I have already stressed the merciless war between marsupials and
placentary mammals of the same type. The dingo, a mammal imported
by man and now run wild, has driven out the larger carnivorous mar-


supials, especially the thylacine, wherever it has gone.


On the other hand, in South America it has been noticed that mar-
supials can survive perfectly well when there are no placentary mammals
of their type, and fill the gaps that they leave. As Sir Richard Owen has


remarked, if a fauna is to be in equilibrium it must have its carnivores,


its insectivores, its herbivores, and so on. All the gaps must be filled.


One can almost say that for this reason there must be a predatory mar-


supial in the mountainous forests of Queensland.


Le Souef and Burrell describe the “striped marsupial cat” of York
Peninsula thus:


Hair short, rather coarse.
General colour fawn or grey, with broad
black stripes on flanks, not meeting over the back. Head like that of a
cat; nose more produced. Ears sharp, pricked. Tail well haired, in-
clined to be tufted at end. Feet large, claws long, sharp. Total length
about five feet; height at shoulder eighteen inches.


It would be almost as big as the small clouded leopard (Neofelis nebu-


losa), or a cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus) with short legs.


So far it seems to be confined to Northern Queensland, where its
habitat is “the rough, rocky country on top of the ranges, country usually
covered with heavy forest, and inhabited chiefly by tree-kangaroos and
rock-wallabies.”” But Le Souef and Burrell add:


We have had a striped carnivorous animal described from North-
west Australia, and Lord Rothschild states, from native reports, that
a similar animal exists also in New Guinea.


And they point out very succinctly why such animals as the York
Peninsula tiger-cat are not better known to science.


This animal is rare, or, to be more correct, it lives in country that man
seldom penetrates, and when he does so he creates such a noise in
getting through the tangled undergrowth that any wary animal makes
off.


There is a rather similar phenomenon in physics.
It is theoretically
impossible to shine a ray of light on to a particle in order to ascertain its
relative position and velocity, without the impact of the light altering
them and giving a false result. This impossibility of making extremely


219


THE LIVING FOSSILS OF OCEANIA


small measurements led the German physicist Wernher Heisenberg to
formulate his now-famous Principle of Uncertainty in 1925.


There ought to be a similar zoological principle, based on the diffi-
culty of making field observations of large animals, man’s natural rivals,
which tend to disappear as soon as man arrives on the scene. The degree
of difficulty depends on their habitat: obviously it is greater in the water
than on land, and greater on land than in the air; greater in mountains
than in plains; greater in the forest than in the savannah or the bush, and
greater in the bush than in a sandy desert. This is why we know so little
about the creatures of the sea and so much about birds—except those
species that cannot fly, The difficulties are almost insuperable when
two coincide, as they do in mountainous country with thick vegetation.
‘That is why most unknown animals live in marshy or mountainous
forests. It is a mere matter of logic.
