THE moa is the oddest of birds. It is, as far as we know, the largest bird
that ever lived. Not only is it unable to fly (like the other running birds,


or Ratitae, such as the ostrich, the emu and the cassowary, which it
resembles a little in outline), but it has not the smallest trace of wings.
There is not even a sign of the collar-bone with which a vertebrate’s
front legs are almost invariably connected to the thorax. It is the truest
of bipeds, and its feathers are so primitive that they seem more like
hairs.


But though a wingless furry bird might be a freak elsewhere it would
not be out of the ordinary in New Zealand. There is a marked tendency
among many different groups of birds on those islands to lose their
powers of flight. There are rails which have forgotten how to fly, such


as the weka or Maori hen (Ocydromus) and the takahe (Notornis), to
which I shall be returning later. There used also to be wingless cranes
(Aptornis). And there is a parrot known as the kakapo or owl-parrot
(Stringops), which has not only become nocturnal (an odd enough thing


for a parrot to do), but has also turned burrower, which is thoroughly
odd for a bird. Its wings are well developed, but it has lost its breast-
bone, that bony keel indispensable to flight. It lives in holes under rocks
and the roots of trees.


New Zealand is the sole home of two families of wingless and tailless
birds with hair-like plumage: the kiwis and the moas, known to science


as Apterygidae and Dinornithidae; while the kiwis have vestiges of wings

beneath their feathers, the moas are completely wingless. Only one
genus of kiwis, Apteryx, seems to survive today; it includes three very
closely related species. The kiwi is a nocturnal forest bird as big as a
chicken. Its appearance, a little head and long beak sticking out of a
bunch of dark brown silk, is familiar from the many pictures of it as the


national emblem of New Zealand and a trade mark for boot-polish. It


is less well known that its nostrils are in the tip of its burrowing beak


and it is the only bird that finds its food by smell—indeed the only one


that has a highly-developed sense of smell. While the African ostriches


have only two toes on each foot and their Australian cousins the emus


have three, the kiwi still has a dim vestige of a fourth toe at the back


of the foot. It is better developed in the other family of New Zealand


63. The New Zealand kiwi.


running birds, the Dinornithidae. These are the moas, of which various
authors have described from 21 to 38 species belonging to five distinct
genera, though they are all—officially at least—said to be fossils.


It is usual to talk of kiwis as dwarfs and moas as giants. The truth is


less simple. The largest moas, such as the Dinornis robustus, stood nearly


12 feet high—3 feet higher than the tallest ostrich—but some, like the


Anomalopteryx parva, were no bigger than a turkey. On the other hand,


it is generally admitted that not long ago there was—and perhaps still is
—a giant Apteryx (Apteryx maxima) which was just the same size. But


it has not been proved that the pygmy moa and the giant kiwi are not


one and the same animal, for the latter is known only from the vaguest


evidence. Where do kiwis end and moas begin? If one is to go only by


external appearance there is no difference except for the length of the


223


THE LIVING FOSSILS OF OCEANIA


beak, and this is not an absolute criterion. One also has to know the
exact position of the nostrils, not an easy thing to verify without the
bird in the hand. In fact all these wingless, furry-looking birds would
be remarkably alike even if they were not so closely related.


Why, you may ask, is it in New Zealand rather than elsewhere that
birds tend to lose the use of their wings, and even their wings them-
selves? The answer is to be found in a fact which Captain Cook was
observant to notice when he explored the New Zealand archipelago in
1773, and found no quadrupeds except dogs and rats.


These dogs and rats were obviously introduced by the natives, so
there were no indigenous quadrupeds in this country. Thus there were
no carnivores that eat birds.


In islands where there are no predatory mammals, birds no longer
need to take to the air at the least danger, but can relapse into a lazy
terrestrial existence—with fatal results. It is hardly surprising that most
birds that have become extinct in historic times have lived on islands,
inaccessible to carnivores, where they have given up flying. For sooner


or later man and his parasites, the dog and sometimes the cat, come to
disturb the peace. The most celebrated victim is the dodo of Mauritius
(Didus ineptus), a huge flightless pigeon which man exterminated in less
than a century. Its name is a very symbol of extinction: as dead as the
dodo.


Of all the islands of any size, the most isolated from any mainland are
the North and South Islands of New Zealand. They are more than 1,000
miles from Australia, the nearest land. In the middle of the Mesozoic


era, during the Jurassic period, these islands were attached to South-East
Asia by a broad causeway that included New Caledonia, the New
Hebrides, the Solomon Islands and New Guinea. It even reached to
Australia. But before the end of the following period, the Cretaceous,


it sank under the waves, leaving only a few scattered islands and cutting
off New Zealand for ever from the rest of the world. This happened
shortly before the great invasion of marsupials, which were thus unable
to spread beyond Australia. Since then the only access to New Zealand
has been by air or by sea. There the only known indigenous mammals
are two species of bats, both called pekapeka by the Maoris; one,
Chalinolobus, also lives in Australia, the other, Mystacina, is found only
in New Zealand. This country could hardly be accidentally populated
by creatures carried there on floating tree-trunks, a common enough pro-
cess between the galaxies of islands, each close to the next, in Oceania.


224


THE MOA, A FOSSIL THAT MAY STILL THRIVE


When land mammals first set foot on New Zealand it was because they
had deliberately steered the tree-trunks there which they had hollowed
out into boats, for they were men. They brought with them their faith-
ful companion the dog, kararehe, now vanished. The rat kiore (Mus
exulans) had certainly not been invited, but its arrival was no accident.


Any species of land quadruped that existed in New Zealand before


this invasion would have to be very ancient, for it would have to have
been there since the Jurassic period at the latest. Such a quadruped


exists. It is the only remaining survivor of the Rhynchocephalians, a
group of reptiles older, geologically speaking, than the dinosaurs, the
tuatara (Sphenodon punctatus), a strange three-eyed lizard which usually
shares its home with a petrel (see plate between pages 72 and 73). Just


as Australia is the last retreat of a past age of marsupials, so New Zealand
shelters the last representative of a reptilian empire that flourished
nearly 200 million years ago.


During the long period between New Zealand’s isolation and its
invasion by man, birds were able to develop richly and into the wildest
forms, such as the giant moas. After losing their power of flight, the
birds in the two main islands evolved along different lines, as is explained
by Professor Ferdinand von Hochstetter of Vienna, one of the greatest
experts on the natural history of New Zealand.


.
.
.as the Apteryx species of the two Islands are different, so also the
Moa species of North Island seem to be different from those found on
South Island. Cook Strait, now separating the two islands, may have
proved to these birds, which could neither fly nor swim, an unsur-
mountable obstacle, preventing them from migrating from one island
to the other. New Zealand was perhaps a large continent when the Moas
were first created. And if we suppose this or at least that the two
islands were formerly contiguous to each other, we of course suppose
also, that the separation took place so long a time ago, that the originally
identical species, after the separation of both islands, may have been
changed in course of time into the present varieties or species.


According to Prof. Owen, the birds of South Island present stouter
proportions, a compact, rather bulky frame of body, such as Dinornis
robustus, elephantopus, crassus and Palapteryx ingens, while those of
North Island are distinguished by more slender and lengthy forms, like
the Dinornis giganteus and gracilis.


These various species inhabited the plains and valleys and had their
hiding-places in forests and caves.
Their food doubtless consisted of


vegetables, especially fern-roots, which they dug up with their powerful


feet and claws. To assist the process of digestion, they swallowed small


pebbles.

This we know because heaps of small round stones, usually chalce-
dony, cornelian, agate and opal, are often found with the bones of moas


or occasionally by themselves. Presumably these round pebbles came
from the moas’ stomachs, for their cousins the ostrich and the emu are in
the habit of swallowing small pebbles to help grind the food and of
regurgitating them from time to time when they have been worn quite
smooth.


The formation of the skull [Professor yon Hochstetter goes on] leads
us to infer that they were stupid, clumsy birds, which we must not
suppose to have been swift runners like the ostrich, but sluggish diggers
of the ground, the nature and habits of which demanded no larger
scope, than such as the limited territory of New Zealand presented.

THE MOA, A FOSSIL THAT MAY STILL THRIVE


Indeed the moa hardly seems to deserve its scientific name of Dinor-


nis, or “terrible bird,” given it by Sir Richard Owen. On the contrary,


it is the very type of a bird that has grown soft from too easy a life and
whose days will be numbered as soon as the first enemy arrives. But did
man exterminate the moa? Yes, say some, going so far as to cite the


evidence of Maoris who point out a Totara tree on Lake Rotorua as the


place where their ancestors killed the last moa.


But for those colossal birds [says von Hochstetter], it would be indeed
utterly impossible to comprehend how 200,000 or 300,000 human
beings could have lived in New Zealand, a country which even in its
vegetable world offered nothing for subsistence, except fern-roots.


And he attributes the Maoris’ cannibalism to their lack of meat when


these wonderfully large and plump birds began to fail. But we know
today that habitual cannibalism is never merely the result of famine, and
that it derives from a magical belief that one can acquire the virtues of
the dead by digesting their bodies. No doubt the Maori cannibalism is


as old as the race itself.


Others no less hotly deny that man exterminated the moa, but this
denial can have two diametrically opposite meanings. Some say that the
moa could not have been exterminated by man, because it was already
extinct when he arrived. The degeneration of this overgrown bird,
reflected in its bones, made the moa die out. Perhaps floods drowned
many of these birds that could no longer fly, and doubtless the violent
volcanic eruptions, of which traces have been found, helped to destroy


a large population. But others say that the moa has not been exter-
minated by man because it is not yet utterly extinct, and this giant bird,


or at all events some moa of smaller size, survives in unexplored regions
of New Zealand. The extraordinary diversity of opinion on this subject


is largely a result of the bitter controversy aroused by the original
discovery of the moa.


The history of the discovery of the moa is even more confused than
the history of the moa itself. For more than a century men have been
©


trying to solve the mystery that surrounds it; and there is no doubt that
some of them, whether from vainglory, incompetence or disbelief, have


ironically only helped to darken the mystery the more. When the moa


was discovered it was variously pronounced to be a contemporary of


present-day man, a bird only recently extinct, and a complete fossil,


Each of these opinions had its own belligerent faction which became


ever firmer in its own conviction, after searching systematically for


227


THE LIVING FOSSILS OF OCEANIA


arguments to support its theory and neglecting any evidence that might
weaken it. Let us try to follow the moa’s discovery without any such


bias.


It officially entered the world of science in 1839 when a fragment of a
huge bone was brought back from New Zealand by a traveller named
Rule and eventually reached the hands of Professor Sir Richard Owen.
The bone seemed to have belonged to an ox, but after careful study he
realised that it was a bird’s femur. On 12 November 1839 he read a
note on this sensational discovery to the Zoological Society of London
in which he said:


Any opinion . . . as to its specific form can only be conjectural; ...
but so far as my skill in interpreting an osseous fragment may be
credited, I am willing to risk the reputation for it on the statement that
there has existed, if there does not now exist, in New Zealand, a Stru-
thious bird nearly, if not quite, equal in size to the Ostrich.


There was no doubt that such a bird had once existed when Rule’s
bone had been identified by such a leading comparative anatomist as
Owen. But that it could still exist or be known to man seemed unlikely
to many people. Captain Cook had heard nothing of it when he visited
New Zealand in 1773 and questioned Chief Tawaihura at some length
about the local fauna. And plenty of travellers had been there since, and
not a single work about the country made the least mention of this
extraordinary bird. This latter objection may have been true until 1839,
but it was so no longer. A Jewish merchant called J. S. Polack had just
published two volumes about New Zealand. He had spent more than
two years, between 1834 and 1837, on the east coast of North Island,
where he said:


That a species of the emu, or a bird of the genus Struthio [ostrich],
formerly existed in the latter island, I feel well assured, as several large
fossil ossifications were shewn to me when I was residing in the
vicinity of the East Cape, said to have been found at the base of the
inland mountain of Ikorangi [Hikurangi]. The Natives added that, in
times long past, they received the traditions, that very large birds had
existed, but the scarcity of animal food, as well as the easy method of
entrapping them, has caused their extermination.


This would have satisfied those who thought the moa was recently
extinct and explained why Captain Cook had heard nothing of such a
monstrous bird being still alive. But Polack goes on to say:


Yet, doubtless, the future ornithologist will be surprised by dis-
covering, among the hidden mountain-gorges and wilds of the Island
228


THE MOA, A FOSSIL THAT MAY STILL THRIVE


of Victoria [i.e. South Island], many birds at present supposed to be
no longer in existence.


I feel assured, from the many reports I received from the natives
that a species of struthio still exists on that interesting island, in parts,
which, perhaps, have never yet been trodden by man. Traditions are
current among the elder natives of Atuas,! covered with hair, in the
form of birds, having waylaid native travellers, among the forest wilds,
vanquishing them with an overpowering strength, killing and devouring,


&c. The traditions are reported with an air of belief that carries con-


viction to the younger natives, who take great delight in the marvellous
and the improbable.


Although a New Zealand printer and amateur naturalist called Wil-
liam Colenso was later to maintain that Polack did not even know how


to write—so that he could pretend that he himself was the first to men-
tion the moa—the book is still the first record of the giant bird. Thus
when Owen published his first article on the subject he mentioned in a
discreet note that Polack’s fossil bones were those of a bird and that
therefore the native traditions he reported were correct. But we should
note in passing that Polack never spoke of “‘fossil” bones, that he said
himself that the giant bones shown him were those of a bird, and that
his book came out before Owen had pronounced favourably upon Rule’s
femur. There is no proof that the zoologist had not read Polack’s book
before he published his conclusions.


Colenso can, however, claim to be the first to mention the name moa
in print. In December 1837, the Rev. William Williams, a protest-
ant missionary, had just published the New Testament in Maori, and
decided to take several weeks’ well-earned holiday with his printer and
friend, Colenso. They left the Bay of Islands on 1 January 1838.
Colenso reported in the Tasmanian fournal of Natural Science:


During the summer of 1838, I accompanied the Rev. W. Williams
on a visit to the tribes inhabiting the East Cape District.
Whilst at
Waiapu, (a thickly inhabited locality about 20 miles S.W. from the
East Cape) I heard from the natives of a certain monstrous animal;
while some said it was a bird, and others “‘a person,” all agreed that’
it was called a Moa;—that in general appearance it somewhat resembled


an immense domestic cock, with the difference, however, of its having a


“face like a man;’’—that it dwelt in a cavern in the precipitous side of a


mountain ;—that it lived on air;—and that it was attended, or guarded,
by two immense Tuataras [Sphenodon], who, Argus-like, kept incessant
watch while the Moa slept; also that if any one ventured to approach

the dwelling of this wonderful creature, he would be invariably

On the strength of this Colenso pretended that he was the first
white man to learn that a giant bird existed in New Zealand. But it
seems clear to me that he did not believe a word of these fantastic
legends, or he would have discussed them with Williams. For when this
missionary returned to the east coast a year later in January 1839 with
a brother missionary, the Rev. Richard Taylor, he had obviously never
believed any story about giant birds—he may not even have heard them.
So it would appear from Taylor’s narrative:


In the beginning of 1839 I took my first journey in New Zealand to
Poverty Bay with the Rey. Wm. Williams (the present Bishop of
Waiapu). When we reached Waiapu, a large pa near the East Cape,
we took up our abode in a native house, and there I noticed the frag-
ment of a large bone stuck in the ceiling. I took it down, supposing at
first that it was human, but when I saw its cancellated structure I
handed it over to my companion, who had been brought up in the
medical profession, asking him if he did not think it was a bird’s bone.
He laughed at the idea, and said, what kind of bird could there be to
have so large a bone? I pointed out its structure; and when the natives
came requested him to ask them what it belonged to. They said it was a
bone of the Tarepo, a very large bird which lived on the top of Hik-
urangi... and that they made their largest fish-hooks from its bones.
I then inquired whether the bird was still to be met with, and was told
that there was one of an immense size which lived in a cave, and was
guarded by a large lizard, and that the bird was always standing on one
leg.


Having bought the bone from the headman of Waiapu for a little
tobacco, Taylor sent it to England, where it eventually reached Owen’s
hands through Sir Everard Home, but not until he had already seen
Rule’s femur and published a note about it. So Taylor’s claim is as


unjustified as Colenso’s when he writes in Te Ika a Maui, or New Zea-
land and its Inhabitants (1855), “I first discovered its remains in 1839, at
Tauranga [Gisborne] and Waiapu.”


When Taylor returned to the Bay of Islands in February he met another
person who had come from Taranaki on the west coast and also claimed


to have heard of the moa, the German naturalist Dr E. Dieffenbach of
the New Zealand Company. When he tried to climb Mount Egmont, a
native chief dissuaded him because the mountain was guarded by a moa
or movie.


Colenso was then a neighbour of Dieffenbach at the Bay of Islands, so
he probably learnt the German traveller’s story and was reminded of the

fantastic tales he had heard earlier about a devil-bird with a human face.
When, like Dieffenbach, he had an opportunity of examining the bones
that Taylor had brought back—in particular a toe—he must have


realised for the first time that the native legends were not utterly without

Two years later Colenso decided to find out more about the mys-
terious bird. He set sailon 19 November 1841 from the Bay of Islands on


alittle boat for Poverty Bay. But he landed much sooner, at Wharekahike,


in Hicks Bay, between Cape Runaway and East Cape, and continued his


journey south on foot, to Rangitukia, a large settlement of the Ngati-


porou tribe on the left bank of the River Waiapu. There he obtained his


first moa bones: five femurs, a tibia and one unidentified bone. At Pov-


erty Bay he met his old friend the Rev. William Williams, who had been


installed as archdeacon at Turanga a year before. He had also collected


a number of moa bones from the natives, intending to send them to


Professor Buckland at Oxford. Colenso added some of his finds to this


collection, but we shall see later that he tried to send his own specimens


to the highest authorities. Leaving the archdeacon, he went on scouring


the east coast, asking the Maoris everywhere whether they knew of moa


bones, and eventually reaching the neighbourhood of the chalky head-


land of Whakapunake, where, according to the traditions he had col-


lected four years before, a moa lived in a cave and terrified the whole


district. But the local natives sent him away elsewhere under the pre-


text that the moa now lived in the Whai-iti Mountains. Another time


the natives showed Colenso a footprint in a clayey rock, a little beyond


Hicks Bay. They said it was that of Rongokako, one of their famous


ancestors. The next footprint was near Poverty Bay, more than 80


miles away—outdoing even the seven-league boots of fable! Colenso


did not guess that it had been made by the creature whose bones he was


collecting, but later it was found to be a moa’s footprint.


When he returned to the Bay of Islands in April 1842 he feverishly set
about completing his collection of moa bones so that he could send them


post-haste to his friend Sir William J. Hooker for Sir Richard Owen.


Meanwhile he wrote an account of his own views about the giant bird,


which he sent to the Tasmanian Journal of Natural Science where it


appears in the volume for 1846.


Determined at all costs to be the first to have told the world of the
giant fossil bird, Colenso always swore that he had never seen Owen’s
1839 note, nor to have heard of it or have met any settler that knew of it.
In fact the New Zealand papers, as one might expect, were full of echoes


231


THE LIVING FOSSILS OF OCEANIA


of this local wonder after Owen’s note appeared, and more than a hun-
dred offprints of the note itself were distributed in New Zealand. The
missionaries, in whose wake Colenso followed, were the most educated
of the settlers and in closest contact with the natives and would have
certainly been the first to receive copies.


Many people in New Zealand claimed to be the first: the first to hear
legends of the giant bird, the first to hear the native name of moa, the


first to collect its bones. And’as they often distorted the truth and con-
tradicted themselves in order to establish their claim, the first reports
have often seemed suspect since. They seemed even more suspect
when there were obstinate rumours that the moa survived. It was no
longer possible to pretend to be the first to have seen bones or heard the
name, so perhaps people were looking for another claim to fame: to be
the first to see a living moa? The seed of scepticism was sown.


In 1842 Archdeacon Williams sent a vast quantity of moa bones
packed in huge wicker baskets to Dr Buckland, who gave them to the
Royal College of Surgeons. From these bones Sir Richard Owen was
able to reconstruct among other things the enormous legs of Dinornis


giganteus, which must, by his reckoning, have stood more than Io feet
high. He also established that there were at least four different species
of varying height and bulk. These were the conclusions of a second note
on the moa which Owen published in January 1843 in the Proceedings
of the Zoological Society.


Then moa bones were found in South Island for the first time, at the
mouth of the Waikouaiti, on thé north of the Otago peninsula, by Percy
Earle and Dr MacKellar. But the richest harvest of all was undoubtedly


that which Walter Mantell, Secretary for Crown Lands and son of the
famous geologist and palaeontologist Gideon Algernon Mantell, col-
lected on both islands between 1847 and 1850. It included no less than
1,000 separate bones and even pieces of the shells of huge eggs that
would have been as much as Io inches long. All these precious remains
were acquired by the British Museum of Natural History, and com-
pleted the rich material upon which Sir Richard Owen based his now
famous monograph On Dinornis. Among Mantell’s bones was the skele-


ton of a moa hardly 5 feet high, but so heavy and massive that Owen
called it Dinornis elephantopus (‘the terrible bird with elephant’s feet”).
Thus there were not only versions of attenuated giraffes and small
turkeys among the moas, but even of pachyderms.


But when did these legendary birds live?
Disregarding native


232


THE MOA, A FOSSIL THAT MAY STILL THRIVE


traditions completely, one can draw valuable conclusions from the bones
and from the geology of the material in which moas left their footprints.
Some of the disinterred bones are, it is true, unquestionably fossilised
and can be dated from the middle of the Miocene period some 15 to 35


million years ago. But most moa bones are in a sub-fossil state. That is


to say they have not had time to “petrify,” or be impregnated with


mineral salts.


The almost undecomposed state of the bones [writes von Hoch-
stetter], their occurrence in the sands of the sea-shore, in swamps,
forests, river-beds, and in limestone caves, together with bones of
animals still living in New Zealand, all this proves beyond the shadow
of a doubt, that those birds belong to the recent period of the earth, and
that their age can only be counted by hundreds, instead of thousands of
years.


As the Maoris had hardly settled in New Zealand two or three cen-
turies before it was sighted by Tasman in 1642, the relative freshness of
the bones is not enough to prove for certain whether man ever knew the
living moa. Moreover, in exceptional conditions bones may remain in


a sub-fossil state for as long as 20,000 or 30,000 years. We must there-
fore turn to the local traditions.


The legends that Polack collected, to say nothing of Colenso’s, hardly
indicate an intimate knowledge of the living bird. Nor does the devilish
and savage nature that the natives along the east coast attribute to the
moa agree with what one can infer about the bird’s habits, which must
have been more sluggish than the ostrich’s. Its description as a sort of
giant cock with a man’s face seems very fanciful. And the fact that the
Maoris attributed its footprint to legendary heroes or demigods seems


to prove that they could not have known it. These arguments drove a
New Zealander called H. Hill to conclude in 1914 that “not a single
Maori known to the missionaries and early settlers ever saw or heard of


a moa, or of its having been’seen by any of their ancestors.” According


to him everything that the natives said about the moa was a myth based


on the discovery of huge bones and on what they had learnt from white


men. He even went so far as to ask if the very word moa was not derived


from English. On 16 July 1912 Urupani Puhara, an old Maori chief of


88, had told him at Pakipani that:


The ‘“‘moa”’ was not the name by which the great bird that lived in
this country was known to my ancestors. The name was ““Te Kura,” or
the red bird; and it was only known as “moa’”’ after the pakehas [white
men] said so.


233


; THE LIVING FOSSILS OF OCEANIA


Hill consulted an expert on Maori folklore, Colonel P. Porter, c.B., of
Gisborne, who had an amusing version of the word’s origin that he had
heard from an educated half-caste: when the remains of the moa were


first discovered, the missionaries and other travellers pestered the
natives with demands for “more bones” which the Maoris had under-
stood as “‘moa bones,”’ taking “‘moa”’ to be the name of the vanished bird.
But Colonel Porter was sceptical of this tale, since he recalled a very old
proverb Ngaro a moa (lost like the moa), an odd Maori equivalent of “‘as
dead as the dodo.”


According to Berthold Seemann, the word moa in the Fijian form,


toa, means a domestic fowl, while the Polynesian name for a flying bird


is manumanu, and that since the Maoris used the word moa they must
have known that the moa could not fly and hence they knew the living
bird. Colenso aiso produced several convincing arguments that man and
the moa lived at the same time. The word moa appears in many names
of people and places: for instance Pukumoa (moa’s belly or entrails),
Taramoa (moa’s spur), Moawhanganui (moa long waited for), Tawake-
heimoa (Tawake able to yoke a moa). It is true that the word moa is
sometimes also used for a hairy waving flaccid and coarse growing sea-
side grass (Spinifex hirsutus) but it may well have been named after the
bird’s hairy plumage. And not only its leaves, but also a local variety of


flax (Phormium), which provides a textile fibre, are called raumoa or


*“‘moa’s feather.” However, it is clear enough that the personal and
place names mentioned above could not refer to a plant.


Colenso says that maimoa is the Maori word for the false birds that
they use as decoys for hunting. Perhaps their ancestors dressed in moa-
skins to deceive the huge birds into letting them come within striking
distance. The fact that ostriches seem to find it refreshing to open their
beaks wide into the wind may explain why the Maoris of the east coast
believed that the moa, which doubtless had similar habits, lived on
nothing but air. Colenso also tells us that moamoa or hamoamoa is the
native name for the little round and shiny stones that are sometimes
found in small heaps. It has since been discovered that these pebbles
come from moas’ stomachs. Their name shows that the Maoris knew


this fact long before we did, and evidently from direct observation.
Colenso, who did not have this last vital piece of evidence, concluded
that New Zealanders had known the moa until prehistoric times (long
before the beginning of their tribal history which went back twenty-five
generations, or about 500 years).


Hill came to exactly the opposite conclusion: that the moa died out

in the Pleistocene period, and probably at the beginning of it, between
300,000 and a million years ago. This is contrary to the palaeontological
evidence and betrays surprising ignorance of some aspects of the prob-
lem.


All the first reports about the moa—upon which Hill based his argu-
ments—came from North Island, and especially from the east coast. It
seems likely that the natives in this area did not know the moa directly.
But could they have known that the huge bones belonged to a bird?
They were not expert palaeontologists. One might argue that since


almost all the other animals on the islands were birds they would have


assumed it to be a bird, and the remains ofits eggs would have confirmed


the theory. For there is little doubt that the Maoris knew these eggs and


thought they had magical properties.


In 1865 a London naturalist called J. S. Stevens received from New
Zealand a Dinornis egg in almost perfect condition. According to the
Wellington newspapers this egg, which was 104 inches long by 7?
inches wide, had been discovered in an ancient tomb at Kaikoura in the


district of Marlborough. A human skeleton, in a sitting position, had
held the egg in its hands.


The natives could have deduced the bird’s existence from the same
evidence as white man, but how did they come to know what its plumage
was like? Polack, it will be recalled, refers to ““Atuas, covered with hair,
in the form of birds.” Of all the New Zealand birds only the kiwi has
feathers like silky hair, and it is incredible that the natives should have
known that the bones and eggs belonged to an outsize kiwi and not to
some other type of bird.


Thus everything tends to show that if the Maoris of the east coast of
North Island did not know the moa themselves or from their immediate
ancestors, their legends are still originally based on an exact description
of the bird. Other men must therefore have known it, travellers, per-
haps, from more southerly corners of New Zealand. And, indeed, when
Governor Fitzroy had a friendly meeting in 1844 with the Maoris at
Wellington at the very south of North Island he had to admit that they
knew the huge birds as well as one would expect these huntsmen to


know their favourite quarry which was now, alas, no more. Hauma-


tangi, an old Maori of 85 who boasted that he had seen Captain Cook in


1773 when he was only 14, said that he had seen a moa for the last time


two years before that memorable date. Kawana Papai, another no less


ancient native, maintained that he had himself taken part in moa-hunts


235


THE LIVING FOSSILS OF OCEANIA


on the Waimate plains in South Island some 50 years before. He gave
very exact details of this sport. The birds were rounded up, encircled
and then killed with spears—not an easy task or a safe one, since the
moa, like the ostrich, fought hard, laying about it with terrible blows of
its feet. The Maoris made use of the fact that it had to stand on one leg
in order to kick with the other. One party attacked it in front and
goaded it into lifting one leg while another party attacked the other leg
with long sticks from behind. The moa-hunters used special spears
which were designed to break off inside the bird’s body. Once dead, it
was cut up with an obsidian knife, and eaten at gargantuan feasts.


This seems to be confirmed by the fact that on both North Island and
South Island, Mantell and another naturalist called Cormack often
found mounds full of charred moa bones near native camps and settle-
ments, the remains, no doubt, of these meals.1 Thus, for the natives of
South Island and of the south of North Island, the moa, which might
weigh as much as a quarter of a ton, was as welcome in the larder as a
Christmas turkey, and became more and more appreciated as the game
grew scarcer. It aroused none of the terror that one finds in the tales
from the east coast of North Island, which perhaps had come from much
further south and been confused in the telling.


On South Island, not only have fresher remains of moas been found,
mummified pieces of the body, the skin and brownish feathers with
white tips still preserved, but much more widespread and detailed
native traditions have been collected. Von Hochstetter relates some of
the more common legends:

describes the land as the haunt of colossal birds. There are yet some

The birds being unable to swim, were driven towards a river or a

was imaginary or not, it could only have been invented by someone who
knew the moa’s habits very well. Hochstetter also cites from Maori


tales the use that was made of the moa:


The flesh and eggs were eaten; the feathers were employed as orna-
ment for the hair; the skulls were used for holding tattooing powder;
the bones were converted into fish-hooks, and the colossal eggs were
buried with the dead as provision during their long last journey to the
lower regions.


The Maoris said it had a brilliant plumage and a high crest on its head.
Altogether it looked like a huge Cochin cock, a fat, gallinaceous bird
with feathered legs. This apparently absurd description has been used


as evidence that the Maoris had never seen moas. Actually it is our
reconstruction that is more likely to be absurd. It is largely based on
one of the running birds still extant in Australia, the emu, which has
bare legs and sober greyish-brown plumage. But we have no proof that
some moas at least did not have brilliant plumage like that other Aus-


tralian bird, the cassowary. The brown feathers that have been found
may belong to females, usually duller in colour than the males. Why do
we always draw the moa with a bare neck like an ostrich, when it could
have been as thickly feathered as an emu’s, which would have com-
pletely altered its outline? And there is no evidence that the moa did
not have feathered legs like a Cochin hen and like the kiwi itself. Only


a fast-running bird of the plains has any advantage in bare legs, and the
moa was not one. In any case the largest moas were not built for run-
ning. Finally, the cranial structure of some of the Dinornithidae in-
dicates that they had a sort of crest on their heads, thus confirming the
Maoris’ picture.


Thus it seems that innumerable moas still lived in New Zealand when


it was first invaded by man. He came from the north, and both islands


would logically have been invaded from the north or north-west and


the moa would have been driven farther and farther to the south. On


both islands moa bones have been found in the largest quantities in the


south-east. Likewise North Island was almost certainly invaded before


South Island, and the moas were therefore exterminated there first. In


any case there is little doubt that most of the moas on North Island had


vanished 500 years before man arrived on the island, which explains why


the Maoris whom Cook questioned, in the north and west of the island,


had never heard of the bird. Perhaps a few isolated flocks of birds were

Colenso thought that the moa survived in South Island at the begin-

this theory. At the beginning of the nineteenth century American


sailors and sealers claimed to have seen monstrous birds 12 to 15 feet


high (an exaggeration, no doubt) running to and fro along the coast of


Cloudy Bay, on South Island, and on the inhospitable shores of the


south-west of that island. According to a letter from Taylor published

on South Island. Finally there is this report quoted from the Nelson

In June, while Messrs. Brunner and Maling, of the Survey Office,
were surveying on the ranges between Riwaka and Takaka, they ob-
served one morning the foot-prints of what appeared to be a very large
bird, whose track, however, was lost among the scrub and rocks. The
foot-prints were 14 inches in length, with a spread of 11 inches at the
points of the three toes. Similar foot-prints were seen on a subsequent
morning, and as the country is full of limestone-caves, it is thought that
a solitary Moa may yet be in existence.


Von Hochstetter did not believe all these stories. According to him


the largest living running bird in New Zealand was certainly a giant


Apteryx (Apteryx maxima), although actually no more is known about


this bird, which is included in the present fauna of New Zealand, than


about the supposedly extinct moas.


Three species of kiwis are well known today, although they are rarely
seen because of their nocturnal habits: Apteryx mantelli confined to
North Island, Apteryx australis confined to South Island, and Apteryx
oweni found in both. Where two kinds are found together the Maoris

The news in the Nelson Examiner came soon after the publication of
Darwin’s The Origin of Species, zoology was in fashion, and everyone
was interested to know if some primitive bird of the moa tribe still lived
in remote New Zealand mountains. Darwin himself had said it was

I do not believe that any bones of this mysterious large kiwi have ever
been found. There are only a few scraps of skin covered with feathers
which adorn a Maori chief’s ceremonial cloak.
So why have some:
authorities considered it as a member of the genus Apteryx? Kiwis
have no “spurs” or well-developed hind claws. Would it not therefore
be more likely to be a small moa, an Anomalopteryx for instance, which
was exactly the size of a turkey? Perhaps they preferred to call it an
Apteryx so that they could assert categorically that every moa was
extinct. But is it more reasonable to assert that there is a giant kiwi that
no one has ever seen?

and saw a party of natives there who gave him a circumstantial account

And one must accept the word of a man who was to become Prime
Minister of New Zealand. Indeed it is not impossible that much larger
moas may have survived until today. We know from Maori evidence
that they were shy birds that liked to be alone. It has always been sup-


posed that the Dinornithidae, like other running birds, preferred to live


in grassy plains. Actually they were a very varied family, large and


small, slender and squat. It is very likely that the different kinds had no


less different habitats, and that there were slim moas of the plains, little


moas of the forests, and heavy moas of the marshes—like the Madagas-


can Aepyornis. And some of them may well have taken refuge, like the


kiwi, in nocturnal habits. Nocturnal moas, living in forests, would have


a good chance of eluding all our searches.


The most encouraging tangible evidence is a discovery made by Dr
R. A. Falla in 1949. In a Maori fowler’s shelter in a confined valley
west of Lake Te Anau in the extreme south-west of South Island, he
found the broken and dismembered skeleton of a single Megalapteryx.
There were also unfaded feathers of wekas, kakapos and takahes, pre-
served flax sandals and weka snares, which could not haye been more
than two hundred years old, and may have been less than a hundred.


In 1950 an expedition of New Zealand and American scientists went
into the almost impenetrable forests around the fiords in the south-west
of South Island. There were reports that they had found some more
evidence that small moas had lived more recently than is generally ad-
mitted. There was never any official announcement to this effect. Per-
haps this was due to the reserve—or caginess bordering on timidity—
of zoologists nowadays; perhaps, too, they did not want to advertise this
thread of evidence until they had followed it up on another expedition.
There is still one honour to be won—to be the first to capture a living
moa.


That New Zealand can still hide an unknown animal of fair size is


strikingly proved by the story of another odd bird, the takahe. It is a


good story, but I have not room here for more than a brief summary.
The reader will find more details in Willy Ley’s Dragons in Amber.


When the moa-hunt first began in North Island, the Maoris often
mentioned another bird, the moho that they had formerly eaten, but it
had now vanished. It was as big as a goose, and it could not fly although


it had wings and feathers that looked like real feathers. But in all the


harvest of moa bones there was none of the less interesting moho, and
the bird was shelved with other Maori myths until 1847, when Walter

Hector found takahe tracks near Thompson Sound and by the central

And extinct it would have remained had not a dog come to the rescue
again. This dog was out rabbiting in the Province of Otago near the


fiords in December 1879 and brought back a takahe still breathing to its


master, who dispatched the bird and hung it from the ridge-pole of his


tent, intending to eat it. Fortunately the Station Manager, Connor, hap-


pened to pass the next day, and recognised it. He carefully prepared the


skin and skeleton of this rarest of birds and sent it to London. There it


was sold by auction and bought by the Dresden Museum—to the dis-


may of the curators of the British Museum, who had told their man “‘to


bid as much as 100 pounds sterling for it.”” The Germans had bought it


for £105.


A detailed examination of the first complete skeleton of a takahe at
Dresden showed that it differed noticeably from that of the moho found


at Waingongoro. The new species was called Notornis hochstetteri as a
consolation prize for the scientist who had searched so hard to find it,
and with so little luck.


Then the takahe played hide and seek for another 20 years. Nothing
was found except an incomplete skeleton in 1884 and a complete
one in 1892—both near Lake Te Anau. They knew where to look,
but the best-organised hunts still yielded nothing. The country was
marshy and covered with thick bush, where a bird could easily hide and


a man could hardly go.


The next live takahe, in 1898, was once again caught by a dog, whose


master, a Mr Ross, recognised the bird and preserved it entire—viscera


and all. This specimen, the only one in the world, was sold for £250


to the New Zealand Government, who offered it to the Dunedin


Museum.


Then half a century went by without a sign of the takahe (whose
name means “the wandering one” or “the one that wanders at large”).


It seemed ta the world of science as if Mr Ross’s specimen really was the


last Notornis. There were, it is true, still vague rumours about foot-
prints in the snow and reports from old Maoris who said that the birds


lived in the mountains and only rarely came down near the lakes. But


these tales were of just the sort that most zoologists obstinately refuse to

notice. This book is full of animals known only from their footprints
and from native legends: evidence that is always greeted with amused
disbelief. The story of the takahe shows how exaggerated and unjusti-
fied this scepticism is. Every time that this bird managed to avoid its
hunters—and their dogs—for a decade the authorities decided that it
must be extinct.


By 1947, just a century after Walter Mantell had proved the existence
—or former existence—of Notornis, only four living specimens of the
bird had been found and there seemed little hope of seeing a takahe
again. But Geoffrey Orbell, a doctor at Invercargill, was undaunted, and
optimistically set off with several companions into the thick forests on
the eastern shore of Lake Te Anau. Three thousand feet up in the
mountains he was surprised to find a small lake which scouts had told
him of, although it did not appear on any map. This lake was well
known in Maori tradition as Kohaka-takahea—“‘‘the nesting-place of the
wandering one.” If one could still discover a whole new lake in this
country, surely there was hope of finding something so inconspicuous as


a bird that could not fly? They had no such luck. They heard unusual
bird-cries and found fresh footprints that might have been made by


their quarry. But no takahe. Dr Orbell was not discouraged. He re-
turned to the place in November 1948, loaded with cameras and ciné-
cameras. His optimism was rewarded. Two takahes were caught in a
single snare. They were tethered by one leg, photographed from every
possible angle, and then released.


A year later Dr Orbell’s third expedition was able to establish several


facts about the takahe’s habits. It was purely vegetarian, it built its nest


level with the ground, and seemed to have only one young one—which
was quite black—a year. A dozen adults were seen. The population of
two colonies in neighbouring valleys was estimated at between 50 and
100.


If it had not been for dogs, which could find the birds when they were
invisible in high forest and scrub, we should pfobably still be unaware
of the takahe. There is therefore all the more reason to think that the
moa may survive. And Dr Orbell, encouraged by his success, has set
about trying to capture a living Megalapteryx. The sceptics will object
that the takahe never vanished for very long, but that the moa has been
lost for a century or two. The recent resurrection of the cahow should
answer this objection.

PASCAL.


PASCAL was exaggerating, of course, but his hyperbole would have
been literally true of those much less conspicuous organs, the waitoreke’s


teats. This animal, which has such cataclysmic implications, is a shy
and ordinary-looking little beast. But it seems to be a mammal, and it


is reported in New Zealand, the only country in the world, apart from
small islands, that contains no indigenous mammals. There is geological
evidence that New Zealand was joined to Australia only until the Jur-


assic period, when reptiles still ruled the world, and was cut off before
the marsupial invasion in the middle of the following period; and there


is the argument that not a single species of indigenous mammal has been
found in New Zealand. If it should turn out that a hitherto undis-
covered animal with teats inhabits that country, palaeogeographical re-
constructions would have to be completely revised and the date of sub-
mergence of certain continental bridges would have to be changed by
several tens of millions of years. For the waitoreke to reach New Zealand
dryshod, the sea would have to have parted, as the Red Sea did for
Moses, and closed again behind it in time to stop the advancing mar-


supials. Thus the face of the world at the beginning of the Cretaceous
period literally depends on whether the waitoreke was
a mammal. But
was it? The creature is certainly supposed to have fur—but in this part
of the world even birds, like the kiwi and moa, look as if they are covered
with hair.


Such a puzzling creature with such revolutionary implications might
be expected to arouse the constant and active curiosity of zoologists.

WAITOREKE, THE IMPOSSIBLE NEW ZEALAND MAMMAL


Actually most specialists have never even heard its name, and those who
have find it simpler to ignore the problems that it implies by denying its
existence out of hand. Nevertheless the waitoreke has good credentials.
In about 1850 Walter Mantell first heard of a mammal which he


called kaureke, He was the son of a famous scientist and was a respon-


sible man, destined to take an important part in New Zealand politics
—not one to spread tall stories. When he was camping at Arowhena,


not far from the present-day coastal town of Timaru on South Island,


the Maoris told him that the kaureke was found some 10 miles inland.


It was a very rare animal, they said, and because of its nocturnal habits


there was little chance of seeing it. But its fur was very light in colour,


almost white, and they said they had several times had a glimpse of it at


its drinking-places. Mantell at once offered a large reward. The Maoris


set off into the heart of the country, but eventually came back empty-


handed. They would not have hunted so hard for a mythical animal.


Their good faith was plain enough, Mantell told his father, adding that


the beast might be extinct, but if so it had only died out recently. A


few years later much more was heard of the creature, and the informa-


tion was far more detailed.
In his great work on New Zealand, first published in 1863, Ferdinand


von Hochstetter is quite explicit:


From certain terms occurring in the Maori language, and from the


most recent observations we may infer beyond a doubt, that New
Zealand still harbours some few sporadic mammalia, which have thus
far escaped the searching eye of science....


After reviewing the Maori names for the various mammals (pekapeka
the bat, kiore the little native rat and kararehe the native dog), which
could all have reached New Zealand after it was cut off, he remarks:


Besides these names we find the name Waitoreke, which has been
only lately clearly defined, having been hitherto applied sometimes to an
otter-like, and sometimes to a seal-like animal. According to the reports
of Dr. J. Haast, the existence of this animal has been recently estab-
lished beyond a doubt; it lives in the rivers and lakes in the mountain


ranges of the South Island, is of the size of a large cony with a glossy
brown fur, and is probably to be classed with the otters.


This information was based on a letter of 6 June 1861 from Dr
Julius Haast, who wrote:

There is so little likeness between the kaureke (whitish and seen at its
drinking-places) and the waitoreke (dark brown and aquatic) that one
may well wonder whether they are not two different animals, or the


first a distorted hearsay version of the second. Certainly we have more
information about the second, which has been reported by white wit-
nesses, so let us concentrate upon it for the moment. As far as I know
nobody has met either animal since.


The description of the waitoreke, vague though it is, reminds me of
three separate creatures. First one thinks of the Australian bunyip which


is sometimes described as a seal, sometimes as an otter. But the bunyip is
too problematical to be used to explain another problem. Then, like von
Hochstetter, one is reminded of an otter—yet how.could a placentary
mammal like an otter have reached New Zealand when Australia, the
previous stage in the colonisation of Oceania, contains nothing but
marsupials? If it is a true otter it could have come by sea, for there is a
purely maritime species: the sea-otter (Enhydra lutris). It sleeps in the
open sea, floating on its back, in which position it usually swims. It
does not even land—as the seals do—in the breeding season. It mates
and gives birth in the sea. When its young are too small to swim under
their own steam it carries them on its belly.


This large animal is much hunted for its fur and has consequently
become much rarer. Now it is said to be found only around the Aleu-


tians and other North Pacific Islands; but in 1938 a pack of 400 were
seen swimming down the Californian coast, and the Marquis de Chat-
teleux, that indefatigable. globe-trotter who signs his travel-books

“Stany,” says he has seen large numbers along the coast of southern
Chile, which seems to imply an extraordinarily long migration.


If this was possible on the east of the Pacific, it could also have hap-
pened on the west, and the sea-otter could thus have reached New
Zealand. It would have been a more hazardous voyage, for after visiting


all the archipelagos between the Kuriles and the New Hebrides—Japan,}
the Philippines and New Guinea—the sea-otter would have had to cross


a wide stretch of sea without a single landmark on the way. It could, of


course, have been driven there involuntarily by the Equatorial Current


from the New Hebrides, that washes the east coast of Australia, turns a


half-circle and warms the west coast of New Zealand. Once the sea-


otter had reached New Zealand waters it could not have returned against


the current, and could easily have given up its migratory habits and


made its way up the rivers to live like its ancestors in fresh water. All


this is pure hypothesis—but only a hypothesis can explain the waitoreke.


Perhaps it might be some kind of platypus. The Australian animal is
very like an otter, and it would not have so far to come as the sea-otter.
To find it—or a relative—in New Zealand would fit in with the family


tree of the mammals and the geography of past ages.


It is wrong to try—as many authors do—to derive each group of
mammals by direct descent from another. The monotremes, marsu-
pials and placentals should be considered as three separate and succes-


sive attempts with varying success at a type of vertebrate with a constant
temperature and able to suckle its young.


The marsupials have often been considered to be the ancestors of the
placentals [writes Jean Piveteau, Professor of Palaeontology at the
Sorbonne]. An anatomical study free of all preconceived ideas shows
that they are nothing of the kind. These two great subdivisions of
mammals developed independently of one another, while still remaining
closely parallel in their adaptations.


At first sight the oviparous monotremes, which have many reptilian


features, look as if they derive from the reptiles, rather than from the


amphibians, the probable ancestors of the other mammals. But a study


of their brain, heart and diaphragm shows that they are indeed true


mammals, but have diverged very early from the original stock and


become very specialised along peculiar lines.


Be that as it may, the three groups of mammals certainly grew and

expanded at quite different periods—as is usual with rival types. There


is not the least doubt that the marsupials spread and flourished before
the placentals. But practically nothing is known of the monotremes’
ancestors. The most one can say is that there was a great crop of repti-
lian mammals (or mammalian reptiles) in the Jurassic period, and that
the monotremes were probably among them. During the Age of Rep-


tiles they could have spread across the world from Asia to Australia and
thence to New Zealand, which were then all connected, without being
noticed much, although the reptile empire would still have been able to
crush any rising of true mammals. If there is an indigenous mammal in
New Zealand which has been there ever since the islands were cut off,
there is a good chance that it is a monotreme. And as it is supposed to
look like an otter—that is to say like a platypus—the most likely theory
is that it is one of this creature’s close relatives. The distribution of the
three groups of mammals would then fit in perfectly with the geological

have been in the Jurassic period. Then in the middle of the Cretaceous
the rising tide of marsupials swept them off the earth except for a few


rare species in Australia and New Guinea, and one, the waitoreke, which
escaped when New Zealand was cut off. Finally the placentals, at the
end of the Cretaceous and beginning of the Eocene periods ousted all
the marsupials but a few in South and Central America and the
Southern States of the U.S.A., from everywhere except the now isolated
countries of New Guinea and Australia.


If, despite all this theorising, it should turn out that the wazitoreke is
neither a sea-otter nor a monotreme, it must have been introduced by
the Maoris when they came to New Zealand. But while it is easy to see
how they carried dogs on purpose and rats by accident it is hard to
understand how they could have brought this strange animal, let it run
wild and then forgotten that they had done so. If the waitoreke is not a
myth it is certainly the devil ofa puzzle.

CHAPTER TWELVE


The Patagonian Giant Sloth


Only one fault he had, which cock-robins have likewise .
.
. that when any
one else found a curious worm, he would hop round them, and peck them,
and set up his tail, and bristle up his feathers, just as a cock-robin would;
and declare that he found the worm first; and that it was his worm: and,
if not, that then it was not a worm at all.


CHARLES KINGSLEY, The Water-Babies.


THE conquistadors who first discovered Central and South America
must have been disappointed to find that although the fauna was so rich
and new, there were no monsters. From the beginning, naturalists have
seen the so-called neo-tropical zone, which stretches from Mexico and
the West Indies to the very tip of South America, as a region of small
animals. The llama, the tallest of its quadrupeds, is merely a rather
thin, humpless small camel, a dwarf compared to a giraffe. The deer


are small and have small horns, the tiny pudu standing only 144 inches


at the shoulder. The tapir, the most massive of the indigenous mam-
mals, is far from the size of its distant African cousins the elephant and
the rhinoceros. The peccary is merely a miniature wild boar. The
jaguar and the puma or cougar are smaller than the lion and tiger.
There is only one bear, the spectacled bear (Tremarctos ornatus), which


lives in the Equatorial Andes of Bolivia and Chile, and it is small in
height and bulk. None of the monkeys is as big as a gorilla or orang-
utan. And the pygmy marmoset (Cebuella pygmaea) is so small that
you can hold it all in the palm of your hand.


Among the birds the phenomenon is less obvious, for South America
can boast one of the largest living flying birds: the condor of the
Andes (Vultur gryphus), which disputes the title with the wandering
albatross, is 4 feet long and its wing-span may exceed ro feet. But the


rhea, the largest South American running bird, is at least a third smaller


253


RIDDLES OF THE GREEN CONTINENT


than an ostrich, and the most typical neo-tropical birds are the family
of humming-birds (Trochilidae) which are found only in America.


On the other hand, the orders of mammals that are usually small are
relative giants in Central and South America. All the largest rodents


are found there—the subungulates as they are called, the paca, agouti
and the capybara, a sort of huge guinea-pig 3 feet long with webbed toes
and weighing as much as 150 pounds. Among the insectivores there is
the very rare almiqui (Solenodon paradoxus) of Cuba and Haiti which
looks like a shrew with big ears but is as large as a rabbit. Its tail alone


is 8 inches long. And there are giants among almost all the groups of
smaller animals, particularly the insects. Some South American Lepidop-
tera—the Atlas moth (Coscinocera hercules), for instance—have a wing
span of over 13 inches. There are wasps and ants (the terrible tucandera,
for example) which are the size of mice; and the largest of the spiders, a
tarantula (Gramostola), is 10} inches across (the body alone is 34 inches
across) and is not afraid to attack chickens and snakes and sometimes
even succeeds in bleeding a rabbit to death.


There is, however, one group of mammals in the neo-tropical zone
which cannot be compared with those in other zones, for they are pecu-


liar to it: the Xenarthra, consisting of the anteaters, sloths and arma-


dillos.1 These creatures, which are odd in more than one respect, vary
considerably in size. The giant anteater (Myrmecophaga jubata) is
sometimes nearly 8 feet long—thanks to its enormous plume of a tail
which is as long as the rest of its body. The pygmy anteater (Cyclopes
didactylus) is hardly as big as a squirrel. The armadillos range from the
giant armadillo (Priodontes gigas), 5 feet long, to the pichiciago (Chlamy-
phorus truncatus), a mere 6 inches. The sloths, the most phlegmatic of
mammals, are never larger than a young chimpanzee.


As a general rule the animals in the neo-tropical zone are fairly small.
So, even though much of South America is still unexplored, one is not
inclined a priori to put much credit in certain legends there about quite
enormous beasts.

a description, very vague it must be admitted, of a large nocturnal

It is a large heavy beast, as big as an ox but with shorter legs and
covered with thick short coarse hair. Its appearance is very frightening.


It is armed with enormous hooked claws, just like an anteater’s, with
which it digs a huge burrow, where it sleeps all day: that is why it is
hardly ever seen. According to some versions its habits are amphibious.
There is some doubt whether it is savage or not, but all agree that it
cannot be harmed by arrows or bullets, and oddly enough, this last
fabulous-looking characteristic is the best evidence that the monster is
not a fable.


The a prior reasons for discounting such tales are somewhat weak-
ened when one learns that South America was not always inhabited only
by relatively small mammals. The first irrefutable proof of.this was
established in 1789, when gigantic bones which seemed to belong to an
animal almost as large as an elephant were found in mud on the banks
of the Rio Luyan not far from Buenos Aires. The peons were the only
people not to be surprised at this discovery: it was a giant mole, they


said, which died whenever it had the misfortune to be exposed to sun-


light.1 This naive explanation satisfied no one else, so the Marquis of
Loreto, then Viceroy of the colony, had the bones sent to King Charles
IV of Spain, who presented them to the Royal Museum of Madrid,
where they were entrusted to José Garriga. This naturalist at once set

He used to talk about all kinds of sciences [wrote de Blainville], and

studied them; for this it was enough to have had a conversation with the
specialists or to have read some of the notes that they had written, and
he had the art of connecting and linking everything together making it
so wonderfully interesting that one would have thought that he under-
stood the subject thoroughly.


This facility coupled with ambition and utter lack of humility led

THE PATAGONIAN GIANT SLOTH


It would be very hard to find the causes of its destruction in its struc-
ture alone; but if it still existed, where could it have hidden from all the
searches of hunters and naturalists?


Its similarities relate it to several kinds of edentates. It has the head
and shoulders of the sloths. The legs and feet provide a strange mix-
ture of characteristics belonging to the anteaters and the armadillos.


We can now see that there is nothing monstrous in this mixture, since


all the ingredients come from very closely related animals. But everyone
was surprised at the size of this South American animal. When it stood
on its hind-legs it was about 15 feet high.


Unlike present-day sloths, it could not have lived in trees. From all
W/


71. Reconstruction of the Megatherium.


that we now know about it, it seems to have been a sort of huge and
hairy bear, armed with terrible claws like so many sickles. It must have
usually stood upon its hind-legs. Its heavy and powerful tail, the struc-
ture of its pelvis and hind-legs forming an enormous supporting base,
the type of articulation of its vertebrae, all show a clear tendency to an
upright posture. Subsequently, at Carson City in Nevada, huge foot-
prints, 18 inches long by 8 inches wide, were found to confirm this


theory.1 If the creature sometimes put its fore-feet on the ground (like

the kangaroo when it walks without jumping), it must have been so

The Megatherium’s great height enabled it to feed on the foliage
of


trees, hooking its claws firmly on to their branches so that it could
browse lazily with the least effort. With its powerful claws it must even
have been able to uproot taller trees so that it could graze on their


leaves. Certainly it was strong enough to do so, but if it was as indolent


as its little nephews the ai and the unau, it might well have scorned the


effort.


Naturalists were so impressed by the size and strangeness of this
creature that at the end of the eighteenth century and for most of the
nineteenth they did not dream that it could possibly have survived until
our time. In Europe the large animals, like the ancient elephant, the
mammoth and the rhinoceros, had been extinct since a geological era
which according to Cuvier’s Theory of Revolutions of the Globe had
preceded our own. On this analogy the Megatherium was thought to
have perished in the Tertiary era. Man could never have known this
monster of a past age.


This did not prevent King Charles IV from being so struck by the
description of the animal that he at once ordered the officials of his
transatlantic colony to send him one dead or alive. Several generations
of scientists laughed at the King’s folly. But since then much evidence
has shown that the King was nearer to the truth than the scientists.
Today no zoologist dare swear that it was impossible to grant at least
part of the King’s wish and send him the body not of an actual Mega-
therium, but of a relative almost as large. For the Megatherium is not
the only giant in the group of sloths, which collectively are known as
gravigrades.
In pampean and even in post-pampean deposits they
were represented by a whole series of giants, among which were the
Mylodons (Mylodon, Glossotherium, Grypotherium) which were very like
the Megatherium, except that they were about the size of an ox and had
much longer tails.


The Tehuelche Indians’ legend seems much less absurd than it did


at first. But other evidence was soon to give it a peculiar weight. Little
by little as the years went by it became evident that the giant gravi-
grades, though huge and fantastic, were not such old fossils as the extinct
‘pachyderms in Europe. And scientists eventually had to admit that
the mammoth and the rhinoceros had been contemporary with man
during the Quaternary era, when pictures of them were found in caves.

THE PATAGONIAN GIANT SLOTH


Given the clearly recent date of the pampean deposits, to say nothing of
the post-pampean, in which the remains of the Megatherium and other
no less impressive creatures were found, they could only date from the
very latest geological period, either the Upper Pleistocene or even the
present period, the Holocene. That is to say they lived less than 30,000


years ago. But as it was almost universally believed that man did not


invade America, by way of the Bering Strait, until quite recently—


between 2,000 and 20,000 years ago according to various estimates (and


in the nineteenth century scientists inclined to the shorter period 1)—no


one thought at first that human beings could have known these monsters.
And no prehistorian had ever been able to show the smallest drawing of


the giant edentates comparable to the French cave-paintings of mam-


moths and reindeer.


In 1870, however, the first evidence was found that man in South
America had been contemporary with some of the vanished gravigrades.
In a terrace of the little valley of the Rio Frias near Mercedes the famous
Argentine palaeontologist Florentino Ameghino discovered some very
decomposed human bones, and with them were some cut stones, char-
coal and some animal bones that had been pierced or incised, the re-
mains of another huge monster: the Glyptodon (see illustration on page
303). This was not a giant sloth but a giant armadillo that had evolved
a rigid carapace like a tortoise’s shell, which alone was sometimes as
much as 12 feet long. Everything outside this armoured dome was
covered with plates, and in one of them (Doedicurus) the massive tail
ended in a spiny ball like a mediaeval mace. It was a living tank.


In 1881, near the Rio Arrecifer, Professor Santiago Roth found in
deposits at Fontezuelas an almost complete human skeleton curled up
under, or at least very near to, a Glyptodon’s carapace. Further similar
finds—carapaces that had been tipped up or turned over by man;
worked flints and traces of hearths under these animal cupolas—soon
showed that the first South Americans used Glyptodon carapaces either


as houses or as tombs.


I need hardly say that these discoveries, which flatly contradicted the
accepted theories of the day, were bitterly disputed. Anthropologists


refused to believe that man could have come to America as early as the


date when giant edentates were supposed to have lived. Palaeontologists

most.”—Boule and Vallois, Les Hommes Fossiles, 4th ed., 1952.

denied that these creatures could have survived so Jate as man’s arrival

It could no longer be pretended—somewhat disingenuously—that
recent Indians had merely been using fossil carapaces, when the
charred bones of gravigrades were dug up and found to bear marks of
crude implements it was clear that after cutting off the meat the Indians
had split the bones to get at the marrow. And one day a giant sloth’s
skeleton was found at the bottom of what had once been a pit in a posi-
tion which made it possible to reconstruct exactly how it had died. The
four legs were still complete, but all the middle of the body had been
more or less destroyed and had been replaced by charcoal and ashes.
Obviously the sloth had been trapped in the pit, and as they were unable


to get it out the Indians had roasted it im situ by lighting a fire under its


belly.


There was now no doubt that the Megatherium had lived at the same
time as man. But for how long had it continued to do so? Man’s first
migrations in Alaska, according to the most exact estimates, seem to
have happened about 12,000 years ago, around 10,000 B.c, But when
did the first men reach the very tip of South America? Several thousand
years later, no-doubt—let us say 7,000 B.c.1 Thus the first American
Indians could equally well have caught giant edentates and eaten their
flesh in historical times or several thousand years earlier. The date the
monsters had become extinct was still very much in doubt—if they really
were extinct. No one, it is true, has yet killed one or shown one in a
zoo, but Patagonia is huge and little known, especially the almost
fathomless boscosa, the forest region between the pampas and the Cor-


dillera of the Andes. And there was still the Tehuelche legend.


Then, in 1898, someone brought Professor Florentino Ameghino, of
the Buenos Aires Museum, a lot of little bones the size of beans from
southern Patagonia and asked him what animal they could have come
from. They had been extracted from a piece of leather ? inch thick and
covered with long reddish-grey hairs in which they had been embedded


like small cobbles in a road. This skin belonged without the slightest
doubt to a large ground-sloth, and Ameghino was even able to deter-
mine its origin more exactly. It was already known from palaeonto-

Lista had seen must have been a quite different animal. But this does


not necessarily follow, since even a rhinoceros is no bigger than a calf


at one stage of its existence. Finally he pronounced that the animal was


certainly no longer extant:


It is absolutely impossible to think that this animal, if it was still
among living beings, could have eluded the sharp eyes of the native
Indians.
Even if it had exclusively nocturnal habits, and hid itself
during the daytime in the most desolate places, the hunting Indians
must have come across it now and then, and they must certainly have
observed its tracks, its traces where it had broken off branches and
twigs when feeding, its scratchings or diggings in the earth, its excre-
ments, etc.

Dr Moreno, who had to go to England at that time, took with him the
square of skin, and on 17 January 1899 showed it to the members of the
Zoological Society of London, who could hardly contain their excite-
ment. Nevertheless he claimed not to be astonished by his examination
of the skin, which was obviously fresh and had been cut off by human
hands. For it had now been established that Mylodons were contem-
porary with man farther north in the Argentine. Moreover Moreno had
himself found in a neighbouring cave another mummified body, also
very well preserved, of a man of an extinct race quite unknown to the
Tehuelche who now inhabited the area. He therefore maintained, with
Professor Seeley’s support, that the Mylodon’s skin could have remained
in an apparently fresh state untold ages, just like the moa’s skin and
feathers.}


The whole meeting disagreed with this view, and were sure that the
skin belonged to a recently dead animal; it was still fairly supple, and
one could see remains of muscles and ligaments and a “‘coating of dried
serum was still preserved on the old cut edges,” as Sir Arthur Smith

Portugal. Even in the Pleistocene period no traces of this rodent are found
south of England.

It was at this point that Professor Ameghino’s second note appeared.
After remarking that the Tehuelche name for the strange quadruped he
had already mentioned was iemisch, or in Spanish tigre de agua (water-


tiger), he said that he was now in a position to reveal more about this


creature, thanks to the discoveries of his brother Carlos, who for two


years had been constantly travelling in Patagonia collecting fossils and


doing geological research. In the middle of the previous year, 1897, he


had written to Ameghino as follows, sending him several little bones:


I have at last obtained some valuable data about the famous iemisch,
which is not a myth as we imagined but actually exists. I have seen in
an Indian’s hands a piece of the iemisch’s skin in which were embedded
the little bones that I am sending you, similar to those we have found
in a fossil state with Mylodons’ skeletons. Moreover Hompen, another
Tehuelche Indian, has told me that when he was going from Senguer
to Santa Cruz he had met a temisch on the road which had barred his
way: he opened fire and shot it dead. According to the Indians the
animal is amphibious and walks as easily on dry land as it swims in the
water. Today it is confined to the centre of Patagonia, in caves and
lairs on the banks of Lakes Colhué, Fontana, and Buenos Aires, and the
Rivers Senguer, Aysen, Huemules etc.
But according to tradition, it
once spread north as far as the Rio Negro; and in the south, as old
Indians recall, it used to live in all the lakes on the eastern slopes of the
Andes, right down to the Straits of Magellan. Thus, around the middle
of the century, a iemisch, which had come down from lakes in the Andes
by the Rio Santa Cruz, landed on the northern bank of this river near
Pavon island. The terrified Indians fled into the interior, and as the
only reminder of its inopportune arrival gave the deserted place the
name it still bears today: Jemisch Aiken (that is, ‘‘temisch’s harbour or
port of call’’). This animal is of nocturnal habits, and it is said to be so
strong that it can seize horses with its claws and drag them to the bottom
of the water. According to the description I have been given, it has a
short head, big canine teeth, and no external ears; its feet are short and


plantigrade, with three toes on the fore-feet and four on the hind; +


these toes are joined by a membrane for swimming,
and are also armed


with formidable claws. Its tail is long, flat, and prehensile. Its body is


covered with short hair, coarse and stiff, of a uniform bay colour. Its


size is said to be larger than a puma’s, but its paws are shorter and its
body thicker.
