Professor Ameghino seems to have gone completely astray in accept-
ing this theory of his brother’s that the armoured skin came from the
Patagonians’ iemisch, which hardly agrees with one’s idea of a ground-
sloth like a Mylodon. A monster of this kind might have been rather
frightening because of its enormous size and impressive claws, but it is
too much to believe that this undoubted vegetarian seized horses and
drowned them. It is especially suspicious that a vegetarian should have
canine teeth, or indeed that an edentate should have ordinary teeth
that looked like canines. The iemisch’s alleged amphibious habits—
which its webbed feet confirm—are a long way from the traditional pic-
ture of the Mylodon, not that a creature’s habits are necessarily certain
from its skeleton. Several large vegetarians, like the tapir and hippo-
potamus, lead an amphibious life, although nothing in their skeletons
betrays the fact. It would be very strange for a water animal to have
huge burrowing claws—but it would not be the first paradoxical feature
in an animal. More information about the Mylodon’s habits was needed.


Meanwhile several more scientific expeditions had been to the Cueva
Eberhardt.


The first consisted of Swedish scientists, led by Erland Nordenskjéld,
cousin of the Otto already mentioned, who excavated the cave and
brought back a large quantity of the little bones mixed with dung and
finely chopped hay which constituted the soil in the place where the
skin had been found. After a very thorough comparative study Norden-
skjéld remarked that the little bones and the skin itself could be attri-
buted to aknown Mylodon, Glossotherium darwini, whose fossil remains
had been found in pampean deposits and described by Sir Richard
Owen. Assuming, for lack of information to the contrary, that Ameghi-
no’s bones had come from the Cueva Eberhardt, his name of Neomylo-
don listai was a needless synonym for Glossotherium darwini. This was a
blow to the professor, who had a passion for naming animals, and had
baptised such astronomical numbers, especially of fossils, sometimes
hastily and often mistakenly, that many palaeontologists refused to
accept his names for them. I am not surprised that after Nordenskjéld’s
statement he should have hastened to publish his second note to prove


that his bones had not come from the Cueva Eberhardt; and I should
point out that whereas in his original note he said that he had received
them from someone who asked him what animal they could have come
from, in the second note his brother tells him what animal he thinks
they came from.

The peculiar arrangement of the place, the skeleton that Eberhardt
and his companions had already found there, the kitchen midden, the
various walls, the heaps of dung and fodder, 3 feet deep in some places,


all seemed to show that giant sloths had been kept alive in this special
enclosed part of the cave. The excrements were obviously those of a
large animal, since the best-preserved ones had kept their shape and
were almost as large as an elephant’s. Moreover, an examination of the
skull of a sloth revealed that man must have brained it with large stones.
Clean-cut bones showed that the beasts had then been dismembered
with sharp cutting-tools and were, of course, finally eaten.


The men who lived there ages ago [concludes Dr Hauthal] were
accustomed to stable their domestic animals in this part of the cavern,
reserving the rest for their own dwelling place.


It seemed indisputable that giant sloths were kept alive in the cave.
Subsequent analysis of the excrements by a British expert called Spencer
Moore showed that the animal’s food was too cleanly cut at the end to
have been done only by its blunt teeth. It must have eaten fodder that
had been reaped by man.


Can one call these sloths true domestic animals? Dr Nehring and
other scientists think not. Is it not more reasonable to suppose that the
Mylodons were accidentally caught in the cave and that the Indians kept
them prisoner as a supply of fresh meat? Or rather, since the depth of
dung shows that a series of sloths were stabled there, that the Indians
were in the habit of catching them and keeping them alive as a reserve
in case food ran short? The most likely, considering the prodigious
strength of these animals, which, though not savage, were well armed,


is that men used to drive them into such caves, just as in India wild
elephants are caught by driving them into stockades. This is far more
probable than that they were really domesticated. No species of animal


is less likely to become extinct than a domesticated one—and with good


268


THE PATAGONIAN GIANT SLOTH


reason. If the sloths were actually domesticated by the Indians—that


is to say they bred in captivity—why does this happen no longer? No
other instance is known of an animal which has ceased to be domes-


ticated, and it is hard to see why anyone should abandon such an
advance so useful to a people who live in dry plains where famine always


threatens. But whether truly domestic or not, the giant sloths certainly


lived side by side with men who fed them with grass, leaves and roots.
This does not in the least agree with the terrifying description of the


Tehuelches’ monstrous iemisch.


The bitter controversy between the various factions about the beast’s
nomenclature and classification, too complex to be explained in detail
here, was complicated even further when Dr Santiago Roth, Hauthal’s
colleague, took the fatal step of dragging in the native word iemisch and
using it as a scientific name for the large carnivore, the end of whose
femur had been found in the dung in the Cueva Eberhardt, justifying
himself thus:


This animal coincides in part with the description that Ameghino
gives of the Neomylodon, even if it does not agree entirely, and I pro-
pose to give it the specific name of listai, replacing the generic name of
Neomylodon, which is not adequate, by that of Iemisch.


This habit of deducing an entire animal from no more than the re-
mains of a femur is all too frequent among palaeontologists misled by
Cuvier’s principle that “any sort of creature can, strictly speaking, be
recognised by any fragment of any of its parts.” Cuvier himself was led
wildly astray by it, mistaking some pieces of a dinosaur first for those
of a rhinoceros and then a hippopotamus. And as to this femur, it was


at first thought by Sir Arthur Smith Woodward to belong to a fossil bear
(Arctotherium) and finally attributed by Erland Nordenskjéld to a large
jaguar many of whose bones he had found in the Cueva Eberhardt.
Professor Roth was still firmly convinced that his own temisch was the
origin of the Tehuelche legend, remarking:


It is very probable that it lived at a not very distant period, on the
banks of lakes and rivers in the Andes and that it was the tiger
nahuel, which gave its name to Lake Nahuel-Huapi.


Although certain cats swim very well, like the jaguar, for example,
which prefers to live near rivers and lagoons, I do not think, however,
that there can have been a species of the Felidae which dwelt both in
the water and on land.

In his

In the deepest waters there usually hides an animal larger than any
hunting-dog, called tigre de agua by the Spaniards and yaguaro by the
Guaranis.
It has a woolly hide, a long and tapering tail, and powerful
claws. Horses and mules swimming across these rivers are dragged to

Soon afterwards one sees the intestines of the animal,
disembowelled by the tiger, floating on the surface.


A similar, but more detailed, description, is found in a book by an-
other Jesuit, Thomas Falkner, A Description of Patagonia, and the
Adjoining Parts of South America, 1774:


In my first voyage to cut timber, in the year 1752, up the Parana, be-
ing near the bank, the Indians shouted yaquaru, and looking, I saw a
great animal, at the time it plunged into the water from the bank; but
the time was too short, to examine it with any degree of perfection.


It is called yaquaru, or yaquaruigh, which (in the language of that
country) signifies, the water tiger. It is described by the Indians to be
as big as an ass; of the figure the size of a large, over-grown river-wolf 1
or otter; with sharp talons, and strong tusks; thick and short legs; long,
shaggy hair; with a long, tapering tail.


The Spaniards describe it somewhat differently; as having a long
head, a sharp nose, like that of a wolf, and stiff, erect ears...


It is very destructive to the cattle which pass the Parana;
for great
herds of them pass every year; and it generally happens that this beast
seizes some of them. When it has once laid hold of it’s prey, it is seen
no more; and the lungs and entrails soon appear floating upon the
water.


It lives in the greatest depths, especially in the whirlpools made by
the concurrence of two streams, and sleeps in the deep caverns that are
in the banks.


That the jaguar should be described as an amphibious animal is not at


all surprising. Its habits may not be so aquatic as the otter’s, but it is an
excellent swimmer, always ready to leap into the water to catch its prey


(especially otters) or to flee from danger. The great naturalist Felix
de Azara in his Apuntamientos para Historia Natural de los Quadrupedos


1 “River-wolves” writes Father Falkner elsewhere, “(which I take to be of

de Paraguay y Rio de la Plata (1802), tells a story, which he verified
personally, how,


a yagouareté, after crossing a broad and deep river, came and seized the
horse in its teeth and, dragging it sixty paces across ploughed land,
recrossed the river and reached the other side with its prey.


These early descriptions of the “water-tiger” remind one very forcibly
of what the Tehuelche believed about their temisch.
The jaguar’s
physical appearance, its large size—larger than the puma—its impressive
claws, its aquatic habits, its grim fondness for dragging horses and mules
under water—everything fits.
Dr Lehmann-Nitsche thinks that confusion has arisen in the Patago-
nians’ minds between the local species of otter (Lutra felina) and the
jaguar (Felis onca), because the jaguar used once to spread to the very
tip of South America, but is now known there only by hearsay. The
Indians have gradually transferred its characteristics to the only aquatic
beast of prey they know: the otter. That the jaguar was once found in
the whole of Patagonia is proved by the early accounts, which assert that
the country is infested with “tigers,” and by the number of place-
names in which the Araucan word nahuel appears. Rivers, lakes, islands
and even farms are all named after the tiger. In the Province of Buenos
Aires alone Dr Lehmann-Nitsche found no less than 43 places named
after the tiger, of which 29 referred to watercourses or other aquatic


sites, the jaguar’s favourite habitat. And these names are found even in
southern Patagonia. Moreover, the tiger, nahuel, plays a great part in
Araucan legend. Finally, Antonio de Viedma reports in 1781 that the
Indians in the Santa Cruz territory told him that the local fauna included
“the tiger or nahuel and the lion or pagi (the puma).” There were
jaguars near the Straits of Magellan until the end of the eighteenth
century. It is only since then that they have gradually withdrawn to the
north. The actual presence of jaguars at the very tip of South America


is confirmed by the palaeontological discoveries, including the remains
of the large jaguar found in the Cueva Eberhardt, to which Professor
Roth gave the scientific name of Jemisch.


Dr Lehmann-Nitsche also collected, through his Araucan friend
Nahuelpi, the traditions corresponding to the zemisch in the folk-lore of
this neighbouring people. They told of an aquatic animal, with webbed


feet, known as niiriifilu, or zorro-vibora (Spanish for viper-fox)—a good
description of the otter’s serpentine movements in the water.
This
monster, which the Araucans fear more than anything else, is reputed

wae

to drag people into the water by winding its tail round them. Since the
otter has no huge claws with which to snatch its victims, its supple and
flattened, though not actually prehensile, tail has acquired this evil
power in popular belief.


We now have all the details of the Tehuelche iemisch, which is surely


a composite of the jaguar and the otter, and it is difficult not to accept
Dr Lehmann-Nitsche’s argument. There is still Tournouér’s evidence
of an animal the size of a large puma, but the German anthropologist


does not reject out of hand the theory that larger species of otters live


in some little-explored Patagonian lakes. Such rumours are not new,


nor confined to the Argentine. Buffon in his Addition al’ Article de la


Saricovienne (a name for the La Plata otter) wrote:


M. Aublet, a botanical scientist, whom we have already quoted, and
M. Olivier, surgeon to the King, who have both lived for a long time in
Cayenne and the Oyapok country, have assured me that there are otters
so large that they weigh as much as ninety or a hundred pounds; they
keep to the large rivers which are little frequented, and one sees their
heads above the water; they give cries that can be heard from very far
off, their fur is very soft, but shorter than the beaver’s; their ordinary
colour is a very faint brown: these otters live on fish, and also eat any
seeds that fall on the water from the river-banks.


The existence of this giant otter is now well established.
It is the
Pteronura brasiliensis known to the Brazilians as ariranha and to the
Guaranis as arirai. The Uruguayans call it Jobo corbata (cravat-wolf) or
lobo gargantilla (collared wolf); it frequents certain rivers in eastern
Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay and the north-eastern tip of the Argentine.
It may reach a length of 7 feet, of which 3 feet are tail. It is as large as a
puma. It is by no means impossible or even improbable that an equally
large species of otter may live in southern Patagonia. The otter is one
of the hardest mammals to see because of its shy and amphibious habits.
This is no doubt the reason why there are so many legends and super-


stitions about otters and other such amphibious mammals as the water-


opossum or yapock (Chironectes) among the marsupials and the platypus
among the monotremes.


After all, what is the iemisch but a Patagonian version of the Australian


bunyip?


With the iemisch out of the way, the problem of the survival of a
ground-sloth is still unsettled, though many zoologists seem tempted to
think otherwise. What was the “hairy pangolin” that Ramon Lista

RIDDLES OF THE GREEN CONTINENT


vainly shot at? And we must not forget that several people reported
Tehuelche legends not about a large, savage and amphibious carnivore,
but a burrowing and harmless animal that was said to be invulnerable.
Its description agrees much better with one’s idea of a sloth which had
not, like the ai and unau, decided to live in trees. We must start again
at the beginning and try to ignore the bitter controversy that poisoned
the whole atmosphere and from which few of the protagonists emerged
with honour.


Our first witness is Dr Moreno, whose evidence cannot be suspect
because he does not believe that giant sloths survive. He reports that
the Tehuelche and the Gennake tell of a sort of terrifying hairy beast,
which is very rare, and of which they have received traditions from their
ancestors. And in 1875, an old chief called Sinckel showed him a cave
which was said to be the lair of one of these unknown animals which
were called ellengassen. But the Indians never told him that the animal


still lived.


Our second witness is Ramon Lista, whose works are still the authori-


ties on Patagonian ethnography and geography. He says that the Te-
huelche believe that in the Sierra Carhuerne (Santa Cruz territory) live
evil spirits and monstrous quadrupeds which, according to their tradi-
tions, once carried off a whole family of Indians who were returning on
foot from an excursion to Charre. (the Patagonian name for Lago
Argentino). This story can only be pure surmise, since no one lived to


tell the tale. The only fact is that people attributed this family’s dis-
appearance to terrifying wild beasts.


Professor Santiago Roth is’ the third witness. The Tehuelche chief
Kankel told him several times that his grandfather used often to speak
of a very savage beast in the neighbourhood of Lake Buenos Aires
(Santa Cruz territory). When this beast roared, all the other animals
fled; and one day when his grandfather was hunting rheas near the lake


it killed a herd of his horses. Poor Kankel was so frightened of this
monster himself that no promises Roth could make would induce him
to go within half a mile of the lake.


Our fourth witness is Rudolf Lenz, an authority on Araucan folk-lore.
In one of the epics that he reports there appears a wild beast whose
name the Araucans translate into Spanish as Jofo-toro (that is lobo-toro)


or, as Lenz translates it, “wolf-bull,” the “wolf” being used as a sign
of the beast’s savagery. But he seems to me to have fallen into the mis-
take, natural to a German or an Englishman, of assuming that the first
word is an adjective qualifying the second, whereas Latin languages are


276


THE PATAGONIAN GIANT SLOTH


constructed the other way round. Thus when the Araucans describe
the otter in Spanish as zorro-vibora they mean a viperish fox, not a foxy


viper. The name Jofo-toro therefore means a bovine wolf, and not a
wolvish bull. If one has only the actual Patagonian animals as terms of
reference, one can hardly describe the appearance of a Megatherium or
Mylodon better than by calling it a wolf
as big and heavy as a bull, for


the wolf is the only coarse-haired and rather shaggy beast, fairly low on


its feet, in the country, and the bull introduced by the whites is the


largest animal known there. Of course this is only very indefinite evi-


dence, but it helps to reinforce what has been cited above. There is


therefore little doubt that the Tehuelche and the Araucan traditions


include a memory of a large and frightening hairy beast. From what we


know of the present and the sub-fossil fauna of this area it can only be


some kind of large ground-sloth.


It may be objected that the terror that these monsters arouse in the
legends about them is incompatible with the domesticated or half-
domesticated state in which gravigrades lived in the cave at Ultima
Esperanza. But the people who kept Mylodons in these stables were not
Tehuelche or Araucan but a preceding race, and in India many peoples


are terrified of wild elephants, although others tame them.


Dr Lehmann-Nitsche thinks that all these legends refer to the past
existence of jaguars and to oxen that have gone wild, and that there is no
trace of any tradition among the Patagonians that recalls a memory of
giant sloths; to imagine otherwise is needless and far-fetched, since he
believes that these animals, once domesticated by a vanished race, have
been extinct for many thousands of years. Personally I think it is going
too far to say that these animals were extinct so long ago, for reasons that


will follow.


Professor Florentino Ameghino was not always so misguided as when
he introduced his iemisch into the controversy. After the publication of


his first note, while other scientists were excavating the Cueva Eber-
hardt, he began burrowing no less busily into the early accounts of the


discovery of the New World. In the Historia de la Conquista del Para-


guay, Rio de la Plata y Tucumdn (1740-6) by a Portuguese Jesuit called


Pedro Lozano he read that from the frontiers of the province of Rio de


La Plata to Patagonia there was a large and very savage beast called su


or succarath, which was in the habit of carrying its young on its back.


The natives were said to hunt it and make cloaks out of its skin. There-


fore, thought Ameghino, it must be too thick and stiff to be used for


277


RIDDLES OF THE GREEN CONTINENT


-
finer garments; this all fitted the Eberhardt Mylodon.
Its method
of carrying its young is a characteristic of existing sloths and also
of the anteaters which, apart from their size, fit the succarath fairly


well.


The name su reminded other scholars that Father Lozano’s animal
had long been known even in Europe and had been mentioned in the
Historia Animalium (1551-8) by that Swiss Pliny, Conrad Gesner. This
vast work was certainly not compiled in the critical spirit of modern
zoology, and it includes several fantastic monsters alongside familiar
animals. It is, however, a summary of all the zoological knowledge avail-
able in the sixteenth century and remained a work of reference for 200
years. It mentions the su (de Subo) after the Descriptionis Americae (cap.


Ivi) of Andreas Theuetus.


To get to the bottom of the matter let us refer to André Thévet’s
original work, which turns out to be called Les Singularitéz de la France
Antarctique, Autrement Nommée Amérique et de Plusieurs Terres et Isles
Découvertes de Nostre Temps. This book, published in 1558, is un-
fortunately little known and its author quite unrecognised. It describes
a long peregrination made three years before by Father Thévet, who
was to become almoner to Catherine de Medici and then historiographer
and cosmographer to Charles IX. It was not only one of the first works
in French about America, but also one of the first to describe the natural
history of the New World, since it appeared only 23 years after Oviedo’s
famous Historia General -y Natural de Las Indias (1535). Thévet, who
was to publish a universal cosmography in 1575, was one of the most


brilliant and learned minds of*the French Renaissance.! Being curious
about “‘prodigies of nature,” he made a natural history collection, and
despite the slanders current about his “bad faith and extreme credulity,”
his writings show that he was a very shrewd observer. In his description
of his travels there are sober and exact descriptions of many strange
birds, such as the penguin (which he calls aponar) and the toucan, as
well as such mammals as the agouti, armadillo, ai (raiit or hatit) and the
manatee, which, I should point out, he does not mistake for a mermaid
—despite all the tales he had heard about those fabulous creatures.
There is thus some reason to credit what he says about the region
“of the Straits of Magellan.”

All in all it seems quite likely that Father Thévet’s su is some kind

At the turn of the century many scientists’ scepticism had been much
shaken by the accumulation of converging evidence: Ramon Lista’s
hairy pangolin—so very like a Mylodon;
the discovery of such well-
preserved remains; the Tehuelche
and Araucan legends, and finally
Father Lozano’s story, whose original source I have just quoted. Even
the Director of the Natural History Museum in London, Sir Ray
Lankester, eventually admitted that large ground-sloths might survive
in some little-known or almost unexplored part of Patagonia. The Daily
Express sponsored an expedition to bring back a living Mylodon, thus
resuscitating King Charles IV’s command, this time with more en-
couragement from the scientists. But when the first searches yielded
nothing, the leader of the expedition, Hesketh H. Prichard, grew im-
patient before he had even reached Last Hope Inlet and went home to
England in a huff, hardly concealing his disappointment and furious at


his own failure, telling everyone that he had been hoaxed and that the
Patagonian legends were a complete invention. This was almost as good


as saying that the Tehuelche were liars, Lozano and Thévet romancers,
the remains of Mylodons were illusions, Ameghino a madman and Lista


a visionary.


Today, half a century later, the matter is still at a dead end. Caven-
dish’s and Koslowsky’s expeditions came back as empty-handed as
Prichard’s, and scientists have therefore concluded that living Mylodons
no longer exist. It has also been pointed out, very justly, that the Te-
huelche accounts never come from direct witnesses but always refer to
third parties, who doubtless never saw the fabulous beast either. Dr
Carlos Rusconi of the Natural History Museum of Mendoza came to


this disappointingly negative conclusion when he drew up a summary of
the affair, putting things in their proper perspective, in 1949. All the
same he had in all honesty to admit that people still regularly came to


him with “more or less trustworthy reports about the existence of a


large animal in certain lakes in the mountains to the west of the Santa


Cruz territory.” The inhabitants of the south of Malalhue in the pro-


vince of Mendoza told him of “‘the existence of rare and fierce animals


which gave a howl like a wolf but were neither foxes nor pumas: in fact


281


RIDDLES OF THE GREEN CONTINENT


~
they are very well-known to these people as much by their habits as by
their tracks which they leave in moist earth where they are known to
come to attack their prey.”


Who knows what may be found when the most hidden corners of
Patagonia are more thoroughly explored? F. Outes has pointed out that
in the area of the Rio Salado and the Tapalqué stream the bones of two
other supposedly fossil animals have been found in a surprisingly fresh


state: the Glyptodon (Doedicurus), a sort of living tank which I have
mentioned above, and a sabre-toothed “tiger,” the Smilodon. And in
1884, in a cave near the Rio de los Patos in the Cordillera of the Andes,
Dr Moreno found paintings in ochre which he thought represented a
Glyptodon’ s shell.


But is Patagonia the right place to look for any survivors of these
animals? There is not the slightest doubt today that in South America
man knew all these giant mammals that seem to belong to a vanished
age. It is also well established, on irrefutable palaeontological proof,
that many of them once migrated to North America, where they were
contemporary with man about 10,000 years ago. From the Miocene to
the end of the Pleistocene, and even at the beginning of the present
period, giant sloths spread north through Uruguay, Brazil, Bolivia,
Colombia, Central America, Mexico and even part of the United States,
where their remains have been found in kitchen middens.


It is now proved beyond a doubt that the remains of Mylodons un-
earthed at the southern tip of Patagonia have been preserved in their
cave for many centuries and that these huge and harmless beasts were
exterminated there by the Indians who preceded the Tehuelche. The
Carbon 14 method of dating has fixed the age of the dung in the Cueva
Eberhardt in which the Mylodon’s bones and skin were found at about
10,000 years (to within 400 years either way). On the other hand, one.
may suspect that giant sloths—or at least smaller related ground species
—were known farther north in the Argentine at the time of the conquest
of America, as appears from the old chronicles. And perhaps some few
survivors were responsible for the legend current among the Tehuelche
during the last centuries and for Ramon Lista’s more recent report.
No doubt the sloth empire covered its greatest area some 10,000 years


ago. At this time there must have been a large number of intermediate
forms between the giant species in the savannah and the little species in.
the forests. Slaughtered by the nomadic hunting Indians, both in the
pampas of the south and the green prairies of the north, the largest


sloths would have retreated, as the jaguar did, to the tropical forests,


‘
282


THE PATAGONIAN GIANT SLOTH


where they could find a safer refuge. All the same, it is unlikely that the
really gigantic species could have adapted themselves to the inextricable
virgin forests, the habitat in which the small tree species flourished. On
the other hand, it is not difficult to see how the medium-sized ground-
sloths might have survived in wooded savannah or sparse forest, or even
on the fringes of or in clearings in the densest of jungles. For the great
ground-sloths were not destroyed by any revolutionary geological or
climatic change. From the number of their remains in kitchen middens
it is clear that these large and peaceable beasts, like so many other spe-


cies, were victims of man’s gluttony. If such is the case, what has hap-
pened to them in their impenetrable retreat in the vast Amazonian selva
and the boscosa of the Andes, through which they passed in the course of
ages? Itis hard to see what, in the peace of these forests rarely inhabited
by man, could have led to their extinction. Only human traps were able


to put an end to these armoured brutes against which beasts of prey were
powerless. Might they not still live in this “green hell” and find it a
heaven of peace? At all events, as we shall see, this would explain some
of the rumours that are still current in an area where “nothin’ would
surprise.”

JouHN MILTON, On the Morning of Christ’s Nativity.


IN 1906 the race for rubber was on, and to get it dirt cheap settlers did
not shrink from enslaving the Amazon Indians, flogging, torturing and
even killing them at the slightest whim. The tribes that resisted were
massacred, their villages pillaged and burnt. Officials and soldiers sent


to keep order were as savage and cruel as the seringueiros. In the rich
rubber plantations along the Rio Abuna and the River Acre (Rio
Macarinarra), which marks the southern boundary of western Brazil,
the northern frontier of Bolivia and part of that of Peru, a bitter dispute
arose between the three countries about the exact position of their
frontiers. War was on the point of breaking out.


The Royal Geographical Society of London was called in to act as
mediator and sent Major Percy Fawcett, an artillery officer of 39, to
make a thorough survey of the area in dispute. It was to perform this
thankless task that he first penetrated the vast forests of the Amazon,
in which he was to vanish without trace 20 years later.


It was in January 1907 that he first heard of gigantic snakes in the


little out-of-the-way hamlet of Yorongas, a mere barraca of two or three
of the seringueiros’ sheds, not far from the source of the River Acre.
It was the last outpost of civilisation on the fringe of utterly unexplored
country.


The manager at Yorongas [Fawcett writes in his memoirs] told me he
killed an anaconda fifty-eight feet long in the Lower Amazon.
I was
inclined to look on this as an exaggeration at the time, but later, as I
shall tell, we shot one even larger than that.


284


THE GIANT ANACONDA AND OTHER INLAND “SEA-SERPENTS”


This happened two or three months later on the Rio Abuna, upstream
of its junction with the Rio Rapirrao:


We were drifting easily along in the sluggish current not far below
the confluence of the Rio Negro when almost under the-bow of the
igarité there appeared a triangular head and several feet of undulating
body. It was a giant anaconda. I sprang for my rifle as the creature
began to make its way up the bank, and hardly waiting to aim smashed


a .44 soft-nosed bullet into its spine, ten feet below the wicked head.
At once there was a flurry of foam, and several heavy thumps against


the boat’s Keel, shaking us as though we had run on a snag.

With great difficulty I persuaded the Indian crew to turn in shore-
wards. They were so frightened that the whites showed all round their
popping eyes, and in the moment of firing I had heard their terrified
voices begging me not to shoot lest the monster destroy the boat and
kill everyone on board, for not only do these creatures attack boats when
injured, but also there is great danger from their mates.


We stepped ashore and approached the reptile with caution.
It was
out of action, but shivers ran up and down the body like puffs of wind
on a mountain tarn. As far as it was possible to measure, a length of
forty-five feet lay out of the water, and seventeen feet in it, making a
total length of sixty-two feet. Its body was not thick for such a colossal
length—not more than twelve inches in diameter—but it had probably
been long without food. I tried to cut a piece out of the skin, but the

beast was by no means dead and the sudden upheavals rather scared
us. A penetrating foetid odour emanated from the snake, probably its
breath, which is believed to have a stupefying effect, first attracting and
later paralysing its prey.1 Everything about this snake was repulsive.


Such large specimens as this may not be common, but the trails in
the swamps reach a width of six feet and support the statements of
Indians and rubber pickers that the anaconda sometimes reaches an
incredible size, altogether dwarfing that shot by me. The Brazilian
Boundary Commission told me of one killed in the Rio Paraguay
exceeding eighty feet in length!


This did not prevent Fawcett from being called an arrant liar when
he came back to London and claimed to have shot an anaconda 62 feet
long. Yet one can read through his notebooks from end to end without
finding any trace of exaggeration about the size or ferocity of the animals
which he met on the Amazon. On the contrary, one is more apt to find
notes like the following, written after he had been attacked by a suru-
cucu or “bushmaster” (Lachesis muta) upon which he had nearly
stepped:


It was quite nine feet long and about five inches thick, and the
double fangs, if in proportion, would be over an inch in length. Experts
claim that these snakes reach a length of fourteen feet, but I have never
seen one so big.


Fawcett was certainly a dreamer, and his dreams sometimes led him


to cherish the wildest hopes, but he was not a liar. What he saw he
always reported in a very matter-of-fact way; his interpretations are
sometimes fantastic, but his observations never are. The most striking
thing’in his memoirs is the contrast between the sordid hell he describes
and the splendour of the lost cities that he searched for till his death.


What then is the official record size for an anaconda (Eunectes murinus)
in the zoological textbooks? Most of them will allow 30 feet. The
American herpetologist Thomas Barbour, the great Brazilian expert Dr

Melo of the Rio de Janiero Zoo all agree on 45 feet; but other experts


are more cautious. Hyatt Verrill, for instance, writes:

A tanned snakeskin is always noticeably longer than it was on the
living animal, since it has to be stretched in the drying. If itis unscrupu-

been stretched to this length from only 20 feet, or that such a reputable

And you can’t stretch a living snake.

specimens which are known with certainty.


Verrill admits the second, but seems ignorant of the first.
I should also add that at El Fayum in Egypt, parts of the spinal column
of a python called Gigantophis belonging to the Middle Eocene period


were dug up; the entire animal was reckoned to be between 42 and 65


feet long. Fawcett’s snake would not necessarily have been the longest.

and Indians often attribute to anacondas are due to the difficulty of
judging the size of a living snake. It is a fact which I have proved for

myself that it is extremely hard to judge the length of a creature coiled

helpless when dealing with a curve. Ask anyone to tell you the length
of a circle, the perimeter of a pool, for instance, and you will be sur-
prised what huge errors they make. ‘You always have to resort to a
formula to measure a curve.1

The camera man, who had never before been in the jungle, said sixty

The Indians’ estimates varied from twenty to forty feet; my camp boy,

de fac’s of da case in consi’ation, I don’t can state posritively, chief, but
Ah knows for de truf tha’ camudi (anaconda) is jus’ too long.”’


A twenty-two rifle bullet through the.head brought an end to the big
anaconda’s career and when he was straightened out and measured he

a monster! About his middle he measured thirty-three inches and a
fraction and he weighed over 360 pounds and was a heavy load for five
Indians. So huge were his proportions that even after we had measured
the creature it was difficult to believe that he was so “‘small.”’


Verrill’s argument is sound enough, but is his experiment as instruc-


tive as he would have us think? The Indians who judged that a coiled

while those who put it at 40 feet would surely have been much more
accurate if they had seen the snake uncoiled. And even if, on the evi-
dence of the missionary, we must halve the dimensions of snakes re-
ported by people who know the country well, we shall still find many
instances of specimens much larger than the record skin in the Institute


at Butantan.

to any great extent, since he measured it dead on the river-bank. His

Those generally met with along the rivers measure between 20 and

He once shot an anaconda about 25 feet long; it fell into the water

water. His canoe-men replied that it was a waste of powder to shoot
such a small snake and a waste of time to stop and pick it up. They also
told him:


On the Rio Guaviare, during floods, chiefly in certain lagoons in the
neighbourhood, and even near the confluence of this stream, we often
see snakes which are more than double the size of the one you have just
shot. They are often thicker than our canoe.


These snakes need not belong to a new species. They could be out-


size individuals of a known species. Dr Maurice Burton has pointed


out that


there is always a percentage, admittedly small, of individuals in every
species which grow to an unusually large size. I have shown elsewhere
that if the average height of a male Londoner be taken as § ft. 8 in.,
then an unusually tall man would be one 6 ft. 4 in. high, but the record
height is 9 ft. 3 in. If we take the various species of mammals for which
reliable measurements are available, we find that the outsizes of species


are: 68 per cent. above average size, and 40 per cent. above the unusu-


ally large.

Of course, anacondas are not mammals, and reliable measurements
are not available. All the same this rule should hold good for reptiles,
and if, as the seringueiros and many hunters and explorers maintain,
anacondas 30 feet long are quite often seen, there might be unusually
large specimens 38 feet long and monstrous freaks over 50 feet long—
which is not so very far from Fawcett’s 62 feet.


The stories of anacondas 70 feet long seem to be quite incredible.
Yet I have heard from the witness’s own mouth a circumstantial
account of how a specimen of this astonishing size was killed. Having
questioned and cross-questioned my informant for several days, I am as
convinced of his sincerity as if I had witnessed the incident myself.


In 1947, after the Chavantes had massacred several Brazilian officials,
Francisco Meirelles, of the Service for the Protection of the Indians,
organised a new expedition to try to establish peaceful relations with


this wild tribe on the Middle Araguaya. This undertaking, which lasted
from February to July, was eventually crowned with a faint measure of
success. The party of some 20 men included two Frenchmen: the very
young explorer Raymond Maufrais, who was later to disappear in the
Tumac-Humac in Guiana where his father continues to search for him
with untiring courage, and the painter Serge Bonacase of Paris, who told
me this story.


At the end of March the expedition had reached Ilha do Bananal, an
island between two branches of the Araguaya, and set up its base camp
there. The members of the expedition spent several days preparing
themselves for life deep in the sertdo, as the wilderness is called, by going


off on long reconnaissance and hunting expeditions, as much as 60 miles
from their base camp. During one of these trips a party of seven or
eight men went hunting capybaras in the swampy area between the Rio
Manso—known as the Rio das Mortes, or River of Death, because the
Chavantes killed anyone who crossed it—and the Rio Cristalino.


The guide [Serge Bonacase told me] pointed out an anaconda asleep
on a rise in the ground and half hidden among the grass. We approached
to within 20 yards of it and fired our rifles at it several times.
It
tried to make off, all in convulsions, but we caught up with it after
20 or 30 yards and finished it off.
Only then did we realise how
enormous it was; when we walked along the whole length of its body
it seemed as if it would never end. What struck me most was its
enormous head, which was like this. [He stretched out his arms in
front of him with his hands together, thus forming a triangle with
2-foot sides and an 18-inch base.]

As we had no measuring instruments, one of us took'a piece of string
and held it between the ends of the fingers of one hand and the other
shoulder to mark off a length of 1 metre. Actually it could have been


a little less. We measured the snake several times with this piece of


string and always made it 24 or 25 times as long as the string. The


reptile must therefore have been nearly 23 metres long [75 feet].


Even if the piece of string was only 90 centimetres (3 feet) long—and
I don’t think we can allow a margin of error of more than 10 per cent—
the snake would have been between 72 and 75 feet long.


Serge Bonacase added that the animal’s diameter was almost half the
length of the measuring-cord, probably nearly 18 inches. The beast was
so heavy that they could not lift it up in the middle of its body. They
could only guess at its weight.


No doubt the reader will wonder, as I did, why they did not take
photographs of such a trophy. The reason is simple. The Service for
the Protection of the Indians had forbidden them to take cameras—
which could easily have terrified the Chavantes and caused another
massacre—on their particularly tricky mission.


But why didn’t they think of bringing back its skin or its head?
Serge Bonacase’s answer to this question was:


First of all, none of us seemed to realise that there was anything ex-
ceptional about our prize. There were no zoologists among us. The
Brazilian officials who had spent much of their lives in this country did
not seem to be particularly surprised. As for me, I had heard so many
tales of giant snakes that I supposed the whole of the Amazon was
crawling with monsters of this size.


Of course, we should have liked to take the snake’s skin back, but we
had neither the time to skin the beast nor to prepare its hide. We were
also very tired, and in that country you must never let yourself linger by
the way or encumber yourself with extra luggage. Think what a piece
of skin more than 60 feet long by 4 feet 6 inches wide would have
weighed! We should have had our work cut out to carry it—or for that
matter the head. Besides, who would have been crazy enough to lug a
piece of rotting meat on his back in that heat through country infested
with insects?


It was undoubtedly an anaconda of the known species. “It was a very


deep dark brown,” Bonacase told me, “‘marked on the sides with almost


black irregular oval rings.”


This would seem to imply that a length of 30 feet, which is supposed


to be exceptional for an anaconda, is really less than the normal size of
an adult. Or are there two geographic races of Eunectes murinus of
different sizes?

To return to the Marquis de Wavrin, let us proceed to what may be
another kind of snake. His canoe-men went on to tell him of many en-
counters with real monsters, fresh-water sea-serpents, as it were:


During a flood some Piapoco Indians tried to go directly from their
hut well upstream of the Rio Uva to the Rio Guaviare by taking short
cuts through the marshes and lagoons. They had just crossed one of
these little lakes, when they heard a sound behind therm like thunder;
yet the sky was clear and there was no wind. However, they saw the
surface of the lake in turmoil; waves broke even on the bank which they
had just reached.
It must therefore be an animal thrashing about in
mid-water. For an instant they could see a monstrous snake’s head.
The reptile swam for a moment on the surface and then dived. If their
canoe had been out in the lagoon they would probably have been
devoured; as it was they were capsized. They vowed never to risk
going that way again.


Naturally. It was also natural that the Marquis de Wavrin should have
been inclined to believe their story when later he reached the Rio
Putumayo the day after an ox had been carried off by a monsttous
snake. The people “wete all still shaken by what had happened.”
Which was also very natural.


Lorenz Hagenbeck, late director of the Hamburg Zoo, also seemed
convinced of the existence of a kind of South American water-snake
larger than the largest afiaconda and of quite staggering size. The son of
the great Carl, he was brought up to the business. For more than a
century travellers and animal-catchers sent zoological information from


all over the world to the Hagenbeck dynasty, who were proud to supply
zoos in every country with specimens of rare and sometimes even sup-
posedly extinct animals. It was an explorer sent out by a Hagenbeck
who caught the first pygmy hippopotamus. But the Hagenbeck family
papers also include several reports, transcripts of which I have seen,
about an aquatic snake from the Amazon which is much larger than the
largest anaconda and which the Indians seem also to distinguish by the
name of sucuriju gigante or “‘giant boa.”


Here I should explain that the anaconda (Eunectes murinus) is a mem-
ber of the boa family and is often called the water boa, meaning thereby


that while other boas only occasionally diye into the water, the anaconda,
whose nostrils can close hermetically, remains immersed much longer
and is more truly aquatic. There is only one species of anaconda: it is
marked with oval or lozenge-shaped spots and rings of dark or blackish
brown on an olive-green, grey or brownish background. Among the


292

many species of boas the colour varies greatly. The back is often
marked with light oval patches, generally pinkish, on a darker back-
ground, usually a rich brown. The boa-constrictor is the largest known


to herpetologists, who state that no specimen caught or killed has been
much longer than 12 feet. Nevertheless there have always been stories


of much larger boas. One John Browne wrote of an “‘ibibaboka” so


fearsome and monstrous (see plate facing page 273) that one is sur-


prised to learn that it was only 27 feet long. But this story of the sole


survivor of a party of six deserters from the garrison of artillery at St


Helena who got lost in the virgin forest in 1799 and found themselves


in the middle of one of the most romantic of love stories has never gairied
much credit.


George Gardner’s evidence in his Travels in the Interior of Brazil is
much more trustworthy. After stating that boa-constrictors are found
throughout the Province of Goyaz, especially on the wooded banks of


lakes, marshes and rivers, he adds that some are found which reach the
enormous length of 37 feet.


The largest I ever saw was at this place, but it was not alive. Some
weeks before our arrival at Sapé, the favourite riding horse of Senhor
Lagoeira, which had been put out to pasture not far from the house,
could not be found, although strict search was made for it all over the
Fazenda.
Shortly after this, one of his vaqueiros, in going through a
wood by the side of a small river, saw an enormous Boa, suspended in
the fork of a tree which hung over the water; it was dead, but had
evidently been floated down alive by a recent flood, and being in an
inert state, it had not been able to extricate itself from the fork before
the waters fell. It was dragged out to the open country by two horses,
and was found to measure thirty-seven feet in length; on opening it, the
bones of a horse, in a somewhat broken condition, and the flesh in a
half digested state, were found within it, the bones of the head being
uninjured; from these circumstances we concluded that the Boa had
devoured the horse entire.

Besides these witnesses’ accounts there are also two striking photo-
graphs of incredible monsters, killed 15 years apart. They were pub-
lished in a Rio de Janeiro newspaper. Photographs can be faked, so to
make quite certain Father Heinz sought out the proprietor of the Bazar
Sportivo at Manaos who had developed them both. It may seem odd
that both rolls of film should end up in the same shop so many years
apart, but Manaos is the largest town on the central Amazon and lies
near the confluence of many tributaries to the great river; it is the first
really civilised place that anyone coming in from the Amazon basin
would reach and it cannot have many shops equipped to develop photo-
graphs. At all events the proprietor assured the priest that the negatives
had not been retouched.


The officials of the Boundary Commission, who brought the first
photograph to be developed in 1933, told him how they had killed the
giant snake with a machine-gun. The wounded animal had, it seems,
risen up some 30 feet, smnashing bushes and even small trees in its fall.
Four men had been unable to lift its head.


The second photograph was taken in 1948. The snake, which was said


to measure 115 feet in length, crawled ashote and hid in the old fortifica-
tions of Fort Abuna in the Guaporé territory. It needed 500 machine-
gun bullets to put paid to it. The speed with which bodies decompose
in the tropics and the fact that its skin was of no commertial value may
explain why it was pushed back in the stream at once.


On the strength of all these reports Hagenbeck asserted that the

Even if we admit that the dimensions of these monsters are very likely


to be exaggerated by the alarmed witnesses who saw them, we must also
admit that the arguments against their existence are even less reliable.
The purely negative attitude of the sceptics who refuse to believe any of
these stories, and insist that the witnesses must be liars and the photo-
graphs fakes, need hardly be discussed. But there are others who have
tried to prove “scientifically” that such monsters are impossible, and
this deserves discussion.


A very learned naturalist Louis Marcellin has attacked the legends on
mathematical grounds:


Let us be generous and allow a certain margin to these proportions:
40 to 45 feet as serious authors have supposed without however adduc-
ing the beginnings of a proof. We are still a long way from the 130 feet
in question and even more from the actual weight of a snake 30 feet
long which weighs 250 lbs. Let us allow an average of 9 lbs. per foot. A
“‘monster’’ of 130 feet would weigh at the maximum half a ton.


M. Marcellin (who incidentally is not so generous as he pretends, since


Verrill’s 194-foot snake weighed 360 pounds, an average of nearly 19
pounds per foot) is a poor mathematician. And Dr Jose Candido de Melo
has made a similar mistake in asserting that a 5-ton snake would have to
be 500 feet long. The weight of a snake would be directly proportional
to its length only if its thickness were constant, and no one has been so
foolhardy as to pretend that the diameter of a 130-foot snake is the same
as that of a 20-foot one. If the proportions of the two are the same the
weight depends upon the volume, that is upon the cube of the length.
Worked out correctly, the weight for M. Marcellin’s snake would
therefore be just under 7} tons, and if it had the proportions of Verrill’s


it would be no less than 45 tons. Both these calculations assume that
the proportions of these giant boas are the same as those of smaller


shakes. Since Hagenbeck has given us the snake’s diameter as well as its


297


RIDDLES OF THE GREEN CONTINENT


length we can go to work another way (calculating for ease of arithmetic
in the metric system). His snake is 40 metres (130 feet) long, 80 centi-
metres (2 feet 6 inches) thick and it weighs 5 metric tons (almost equal
to § British tons). Now, since it is an aquatic snake, it must, like all
other aquatic animals, have a specific gravity almost equal to that of
water. In other words, every cubic metre of snake weighs the same as


a cubic metre of water: I metric ton. Now assuming that it tapers
considerably at the tail, and Hagenbeck’s 80 cm. is a maximum dia-
meter, let us consider the snake as a cylinder of, say, 50 cm. diameter,


i.e. 25 cm. radius. Its weight is then 40 x 0:25? < 7, which is about
7} tons. By the same method we can say that if a perfectly cylindrical
40-metre snake were to weigh 5 tons, its diameter would be 39 cm.


All in all, I think 5 tons a very reasonable weight for a 130-foot snake,
and I am surprised that the people who shot it and had no means of
weighing it at hand were able to judge its weight so accurately.
_


If this is the normal weight for these monsters it is less surprising that
none of the people who claimed to have shot one should have brought
back a specimen, or waited until the flesh had rotted off the bones to
bring back a bone. In the tropics flesh putrefies quickly, and the stench


that would rise from § tons of rotting flesh defies the imagination.


Five-ton snakes are not the only monsters reported from this part of
the world. The Marquis de Wavrin writes:


Around the Upper Paraguay they give the name mifiocao to a more or
less fabulous snake; the natives say that it can reach the size of a canoe.
They suppose that it is.a sucuriju or boa-constrictor that has grown very
old and turned into a water-snake.
On the Upper Rio Parana, in
Brazilian territory, I have also been told of these enormous snakes,
capable of dragging a canoe to the bottom. These monsters frequent
deserted places, and never leave a river. The fear they arouse is quite
superstitious.


The mifiocao or, in its more usual Portuguese spelling, minhocao,
“sounds at first as if it were one of the giant boas we have been discussing,
a sucuriju gigante. But when we have looked more carefully at the legen-
dary description of the minhocao and reports of eye-witnesses who have
seen it we shall find that it is neither an anaconda nor a boa-constrictor,
and may eventually doubt whether it is a snake at all.


The first scientist to be interested in the minhocado was Fritz Miiller
(1821-97), a German, who, after studying the embryology of certain
crustaceans, noted that the various forms the individuals took in the

THE GIANT ANACONDA AND OTHER INLAND “SEA-SERPENTS”


course of their development corresponded to those their species had
taken in the course of its evolution. This novel idea inspired Ernst
Haeckel to formulate his famous Recapitulation Theory: ontogenesis
reproduces phylogenesis—or, in plainer language, during its life-history


an animal climbs up its family tree.


It was in Brazil, where he had gone as a trader, that Fritz Miiller
spent his spare time studying the development of crustaceans and where
he was able to collect numerous tales about the fabulous minhocao. At


first he took no notice of what seemed absurd stories about an animal
50 yards long and 15 feet across, covered in bony armour, overturning


trees like blades of grass, shifting the courses of rivers and turning dry
land into fathomless marshes. But gradually he collected evidence from
people who claimed to have seen it and spoke of it not as a monster but


a very large unknown animal, until he wrote a report on the probable
existence in Brazil of a huge amphibious creature. The word minhocdo
was, according to Miiller, the superlative of sinhoca (earthworm), and
thus meant “giant earthworm.” In the late 1860s it made a very re-
markable appearance in the neighbourhood of Lage. Some six miles
from the town, a certain Francisco de Amaral Varella who lived in
Baguaes saw a strange animal of gigantic size on the banks of the Rio
das Caveiras. It was 3 feet thick, but not very long, with a pig’s snout,
but he couldn’t say whether it had any feet. He dared not attack it
alone, but when he called his neighbours it lumbered off clumsily, leav-
ing a trail of deep furrows about 3 feet wide before it disappeared into
the ground.


Some weeks later, a similar trench which could have been made by
the same animal was seen on the other side of Lage, nearly four miles
from the first. They followed the animal’s track which finally led under
the roots of a large pine and then were lost in swampy ground. A Ger-
man merchant called Friedrich Kelling, then living at Lage, was an eye-
witness of this.


Another German, Emil Odebrecht, was surveying a route for a road
from Itajahy into the uplands of the province of Santa Catarina, and in
a broad, swampy plain intersected by a branch of the Rio Marombas his
progress was held up by winding trenches along the course of the stream.
They were too wide for him to step across, but not too wide for him to
jump them. Thus they were about the same width as Kelling’s. At the
time he did not know what to make of them, but later attributed them


to the minhocao.

One evening in 1849, after a long period of rains, a sound of falling
rain was heatd in Jodo de Deos’s house near the Rio dos Papagaios, a
tributary of the Iguassu in Parana province, but the sky was clear and

route the beast had taken into the bed of a stream that ran into the
Papagaios. Three years later a rich landowner called Lebino José dos

found the tracks still there, and concluded that there had been two
animals some 6-10 feet thick.


Senhor Lebino also related that in the same district, a negress, who

than a lasso” (about 80 feet) with two movable horns on its head lying
close to its body. It was wallowing in the mud.

The Gaceta de Nicaragua of 10 March 1886 published a letter from
Paulino Montenegro telling how during a journey to Concordia in

cause the subsidence.
Little by little, trees were loosened, great oaks
were even overturned, and huge chunks of rock thrown up until in

Fawcett also seems to refer to the minhocao when he writes:


In the Paraguay River there is a freshwater shark, huge but toothless,
said to attack men and swallow them if it gets a chance. They talk here

Bolivia, enormous tracks have been found, and Indians there talk of a
huge creature described at times half submerged in the swamps.


The reports are usually rather vague about the animal’s size and shape.
Indeed it has been assumed on too little evidence to be a monstrous
earthworm, merely because it leaves grooved tracks like a worm’s. It
might well have feet concealed below the earth or mud, although no
observer mentions them. Dr Budde, who summarises Miiller’s report
in his Naturwissenschaftliche Plaudereten, remarks:


If the animal has no feet, we must allow that it moves by crawling
like a worm: its scales would serve to give it a grip when forcing a
subterranean passage. The pig’s snout and the horns, if they can be
trusted, remind one of certain reptiles that lead a similar life to the
minhocdo’s.


This last phrase seems to refer to the horned viper which burrows in
the sands of the Sahara and Arabia Deserta.

Only one of the minhocdo’s habits seems surprising in a Glyptodon: it


is amphibious. Armadillos certainly are not, though it is now known
that they are excellent swimmers. They cross narrow streams by run-
ning across the bottom, and for larger rivers they fill their intestines
with air until they float in spite of their heavy armour. There is no
reason why a giant armadillo should not take up a semi-aquatic life.
It would not be the only mammal to be both a burrower and amphi-
bious: besides the platypus there is the insectivorous water-shrew
(Neomys fodiens) and rodents like the beaver and the muskrat. Like the
giant dinosaurs, such as the Diplodocus, it might have taken to a medium
denser than air, where its heavy body, laden with its great carapace,
could move more easily. With its scales it. could easily be mistaken for
a giant snake if only its head and the huge dome, more than 3 feet
wide, of its carapace were visible above water.
The legends about
gigantic reptiles might be due to people seeing Glyptodons and very
large water-boas and mixing the two together. More evidence is needed

RIDDLES OF THE GREEN CONTINENT


before one can draw such a bold conclusion, but given the compara-
tively recent date of the Glyptodons, which have certainly been con-
temporary with men, their survival would not be so surprising.


Personally I am inclined to think that a third animal may have con-
fused the story. The monstrous water-snakes are so similar to the great
sea-serpent—which is certainly not a snake, since it wriggles up and
down, and not from side to side—that I wonder whether they may not
be primitive Cetacea (Archaeoceti). As Remington Kellogg suggested in
1936 in his Review of the Archaeoceti, the first stages in the history of the
Cetacea (whales, etc.), which are mammals that have reverted to the sea,
may have occurred in freshwater lakes and rivers. Some of the Archaeo-


ceti had a coat of mail consisting of rings of horny scales around the
body. The rows of nodules on the skin on some porpoises’ backs (genus
Neomeris) are a vestige of this ancient armour.


If a primitive cetacean had survived today, its head, rising above the
surface on a neck as flexible as a seal’s, and its scaly back would make it
look very like a monstrous serpent. Ivan T. Sanderson no doubt had
this in mind when he wrote:


Perhaps there are Acrodelphids still cruising the oceans, Zeuglodonts
browsing in lakes, lochs, and fjords, the ancestors of these in tropical
rivers, and even some “First Ancestors’? [Archaeoceti] on their banks.


But all this can be no more than a theory, for we know far less about
the minhocdo than about the great sea-serpent or the Loch Ness monster.
At all events it is more probable than that the surviving giants should
be those dinosaurs that seem to leap into romantic minds whenever they
learn of the discovery of huge footprints or glimpses of vast aquatic
animals in the Green Continent.

SIR WALTER RALEIGH on the tales of hairy
men that he heard in South America.


CANDIDE and Cacambo were lost in the Amazon jungle when they
heard faint cries that seemed to be uttered by women.


They could not tell [writes Voltaire] whether they were cries of pain
or of joy; but they rose hastily with that alarm and uneasiness caused by
everything in an unknown country.


The cries came from two completely naked girls who were running
gently along the edge of the plain, while two monkeys pursued them
and bit their buttocks. Candide was moved to pity; he had learned to
shoot among the Bulgarians and could have brought down a nut from
a tree without touching the leaves.
He raised his double-barrelled
Spanish gun, fired, and killed the two monkeys.


“God be praised, my dear Cacambo, I have delivered these two poor
creatures from a great danger; if I committed a sin in killing an In-
quisitor and a Jesuit, I have atoned for it by saving the lives of these two
girls. Perhaps they are young ladies of quality and this adventure may
be of great advantage to us in this country.”


He was going on, but his tongue clove to the roof of his mouth when
he saw the two girls tenderly kissing the two monkeys, shedding tears
on their bodies and filling the air with the most piteous cries.


“I did not expect so much human kindliness,”’ he said at last to
Cacambo, who replied:


“You have performed a wonderful masterpiece; you have killed the
two lovers of these young ladies.”’


‘Their lovers! Can it be possible? You are jesting at me, Cacambo;
how can I believe you?”’


““My dear master,’’ replied Cacambo, “you are always surprised at
everything; why should you think it so strange that in some countries

RIDDLES OF THE GREEN CONTINENT


there should be monkeys who obtain ladies’ favours? They are quarter
men, as I am a quarter Spaniard.”


"
“Alas!?? replied Candide “I remember to have heard Dr Pangloss
say that similar accidents occurred in the past and that these mixtures
produce Aigypans, fauns and satyrs; that several eminent persons of
antiquity have seen them; but I thought they were fables.”


“You ought now to be convinced that it is true,”’ said Cacambo.


The ancient myth that satyrs and fauns were hybrids between men
and beasts is now known to have been based on garbled descriptions of
anthropoid apes.


Voltaire was of course more interested in the women’s behaviour than
the monkeys’ existence. AH the same he garnished Candide with fact
wherever possible. What made him think that there were large apes in
South America when in fact the only species of monkeys there known to
science are small and have long tails? One cannot be certain, but it is
more than likely that he drew his information chiefly from the memoirs
of those Jesuit missionaries whom he so loved to make fun of. The
Noticias Curtosas e Necesarias das Cosas do Brasil by Father Simao de
Vasconcellos, s.J., provincial of Brazil, is a mine of curious information
and contains several references to man-faced monsters that haunted the
Brazilian forests. There are, for instance, dwarfs called goazis or guaya-


zis; the matuyus, wild men with their feet the wrong way round;
curinquéans, giants 16 spans (about 11 feet) high, the most courageous of
creatures, with their lips and nostrils adorned with nuggets of gold, for
whom everyone showed the greatest respect.


These legends are so like those which had been known in the East
since time immemorial that one might easily suppose that the first ex-
plorers, who thought they had arrived in Asia, had innocently fathered
on the new continent the wonders that Ctesias and Megasthenes had
reported of the Indies; in which case it would hardly be surprising that
the legend of Indians who coupled with beasts ‘“‘under the influence oe


a vile sensuality” should also be found in America.


But subsequent explorations showed that it was not the Conquista-
dors who had introduced these tales; they were current among the most
remote tribes which had had no contact with the whites. Moreover,
most of them had a foundation in fact. The first reports about the New
World therefore deserve careful attention. During their discovery of the
“Empire of Guiana” in 1595 and 1596 Sir Walter Raleigh and his con-
tinuator Laurence Keymis heard tell of monstrous creatures remini-
scent of the “‘Aigypans, fauns and satyrs” of the Old World. And of

It is also said that in other places there are (though for myself I have

monkey in question was far larger and more massive than any spider-

This absence of tail, a feature in common with the African and Asian

hand, it is hard to deny that Loys’s monkey has a more massive body
and thicker limbs than the ordinary spider-monkeys. A detail which I
do not think has been pointed out is that its thorax seems to be flattened
dorso-ventrally, like an anthropoid’s—as one can see from its broader
shoulders—and it is much longer than a spider-monkey’s. Its face is
also much more oval. Its hind-legs seem to be shorter than its fore-legs,


like those of the anthropoids, but this is not enough to put it into a
different genus; all the spider-monkeys have a similar tendency.


There is one other very important characteristic in which the Platyr-
rhinian monkeys of the New World differ from the Catarrhinians of the
Old World. The former have 36 teeth, the latter 32. Loys asserts that
the animal he shot had only 32. We cannot verify this figure without
examining the monkey’s dentition in detail. Alas, the expedition’s cook
who prepared and preserved the animal’s skull was rash enough to turn


it into a salt-box. It dried and disintegrated in the heat and little by


little the pieces were lost.


If Loys has given the number of teeth correctly, the monkey might


still have a Platyrrhinian’s normal dentition, if the last molars had not
yet appeared, though this would be most extraordinary in an apparently
adult animal. It would have to be a freakish reduction in the basic num-
ber, which, as Dr Charles Bennejeant has pointed out, is extremely rare:
the American monkeys are more apt to increase the number of their
molars. Nevertheless, in an unpublished treatise quoted by Professor
Beccari, Dr Schultz of Baltimore, who collected some 400 specimens of
monkeys in Nicaragua and Panama, has shown that the spider-monkeys


are an exception to this rule and often lack the third molar.


If Loys’s ape is, as it seems, a highly developed spider-monkey, one
would expect that what is a tendency in the rest of the group would be a
normal characteristic for it, in which case de Loys was telling the truth,
and we should be all the more inclined to trust the rest of his account,


especially about the absence of tail.

According to M. Cintract, a photographer, who judged from the
number of planks in the crate, it must have been about 20 inches high,
and the animal’s height was between 5 feet and 5 feet 3 inches. On the
other hand the standard size for petrol-crates is 17$ inches high, and
as the animal is three and a third times the height of the case, this
implies a height of 5 feet.


Which confirms the accuracy of Loys’s measurements. The monkey
would therefore be taller than the chimpanzee, the female of which
rarely exceeds 4 feet 3 inches in height. No wonder Loys was so sur-
prised. On the strength of this photograph and information given him
by the geologist, Professor Montandon published a careful description
of the unknown animal in 1929, naming it Ameranthropoides loysi, to
mark its anthropoid characteristics and honour its discoverer. Gosse’s
prediction had come true.


This talk of an American “anthropoid” shocked some zoologists who
wanted to keep this term strictly to a few of the Catarrhinians. Actually
it has no ptecise meaning in systematic classification, but is generally
used to embrace two distinct families, the Hylobatidae or gibbons and
the Anthropoidae (or Pongidae) the gorilla, the chimpanzee and the
orang-utan. To my mind the family of Anthropoidae is by no means
homogeneous: in some characteristics the orang-utan is nearer to the
gibbons—which are Asians like itself—than to the African chimpanzee
and gorilla. I am very tempted to believe that the gibbons and orang-
utans are giant types derived from the Asian langurs, while the gorilla
and chimpanzee have sprung from a group of little African monkeys
related to the baboons. Thus the term “anthropoid” merely means


all the large tailless apes with arms longer than the legs and a flattened
chest, irrespective of their origin. These characteristics betray a special
form of locomotion: brachiation, that is ta say moving usually by swing-
ing from their arms (the other monkeys which employ cruriation, or

To his description of Ameranthropoides loysi, Dr Montandon ap-

Monstrous stone statues like gorillas, coming from the gorilla-less

of any legend which explains their significance, and the inhabitants of

Professor Montandon also remarks that according to the Indians,

might very well be large apes, especially if they had particularly human

Thus we see that the legend of those dwarfs the guayazts is by no means
far-fetched. Montandon goes on to make higher claims:


If our subject’s well-developed forehead is not merely the result of an

the Hominidae which would put it on a level with the genus Pithe-
canthropus.

sort of “Missing Link” between monkeys and man, not so much for the

development of the monkeys of the New World, as regards both weight

If, as in the African and Asian monkeys, the intelligence of the Ameri-

chimpanzee or gorilla. Even if it is merely a giant spider-monkey, its

than the Pithecanthropus’s and perhaps even than man’s. If a spider-
monkey or a capuchin kept its usual proportions but were as large as a
man it would obviously have a larger brain than his; and the Ameran-
thropoid (5 feet 13 inches) is the height of a human pygmy (5 feet or


less) or even a short man. Even though it certainly has an intellect far
inferior to the most backward of men (otherwise it would have con-
quered the world!), a comparative study of its anatomy and physiology,
especially that of its brain, with those of a man of the same size would
be of immense interest and might enable us to establish for certain the


relation between the weight, volume and shape of the brain and the
degree of intelligence.


The zoological problem of Loys’s monkey demands a solution.
Some eminent naturalists, like.Sir Arthur Keith, have coolly avoided
the issue by maintaining that it is merely a variety of ordinary spider-
monkey and that the tail has been hidden in the photograph—thus im-
plying that Loys is a fraud. Quite apart from the size of the animal—
which can still be disputed, though unfairly—it seems to me that the
photograph proves that this is an unknown kind of monkey, and I am
forced to the irreverent conclusion that Sir Arthur has never had a good
look at an ordinary spider-monkey.
Philip Hershkovitz, an excellent
American mammalogist who during the War prospected the area that
Loys had explored but found no trace of the Ameranthropoid, even
claims to have determined the species of spider-monkey to which it
belongs, the mulatto spider-monkey (Ateles hybridus). I therefore spent


a long time in the Natural History Museum in Paris studying the “‘type”
of this species, collected by Le Plée in Colombia in 1826, but I was not
in the least convinced. While it is true that the mulatto spider-monkey
has much thicker limbs than the other spider-monkeys (at least it had

and fur not unlike the Ameranthropoid’s, its size, the length of its thorax

Legends of large monkeys are not confined to the Colombo-Vene-
zuelan border, but are found all over the country of the Amazon. The
Marquis de Wavrin writes:


I have been told of the existence of large monkeys in the region of the
vast forest north of the Matto Grosso, between the Paraguay and the
Amazon basins. I have not seen them. Although large monkeys are
reported everywhere in the Amazon basin, if relatively rarely, it is
around the Orinoco that they seem to be more frequent. They are
called maribundas.
Their height when standing upright, a position
they readily adopt to walk on the ground, is supposed to be about § feet.
The only civilised man who lives with his family on the Guaviare on
the upper reaches of this river, told me he had brought up a young
maribunda at his house.
It was very friendly and amusing in all its
pranks; finally its owner had to kill it because it did too much damage.


The maribunda’s cry sounds strangely like a human call. On the
Guaviare in particular I several times thought at first that it was Indians
calling.


Once maribundas spread panic among his servants, who thought they
were being attacked by the terrible Guaharibo Indians. Are these mari-

or marimonda is the native name for what in English is called the
marimonda spider-monkey (Afeles belzebuth)—but this is never more
than 3 feet 7 inches high. And Wavrin adds: “According to what the
Indians told me, this monkey’s body is rather slim. It likewise has a
prehensile tail”-—which does not agree at all with Loys’s description.
Rather than suppose that there is a giant species of marimonda spider-
monkey, might there not be a confusion in the Indians’ minds between
a marimanda of ordinary size and our large tailless spider-monkey which
according to Loys is greyish brown?
In any case the Marquis de
Wavrin’s observations are far from solving the problem.


At first sight Roger Courteville’s evidence appears more helpful. A


civil engineer who once led an ethnographic expedition in South
America, he was, in 1926, the first man to cross the entire continent,
from Rio de Janeiro to La Paz and Lima, by car. He claims that in the
area that Loys explored he twice met a large tailless ape. He informs
me that his encounters occurred in 1938 and 1947.
In his book
Les Indiens Inconnus de ? Amazanie he tells how he was in virgin forest

Was it a man? Was it a monkey? It seemed rather a monstrous

Its upper arms seemed longer

The apparition had not lasted a minute. But I think that I shall never
forget it as long as I live.

But in fact the spider-monkeys (and the

It is quite possible that Courteville really met an Ameranthropoid, as

think so.


This suspect evidence must not be allowed to cast suspicion on Loys’s
account, which is supported by an indisputable document in the correct
sense of the word.

This great ape appears not to be confined to a narrow strip in the
north-west of South America. In 1868, a century after Dr Bancroft,
Charles Barrington Brown, who was then Government Surveyor in
British Guiana, heard new rumours on the Upper Mazaruni on the
Venezuelan frontier that a sort of hairy men lived there. Oddly enough,


it was after hearing the “plaintive moan or howl” which Cieza de Leon
also alleged these ape-men made.


The first night after leaving Peaimah we heard a long, loud, and most
melancholy whistle, proceeding from the direction of the depths of the
forest, at which some of the men exclaimed, in an awed tone of voice,
“The Didi.’’ Two or three times the whistle was repeated, sounding
like that made by a human being, beginning in a high key and dying
slowly and gradually away inalowone....


The “‘Didi’’ is said by the Indians to be a short, thick set, and power-
ful wild man, whose body is covered with hair, and who lives in the
forest. A belief in the existence of this fabulous creature is universal
over the whole of British, Venezuelan and Brazilian Guiana. On the
Demerara river, some years after this, I met a half-bred woodcutter,
who related an encounter that he had with two Didi—a male and a
female—in which he successfully resisted their attacks with his axe. In
the fray, he stated that he was a good deal scratched.


In 1931 Professor Nello Beccari, an Italian anthropologist, Dr Renzo
Giglioli and Ugo Ignesti, made an expedition to British Guiana, where
one of their secondary objects was to attack the problem of Loys’s ape.
For in this area the fauna, flora, climate and indeed the whole ecological
pattern—what is now called the “biotope”—are the same as in the Sierra
de Perija4; and Beccari had read in Elisée Reclus’s geographical encyclo-
pedia that according to Indian legend the. forests in British Guiana
were haunted by fabulous hairy men called di-di, which all the Indians
fear, although they have never seen them. But it was not until he was
just about to return to Italy that he heard any definite information about
where this beast lived.


On his return from several months in the interior, he met the British
Resident Magistrate, Mr Haines, who was then living on the Rupununi.
Haines told him that he had come upon a couple of di-di many years
before when he was prospecting for gold. In 1910 he was going through
the forest along the Konawaruk, a tributary which joins the Essequibo
just above its junction with the Potaro, when he suddenly came upon
two strange creatures, which stood up on their hind-feet when they saw
him. They had human features but were entirely covered with reddish-
brown fur. Haines was unarmed and did not know what he could do if
