CHAPTER SIXTEEN


Three Large Pygmies: the Forest


Rhinoceros, the Water Elephant and


the Spotted Lion


There’s a sort of tiny potamus, and a tiny
nosserus too—
... And I think there’s a sort of a something
which is called a wallaboo—
A. A, MILNE, When We Were Very Young.


“In Africa,” Trader Horn has sagely remarked, “the Past has hardly
stopped breathing.” Several legends of unknown animals seem to refer
to creatures of a long-vanished age and are rejected by sceptical scien-


tists on that account. Yet the negroes have not had lessons in palaeonto-
logy and they could not know what prehistoric animals looked like.
Though they interpret what they see in a most original way because their
minds are dominated by sympathetic magic, and though they tend
either from fear or from natural braggadocio to exaggerate the facts they
report, there is always a real observation at the bottom of their stories—
not a dream or a vision. More than once they have shown that they are
good observers and that their interpretations of facts are not so ridicu-
lous as was at first supposed. They were ridiculed for thinking that
fevers were caused by mosquito-bites at a time when western medicine
gave malaria its name in the belief that it was literally caused by “bad


air.” Now the negroes have been proved to be right.


In any case, animals thought to be extinct are more likely to have sur-
vived in Central Africa than elsewhere.
Its climate has remained un-
changed since time immemorial. The Ice Ages had no effect except to
produce long rainy seasons. Geologically it has not changed for tens of
millions of years, and it is the only continent which has not been largely


357


92. Welwitschia mirabilis, a vegetable relic of the Palaeozoic era,
found only in a strip of the south-west coast of Africa.


submerged at some time since the beginning of the Primary era. It has
also escaped the great upheavals of the Earth’s crust. While the Alps
were gradually forming from the end of the Mesozoic era until the pre-
sent day, and the Rocky Mountains, the Andes and the Himalayas were


all appearing, Africa had long been physically settled. So it is not sur-
prising to find in Central Africa living specimens of types which once
flourished in a large part of Europe: macaques, elephants, rhinoceroses,
hippopotami, giraffes, lions and hyenas. The fauna of equatorial Africa


like its flora (which includes the Cycas from the Mesozoic era and even
the extraordinary Welwitschia from the end of the Palaeozoic) has always
been several geological periods behind. For example, in Central Africa
Dinotheriums have been excavated which were only 100,000 years old,
although they vanished from Europe 5 million years ago.


As Dr Frechkop has pointed out, the fact that animals like the okapi,
forest-hog and water-chevrotain (Hyemoschus) are found in Africa
proves that “the equatorial forest is the nature reserve of primitive forms
which have not been able to survive elsewhere.” As it is almost im-
possible to penetrate this dense, dark and unhealthy jungle without dis-
turbing the shy creatures that inhabit it, many of them may live there
without our having the least chance of meeting them except in excep-
tional circumstances. Only the natives who live on the verge of the
jungle, and more particularly the pygmies who live within it, are likely
to know of some of these animals. So it is natural that the legends likely
to interest us are mainly found along the vast equatorial rain-forest.


When Hans Schomburgk brought a pygmy hippopotamus back alive


to Europe in 1913, and thus proved that at least one native legend was
well-founded, he was probably more inclined to pay heed to others, one


358


-
Seay
de


THREE LARGE PYGMIES


of which referred to a sort of pygmy rhinoceros which, according to the
Kroo, also lived in the mountainous part of Liberia. At first he thought
the tales must refer to the forest-hog, a big black pig with large tusks, a
variety of which is in fact found in eastern Liberia. But he soon found


that the Kroo made a clear distinction between the large forest-boar and


the little mountain rhinoceros, and he eventually came to believe they


were right. Unfortunately all his attempts to discover a specimen of this


absolutely unknown species failed—it was a harder task than looking for


a needle in a haystack, since here the needle was on the move, constantly


eluding its pursuers.


There is a good argument to show that this part of Africa may still
conceal a pygmy rhinoceros. Professor Trouessart has said of the pygmy
hippopotamus:


The presence of this pygmy species in this particular area in the loop
of Niger leads one to suppose that this country was an island separated
from the continent at the time when the Atlantic still penetrated the
north of West Africa, that is to say during the Eocene.


It has long been noticed that land animals which live on islands are
generally smaller than the same or similar species living on the nearest
continent. Thus the deer and the rhinoceroses on Java and Sumatra are
smaller than those in India and Indo-China. In the Tertiary era a whole


series of pygmy elephants and rhinoceroses lived on the Mediterranean
islands of Sicily, Sardinia, Malta and Cyprus. This phenomenon, by
which a creature’s size seems to be related to that of the territory it lives
in, has been attributed to what Moritz Wagner calls segregation, in
which the lack of choice of sexual partners, the lack of variety in diet,
and perhaps a less favourable climate all play a part. If the country in
the loop of the Niger was once an island, one might expect its ancient
fauna to have insular and therefore dwarf characteristics. If there were
pygmy hippopotami, why not pygmy rhinoceroses?


No known rhinoceroses, fossil or living, are found in the area south of
the Niger and Senegal rivers. This is odd, since the hippopotami and
the elephants (which like them are pachyderms of similar habits, dating
from the same geological period) spread over this territory. Perhaps the
rhinoceroses in this area have remained unknown, because they are so


small and can shelter in mountains covered with thick forests. The


natives of Liberia are ignorant of this palaeontological argument, so it


is all the more interesting that they should put the pygmy rhinoceros in


the one place in Africa where we have reason to expect to find it.


359


THE TERRORS OF AFRICA


Liberia is not the only part of Africa where rhinoceroses have been
reported in quite unexpected places.
Both the black rhinoceros
(Diceros bicornis) and the white rhinoceros (Ceratotherium simum) live
in open country, mimosa-covered steppe and wooded savannah; they
sometimes venture through forest paths to the rivers where they bathe,
but they never live in the heart of thick wet forest. The vast area they
occupy in the eastern half of Africa hardly touches the tropical rain-
forest except around the foothills of Mount Kenya and Kilimanjaro.


Now in January 1931 an official of the French colonial administration
of the eastern Cameroons, Géraud de Galassus, told Lucien Blancou
that there were rhinoceroses in the forest in the south of the Batouri
subdivision which he administered. At that time Blancou thought that
they must be the remnants of a population of savannah rhinoceroses,
for he did not know the area in question. But when he became chief
game inspector in French Equatorial Africa his opinion changed. Be-
tween 1949 and 1953 he collected, from three other French officials,
Millet, Rolland and Rozan, information confirming the first report:
according to the natives of the Kellé, Ouesso and Dongou districts on
the Middle Congo River there was a species of rhinoceros in the very
depths of the thick forests in those districts. This was confirmed by an
engineer in the Forestry Department called Moiraud who had heard the
same story from Europeans living at Epéna. In such a very peculiar
habitat, the rhinoceros could hardly belong to either known genus.
Blancou concludes:


The Africans in the north of the Kellé district, especially the pygmies,
know a forest animal larger than a buffalo, almost as large as an elephant,
but which is not a hippopotamus.
Its tracks are only seen at long in-
tervals, but they fear it more than any other dangerous animal. The
sketch of its footprint which they drew for M. Millet is that of a rhino-
ceros. On the other hand they do not seem to have said that it has a
horn, though they have certainly not sajd that it has not. While M.
Millet was at Kellé, in 1950 if I am not mistaken, one of the best known
African chiefs in the district came several days’ march to inform him
that “‘the beast had reappeared.”” Unfortunately that is all I can say,
for M. Millet left the district in 1951 and I have not been able to go
there myself. The rewards in kind which this official offered the pyg-
mies for a tangible proof of the animal’s presence yielded no result.


Around Ouesso the natives talk of a big animal which does have a
horn on its nose—though I don’t know whether it has one or several.
They are just as afraid of it as the Kellé people.


Around Epéna, Impfondo and Dongou, the presence of a beast
which sometimes disembowels elephants is also known, but it does not


360


THREE LARGE PYGMIES


seem to be so prevalent there now as in the preceding districts. A speci-
men was supposed to have been killed twenty years ago at Dongou, but


on the left bank of the Ubangi and in the Belgian Congo.


Blancou admits that all the evidence is pretty thin; but points out that
the evidence upon which the okapi, forest-hog and Congo peacock and
many other creatures were discovered was equally thin. He remarks that
in the great wet forest where several of the least-known large species of
mammals survive, there seems to be an “ecological niche” for a well-
adapted rhinoceros. No doubt, like so many other animals, this species
was once widespread but has gradually retreated into a small area of
swamp and steep and thickly wooded mountains. In this it resembles
the forest rhinoceroses of Java and Sumatra to which it may perhaps be
related.


The latter rhinoceros (Dicerorhinus sumatranus) is by far the smallest,
due no doubt both to its insular and forest-dwelling habits. The red
buffalo of the forests is smaller than the black buffalo of the savannah,
and probably the African forest rhinoceros is smaller than its brothers on
the steppes; perhaps it is a true pygmy like its hypothetical Liberian
cousin.


The African elephant is exactly parallel to the African rhinoceros.
There are three sizes, one of which is still excluded from the official list.
At the end of the last century Paul Matschie had already noted that
there were two quite distinct races of elephants in Africa. The first
(Loxodonta africana oxyotis) had rather triangular ears, while in the
second (Loxodonta africana cyclotis) they were definitely rounded.
Matschie thought these sub-species belonged respectively to East and
West Africa, but it has since been shown that actually both types are
spread over most of Africa, the pointed-eared elephant preferring to


live in the savannah or bush, while the round-eared one chooses the


forest. Moreover the first is much larger than the second. A male bush
elephant often stands more than 11 feet high and may occasionally reach


as much as 12 feet 8 inches, while the male forest elephant is never more
than 10 feet high and is generally about 8 feet. The first has light-grey
rough-looking skin and tusks tending to point outwards, while the
second has dark-grey smooth-looking skin and tusks which tend to point
more inwards. Moreover the bush elephant has only four toenails on


the fore-feet and three on the hind-feet, while the more primitive forest
elephant has five on the fore-feet and four on the hind-feet.


They are thus so different that Glover M. Allen has considered that


361


93. Forest elephant compared with the larger savannah elephant.
Note the different shape of the ears.


they are actually different species, and that the savannah elephant (by
the law of priority) should be called Loxodonta africana, and the forest
elephant Loxodonta cyclotis. These two species do not seem to Keep
strictly to their respective habitats. On 19 May 1938, when he was
exploring the Albert National Park in the Belgian Congo, Dr Serge
Frechkop happened to see two herds of elephants feeding close to one
another only 100 yards or so from his camp at Ishango north of Lake
Edward:


One of these herds consisted of larger elephants with brownish-grey
skin; the other included individuals measuring about three-quarters of
the height of the specimens in the first herd and having skin of a blackish
dark brown colour. The two herds moved side by side without mingling
with one another.


Although he could not get close enough to examine the shape of their


ears, he was convinced that one herd consisted of Loxodonta africana
and the other of Loxodonta cyclotis.


Besides these two there seems to be a third much more controversial
species, the pygmy elephant, in which the adult does not exceed 6 feet
6 inches at the withers. There is no doubt that such elephants exist.
Specimens have lived in the Antwerp and New York zoos, but some


362


THREE LARGE PYGMIES


zoologists maintain that this does not prove they are separate species
(like those once found on Malta and other Mediterranean islands); they
may merely be the freak offspring of normal elephants. It is often diffi-
cult to distinguish between true pygmies and pathological dwarfs. To


settle the question one would have to observe the reproduction of pygmy


elephants or prove that there are whole herds of them.


The pygmy elephant was first officially described in 1906 by a German
professor, Theodore Noack of Brunswick from a specimen which was six
years old and came from Ndjoléin Gabon. He called it Loxodonta pumilio.
In 1923 Hornaday reported it in the same area, around Lake N’Gobi,
80 miles south-east of Fernan Vaz, and in 1926 Pohle reported it in
Fernan Vaz itself. Not long ago Professor Bourdelle, one of the world’s
greatest experts on mammals, and Francis Petter published a remark-
able study of a pygmy elephant, killed on 11 March 1948 at Aloombé
on the coast of Gabon between Libreville and Port-Gentil.
It was a
solitary old male, thought to be very aged. It was barely 6 feet 5 inches
high. Lucien Blancou, who has made a careful study of the mammals of
French Equatorial Africa, notes that the negroes make a clear distinc-
tion between the pygmy elephant and the larger species; he remarks that


it is usually hairier than the ordinary elephant and he is convinced that


it is a distinct animal.


In the Congo the pygmy elephants are often said to be aquatic. A


settler living near Lefini in the Upper Congo area, showed Hans Schom-
burgk a piece of thick skin like an ordinary elephant’s but covered with
a fleece of reddish hairs. He said it came from an animal which the
natives called “‘river-elephant” and which had amphibious habits like a
hippopotamus. There were persistent rumours all round Lake Leopold
II about this curious animal, but Schomburgk was unable to find out
the truth of them himself.


In 1911 Professor Trouessart reported that a certain Le Petit had
seen five of these water-elephants at Tomba-Mayi on the north bank of
Lake Leopold II, in the Loukeni region of the Belgian Congo. Their
trunks and ears were remarkably short but their necks, on the other
hand, were longer than an ordinary elephant’s, and they were not more


than 6 feet 6 inches high. At the sight of man they jumped into the


water, leaving only their trunks and the crowns of their heads above it
and swam out into the lake.?


Dr Henri Schouteden, Director of the Congo Museum at Tervueren


in Belgium, thought that Le Petit must have been “the object of a


1 Le Petit’s elephants will be discussed in greater detail on pp. 472-4.


363


THE TERRORS OF AFRICA


complete illusion and that the natives, as often happens in the Congo,
had given a free rein to their imagination.” He was soon to change his
mind. Lieutenant Franssen, a Belgian officer, had promised to make a
systematic search for the animal and send a specimen to the Museum
at Tervueren. “If the animal exists,” he said, ‘I will come back with it;
otherwise I shall not come back at all.”


Lieutenant Franssen came back, as he had promised, with the remains
of a water-elephant captured “after spending thirty-six hours in mud
and water.” Exhausted by his sufferings on this expedition, and shaken
with violent fever, he did not long survive his return. Dr Schouteden
named the water-elephant, or waka-waka as the natives called it,
Loxodonta fransseni in his honour. Although his specimen was one of
the largest in the herd it was only 5 feet 5 inches at the withers. Its
tusks were 2 feet 2 inches long and together weighed under 43 pounds.
They were thus considerably longer than those of an ordinary elephant
of the same size, as Dr Schouteden points out.


According to him the shape of the ears and the fact that there are two
finger-like appendages on the tip of the trunk (L. pumilio, like the Asian
elephant, is supposed to have only one) are enough to justify a new spe-
cies of pygmy elephant. Personally I cannot see much difference in the
shape of the ears in photographs of L. pumilio and L. fransseni, and I find
it hard to believe that there are any elephants in Africa with only one
finger on the tip of the trunk.
It is more likely that L. fransseni is
merely a synonym for L. pumilio—which is hard luck on Lieutenant
Franssen.


Pygmy elephants have been reported in other widely separated parts
of the Belgian Congo, where they do not seem to be particularly amphi-
bious. In 1932, Major P. Offerman, director of the elephant-taming
station at Gangala-na-Bodio, reported that two pygmy elephants had
been captured in the Api (Uelé) area. They measured 4 feet 3 inches
and 4 feet 9 inches at the withers, but had “long and stout tusks almost
touching the ground.” The natives called them abele as distinct from
tembo, the larger elephant.


A.-J. Jobaert, an honorary assistant game-warden in the Belgian
Congo, several times saw pygmy elephants in the Lusambo province,
and thinks that this species lives in “all the large forests in the northern
territory of the province.” These little elephants were never more than
6 feet 6 inches high and they always travelled “in fairly large herds.”


Glover M. Allen maintained in 1936 that pygmy elephants (L. pumilio
and L. franssent) are merely forest elephants (L. cyclotis) which are not


364


THREE LARGE PYGMIES


yet fully grown. All the same there is no doubt that adult pygmy ele-
phants exist which are less than 6 feet 6 inches high. The specimen at
the New York Zoo, whose growth Dr Hornaday followed to the end,
reached a height of only 6 feet 5 inches and a weight of 1 ton 24 cwt.
An adult of the larger species weighs between 5 and 7 tons. The evi-


dence I have already cited shows that there exist small groups and even


large herds of pygmy elephants, so that Allen’s view is hard to maintain


today. Bourdelle and Petter also point out that the pygmy elephant


appears to have a habitat of its own:


Up to the present the pygmy elephant has appeared to be mainly an


inhabitant of the African rain-forest, and especially the marshy parts


of it; this seems to justify its name of ‘‘water-elephant’’ which the
population often give it and which certain authors have used in their
turn.


Thus there are three species of elephants in Africa, corresponding to
three different habitats: the bush elephant, naturally the largest and
with the most developed ears, as is usual with animals that live in fairly
open country; the forest elephant, smaller, darker and with rounder
ears; and the marsh elephant, even smaller and hairier. (In this respect


it is like the Negrillo pygmies which differ from the other negroes in the
same way; perhaps a moist jungle habitat causes these racial differences.)
The size of the adults seems to range roughly between 5 feet and 6 feet
6 inches in the pygmies, between 6 feet 6 inches and Io feet in the
forest elephants, and ro and 13 feet in the bush elephants. There is no
gap between the species, which has always made it difficult to tell them
apart. But to deny that the pygmy elephant exists, even as a sub-species
of Loxodonta cyclotis, shows a most obstinate prejudice. W. R. Foran, a
British big-game hunter, has even affirmed that the pygmy elephant was
invented by ivory-traders. It is forbidden to kill elephants that are not
full-grown, so when poachers shoot a young one they pretend it is a


pygmy.


Many zoologists are still no less incredulous, but with no justification,
especially when one recalls how ready they are to create new species


or sub-species, distinguished only by the slightest difference in colour


or a few extra whiskers.


The reader may feel that the evidence for the pygmy rhinoceros is too


vague and that the pygmy elephant is too well-established to be un-


known. No such objection can be made against the marozzt, the little


spotted lion of the Kenya mountains.


365


THE TERRORS OF AFRICA


Colonel R. Meinertzhagen, who was the first to collect remains of the


giant forest-hog, heard of it several times between 1903 and 1908, but


not until 1931 was any more official notice taken of it. Then Captain
R. E. Dent, a Kenya game-warden in charge of the Fisheries section,
saw four of these large cats crossing the path in front of him, between.
10,000 and 11,000 feet up, near the sources of the Kathita above Meru.
They seemed to him smaller than ordinary lions and of a very different
type. No doubt he would have forgotten about it if a few months later
his boys, who had set leopard-traps all along the eastern slopes of the
Aberdare Range, had not come and told him excitedly that they had
caught an unusual animal. It was neither a lion nor a leopard, but a sort
of cross between the two. Unfortunately for some unknown reason they
were not able to bring the specimen back.


A little later a white farmer called Michael Trent shot two small lions
with strange fur which had been attracted by a waterbuck that he had


fixed as bait some 10,000 feet up in the Aberdares. He was not a
naturalist and did not think their peculiar appearance was important.
Luckily an official in the Game Department happened to see the skins
preserved as trophies and thought them so unusual that he at once took
them back to Nairobi to Captain A. T. A. Ritchie, then Chief Game-
Warden, who recognised that there was something unusual about them
(see photograph facing page 368). They were those of a lion and a


lioness, for one of them had a mane, though it consisted of little more
than side-whiskers.


From their size they seemed to belong to lions at least three years
old—the age of puberty—which was perhaps confirmed by the fact that
they were a lion and his mate. But their skins were spotted. Now lion-
cubs are always born with fur speckled with fairly faint spots, but these
usually disappear quite soon and have quite gone before they are three
yearg old. These skins. were clearly spotted, and the spots showed not
the slightest signs of fading. But without a complete skeleton, or at


all events a skull, which could have definitely established the speci-
men’s age, it was hard for the Game Department officials to give a
verdict.


It was recalled that in 1924 the late Blayney Percival, a famous game
warden and a brilliant naturalist, reported he had killed a lioness and
her cubs which were all very clearly spotted. Might not some indivi-
duals retain their juvenile spotted coat until later than usual? It was
best to be cautious. But Kenneth Gandar Dower, a big-game hunter
who also examined the skins, was more positive about them:

THREE LARGE PYGMIES


They appear to belong to lions two or three years old—the male had
a whiskery mane—and yet the cub spots with which almost every lion is

large for a leopard’s and too small for a lion’s; nor could they be mis-

Undaunted, he published an exciting book about the spotted lion in
1937. It made a good deal of noise in the British Press and brought to

In a letter to the Field he recalls that one day when he had shot an animal
he took for a leopard, although it was unusually large and dark in colour,
his Kikuyu boys told him that it was a damasia, not a chui (leopard), and
that it was as different from a leopard as a lion from a marozt. When he
asked them what a marozi was, they at once replied that it was an animal
smaller than a lion, which one usually met in pairs, though this hap-

Later, in the spring of 1923, I crossed the Aberdares on foot from

An inquiry among the Kikuyu confirmed that they did in fact make a

Raymond Hook, the hunter who accompanied Gandar Dower’s ex-

would have undergone a change in colour to suit its new environment.
But Hook thinks that there is not enough evidence to prove its existence.


Other experts are less cautious. Powys Cobb of Elementeita, who
knows African big-game well, is convinced that a species unknown to
science lives in the thick and little-explored Mau forest. He surprised a
strange beast of the cat tribe, between a leopard and a lion in size, which
had attacked cattle grazing in a corner of his farm near the edge of the

where he had to give up the chase without having come any nearer to


it. Its footprints were like a small lion’s.


These two opinions were quoted after Gandar Dower’s death, by

The natives of Embu told Major G. St. J. Orde-Brown about “a


lion-like forest cheetah” on the south-eastern slopes of Mount Kenya.
There is no doubt that this is our “spotted lion,” for the cheetah is like
the lion in outline: both have high shoulders and usually walk with the
head raised, while the leopard holds its head farther forward and lower
than its shoulders. No doubt this is because the lion and cheetah are
animals of the savannah, while the leopard and tiger usually live in
forests ; and animals living in tall grass have more need to lift their heads
to get their bearings than those which slink through bushy under-
growth.

ntarago, in which he is inclined to believe, having heard its voice.

The voice I heard that evening at Kichwamba was strangeness itself,
and beyond my power to describe with sufficient accuracy, although I

thing else if you add the word liquid or gurgling.


Four natives, one of them an old and trusted tracker, all independently
told Temple-Perkins that it was the ntarago. He was unable to catch
sight of the beast in the firelight, nor could he find any spoor. All the
same he is very insistent that animal is a feline, and is quite emphatic
that it has nothing to do with another frequently reported animal, the
giant hyena.


For some fifty years, then, rumours have been current about this
strange cat in Upper Kenya above Meru, despite the scepticism of some
experts who maintain that it is merely an ordinary lion that has retained


its juvenile spotted coat. Each witness has reported the same features:
the size is smaller than an adult lion and nearer that of a cheetah, the
spots are like a leopard’s, and there is little or no mane.


Most naturalists are apt to be reserved about the spotted lion’s
existence, but not ill-disposed to it. Reginald Pocock, a great authority
on the felines, is distinctly favourable, and brings grist to Gandar

There is, as a matter of fact, some independent evidence, unknown to
Mr Gandar Dower at the time, of the evidence of a small lion in Kenya.
Several years ago, Messrs. Rowland Ward showed me the skulls of an
adult lion. and lioness received without skins or more precise locality
from that Colony. Their unusually small dimensions puzzled me a good
deal. The skull of the lion was less than 4 an inch longer than the
longest lioness’s skull, from Laikipia, in the Washington collection, and
the same width; and the skull of the lioness was nearly 1 in. shorter
and over } an inch narrower than the smallest lioness’s skull, from
Kapiti, in the same collection.


Since these skulls are decidedly smaller, sex for sex, than any out of
the very large numbers that have been measured from many localities
in the plains of East Africa, it seems probable that they came from some
place in Kenya where few sportsmen have shot and preserved lions.
That place may have been the mountain forests of the Aberdares ...

But how does he explain the fact that Michael Trent’s lions did not
change their spots even after they were shot, skinned and examined by

Major W. R. Foran, whose sceptical views about the pygmy elephant
we have already heard, takes the line in an article on ““The Legendary

On two different occasions in 1906 I shot a lion and a lioness on the

somewhat smaller than the average lion and the male was quite mane-

What makes him think these were individual freaks and-not members
of a different race? Elsewhere he makes a remark which contradicts this
point of view:
;


There is nothing unusual in lions being found at such high altitudes:


they are customarily styled “‘forest’’ lions, and on average, they are
smaller than normal beasts found on the plains at lower altitudes.


Certainly it is not unusual to find lions on mountains, but to find them
in thick forests like those on Mount Kenya is quite extraordinary. The
lion is an animal of the savannah. It never ventures into thick forests.
So if one finds lions in such forests they must therefore be a very special
kind of lion. Since racial differences are always shown in differences in
form and colour, it would be quite normal for forest lions to be smaller
and have a spotted coat. As Dr Serge Frechkop has noted about
leopards, “‘there is as a general rule a type of larger size with a lighter
coat in the savannah, and a type of smaller size with a darker coat in
the forest.” Why should not this also be true of lions?

Major Foran does not explain the legend of the marozi very convinc-
ingly. He recalls that zoologists allow only two varieties of lion in East
Africa, the Masai lion (massaica) and the Somali lion (somalica). The
second is smaller, has practically no mane but larger ears; it is always of


a lighter fawn, almost cream-colour. Perhaps, he suggests, the Somali


lion has come into Kenya and settled there. But he seems to forget that


the Somali lion like the other lions, but unlike the marozi, is not sup-


posed to retain its juvenile spots when it is fully-grown.


In any case these varieties of African lions need some qualification.
Dr Frechkop remarks that:


It does not seem that today one can distinguish more than one species
of the genus Leo, unless perhaps the differences between the African
lions and those which are still preserved in a region of India are con-
siderable enough for the latter to be treated as a species (Leo goojraten-
sts) different from that which lives in Africa (Leo leo).


As to the African lions, it is certain that there are fairly marked
differences between the lions found in Algeria [Leo Jeo Jeo (Linn.), the
Atlas or Barbary lion] and those found in Cape Colony, called Leo leo
capensis (Fischer) or Leo leo melanochaitus (H. Smith), as well as be-
tween those which live in Senegal—Leo leo senegalensis (Meyer)—and
those in East Africa.


Dr Frechkop goes on to deplore the creation of a host of sub-species
which he considers to be “‘the exaggeration of systematicians who do not
take into account the animals’ life, nor the complex play of heredity and
individual variation.” “I am far from denying that these names may


refer to different races,”’ he writes, “but it is also necessary that each
specimen from one region should have the characteristics attributed to
the race belonging to that region.” And he goes on to show that even
in the Albert National Park in the Belgian Congo there are two extreme
types, with every possible intermediate form: one is a lion with an
undeveloped mane, confined to the neck and consisting of tawny hairs
with only very few blackish ones; the other has a thick dark mane, reach-
ing beyond the shoulders and even under the front legs where it forms


tufts on the elbows. Obviously this is not a case of separate races but


of individual variations. As most of the sub-species of lions are based


on such slight characteristics as the relative size of the mane or the


relative colour of the fur, I doubt whether they have much value. Yet,


paradoxically enough, the same systematicians who are so ready to


create new species on such trivial data, refuse to admit that the


spotted lion is a separate variety, even though the differences observed


in its size and marking are so distinct that they may well justify the


371


THE TERRORS OF AFRICA


creation of a new species, which could have no better name than Leo
maculatus.


At all events there is little doubt that a race of lions with juvenile
characteristics could have arisen in Kenya, where it has taken refuge in
the thick forests at high altitudes. Cut off there from the lions of the
plains, they must have undergone considerable changes as a result of
the phenomenon of segregation. From all accounts they seem to have
dwindled appreciably, for they are generally said to be between the size
of a lion and a leopard. If a large lion (omitting the tail) is 5 feet 3
inches long, and a large leopard is 4 feet, an adult spotted lion would
be about 4 feet 8 inches from the tip of the nose to the root of the tail.
Perhaps its size is even smaller, since it has several times been compared


to a cheetah, which rarely exceeds 3 feet 3 inches, in which case one
could clearly call it a “pygmy lion,” and, like the pygmy forms of hippo-
potamus (Choeropsis), rhinoceros (Dicerorhinus), siamang-gibbon (Hylo-
bates klossi) and chimpanzee (Pan paniscus), it would deserve to be
raised at least to the status of a new species. Its exact position in the
zoological scale cannot be settled until its skeleton and perhaps also its
internal anatomy have been studied. And we have yet to capture a
specimen.

THE bravest native hunters in Kenya will tremble at the name of the
chemosit. Men who are not afraid to meet a lion with no weapon but a
spear, turn back at once if they come upon its footprints. It is said that
no one who has heard its hideous cry ever forgets it. But if you ask a


settler, whether he be game-warden or professional zoologist, about this
nightmarish creature, he will give you nothing but vague theories, a
frank denial or a sceptical shrug of the shoulders. Yet it would need a
whole book to detail all the tales told by whites and negroes in British
East Africa and the neighbouring part of the Belgian Congo about a


sort of large “bear” of unparalleled ferocity. The British call it Nandi
bear, from the name of the people in whose territory it is chiefly found.


_ Now the odd thing is that there is virtually not a single species of bear
in the whole African continent.! Of course there is no certainty that the
Nandi bear is really a bear, but it looks like one; and the features re-
ported by numerous witnesses are so characteristic that it seems a

reasonable supposition. Moreover, despite the total absence of bears in

Ancient accounts of travels sometimes mention bears even in the

In the centuries that followed, all naturalists agreed that there were
no bears in Africa. It was not until 1905 that Europeans first saw what
came to be known as the Nandi bear on the Uasin Gishu tableland; and
their accounts were not published until there was a particularly persis-

I am asked to describe the strange beast that I once saw up on the
Uasingishu, and it is with some diffidence that I make the attempt since
experience has taught me that descriptions of unrecorded animals do
not meet with much credence.


However, as I now hear that it has been seen again, I feel encouraged
to do the best I can.


Several years ago I was travelling with a cousin on the Uasingishu
just after the Nandi expedition, and, of course, long before there was any
settlement up there. We had been camped on the edge of the Escarp-
ment near the Mataye and were marching towards the Sirgoit Rock
when we saw the beast. There was a thick mist, and my cousin and I
were walking on ahead of the safari with one boy when, just as we drew
near to the slopes of the hill, the mist cleared away suddenly and my
cousin called out ‘What is that?’ Looking in the direction to which
he pointed I saw a large animal sitting up on its haunches not more than
30 yards away. Its attitude was just that of a bear at the ‘Zoo’ asking
for buns, and I should say it must have been nearly 5 feet high. It is
extremely hard to estimate height in a case of this kind; but it seemed
to both of us that it was very nearly, if not quite, as tall as we were.
Before we had time to do anything it dropped forward and shambled

The tales which were current when this very circumstantial account

apparently mysterious—animal they failed to recognise.

This strange beast was first mentioned to me by Mr. Clifford Hill,
who, on the first survey of this railway, had a young Dutch boy with
him who came across one on the Koora Plains (Mile 71).


He had seen nothing like it and could not describe it, so Mr. Hill
showed him a picture-book of animals, and he picked out the bear as
being like the animal he had seen.


The first we heard of it during construction was when we had our
pipe-line discharging water to waste at about Mile 71. Several engi-
neers saw a strange spoor in the mud so formed—all the rest of the
country being dry. It has been sketched to me and described as that of
a bear. [See Fig. 94.]


A native servant of one of the engineers, Mr. Archibald, also reported
that he saw this strange animal, which, he says, stood on its hind legs
and looked at him, but would not run away.


The only other instance of its actually having been seen is reported
by a sub-contractor, Mr. Caviggia, who saw one at Mile 38, and his
description is very similar to mine.


I have been in Africa—East, South, and West—in the wilds in ad-
vance of civilisation, building railways during a considerable part of the
last eighteen years, and I cannot think of any animal I have not seen
in its wild state, but I have never before seen anything like this beast.


The last of Hobley’s reports does not seem at first sight to refer to the
animal in question.


There are also stories of another unknown beast from the lower and
middle valley of the Tana River. Mr. Cumberbatch, the District Officer
of that region, tells me that the German missionaries who have lived
for many years at Ngao state that the Pokomo natives know of a forest
beast called the ‘Koddoelo,’ and is said to have been killed near Ngao
some years back. On one occasion one of the missionaries found that
the whole population of the biggest Pokomo settlement in Kina Kombe
district had deserted their village and crossed the river because this
animal was roaming about in the bush near the village.


The animal was described to the District Officer by a Pokomo (who,
however, admitted that he himself had not seen it) as being as large as a
man, as sometimes going on four legs, sometimes on two, in general
appearance like a huge baboon, and very fierce. The Pokomo native is

not a highly strung or imaginative person, so it is possible that there is
some undiscovered anthropoid beast in the dense bush which is found
in the Tana Valley.


An “undiscovered anthropoid beast” may seem a long way from a
“bear,” but in fact the Nandi think the chemosit is more like a large
monkey. And when Hobley soon afterwards received further details
about the koddoelo from a Mr Rule who had made a thorough inquiry
among the Wa-Pokomo, he published a description which agrees in
many details with that seen by Hickes beside the Magadi railway.


Colour, reddish to yellow; length, about 6 feet; height, about 3 feet
6 inches at the withers; hair long, and all accounts agree on the point of
a thick mane;
tail short and very broad; claws very long; head, fairly
long nose, teeth long but not so long as lion; fore-legs said to be very
thick.


The Pokomo state that several have been killed, and one man says
that he killed one himself a good many years ago. It is said to be very
fierce, and to visit villages and carry off sheep. On these occasions the
natives either cross the river until it leaves the neighbourhood or
frighten it away by beating drums. The Waboni hunters know the
beast well, but say that they prefer to leave it alone.


Hobley goes on to give further information which comes even nearer,
in some details at least, to the descriptions of the alleged Nandi bear.


The Assistant District Commissioner on the Tana also sends a
further account of the animal, based on recent inquiries, and it was
described to him by Pokomo, who said they had seen it, and their
account was as follows:—Light in colour, long hair on neck and back;
usually goes on fore-legs but can go on its hind-legs, not known to
climb trees, rather smaller than a lion, tail about 18 inches long and
some 4 inches broad, is nocturnal in its habits, fore-legs very thick; said
to leave a track with one deep claw mark behind the marks of its four
toes (this is rather obscure). They are agreed about its ferocity and
say it attacks a man on sight. One is said to have killed a rhino near
Makere, but this is rather difficult to credit. One tried to raid a goat
kraal last January, but was driven away by the noise made by the
villagers when the alarm was given.

As the rumours grew all over Kenya, people began to interrogate the
natives to find out whether they knew any bear-like creature, and little
by little it began to appear that an animal like one in some respect or
another was well known to the natives since time immemorial. On the
coast the Moslem Swahili peoples, who from long contact with Arabs
had learnt of the existence of bears, had not been influenced by the
whites in calling the mysterious beast by a name derived from the
Arabic for bear: duba. In the uplands, beyond the reach of Arab in-
fluence, the Lumbwa name is geteit which means “‘brain-eater.” This
becomes gereit, kereit, keteit or kerit on the slopes of the Mau escarp-
ment and in the Nandi country, where it is also called chemosit and chimi-


set or “the devil.” In Ruanda this is altered to 1kimizi, though other
parts of the same country use the quite different name of kikambangwe,
The Ba-Gishu and Sabai of Mount Elgon call it sabrookoo.


But, whatever the name, there is no doubt that the native descriptions


are often very exaggerated, or perhaps one should say poeticised. Ali,
Roger Courtney’s guide, speaks of it as “great, white and hairy, that
walks upright like a man and eats only the brain of its victims.” The
Nandi chief Kitapmetit Kipet described it to Captain William Hichens


as “half like a man and half like a huge, ape-faced bird, and you may
know it at once from its fearful howling roar, and because in the dark of
night its mouth glows red like the embers of a log.” Such tales were
naturally taken for mere superstitions until white men started to see the
Nandi bear and show that they might have a real foundation.


There seems little doubt that there is confusion in the Nandi mind
between a real animal and a devil in their local mythology. Perhaps this


is because they call the beast chemosit in a figurative sense, just as we call
various animals, such as the predatory Tasmanian marsupial, by the
name of “devil.” In his standard work on The Nandi, their Language
and Folklore, published in 1909, A. C. Hollis drew a fantastic picture of
the local devil, some of whose features are apt to turn up in descrip-
tions of the Nandi bear.


There is also a devil called Chemosit, who is supposed to live on the
earth and to prowl round searching to devour people, especially chil-
dren. He is said to be half man, half bird, to have only one leg but nine
buttocks, and his mouth, which is red, is supposed to shine at night like
a lamp. He propels himself by means of a stick which resembles a
spear and which he uses as a crutch.


380


THE NANDI BEAR, AN EAST AFRICAN PROTEUS


Subsequently I. Q. Orchardson, a settler who had lived among the
Kipsigis (another name for the Lumbwa) for 16 years, maintained that


the chemosit should not be considered as entirely mythical.


Among the Kipsigis one finds no belief that the Chemosit is a devil or
spirit or god or man. The only reference to its being like a man is that
some say that at a distance it looks like a huge man because it stands up
on its hind legs. Even those who say it has only one leg say that it has
no arms and that its footprint is something between that of an elephant
and a rhino and insist very strongly that it is only an animal. A few old
men even say that they have seen it at night and give descriptions—very
wild ones but all quite unlike man or spirit, for they include fur, whis-
kers (“‘wawechik’’ = whiskers or antennae of animals and insects only).
The crutch of Hollis’s book is quite unknown here for they say how
could an animal use a crutch. A curious detail is that the urine of the
Chemosit is said to be so evil smelling that no man can stay near it. All
the young men deny having seen it or knowing what it is like, but love
to tell children and unsuspecting Europeans fancy tales of it.


The name Chemosit however might not be said at night just as in the
case of the Chief Witch Doctor. At night it was given another name,
viz. Gononet, of which I do not know the derivation. Chemosit is a fairly
common man’s name and it is also used by mothers to make their chil-
dren obey, e.g. “If you don’t eat your food the Chemosit will come and
eat you.”


Because mothers frighten children with bugbears in our country, it
does not mean that all bears are imaginary beasts. To the Nandi the
chemosit seems to be sometimes a bugbear and sometimes a real bear—


or at least a real animal rather like one.


When settlers tried to set about finding out what this animal was they
could count on little help from the natives, who were all too apt to turn
grey with fear at the mention of its name. “Anyone who has lived in a
‘Nandi bear atmosphere,’” writes the game-warden C. R. S. Pitman,
“cannot doubt the reality of the dread the brute inspires.” Indeed it is
supposed to be a more bloodthirsty monster than any other animal in
Africa. Not only does it slaughter domestic animals, but every year it is
blamed for the death of many natives found with their skulls smashed in


or the top of the head literally torn off.


Charles T. Stoneham, a well-known big-game hunter who searched
for the mysterious animal in the Mau forests, gives some details:


Men told me it came down to the villages at night and murdered the


- inhabitants in their huts. It made its entrance through the roof, killed
the occupants, and ate their brains. That was one of the beast’s pecu-
liarities ; it ate only the brains of its victims. Women gathering firewood


381


THE TERRORS OF AFRICA


in the forest would be missed, and later their bodies would be dis-
covered, always minus the tops of their skulls.


One of the brute’s tricks is supposed to be to lie along a low branch
above a path and wait till someone comes past. Then with a savage blow
of its great clawed paw it rips open his head and eats his brain.


Without going into the way the beast ambushes its victims, but relying
only on the wounds it is said to cause, we can say at once that no cat


kills in this manner. It is much more like that of a large bear, which
would generally stand up to its full height and use its powerful claws to
hit its adversary, very likely scalping him as if he were
aman. The cats
on the other hand almost always finish off their victims by crunching


their teeth into the nape of the neck or the small of the back.


In 1919 a farmer in the Lumbwa country called Cara Buxton told a
circumstantial story which may perhaps provide the key to this parti-
cular problem:


A short time ago a ‘Gadett’ [obviously the same word as geteit]
visited this district. This name is given to the animal by the Lumbwa
and signifies the ‘brain-eater.’


Its first appearance was on my farm, where the sheep were missing.
We finally found all ten, seven dead and three still alive. In no case
were the bodies touched, but the brains were torn out.


Buxton appends “‘a tracing from a photograph of one of the sheep that
was still alive.” The hole through which the brain has been removed is
tiny, no more than an inch across.


During the next ten days fifty-seven goats and sheep were destroyed
in the same way; of these thirteen were found alive. The Lumbwa were
allin a state of great terror, and weird stories were told of the ‘Gadett’:
how it walked on its hind legs, pulled babies out of huts, and was even
able to killa man, Finally it was tracked to a ravine and killed by the
Lumbwa with their spears. It turned out to be a very large hyena of
the ordinary spotted variety.
It had evidently turned brain-eater
through some sort of madness.


This anecdote can hardly be said to clear up the whole problem of the
Nandi bear. The spotted hyena does not agree with the various descrip-


tions of the unknown animal, nor is it completely proved that the beast
the Lumbwa killed was the real culprit. This theory would imply that
spotted hyenas are often seized with a strange “madness” which drives
them to swallow the brains and spurn the rest of the body. Anyway,
how do they set about trepanning the skulls so neatly?


But the most suspicious thing about the Nandi bear is not the way it


382


THE NANDI BEAR, AN EAST AFRICAN PROTEUS


attacks, but that it attacks at all. Most so-called savage beasts never
attack man unless they are wounded, startled or provoked. I therefore
think it is a safe rule that the more nervous the animal the more dan-


gerous it is. The large carnivores usually take no notice of man, whom


they rightly distrust. If they do charge him deliberately it is in excep-


tional circumstances: usually when they have been starving for several


days because they have been unable to obtain the game that is their


usual diet. Hyatt Verrill observes:


As a rule the man-eaters are old, decrepit tigers or lions which, being
unable to bring down fleet footed, wary, wild animals, are forced to
resort to killing easier prey and find human beings the easiest of any.


More general and serious famine affecting beasts of prey of all ages


—and thus indirectly man who is liable to become their victim—may
occur if disease or intensive hunting makes their normal prey scarce.


Famine may also be seasonal, particularly for the lion in the rainy
season. In dry weather he cannot go for long without drinking and must
always remain close to a water-hole where his prey must also come to
drink. Thus he always has food to hand. But when the heavy rains
begin, little puddles form here and there in the bush, and the herbi-
vorous animals leave their usual dangerous drinking-holes. Now the
lion must hunt for food; and if he is an old solitary male with no family


ties he may wander very far afield. Bad luck in hunting may lead to
long days with little food, and then he becomes a public menace, attack-
ing the lonely traveller or leaping over stockades and killing cattle and
even villagers in their huts. If his first attempts sueceed, this way of life
becomes a habit.


This happens but rarely, and serious naturalists are apt to be sceptical
when an animal is said to be a man-eater. The Nandi bear’s reputation
in this respect is, however, based on unequivocal facts. A. Blayney
Percival, the celebrated game-warden, is responsible for what is perhaps
the only report of a chemosit being killed for its misdeeds: it happened in
the Maraquet district not long before 1914.


It is said that at one time one of these animals was so bad that great
preparations were made to kill it, and at last it was killed by a party of
men who put a dummy man in the doorway of a hut and sat inside and
waited till the animal came and tried to take the dummy;
it was then
shot with arrows.


The following story is more circumstantial: in 1925 a village had
suffered so much from one of these brute’s depredations that the vil-
lagers asked the Government of Kenya for help. They said that it had


383


THE TERRORS OF AFRICA


carried off a six-year-old girl one night after having cut a hole chrongh
the mud wall of her hut. What is more it had managed to force a way |
through a thorny hedge 8 feet thick and drag away some calves. Now —
the surprising thing about this is not that it should have carried off a
person or a calf. A large beast of prey can carry a man or even a whole
ox; in fact it is even capable, as many witnesses have affirmed, of leaping
over a 6-foot palisade with such a burden in its mouth! The astonishing
thing is the way the brute reached his victims. Lions and leopards never
try to force a way through the thick and thorny fences round native


cattle compounds because their noses and the pads on the feet are far too
sensitive and vulnerable. They jump over the fence. A brute which
could force its way through such a thicket of thorns must not only have
strong burrowing claws but also an armour of thick hair and hide. Only
a creature like a bear could perform such a feat.


The government official who was sent to investigate these raids has
told the story in Chambers’s Fournal for 1927 in an article signed with
the pseudonym ‘“‘Fulahn,” concealing the identity of Captain William
Hichens of the Intelligence and Administrative Services of East Africa.


Although Chief Kitapmetit Kipet gave such a fantastic description
of the chimiset which was supposed to be to blame, Hichens set to work


as if he were after a real beast.


Kipet informed me that the chimiset seemed to come from a small
forest-clad kopje or boulder hill some five miles from his nganasa.
I
circled that kopje with spearsmen, and, gradually closing in, beat every
bush and twig on it till we got to the summit. We put up baboons,
rock-rabbits, some mongooses, some dik-dik antelopes, a bush-buck
and its does; we put to flight owls, hawks, bats, and guinea-fowls. We
found the lair of a porcupine family and a hyaena hole; we dug both
out. We put up some wart-hogs, and the dogs turned out innumerable
rats, mice, and lizards, and not a few scorpions and snakes. But we
found no chimiset; nor trace of it. Nor did we find a trace of the spoor
of lion or leopard, which might have been the culprits.


I thought of a score of such hunts after the chimiset, all of which had
proved futile, and decided to make quite sure. A huge forest, some
twenty miles square, stretched away from the kopje. I could not search
that forest, but I could make certain if any beast came to the kopje from
the forest and then left the kopje by night for the village.


Around the kopje ran several sandy bush-tracks, which led to water-
holes. Cutting down the bush between, Kipet’s men joined these paths
until they made a sandy track completely encircling the kopje. We
brushed this track clean and smooth, so that even a beetle walking over
it would leave its trail.

aroused, unbarring their hut doors,


I heard my pi-dog yelp just once. There was a crashing of branches

But that howl! I have heard half a dozen lions roaring in a stampede-
chorus not twenty yards away; I have heard a maddened cow-elephant
trumpeting; I have heard a trapped leopard make the silent night miles
a rocking agony with screaming, snarling roars. But never have I heard,
nor do I wish to hear again, such a how] as that of the chimiset.


A trail of red spots on the sand showed where my pi-dog had gone.
Beside that trail were huge footprints, four times as big as a man’s,
showing the imprint of three huge clawed toes, with trefoil marks like a
lion’s pad where the sole of the foot pressed down. But no lion, not
even the giant 9 feet 44 inches long which fell to Getekonot, my hunter,
at Ussure, ever boasted such a paw as that of the monster which had
made that terrifying spoor.


At the first streak of dawn we followed those tracks; they led to the
kopje. Over our sandy path they showed as plain as the print on this
page; on the farther side of the kopje were more footprints leading to
the forest, where, searching with our hearts in our mouths every day
for a week and more, we found and lost and lost and found them. But
we found no chimiset.

One day, when hunting in the forest, I was shown by a palpitating
game-scout a pair of very peculiar animal footmarks. They were two
enormous pug marks, the size of dinner-plates, in a soft patch of ground.
They were spade-shaped and turned inward. The claws must have
been non-retractile, as I could distinctly see the small cuts where they
had dug into the earth. The fact that they turned inward revealed a
bear-like character; otherwise I would have said that they had been
made by the grandfather of all hyenas.


But, then, a hyena enormous enough to leave footprints as big as
those would have himself been a fabulous beast.


There have been rumours that the Nandi bear has six toes on each
foot—which have helped to discredit it in zoologists’ eyes. This absurd
story is based on imprints with six toe-pads and six claws. In Nature
Parade Frank Lane has published a sketch of one of them, found in the
sand “in dry-season river-bed of Dalumo River, Iyambi.” It is obvi-
ously a composite print made by an animal which normally puts its
hind-feet down on the imprints of its fore-feet.


On one point everyone who has examined a supposed chemosit’s track


is agreed: it cannot be a feline animal with retractile claws.


From all over East Africa and for almost half a century generally
consistent rumours about the beast have come, and still regularly come.


It may even be responsible for the depredations of an unknown animal
in much of north Cape Province and the Transvaal in the thirties.
Captain William Hichens writes in 1937, this time signing his own
name:


No one has seen the animal, but its spoor is known and its sav-
age depredations have caused widespread alarm. The natives call it
the khodumodumo, or “gaping-mouthed-bush-monster.”?
In stealthy
silence, under cover of the darkest nights, this marauder invades the
kraals and farms, clambers over six-foot palisades which pole in the
cattle-byres and stock-pens and then, seizing a sheep, goat, or calf,
leaps back over the fence, to disappear with its quarry.


Its spoor on the kraal pathways and bushveld tracks only serves to
shroud the animal in deeper mystery. Its footprints are “round, saucer-
like spoor, with two-inch toenail marks,’ a pug which has so far
puzzled hunters to identify, since it does not fit the paw of any known
wild beast that raids stock. The khodumodumo’s attacks were especially

predatory in the Graaffreinet area, where a posse of over a hundred
settlers turned out to hunt the beast down, a large reward having been
placed on its head.


While this may give an indication of the Nandi bear’s area of distribu-
tion, it tells us little about its possible identity. Major Braithwaite and
C. Kenneth Archer, two experienced British settlers in Kenya, are more
helpful in this respect. They were lucky enough to be able to watch
what they thought was a Nandi bear in the tall grass and shrub of the
savannah. At first they took it for a lioness, but when they saw its


profile they got the impression it had a snout. Its head was very large.
At the withers, which were very high, it was about 4 feet 6 inches
high.


The back sloped steeply to the hindquarters, and the animal moved
with a shambling gait which can best be compared with the shuffle of a
bear. The coat was thick and dark brown in colour. ... Finally the
beast broke into a shambling trot and made for a belt of trees near the
river, where it was lost.


Reports were so common during this century that C. R. S. Pitman
could write:


Not long ago there was scarcely a white man in those districts who
had not at one time or another either actually seen the beast or had some
experience connected with it.


Among the naturalists, game-wardens and hunters, many of whom
stated their belief that the Nandi bear existed—whatever its precise
zoological identity might be—were F. C. Selous, a distinguished
naturalist and one of the greatest experts on African fauna, A. Blayney


Percival, late of the Kenya Game Department, and Captain William
Hichens, who quotes a Uganda game-warden as saying “I believe in the
Nandi bear; it may be a giant hyaena; it may be something different
from anything we know,” and himself adds, ““Some fearsome monster,
named kerit, lurks in the forests of East Africa and yet awaits capture and
identification.”


The Nandi bear has even appeared in official publications. The
Report of the Game Department of the Colony and Protectorate of Kenya
for 1932-1934 contains several accounts gathered by the Chief Game-
Warden Captain A. T. A. Ritchie about “‘our old friend the Nandi bear.”
The first comes from Captain F. D. Hislop, District Commissioner of
Kapsabet, and describes a beast which certainly sounds like a bear.


I have to announce that we believe we saw a Nandi bear! Naturally,
I cannot be positive. Just at dusk, we were about half a mile short of


387


THE TERRORS OF AFRICA


the point where the Londiani and Eldama Ravine roads fork. Sud-
denly, loping along the right-hand side of the road which is bordered by
forest, we saw a dark grey creature, about three feet high to the back,
round and even podgy, with a small pointed head. It moved on all four
legs, but with a slight pronounced power in the hind legs. It went on
for about fifty yards until it found an opening into the forest and
disappeared.


I am unable to say what it was if not a bear. It was not a hyena or a
baboon—of that I am certain. I have never seen any other animal like
this.
Its whole appearance and action was like a bear, and obviously
not afraid of the car, as it moved quite sedately until it found a chance
to cut into the forest. I really think it must have been the legendary
animal, but of course I cannot assert this as a fact.


The second account comes from Gunnar Anderssen at Kaimosi on
the Zinga Estate and seems to refer to the same animal. One rainy day
he heard his boys shouting:


When I came to see what was wrong I found them still shouting, a
few hundred yards from my house, round a killed forest pig. At the
same time I heard a roar from the forest—not like anything I have ever
heard before. That the pig had been killed by a very powerful animal
could easily be seen, and to judge from the roar he was not very pleased
to be driven off.


I asked the boys to help me to track, but they refused absolutely,
explaining that they would not have anything to do with the “Sheitani”’
as it was translated to me from Nandi language. It was no use me going
alone into the forest, so when the boys had cooled down a bit, I took
their description of the beast, without making any suggestions to them:


“Very big, with long black hair and a long tail.”’
“With long black hair, the tail carried like a dog’s, the head not very
big, but baya sana.”’


Very big and powerful it must have been from the way the pig had
been handled. As regards black hair, we found long black hair lost in
the battle, soft hair: this was not from the pig, which had coarser hair.
The boys could not explain in what way the head was baya sana, but
they all agreed that it was very bad.


I could not get a clear foot-mark in the grass. What I could see
looked very large, something like the mark of an old leopard which could
not draw in his claws properly. The pig appeared to have been killed in
an extraordinary way, as if it had been hit with, say, a log, breaking the
backbone; it had then been turned over and the stomach, heart, etc.,
had been eaten.


I suggested to the boys that it must have been a hyena with longer
front legs than hind legs, but they said no. They knew about the very
big forest hyena, but that hyena was not black, more the colour of my
washed-out corduroys. No: this was the “devil” and they would not

have anything to do with it. However, they got the pig, and they did
not seem to mind who or what had killed it


As rain started again, I could not follow the tracks to get the foot-
marks on softer ground. This story may sound a bit funny—I think so
myself—but so it happened.


Finally, to complete the record, I shall add the strange encounter
which Charles T. Stoneham tells in his book Hunting Wild Beasts with
Rifle and Camera (1933). He had set up a trading-station at Sotik on
the edge of the Lumbwa Reserve.


My bedroom was a little round hut, some distance removed from the
others. Beside it grew a patch of evergreen bush, behind it the grass
sloped away to a valley wherein a narrow stream gurgled along the
declivities to join the Kipsanoi river, half a mile below.


One night, thinking I heard a noise, I sneaked quickly from my hut
and stood against the wall of it, shaded by the thatched eaves. ..
. Mist
hung over the feathery grasses, pale silver and quiet; there was not a
breath of wind. I saw some beast travelling towards me through the
mist, and I could not think what creature it could be. It was the size of
a lion, but its movements were unlike Simba’s slouching stride. The
grass came up to its belly, its head was held low before its bulk, it
appeared to have an enormous tail. Slowly and quietly it approached,
and I waited, intensely interested, knowing it could neither smell nor
see me. The moon passed behind a cloud; the animal became indistinct
in the mist. When within a dozen paces it stopped, and at that moment
the moon shone out again clear and brilliant.


I received a dreadful shock. The beast was like nothing I had ever
seen or imagined.
It had a huge square head, and the snout of a pig;
its eyes, two black spots, were fixed upon me in an observant stare.
Large circular ears, the size of plates, stood up from its head, and they
were transparent—I could see the grass through them. The creature’s
body was covered with coarse brown hair, its tail was the size of a tree
trunk.


There is an ant-eater in Kenya, a survival of the age when the cave
bear and the woolly rhinoceros roamed the earth, but this beast, though
like to that rare species, was not of it.


Stoneham ran indoors to fetch his rifle, but when he came back he
saw the beast’s hindquarters disappearing into the mist. He did not fire


for fear of merely wounding it and making it dangerous.


When he told his friends about his adventure the next day they all
were inclined to think he had seen the Nandi bear.


But I am inclined to think I saw some weird, hybrid ant-eater, and
am sorry I had not the pluck to go after it and find out all about it.

That is the chief evidence for the Nandi bear. Now for the experts’
opinions. Blayney Percival writes:


The stories vary to a very large extent, but the following points seem
to agree. The animal is of fairly large size, it stands on its hind legs
at times, is nocturnal, very fierce, kills man or animals.


C. R. S. Pitman, who does not believe that the Nandi bear is an
unknown species, has underlined the contradictions in the numerous
reports he had collected personally:


By day, a dark rufous or tawny-hued creature resembling either bear
or gigantic ape, almost invariably viewed indistinctly at a distance and
usually in longish grass; and by night a long-haired brute having the
appearance of a bear, abnormal hyena or South American giant ant-
eater.


And indeed the beast would have to be Proteus himself in order to
look like all the animals it has been said to resemble: a gorilla, an ant-


eater, a hyena and a bear, and to be black, tawny, red and grey in colour,
sometimes tailless and sometimes with a brush, sometimes earless and
sometimes with distinct ears.


The most obvious conclusion is that it is an animal belonging to one
of the types just mentioned, and that all these puzzling divergences are
due to people observing other animals which have nothing to do with
the question. Let us begin with C. R. S. Pitman’s list and proceed by
elimination. We can discard the giant anteater at once, for it is a spe-

97. The aardvark.

cifically South American animal, belonging to a group found only in
America. I feel sure that the animal actually referred to by this term


is the aardvark, an African burrowing anteating animal whose Latin
name is Orycteropus and whose English one is the Afrikaans for “earth-
pig.” This animal is very rarely seen, since it spends the day in burrows
under the earth and prowls only at night. It has a pig’s snout and huge


ears. Its skin is usually almost bare with only scattered bristles, though


sometimes it is hairier, especially on the lower part of the body (this is


a distinctive characteristic of the South African species, Orycteropus


capensis, compared with the Central African and Abyssinian, O. aethio-


picus), and then its coarse yellowish-brown to russet hair does remind


one a little of a bear’s. It has a powerful tail, upon which it can lean


like a kangaroo, and often stands on its hind-legs: a second bear-like


feature. And it is often known as an ant-bear. Could the Nandi bear be


an aardvark?


Certainly it is so rare to see one that people might easily be bewildered
by meeting an aardvark. Personally I am almost certain that it was an
ordinary aardvark that Charles Stoneham saw, whatever he may think.
No doubt he had seen this beast only in drawings and photographs, and
in the moonlight and mist it seemed to him even more extraordinary
than it really is. His description is so full of features that betray the
animal’s identity—the pig’s snout, round ears that sometimes hang
down on the side of the head and have skin so thin as to be translucent,
the brown fur, the tail as long as a tree-trunk—that there can be hardly
any doubt. We can therefore dismiss this report.


It is also possible that the aardvark’s footprints may have sometimes
been attributed to the Nandi bear by puzzled witnesses; for when it
stands up on its hind-legs it may put a large part of the sole of its
foot on the ground and leave the marks of five toes with stout claws:
which are actually little pointed hooves with which it digs in the


earth.


Though this elusive and infernal creature (for the infernal regions are
always underground) is treated with superstitious fear by the Watussi


of Ruanda, there is no justification for their fear. The aardvark cannot


be blamed for any bloody depredations; it eats ants and termites, and


has nothing to gain by slaughtering cattle or human beings. It does not


look in the least like most of the descriptions of the Nandi bear. Wil-


liams and Hickes both stress the small ears and inconspicuous tail; and


the aardvark has the thickest tail and most conspicuous ears of any of


the larger mammals.

So the Nandi bear is not an aardvark.


It might seem self-evident that the Nandi bear is a bear. Most wit-
nesses compare the chemosit to one, and the Wa-Swahili give it the Arab
name of duba. The zoogeographical argument that bears are conspicu-
ously absent all over Africa is not conclusive, since they are found in the
mountains of Spanish Morocco—or were found there until lately. If
they could reach Africa from Europe before the Straits of Gibraltar
were formed, why could they not continue their journey to Central and
East Africa?


This argument is sound enough, but most of the accounts do not
agree with a bear. Many of them mention a clearly visible tail, and the
others never speak of a stump of a tail, so characteristic of the bear, but
say that it was indistinct or not visible, implying that it could well have
been tucked between the legs. There are also descriptions of a slender
beast, and of one with short legs. And what are we to make of those that


insist that it has a mane and smoother, less hairy, hindquarters? All the
bears, whether long- or short-haired, are remarkably evenly covered
with fur. Moreover, when in a hurry, but not actually galloping, they
adopt a gait which is so characteristic that it is not easily overlooked.
Now although some witnesses have said that it had “‘a gait similar to
that of a bear—a kind of shuffling walk” or “‘a shambling gait which can
best be compared with the shuffle of a bear,” no one has actually said
that it ambled, that is to say that it ran by simultaneously moving both
legs on one side of the body. This is most important, since no ape runs
in this way, and the only carnivores to do so are the bear, the hyena and
the South American maned wolf. That a heavily-built animal should
shuffle or shamble is quite natural, but so would a gorilla, a bear, an old
lion or a wild pig. At one moment I thought I had found an exception
when I read in Geoffrey Williams’s account, quoted in an American
magazine, that the beast “ambled away.” But on checking with the

_—

original text I found that he had actually written “shambled away.” It


is always best to check one’s references.


The only witness who has described the beast’s gait in detail is Hickes,
who followed it for a good while along the Magadi railway. He says it
“loped off—running with its fore-legs and with both hind legs rising


at the same time.” This is none too clearly put, but it does imply that
when the beast trots or gallops its two hind-feet always leave the ground
together, while its fore-feet do not move together. This irregular gait
in which the fore-legs touch the ground in turn, while the hindquarters
move as a single unit, is like the so-called “‘pithecoid” gallop so charac-


teristic of monkeys in a hurry. The fore-feet always move forward at a
slight angle. Williams’s cousin’s phrase “‘a sort of sideways canter” is a
good description.


This brings us to the next theory: is the Nandi bear an ape? The
negroes of the Mau and Nandi country usually think of the chemosit or


Rerit as a sort of giant ape, and the Wa-Pokomo describe the koddoelo as
an enormous baboon. The beast that the Nandi villagers killed because


it had climbed on the roof of a hut could hardly have been a lion or a
hyena. It sounds more like an ape. Even the white men’s descriptions
often suggest an ape. “In most stories,” Blayney Percival points out,
‘the resemblance to a monkey of sorts is very noticeable, but the fact
that the animal is nocturnal, a point on which all native accounts agree,


at once makes this impossible.”


This a priori argument is not really tenable. Primates as a whole
show a clear tendency towards a nocturnal life, natural enough for such
generally defenceless animals.
The tarsiers and most lemurs have
chosen this life and are partly adapted for it. Among the true monkeys,
there are several species with nocturnal habits, especially in America.
The douroucouli (Aotes) is purely nocturnal. The howlers belong more


to dawn and dusk. And many of the American monkeys may be fond
of excursions at night. I have a little capuchin monkey from Brazil,
which when I am in the south of France enjoys complete freedom and


can if he wishes go and play in the bushes around my bungalow. Very


often he goes out on moonless nights, and although it is far too dark for


me to see him, I can hear him jumping about among the leaves with


perfect confidence. He is usually timid, but at night he is not only not


afraid of the dark, but actually seems to enjoy it, and even to be able to


see clearly.


It would not be so extraordinary if an African ape were to have

Hichens writes about this theory:


Some of us who have hunted the brute share the view that it may be

Now, while there are no known baboons as large as the “Nandi bear”
—though the last to be discovered, the gelada, is the biggest—they
existed in the past. Palaeontological discoveries have established that in
India there was once a sort of giant baboon, the Simopithecus, which was
twice as high as the present baboons. Moreover Dr Broom has found
remains of giant baboons in Africa itself; and he has given them the


scientific name of Dinopithecus. May not their descendants have given

events a reconstruction of a giant baboon is extraordinarily like most of

a beast survived it is easy to see why the chemosit arouses such terror.
The mere thought that there may be a living animal as huge and strong


as a gorilla and as brutally sayage as a baboon is frightening enough.


This theory, which I do not think anyone has put forward before, is
too daring for the sceptical zoologists who prefer the more common-

maintained that the Nandi bear is merely the common spotted hyena
(Crocuta crocuta), which has a head and general outline strikingly like a
bear’s and which moreover ambles like a bear. It is also savage enough
to be the monster.


The spotted hyena is very cowardly, and often shrinks from attacking
herds for fear of their hooves. It usually makes do with carrion. But
carrion is often short where the vultures are always the first on the scene.
Then the starving hyena creeps into the native huts to seize someone
asleep. The children are usually put to sleep in the passage at the en-

have seen hyenas attack people in broad daylight when they were resting

The Nandi bear’s fur is sometimes described as black, sometimes as
reddish. Pocock has pointed out that the spotted hyena varies greatly in
colour in the course of its growth; and just as there are white mutations
(albinism) in many mammals, that is to say abnormally coloured off-
spring of normal parents, and black mutations (melanism) of the panther,


so there are red mutations (erythrism) of the spotted hyena, which
Pocock suggests may be the origin of the legend of the Nandi bear.
These mutations are commoner in the north (Somaliland and Sudan)
than in East Africa, where they might be taken for unknown monsters.
Pocock therefore thinks that the red hyena is “the Chemosit, Kateit, and
