Charles Stoneham tells a story which is much better evidence for the
hyena theory:


In 1930 a man brought me a skull like a hyena’s skull, but of larger
size. He had a farm at Koru, where at about that time cattle and sheep
had been killed by some mysterious agency. The Lumbwa herdsmen
ascribed these deaths to the chemoiset. The farmer had set numerous
traps, and one day, on returning from a week’s holiday, his boys in-
formed him that the marauder had been caught. It was a young che-
moiset, they said. Being unwilling to lay hands on the beast’s body they
had tied a rope to it and towed it away into the bush. There the farmer
found all that remained of the body, and he brought the skull to me.


I am no zoologist, so I turned the skull over to the Game Depart-
ment, with a request for their opinion. They pronounced it to be the
skull of a hyena. A few days later Mr. Leakey dropped in; without com-
ment I showed him the skull. He was puzzled and interested. Accord-
ing to him the teeth were not those of either the striped or the spotted
hyena; he wanted the brains and hair of the beast to send to the British
Museum.


A short while later he wrote to say that the skull was that of a solitary
brown hyena, a species observed in Rhodesia, but never before seen in
Kenya. I communicated with the farmer, and managed to procure some
scraps of hair and a few bones, which were sent off for classification.
After a lapse of months I heard from Mr. Leakey that he had found
other specimens of the same beast, and did not think it much of a rarity.
So once again the trail of the Nandi bear led to an impasse.


The brown hyena (Hyaena brunnea) was described in 1820 by the
explorer and zoologist Carl Peter Thiinberg. It is closely related to the
striped hyena (Hyaena hyaena), and is the same size—smaller than the


400


THE NANDI BEAR, AN EAST AFRICAN PROTEUS


spotted hyena (Crocuta crocuta). It can be recognised by its uniform
dark-brown colour, marked only with a few whitish spots on the legs,
and by the length of its shaggy fur, which forms a lighter mane on its
shoulders and falls like a coat on its sides. It is the one hyena massive
enough to remind one of a bear. But its plume of a tail and its parti-


cularly long and upstanding ears make it difficult for one to see how


there could be any confusion.


The brown hyena lives chiefly in South Africa, where it roams at
night on the edges of streams or on beaches. For this reason the Afri-
kaaners call it “strand wolf.” It feeds mainly on crabs and dead fish, but
sometimes attacks young cattle.


The brown hyena is not usually supposed to be found north of the
Zambezi, but its area of distribution seems once to have reached as far


as Kilimanjaro. Thus it is not impossible that there may still be very


rare specimens in Tanganyika and even in Kenya. Naturally the un-
usual appearance of one of these dark-maned hyenas would be most dis-
concerting and liable to produce plenty of fantastic interpretations. And
Stoneham’s story shows that even the natives could mistake a brown
hyena for a young chemosit.


Pocock’s skin and Stoneham’s relics made the Nandi bear a laughing-
stock for a while, and much bitter controversy flew back and forth be-
tween sceptics’ armchairs in London and embattled witnesses in Africa,
for whom Captain Hichens speaks as follows:


As to the oft-repeated suggestion that the beast accounted for by
Africans as a Nandi bear is really no more than a hyena, I have never
been impressed by that explanation which seems to me to be an evasion
rather than an explanation.
Hyenas are as common around most
African villages as rabbits around English villages; their habits, appear-
ance and spoor are thoroughly well known to every villager and to sug-
gest that, not once, but dozens of times in many places, kraalsmen would
mistake a hyena for a Nandi bear is on a par with suggesting that
countryfolk all over England could mistake a rabbit for, say, a fox.


It is quite clear from almost all the descriptions that the beast cannot
be a hyena, unless it is some strange crossbreed with a spotted hyena’s
round ears and an even shorter tail, combined with the brown hyena’s


thick dark fur. The hyena is a digitigrade animal and would find it as


hard to stand up on its hind-legs as a dog or a cat. And a hyena that


stood 4 feet 6 inches at the withers would be an unknown animal as


remarkable as a giant baboon.


Moreover, as Captain Hichens has pointed out, the khodumodumo’s

method of stealing cattle in the Transvaal would be impossible for a
hyena, which drags its victims. It is as incapable of leaping over a 6-foot
fence with a calf in its mouth as it is of forcing its way through a wall of
thorns. Besides, the hyena is a noisy brute: it wails before killing its
victim and gives piercing cries immediately afterwards.


So the Nandi bear is not an aardvark, bear, known ape or ordinary
hyena. We have been multiplying possibilities without simplifying the
problem. And indeed it is the very quantity of evidence that makes it so
complex, as Blayney Percival implies when he writes in A Game Ranger’s
Notebook (1924):


For many years now I have been trying to discover upon what

becomes to reconcile this creature with any known species. ... Time
will show, no doubt; meantime I do no more than state my belief that
there is an animal of arboreal and nocturnal habit in the Nandi forests
awaiting discovery, description and Latin name.

.

But he adds:


The strongest point in favour of there being such an animal is that it
has a native name, and appears to be well known amongst the Nandi.

of the time. Major Toulson’s and Corbett’s animals are obviously not

the same as Hickes’s. The same animal could not leave plantigrade foot-

I look upon the reports from the Nandi and from Magadi as referring

Now he was certainly right in considering the Nandi bear as a com-

unknown animal, and that other known animals had crept in to blur
the picture. Let us see what these known animals are,


Here I am glad to be able to offer a very pertinent description of
what at first seems to be an unknown animal given me by Georges Sand-


rart, who did some ethnological research in the Belgian Congo when he
was the Resident in Ruanda-Urundi.


In 1936 I was on an excursion on the ridge of the Congo—Nile water-
shed, at an altitude varying between 8,000 and 11,500 feet, where some
of the last patches of virgin forest still survive. One day in broad day-
light about noon I saw a little bear, slightly smaller than a Carpathian
bear, round a bend in the path. I was astounded, so I took great care to
examine it minutely.
Its fur was shining blackish brown and I could
see a triangle of silver hairs on the peak of its forehead. The apparent
absence of tail, the shape of the head, the large snout, the little round
ears, the slope of the back, the relatively long legs, everything about the
animal reminded me of a bear. But a bear in Africa....


He wasn’t dreaming. The late Chief Semu Geshi, who happened to
be with him, confirmed every detail of his description. Another Euro-
pean had seen the animal; and two pygmies had seen one attack a forest-
antelope and furiously try to bite its leg. They called it zsata, or “honey-
eater,” and even produced a skin. It turned out to be an animal that is
rarely met, because it is both nocturnal and burrowing, but which is
well known to zoologists: the honey-badger or ratel (Mellivora ratel),
which G. S. Cansdale says is probably seen less often than any other
small carnivore. All the same it is found all over Africa as well as in
Arabia and India.


The ratel is not strictly speaking a bear, even though it has a similar


head, general shape of the body, thick coarse hair and powerful claws,


and, thanks to its almost plantigrade feet, also tends to stand up on its


hind-legs. It belongs to the closely related family of Mustelidae and is a


sort of plump badger, all black except for the top of the head and the


403


99. When the ratel turns black with age it is very like a bear.


back, which are covered with a clearly defined band of silver hair. As
both its Latin and its pygmy name imply, it is reputed to eat honey.


Was this then what so many people took for a bear? There is no doubt


it is what Sandrart saw (the triangle of silver hair on the forehead is very
significant), but even so he is convinced that it was a giant species, still
unknown to science.


I must admit that for a long time I believed that the ratel was a small
creature, not so big as a European badger, but Sandrart’s account set me
researching, and I was astonished to find that some ratel skins from
Central Africa are as much gs 3 feet 6 inches from the nose to the tip of
the tail (which is quite small and no more than 8 inches long). It is al-
most as big as the smallest of the bears, the Malayan sun-bear.


But if some of the Nandi bears were ratels, why had nobody men-
tioned the conspicuous band of white down the head and back? This
puzzled me for some time, until I discovered that in 1906 Lydekker had
described, under the name of Mellivora cottonit, a West African ratel
which had no silver band and was therefore entirely black. As his
description was based on a single specimen, he suggested that it might
be an individual case of melanism, though this did not prevent him from
describing it as a new species.


We now have proof that in Africa one may meet a little-known animal,
looking very like a small black bear; and this explains some of the de-
scriptions of the Nandi bear. There is no doubt that what Major Toul-


son, Captain Hislop and Anderssen’s boys saw was a black ratel. A

“round and even podgy” beast, 3 feet long and between 18 and 20
inches high, with short legs and covered with long black hair, a small
pointed head, the tail carried like a dog’s with non-retractile claws—
what else could it be?


Blayney Percival tells how he had to go and inquire in the Sotik
country about an animal very like the Nandi bear. It was supposed to be
fairly large—the size of a pointer—and it stood on its hind-legs and was
very fierce. It turned out when he showed them a picture of the ratel
that this was what it was. I think the ratel may also be the answer to the
problem of the too, an animal Schomburgk heard rumours about in
East Africa, “as big as a goat, with teeth like a dog’s, dark black fur and
an evil character.”


Pursuing the question of black ratels I found that the truth was more
relevant than I had expected. In 1909 Pocock published a note on the
ratels in Africa listing no less than four species, differing only slightly in


size and in the extent of the silvery grey band on the back. Mellivora
leuconata, for instance, had a light strip all along the back, but as it grew
older the hindquarters darkened. In the London Zoo was an old speci-
men with no white except for a crescent on the top of its head, its back
being merely sprinkled with grey. He cautiously added that “It may be
that the datk hue of the dorsal surface is a sign of age,” but did not
draw the logical conclusion that differences were not due to different
species but to different individuals of different ages. Far from it, he pro-
ceeded to describe yet another species, Mellivora signata from Sierra
Leone, on the evidence of a young specimen in which the dorsal patch
was already no more than a crescent on the top of the head.


Soon afterwards Dr F. D. Welch gave a much more detailed account
of the changes of colour which a ratel may undergo. He had observed
the old specimen in the Zoo for more than 12 years and remarks, “It is
now very different from what it was when first observed.” When this


ratel of the characteristic East African species, Melhvora ratel, arrived


at the Zoo in 1890 it appeared to be adult. It was therefore more than
20 years old in 1909 when Dr Welch wrote:


When I first knew it twelve years ago its colour was as follows :—Scalp,
back of neck, and dorsal surface were very pale grey with a few black
hairs scattered at intervals over the posterior half of the back, no black
hairs whatever on scalp, back of neck, and anterior half of back;
this
dorsal patch of grey was very sharply defined from the black of the
under parts by a straight, very distinct line. Tail was quite black on
upper and under surfaces, as I shall remark on later.

It was then as large as now, and much larger than a female Mellivora
ratel which lived with it many yéars and was adult.


It retained its original colour, not altering in any way, till the begin-
ning of 1907, when the pale grey dorsal patch commenced turning
black, the change being very gradual and evenly distributed over the
posterior half of the back and not in patches, and later on spreading to
the anterior half of the back and neck.


This change went on very gradually, the well-defined margin of the
dorsal grey patch at its junction with the black of the under surfaces and
limbs and tail becoming gradually lost; the black of the under surfaces,
limbs and tail becoming gradually continuous with the new black of the
back, leaving only scattered grey hairs mixed with black where formerly
there was the well-defined line of all grey hairs.


At present all the back is “black merely sprinkled with grey,” as Mr.
Pocock remarks, but on the scalp there are more grey hairs in propor-
tion to black than on the body, and the black of the dorsal surfaces
cannot now be distinguished from the black of the under parts...


Mr. Pocock has suggested senility as the cause of this change, and as
the animal is otherwise in good health, I do not think there is any doubt
on this point.


Almost entirely black ratels may not therefore necessarily belong to a
dubious species (Mellivora cottoni) confined to West Africa, nor need
they be exceptional melanistic mutations. It seems to be quite normal
even for East African ratels (Mellivora ratel) to become black at the end
of their lives, when their size is largest. The largest ratels are therefore
also the blackest, and would naturally not be recognised as the same
animal as the young ratels, which are smaller and strikingly marked.


This does not necessarily mean that Sandrart was wrong in thinking
the Nandi bear to be a distinct species of giant ratel. Dr Welch has
pointed out that the ratel which he watched blackening with age was
much larger than another adult ratel living with it. On the basis of the
measurements of five living animals and 26 skins and skulls, all from
Africa and Arabia, he concludes:


There is in this species considerable range of size, which in my mind
raises the question as to whether the skins hitherto regarded as M. ratel
may not be divisible into two species differing only in size. However,
most of the skulls have no sex stated, so no definite conclusion can be
come to on this latter point, as the male would be naturally larger than
the female skulls.


In short, some descriptions of the Nandi bear may refer either to very
old males of the species M. ratel or to elderly individuals of a larger
species—or rather sub-species, since there is no reason to create a new

My friend Charles Dewisme has suggested that the legend of the
Nandi bear may be based on two separate animals: the spotted hyena
and the ratel, the hyena’s bloody deeds being attributed to the mysteri-
ous little “bear” which is so rarely seen.
It is natural for any little-
known animal to be blamed for every crime, just as a stranger in a village
is always the first to be suspected.


Patrick Bowen has suggested to Frank Lane that the Nandi bear may
be a scapegoat in a more sinister sense and that native witch-doctors may
well be responsible for the massacres attributed to the mysterious ani-
mal. They are very clever at imitating animals’ cries and making false
tracks as a means of stealing cattle and revenging themselves on their
enemies with complete impunity. Just as in the Belgian Congo and
Nigeria there is a secret society of leopard-men called Aniotos, and in
Europe in the Middle Ages there were men who were werewolves, there
may well be a sect of bear-men, based on Arab folklore, hyena-men, or
even ratel-men in Kenya and Uganda. The Aniotos cover their heads
and backs with leopard-skins and use mummified paws on the end of


sticks to imitate the beast’s tracks. They attack their enemies at night
and maul their necks with gauntlets armed with iron claws, thus pro-
ducing horrible wounds indistinguishable from those made by a large cat.
In the same way they might easily imitate the bear’s method of killing.


This would explain those native descriptions of the chemosit as half-
man, half-bird, with an ape’s head and walking upright. And the foot-
prints like those of an old leopard which could not draw in its claws
properly could well have been made by a lion’s foot stuffed with straw or
sand, or worn on the real criminal’s foot. All this is pure conjecture. But
the terrible atrocities of the Mau-Mau in Kenya have shown the cruel
lengths that the Kikuyu would go to, and make this theory all too possible.


Actually there is no need to consider the ratel as a harmless scapegot
blamed for hyenas’ or witch-doctors’ misdeeds.
It is not always so

harmless. True, it is fond of honey (like the bear) and also feeds on
small mammals, birds, reptiles and insects (also like the bear). It is one
of the poultry-farmers’ worst enemies. In Algo-abai, where the peas-
ants were battling with it over the eggs their hens had laid, it won the
day by breaking all the hens’ necks one night—there were some 30
of them—and carrying off three to its lair. The pygmies’ report of see-
ing it at grips with an antelope shows that it will attack animals much
bigger than itself. Brehm says that “at the time of rut it is so excited,


so furious, that it will even attack man and bite him savagely.”


Guy Babault, a French naturalist who has been observing the fauna
of Central and East Africa for 30 years, writes of the ratel:


The courage of this little animal is unparallelled. A lion will let a
determined man pass, but not the ratel. When disturbed it will attack
and only retreat in order to return more bitterly to the charge.
It is
wonderfully tenacious and brave. Moreover it is armed with strong
jaws and powerful claws, for it is a burrower that can dig itself deep
earths.


Professor Pierre Grassé notes in his monumental Encyclopédie de
Zoologie that ‘‘Besides honey and brood-comb the ratel eats insects,


small mammals and even small antelopes.”’ Its lust for meat must some-
times be very~-violent, since in India it has the odious reputation of
stealing corpses from cemeteries. It is as gluttonous as the hyena, whose
cowardly thirst for blood often drives it to atiack solitary or sleeping
people.


This behaviour is not surprising. The ratel belongs to a very fierce
family of carnivores. The Mustelidae have not the panther’s or the


tiger’s reputations only because they are smaller. But relative to the


size of their victims, they are really much more cruel, fearless and ag-
gressive than the felines. The wolverine or glutton (Gulo Juscus) of the


arctic, which is no bigger than a large ratel, well deserves its name, since


it lives upon large herbivores like the reindeer and even small elk. The
tiny stoat (Mustela nivalis), hardly 15 inches long, is even more voracious.


It has been known to attack horses and cows and even man, causing
frightful wounds, Nothing can be more sadistic than the stone-marten
(Martes foina), which causes wholesale massacres among the inhabitants
of hen-houses and rabbit-warrens, without the least excuse, since it
carries off only one of its victims. Finally the badger, the nearest ap-
proach to a ratel in Europe, is justly renowned for its courage. I have
even found a case of one attacking a young man. It is described thus
by Jean Mathis, the victim’s father:

I recently sent my fourteen-year-old son to draw water in a pasture

up unhurt, but was not a little surprised to see a greyish brown animal
charging at him, snarling and showing its teeth. Leaving his bicycle on

climbed over a fence and ran towards a hut where he hoped to take
refuge; but he was still pursued and had to run round the cabin several
times with the beast at his heels. Finally he managed to get hold of a
large stick and to give the animal a heavy blow on the skull. He only
succeeded in increasing its fury and a desperate battle ensued until the
beast was completely stunned.


It was a male badger, about a year old and weighing 16 pounds. In
all my experience of hunting I have never before heard of such a
pugnacious badger.


All of which shows that a large ratel about the size of a wolverine
might well kill pigs, sheep and even cattle; and that it might possibly


kill a man.


Moreover the ratel is one of the few mammals one might suspect of
penetrating a wall of thorns to reach its prey. Its dense fur and a thick
layer of sub-cutaneous fat make it impervious to the stings of wasps and
bees when it raids their nests. Brehm reports that the Indian ratel


prowls round native dwellings at night; it passes through thick thorn
hedges, or burrows an underground passage beneath them.
In ten
minutes it will dig such a passage into the hen-roost which it is raiding.


The African ratel, which is larger and stronger than its Indian cousin,
could well kill much larger prey. But could it carry them off? The
following passage from Frank Lane’s Nature Parade may provide an
answer:


It is an interesting fact that strength in the animal world seems to in-
crease in inverse proportion to the size of the creature. Big-game hun-
ters say that a large carnivore is capable of carrying a full-grown bullock
over a five-barred gate practically without pausing in its stride... But
such a feat is eclipsed by a weasel dragging a hare. Worked out on the
basis of cubic capacity, the smaller animal’s feat is equivalent to a lion
dragging an elephant at five miles an hour.


In its method of killing its prey by a blow with its paw on the top of


the head and then disembowelling, the Nandi bear is much more like


an animal with powerful claws, like the ratel, than one with powerful


fangs, like the hyena or lion. The ratel is therefore perfectly capable of


committing many of the misdeeds attributed to the Nandi bear.


Bears, which are usually peaceable and gentle and live on fruit and

insects, sometimes become complete carnivores when they are old soli-

This theory is now a simple demonstrable theorem:
The Nandi bear is described by the Kenya settlers as a small black
bear of bloodthirsty habits. But a dangerous black bear is an altogether
unusual sight in Africa.


When a ratel grows old it changes so much in its appearance and its
nature that it is also a very unusual sight.


Now when an old ratel turns black all over, reaches its full size and
becomes a more bloodthirsty carnivore, it looks and behaves just like

Therefore the Nandi bear is an old ratel. Q.E.D.


Of course this theorem is valid only if you begin by accepting that the
Nandi bear looks like a small black bear. As I have already shown, the


settlers have often used the name for an animal which seems more like

natives as a big hairy biped, and the koddoelo as an enormous baboon.
I believe the whole confused question of the Nandi bear was based on
a misunderstanding.


When Geoffrey Williams and his cousin saw a strange animal, which

the Wa-Swahili knew an animal which they called duba from the Arab

Finally some plantigrade footprints were found which might have

The Nandi bear is now a bear no more. It is a whole Apocalypse of

I have been able to disentangle the four horsemen: the giant baboon,
the old black ratel, the unfamiliar hyena and the witch-doctor.


Only the first, the chemosit, the Nandi’s terrible two-legged demon

alive or dead. Even so, attempts have been made. Frank Lane tells of
an enthusiastic hunter who “was so confident of success that he had a
large cage in readiness which required 40 porters to move when empty!”
I need hardly say that his optimism was not rewarded. On the other
hand, K. R. Williams, who lived in Uganda, is said to have killed a

was just like a bear’s. An old witch-doctor said it was not a hyena but a

his camp to get something to skin it with, real hyenas arrived and carried
off this specimen which might have solved one of the most puzzling of
zoological mysteries.


Scientists have put forward the most daring theories in their attempts


to explain the Nandi bear. In 1923 Dr E. G. Wayland, Director of the
Geological Survey of Uganda, made a sensational discovery on the
Bunyoro side of Lake Albert in a very recent stratum, probably dating
from the Pleistocene. This happened on the scene where the engargiya
(the local version of the chemosit) had committed its crimes. The bone
that he disinterred was an incomplete phalanx belonging to a member of
one of the strangest groups of mammals the earth has ever known, the
Chalicotheria or Ancylopoda.


These Perissodactyls, which are distantly related to the horses, were a
headache for the palaeontologists for a long time, because, while they
have an ungulate’s skull and teeth, their feet have three toes armed with
formidable claws. When the first sparse remains of these beasts were
discovered in 1823, Cuvier attributed the feet to “‘a giant pangolin” and
the teeth to some sort of Perissodactyl: according to his Law of Correla-
tion between the Organs an ungulate with claws was an impossibility,
and his word remained law until the day when a whole skeleton was
found. It showed that the pangolin’s feet really did belong to an ungu-


late, despite the Father of Palaeontology’s edicts.


It is now thought that the Chalicotheria used their claws to tear
down the leaves which were no doubt their food.


The remarkable thing about Dr Wayland’s find was that it was the
first time that remains of one of the Chalicotheria had been dug up in
Africa. Until then several species had been discovered in Europe, Asia
and even in America, but never in Africa.


When the precious phalanx reached the British Museum of Natural

sentative hidden in the African forests?


These clawed ungulates, with their short hind-legs and very sloping
back, their heavy head and short tail, must have been very like a hyena
in outline—but a hyena as big as a horse. Dr Andrews therefore won-
dered whether some belated Chalicotherium might not be at the bottom
of the persistent rumours in Africa about the so-called Nandi bear.


Of course this indisputable vegetarian could not be saddled with the
crimes attributed to the chemosit—which could often be due to spotted
hyenas. But there is no doubt that if a Chalicotherium were clad in a
furry coat—which is pure supposition—it would agree perfectly with


413


THE TERRORS OF AFRICA


most witnesses’ descriptions. And that is all that one can say for the
moment.


Science is a long way from officially adding the Nandi bear to the list
of African fauna. We have only the most dubious remains of it. Ivan T.
Sanderson says that in the British Museum of Natural History there is a
piece of fur covered with long brown hair which may come from the
animal about which arm-chair experts are so sceptical, but whose exis-
tence it is rash to deny in many villages in Kenya.

CHAPTER EIGHTEEN


Mngwa, the Strange One


At night all cats are grey.
French proverb.


IT is dawn in a small village on the coast of Tanganyika. Suddenly the
silence is broken by a woman’s shrill scream. On the still-fresh sand in
the market-place lies a shapeless heap of flesh, the unrecognisable body
of a man, ripped and pounded to mincemeat by some incredible killing-
machine. The scavenging birds fly off their carrion, and one by one the
villagers gather round in a circle, silent until one of them notices a few
greyish hairs among the drying blood and exclaims: ““Mngwa.”


The mngwa is the most feared of all Africa’s mysterious beasts, al-
though the whites do not know it at all, and even to the blacks it is largely


a mystery; for its name comes from the Kiswahili mu-ngwa, which
means “strange one.” East African settlers often confuse this animal,
which the natives also call munda, with the Nandi bear. But the terrors
of Africa do not all come in one shape. Whereas the chemosit is a lum-
bering beast reminiscent of a bear or a huge baboon, the mngwa is dis-
tinctly feline, a silent machine with muscles like steel springs, control-
ling an armoury of teeth and claws. And while the chemosit’s misdeeds
occur all over the interior of East Africa, the mngwa is found only along
the coast of Tanganyika. If the »mgwa can be compared to any unknown
animal in the uplands it is to the ndalawo of the Uganda forests, a savage
man-killing carnivore, which is said to be the size and shape of a leopard,
but with black fur on its back, turning to grey beneath its body. The
mngwa is supposed to be larger. The natives who have seen it say that it


is as big as a donkey and striped with grey like a tabby cat. It may seem
extraordinary that Africa should conceal an unknown feline the size of
lion, and Captain William Hichens writes:


It can be said that such a beast is “impossible’’; but, having trekked
many a long mile in its reputed haunts and helped to patch up more

THE TERRORS OF AFRICA


than one of its mangled victims, I am convinced that some beast an-
swering to the mngwa’s description does lurk in the dense jungle which
fringes parts of this coast. Patches of this dark jungle-growth have not
been trodden by human foot for centuries, as may be judged from the
fact that a large town of ruined stone mansions has stood in the bush
not an afternoon’s car-drive north of Mombasa, for over five hundred
years, and was utterly unheard-of until rediscovered about four years
ago [i.e. around 1933].


The mngwa appears in many Swahili songs and tales. Hichens quotes


a war-song dating from about I150 A.D.


Sikae muyini kewa kitu dunt
Nangia mwitunit haliwa na mngwa
(I dwell not in the city to become a worthless idler,
I plunge me in the forest to be eaten by the mngwa!)


From the legend of the Sultan Majnin quoted by Edward Steere in

folklore as dragons did in Europe in the Middle Ages.


One day the Sultan’s cat escaped and slaughtered its master’s poate

The moral of this interesting legend might well be: Never mistake a
nunda for any ordinary creature.


What is a nunda or mngwa? Until the 1920s it was thought to be quite
imaginary, but then, as Frank Lane remarks,


a series of events took place in some of the fishing villages on the coast
of Tanganyika which brought the nunda from the realm of native fan-
tasy to that of Government reports.


One of these villages was Lindi where Captain William Hichens was
Native Magistrate, and where he tells us that the following events took
place in 1922:


It was the custom for native traders to leave their belongings in the
village market every night, ready for the morning’s trade; and to pre-
vent theft and also to stop stray natives sleeping in the market place,
an askari or native constable took in turns with two others to guard the
market on a four-hour watch.


Going to relieve the midnight watch, an oncoming native constable
one night found his comrade missing. After a search he discovered him,
terribly mutilated, underneath a stall. The man ran to his European
officer, who went with me at once to the market. We found it obvious
that the askari had been attacked and killed by some animal—a lion, it
seemed.


In the victim’s hand was clenched a matted mass of greyish hair, such
as would come out of a lion’s mane were it grasped and torn in a violent
fight. But in many years no lion had been known to come into the
town.


We were puzzling the problem at the boma next morning when the
old Arab Liwali or native governor of the district hurried into our office

THE TERRORS OF AFRICA


with two scared-looking men at his heels. Out late the previous night,
they said, they had slunk by the market-place lest the askari should see
them and think them evil-doers; and as they crept by they were horri-
fied to see a gigantic brindled cat, the great mysterious nunda which is
feared in every village on the coast, leap from the shadows of the market
and bear the policeman to the ground.


The Liwali, a venerable and educated man, assured us that within

animal, not a lion or a leopard, but a huge cat as big as a donkey and
marked like a tabby. I had heard this tale, and had put it down as silly
superstition, but the Liwali’s assertion put a different light on things.


That night we kept watch with two armed askaris at the market:
nothing happened. On parade next day we read the native constable a

It seemed that we were slightly premature. That same night another

The native constables refused to mount watch at night, even though

For a month the mngwa kept up its terrible depredations in the coastal
fishing villages and every attempt was made to kill it. Pits, traps and
poisoned meat were set in its way. Armed police patrolled the district.
A few cautious sallies were even sent into the skirts of the forest. But
the beast went on with its slaughter unseen and untouched. Then as
suddenly as they had begun the raids ended—but not for good. Years


later they began again, and this time Hichens was less sceptical of the
native “superstition.” In 1937 he wrote:


Not long ago a man was brought in to me at Mchinga (a small Tan-
ganyika coastal village) on a litter and terribly mauled by some great
beast. He said it was a mngwa, and as he himself was a brave and skilful
native hunter, who had often tracked down lions, leopards and other
“killers’’ with me and other white men, why should we suppose that in
this case he mistook a lion or a leopard for some other beast? He had
nothing to gain by telling me lies; on the contrary, as a hunter he
depended for his livelihood on being absolutely truthful and trust-
worthy. ...


Nor is the African native a fool in the ways of the bushveld and its
beasts; he does not assert that a beast is a mngwa when any old woman

in the kraal could tell by a glance at its spoor or by the way that it

tells of the simba (lion), msui (leopard) and the mngwa all in one verse,
plainly showing that there is no confusion in the native mind between

Even Patrick Bowen, who was so sceptical of the Nandi bear, attribut-

existence, because he saw its spoor after a raid in which a little boy was
carried off by the beast. Bowen and another hunter went to the village
where the raid had taken place and followed the culprit’s tracks. At


first he thought it was a lion, but eventually the track crossed some hard
wet sand, where the spoor was exceptionally clear, and then there was
no doubt that it was not a lion. “The spoor we were following,” he told
Frank Lane, “appeared to be that of a leopard as large as the largest
lion.” The beast’s hairs, found on the stakes where the mngwa had
forced its way into the kraal, were brindled and quite different from a
leopard’s.


And that is all we know about the mngwa. What are we to make of it?
It would not be the first strange and unknown feline animal to be dis-
covered in Africa in our time. The story of the msui-fisi is most instruc-


tive in this respect. Alarming tales about this beast, whose name means
*“‘hyena-leopard,” have long been told in Rhodesia, where the natives
believe it is a cross between these two carnivores. It is supposed to look


like a leopard, but it is striped with black and white like a striped hyena
and its claws are not retractile. As one might expect of such a hybrid,


it is extraordinarily swift, crafty and ferocious.
It always attacks at
night, forcing its way through the gates of cattle-kraals or between the
branches that form their roofs, turning them into a slaughter-house and
always carrying off a goat or a sheep. As usual, the whites disbelieved
these tales and thought them mere superstitions.


Then one day in 1926 Major A. L. Cooper saw a most unusual cat-like
beast near Salisbury in Southern Rhodesia and immediately shot it. It
proved to be a strange animal very like a cheetah but covered with fur


as thick as-a snow-leopard’s and marked with spots which ran together to
form stripes. Cooper was puzzled by the beast and wrote to the Field
(October 1926) suggesting it might be a cross between a leopard and a
cheetah. Then other specimens were obtained; they all had non-retrac-


tile claws—a feature peculiar to the cheetah—and there was now no
doubt that they belonged to a new variety of cheetah distinct from the


419


THE TERRORS OF AFRICA


one species, Acinonyx jubatus, found in both Africa and Asia. R. I.
Pocock, the famous British zoologist, baptised it Acinonyx rex—or, in
plain English, king cheetah—remarking that it was “most extraordinary
that so large and distinct a species should remain for so long unknown.”


It is not at all extraordinary. As we have seen, it has happened dozens
of times; and it will go on happening so long as the whites go on thinking
the people they are apt to call “savages” are liars or fools.


Nevertheless it is by no means proved that the king cheetah is a new
species. Many zoologists think it may merely be a matter of individuals
with abnormal markings. From an evolutionary point of view, the
spotted coat of many felines derives from a primitive striped coat; the
spots are due to the stripes breaking up. In domestic cats one can some-
times see several intermediate stages between spots and stripes all in the
same litter. In the spotted species of felines stripes may reappear as a


result of atavism in certain individuals. Thus several very rare cases of
striped leopards have been described, and there is no doubt that they
belong to the Known species.


It is therefore not impossible that striped cheetahs may also be mere
abnormalities. The fact that the few known specimens all come from
the same area does seem to contradict this theory. But there could well
be ecological reasons which favoured these abnormal offspring, or these
abnormalities could be connected with the genetical ancestry of a group
of animals in a confined area. For instance black panthers are fairly
common in Indonesia but very rare in Africa.


The reader may wonder whether the legend of the mngwa may not


also be based on abnormally coloured individuals of a known feline
species. It is possible, but it is hard to see how the odd brindled coat of
the “strange” beast could be an individual variation of lion or leopard.
The mngwa is much more likely to be an unknown species than the


nsui-fist.


Perhaps the best observation is yet another line of Swahili, which seems


to have been made by some negro Hamlet to a no less black Horatio:


Si taajabuni, waana Adanu, mambo yalio duniani
(Do not wonder, O sons of men, at the things which are in
this world.)


CHAPTER NINETEEN


The Little Hairy Men


Up the airy mountain
Down the rushy glen
We daren’t go a-hunting
For fear of little men.
WILLIAM ALLINGHAM.


TERROR is more dreadful when it wears a human face. The werewolf is
more fearful than any ordinary wolf, since it is a man turned into a wolf.
The most terrifying monsters of antiquity had human features: the
Cyclops, the Sphinx, the sirens, the Gorgon, the manticora and the in-
numerable host of ghouls, vampires and harpies. The most successful
horrors manufactured by the film industry, Frankenstein’s monster, Mr
Hyde, Dracula and the Phantom of the Opera, all have human faces. It
may seem paradoxical that we should be most frightened by something
most like ourselves. But while mere brutality is the act of brutes, evil is
the prerogative of man.


This explains why the Nandi make their most feared animal, the


chemosit, so man-like—while on the other hand the man-like anthropoid
apes are unduly dreaded as ‘‘man-faced monsters.” In the areas where
they live they are often feared by the natives, and credited with the most


evil instincts; naturalists and explorers are usually powerless when the
natives are too frightened to help. And of course these great apes’ in-
telligence enables them to elude our attempts to observe or approach
them, which also helps to prolong our ignorance, thus giving rise to
much confusion.


The mountain gorilla, which is the largest of all, the pygmy gorilla,
which has never been observed in nature and of which we have only a
few skins and skeletons, and the pygmy chimpanzee were still unknown
in the last century. So it is not impossible that Africa still hides some
anthropoids unknown to science.


421


THE TERRORS OF AFRICA


By far the most mysterious of African tales about man-faced monsters


are those about the agogwe, little hairy men, barely 4 feet high, which
walk on their hind-legs. Captain Hichens, whom I have had several
occasions to quote, tells how:


Some years ago I was sent on an official lion-hunt to this area [Ussure
and Simbiti forests on the western side of the Wembare plains] and,
while waiting in a forest glade for a man-eater, I saw two small, brown,
furry creatures come from the dense forest on one side of the glade and
disappear into the thickets on the other. They were like little men,
about four feet high, walking upright, but clad in russet hair. The
native hunter with me gazed in mingled fear and amazement. They
were, he said, agogwe, the little furry men whom one does not see once
in a lifetime. I made desperate efforts to find them, but without avail
in that wellnigh impenetrable forest. They may have been monkeys,
but, if so, they were no ordinary monkeys, nor baboons, nor colobus,
nor Sykes, nor any other kind found in Tanganyika. What were they?


When he made inquiries in the neighbouring villages, the natives told
"him the strangest stories about the agogwe: if you put a large gourd full
of ntulu beer and a bow! of food in the grain plantations, these little men
would collect these gifts and come and weed and hoe at night to show


their gratitude. ‘““That,”’ remarks Hichens, “I can well believe, is myth;
but my little brown men were real enough.”


Personally I find this legend disturbing, to say the least. It is like
those in northern Europe about those elves called leprechauns in Ire-
land, brownies in Scotland and mutons in Scandinavia. Unless they are


all based on authentic and similar facts it is hard to see how they could
have arisen independently in countries as far apart as northern Europe
and East Africa. And as to these facts, let me recall the discovery at the
end of the last century at Schweizersbild near Schaffhausen in Switzer-
land, of bones of tiny men, pygmies of the Later Stone Age. Kollmann,
who examined the bones, maintained that they were certainly not patho-


logical dwarfs. James Geikie, the Scottish geologist, has written:


It is possible, as Dr, Ntiesch suggests, that the widely-spread legend
as to the former existence of little men, dwarfs, and gnomes, who were
supposed to haunt caves and retired places in the mountains, may be
a reminiscence of these Neolithic pygmies.


But that is another story.
The East African leprechauns seem to be more than a remini-
scence. S. V. Cook wrote as follows in the Journal of the East Africa and
Uganda Natural History Society in 1924:

THE LITTLE HAIRY MEN


Fifteen miles east of Embu Station there rises from the Emberre
Plains the lofty hills of Kwa Ngombe, nearly six thousand feet high.
They are inhabited, the Embu natives say, by buffalo and a race of little

Cook naturally disbelieved this story and thought it no more than a
charming fairy tale. But Hichens’s report puts it in a different light.
After all the Kwa Ngombe hills are only 350 miles north-east of the
Ussure and Simbiti forests.


In support of Hichens’s story, Cuthbert Burgoyne wrote a letter to
Discovery, in which it had appeared. This was published in a subsequent
issue, and the gist is as follows:


In 1927 I was with my wife coasting Portuguese East Africa in a
Japanese cargo boat. We were sufficiently near to land to see objects
clearly with a glass of twelve magnifications.
There was a sloping
beach with light bush above upon which several dozen baboons were
hunting for and picking up shell fish or crabs, to judge by their move-
ments. Two pure white baboons were amongst them. These are very
rare but I had heard of them previously. As we watched, two little
brown men walked together out of the bush and down amongst the
baboons.


There were certainly not any known monkey and yet they must have
been akin or they would have disturbed the baboons. They were too
far away to see in detail, but these small human-like animals were
probably between four and five feet tall, quite upright and graceful in
figure. At the time I was thrilled as they were quite evidently no beast
of which I had heard or read.


Later a friend and big game hunter told me he was in Portuguese
East Africa with his wife and three hunters, and saw a mother, father
and child, of apparently a similar animal species, walk across the
further side of a bush clearing. The natives loudly forbade him to
shoot.


Now there is no known ape, even among the anthropoids, which
normally walks upright on its hind-legs. While a monkey may stand up


on its hind-legs for a moment, the position is unusual, if not uncom-


fortable. In fact only the gibbon, which is found only in the Far East


and the Malay archipelago, is a biped, its long arms acting as balancing


423


THE TERRORS OF AFRICA


rods; but it is specially adapted to swinging from its arms in trees and
rarely descends to the ground.


Perhaps the agogwe are therefore really little men. Their description
seems at first sight to apply pretty well to the African pygmies. Pure-
blooded pygmies are never more than 4 feet high, and their bodies are
not so smooth as those of the other Africans. Their skin, sometimes very
dark and dull, but more generally a reddish or yellowish brown, is
covered with yellow down, especially on the back, arms and legs. Their
short and woolly hair is a dark rusty brown. Their arms are relatively
long and their legs short, like those of some monkeys.


It may seem odd that these little men should live on good terms with
baboons—but it would not be miraculous. If all wild animals run away
from man, it is man’s fault, since he cannot see a wild animal without
using it as a target. But in uninhabited countries, like the Antarctic,
we find that seals and penguins and many other animals can be man’s
neighbours without being afraid or hostile. The same is true in Bud-
dhist lands where all animals are sacred.1 Some supposedly savage
beasts even seek man’s company, and it was only after much treachery
on man’s part that he broke off relations with the puma, which the first


travellers called el amigo del Christiano, the Christian’s friend.


It would not-be so very extraordinary to find unknown tribes of pyg-
mies in Tanganyika or Mozambique, where there is thick forest, which


is the pygmies’ favourite habitat. Driven southward and eastward by
the Masai, they could easily have reached the great lakes.


Georges Sandrart who used to be the Resident in Ruanda-Urundi has
suggested to me that the little men could equally well be full-blooded
Bushmen, who are hardly taller than the pygmies, varying in height
between 4 feet 8 inches and 5 feet 2 inches. Their skin is the colour of
light tan leather, much lighter than the rest of the Africans. It is true
that today pure-blooded Bushmen are confined to the Kalahari Desert,
driven there by the Kaffir tribes. But they once covered a very large area
and many tribes know them. The Zulus call them Aba-twa, the Bechu-
ana Ba-roa and the Hottentots Saan. The influence of their language is
found in place-names all over Africa south of the Zambezi. Sir Harry
Johnston has even found their characteristic stone implements farther

In the Ivory Coast, almost at the opposite end of Africa, there is a

“Yes, about 500 yards from here.”
The professor nearly fell out of his chair in surprise. The Institute
was surrounded by forest, but though it was thick in places it was very
well known and natives were constantly passing through it. The story
seemed most suspect.


“Why didn’t your friend come and tell me at once?” he asked suspi-
ciously,
:


The young man explained that since the whites disbelieved the
rumours about pygmies in the neighbourhood his friend had been loath


to be laughed at or thought to be mad. But he knew the man well
enough to know that he had not made it up, so he decided to make in-
quiries for him himself.


Professor Ledoux was more and more intrigued and insisted that the
eye-witness should come and see him. He promised that he would not
make fun of him and would not tell anyone of his story.


The next day [the Professor tells me] I had a visit from the boy re-
sponsible for the observation. He was well-educated and had a certifi-
cate for primary studies. I asked him about the circumstances in which
he saw the “pygmy.”


It had happened near the Meteorological set when they were taking
their daily readings at 8 o’clock in the morning. Among the roots of a


426


THE LITTLE HAIRY MEN


silk-cotton tree [Bombax] there suddenly appeared a little man with
long reddish fur and long hair on his head—“same like white man”—
but also reddish.


At once the little red man and the large black one took to their heels
in opposite directions. For, according to the legends, the little forest-
men brought bad luck. You only saw them once in a lifetime and you
had to be alone.


I went to the place with my two informants. It lay in the shadow of
thick forest, but was not too overgrown since the silk-cotton tree grew
near a path. It was very likely that if there had been anything there it
would have been easy to see.


I asked to be informed at once if a similar meeting occurred again,
but this never happened.


Professor Ledoux admits that he was then very incredulous.
It
seemed unthinkable that within 12 miles of a big town like Abidjan, and
500 yards from huts inhabited by six Europeans and some 300 Africans,
there could be unknown creatures in forest which though thick was far
from virgin. Moreover the African who claimed to have seen the mys-
terious pygmy did not come from the Lower Ivory Coast but from the
Middle Coast, which is wooded savannah country. Perhaps the great


forest, which is most impressive, had over-excited his imagination. And
in his solitary walks in the forest the professor had often put up bush-
buck. If the African had seen the russet back of one of these antelopes
among the bushes it was not impossible that his imagination should have
led him to think that it was one of the “little hairy men” of the legends.
At all events when the professor showed him a book containing pictures
of Central African pygmies he insisted that his creature was not like
them.


Despite his scepticism Professor Ledoux decided to make discreet in-
quiries about the native legends and what they were based on. He ques-
tioned several Africans who trusted him, and he pretended that he fully
believed their stories, thus putting them at their ease and getting much
more detailed information.
In this way he came to visit most of the
neighbouring villages.


As a matter of fact I did not obtain any important information, for
while there were plenty of men who “‘had seen”’ (?) them, they were
reticent on the subject, always concluding that they were probably
mistaken for all the encounters had taken place at nightfall. This is
likely enough.

There was one relatively exact fact. In March 1946 a team of work-

I was at once deluged with stories of dwarfs with their feet back to

One of them told me the following:
During one of his expeditions in the course of 1947 the great

All the same I doubt whether it would have been successful since en-

In 1951 the professor’s new boy, in reply to his usual barrage of ques-
tions, told him that when he was young, probably around 1941, he had
himself seen a hunter at Seguéla bring back a little man with red hair in
a cage. The local official had put clothes on it for decency’s sake and
sent it to Abidjan by way of Bouaké. The boy did not know what hap-
pened to the little prisoner afterwards.


This tale seems to me to have been embroidered somewhat. If the
creature was really human it would not have been put in a cage, and if it
was an ape the official would not have worried whether it was decently
dressed. Either it was.a creature half way between man and an ape, or
more likely, it was an unknown primate which had been dressed up as a
joke, as tame monkeys so often are.


Professor Ledoux remarks that these tales of an unknown reddish-
brown primate in the Ivory Coast are overlaid with the very firmly held
belief that there are pygmies in the forest between the Sassandra and
Cavally rivers.

According to an African technician of mine from Toulépleu called

there was recently a system of barter between the negroes and these


forest creatures; various manufactured goods were left in the forest in

to the negroes themselves. The Guérés called them Séhité.


It is possible that these Séhités may be true pygmies like those in
Central Africa.


The professor’s inquiries among the Europeans brought out a sig-
nificant fact. Those who had never spent any length of time between
the Sassandra and the Cavally denied out of hand that there could be
any little men in the forest, whether they were true pygmies or unknown
primates. On the other hand those who had lived in this area were
seriously prepared to consider that pygmies might have lived there in
the past and also that there might be a real basis for the legend of the
red dwarfs. His own impression was that the legends and rumours in
the Ivory Coast were based on the fairly recent presence of pygmies
and the present existence of reddish-haired primates whose exact nature
was still problematical.


Although the “‘little hairy men” reported in Mozambique and Tan-
ganyika as well as the Ivory Coast agree with nothing known to the
zoologist or the anthropologist, their description could not agree better
with a creature well known to palaeontologists by the name of Australo-
pithecus, which was still living in South Africa, not more than 500,000
years ago, at a time when all the existing African species were already
formed.


The Australopithecus, which once lived on the grassy plains in the
valley of the Vaal, was a little creature, about 4 feet high, with a face like


a chimpanzee, although its dentition was almost human, but which
walked upright on its hind-legs and was proportioned like a miniature
man. The first skull of one of these odd gnomes was discovered in 1924


at Buxton in the Taungs area of British Bechuanaland by men quarrying
limestone in one of the caves filled with chalky tufa which have been


exploited in the broad Harts River valley since the first world war. The


skull, which was embedded in a block of stone, was sent to Professor
Raymond Dart of the University of Witwatersrand, who gave its owner


the name of Australopithecus transvaalensis. It was so strikingly human


that the people who found it are said to have thought it was a Bushman’s.


Professor Dart maintained that this creature had a much better claim

Actually the Australopithecus’s remains were found in caves and not


in geological strata, so that it is very difficult to reckon their age. The


estimates are based on the kinds of animals found with them; but this
method has not the slightest scientific value, since it is impossible to


state for certain the date at which a species became extinct. Today
many palaeontologists admit that the Australopithecus must have been
contemporary with man, indeed man has been blamed for its extinc-


tion.


Loren C. Eiseley, head of the Anthropological Department of the
University of Pennsylvania, affirms


That the Australopithecines have vanished while many simple
arboreal relatives of ours survive is not surprising. The man-apes tried
to occupy the same environmental niche as man, and as a consequence
man destroyed them.


This mass-extermination cannot have happened more than 500,000
years ago.


But if the Australopitheci were really as intelligent as everyone thinks
they were, would they have let themselves be killed without flinching?
Surely, like many less cunning animals they would try to move out of
range of an obviously stronger enemy, by taking refuge in a less agree-
able but safer area. Since man meant to be master of the plains, the


little hairy hordes would have adapted themselves to the forest, just as
the East African pygmies were to do when driven by the invading Masai.
The forest would have suited such ape-like creatures well.”


In the thick forests of Africa, the last refuge of so many “‘relic” spe-
cies, might not the Australopithecus’s descendants still survive? Cer-
tainly the agogwe are extraordinarily like Dart’s “intelligent, energetic,


erect, and delicately proportioned little people.” And the account of
them mixing freely with baboons agrees with the fact that the two crea-

some sort of “gentleman’s agreement” between these two very distantly
related primates to live together in a sort of symbiosis, so frequent among
animals. The baboons have a more highly developed social instinct than

Traditional tongue-twister.


AT half-past eleven on the morning of 23 December 1919 Captain Lei-
cester Stevens boarded the Southampton train at Waterloo station on his
way to hunt the Brontosaurus in Central Africa.


“T am leaving for Cape Town on Christmas Eve,” he told a news-
paperman who followed him to his compartment. ‘From Cape Town
I shall go 1,700 miles north to Kafue, where my expedition will be
organised.”


His only companion was his faithful Laddie, a former “barrage dog,”


a mongrel of dog and wolf, which had often carried messages under
heavy artillery fire during the,first world war, and was to help its master
track the monstrous dinosaur and win the million-pound reward offered
by the American Smithsonian Institution.
Captain Stevens put his


trust in his Mannlicher rifle, for the huge reptile was supposed to have a


vital spot.


“Where that spot is,” remarked the new St George with an unduly
mysterious air as the train moved off, “is one of my secrets.”


His brown, weather-tanned face broke into a broad smile and his very
light blue eyes twinkled as he waved goodbye. He was a tall muscular
fellow in his thirties, and seemed perfectly sane.


This story is not a science-fiction writer’s dream but is taken from the
Press of the time. To go dinosaur-hunting in the twentieth century is
surely madness—yet plenty of people were infected by it. When Cap-


tain Stevens first announced his bizarre intentions, he was flooded with


letters from hunters, sportsmen and bored demobilised officers all asking

to come with him. An old lady who had long been a member of the

For several weeks the most exciting news in the papers were Carpen-


tier and Beckett warming up for their famous boxing match and that two
different travellers had recently met a prehistoric monster in the Belgian
Congo.


On 17 November The Times had published a small news item; it was,
as usual, under the smallest and most discreetly unsensational of head-
lines:


A TALE FROM AFRICA
Semper aliquid novi


The Central News Port Elizabeth correspondent sends the following:
The head of the local museum here has received information from a
M. Lepage, who was in charge of railway construction in the Belgian
Congo, of an exciting adventure Jast month. While Lepage was hunting
one day in October he came upon an extraordinary monster, which
charged at him. Lepage fired but was forced to flee, with the monster
in chase. The animal before long gave up the chase and Lepage was
able to examine it through his binoculars. The animal, he says, was
about 24 ft. in length with a long pointed snout adorned with tusks like
horns and a short horn above the nostrils. The front feet were like those
of a horse and the hind hoofs were cloven. There was a scaly hump on
the monster’s shoulder.


The animal later charged through the native village of Fungurume,
destroying the huts and killing some native dwellers. A hunt was at once
organised but the Government has forbidden the molestation of the
animal, on the ground that it is probably a relic of antiquity. There is
a wild trackless region in the neighbourhood which contains many
swamps and marshes, where, says the head of the museum, it is possible
that a few primeval monsters may survive.


The dinosaur which the animal described in this dispatch most re-
sembles is the Triceratops (Fig. 53, page 188), which was some I9 to
26 feet long, and did have a horn on its nose. But it had “horns like


tusks” rather than the other way round, and all four feet were thick and


heavy like a pachyderm’s. For some reason (mere journalistic ignorance


is the most likely one) everyone began calling it a Brontosaurus, though


this dinosaur is related to the Diplodocus (Fig. 52, page 188) and shares


its characteristically long neck and tail, and, like it, has neither horns


nor tusks.


The Brontosaurus seems to have first reared its head in this affair in


a delayed Reuter message from Bulawayo, dated 4 December but not


435


THE TERRORS OF AFRICA


printed in the London papers until the twelfth. It was all the more
uncalled for as the beast described in this new report was even more like


a Triceratops, or rather its cousin the Monoclonius, the two “tusks like
horns” (or vice versa) having disappeared.


News apparently corroborating the report of the existence in the
Congo of a monster known as a Brontosaurus (the thundering Saurian)
comes from Elisabethville.


A Belgian prospector and big game hunter named M. Gapelle, who
has returned here from the interior of the Congo, states that he followed
up a strange spoor for 12 miles and at length sighted a beast certainly of
the rhinoceros order with large scales reaching far down its body. The
animal, he says, has a very thick kangaroo-like tail, a horn on its snout,
and a hump on its back. M. Gapelle fired some shots at the beast, which
threw up its head and disappeared into a swamp.


The American Smithsonian expedition was in search of the monster
referred to above when it met with a serious railway accident, in which
several persons were killed.


Now the Brontosaurus, which is a reptile, is certainly not “‘of the
rhinoceros order.” As all the rest of the description—thick and power-
ful tail, large scales on its sides and humped back—seems to refer to
some horned dinosaur belonging to the group of Ceratopsians (Tricera-
tops, Monoclonius, etc.), perhaps M. Gapelle meant that it was like a
rhinoceros in general size and appearance and particularly in that it had


a horn on the end of its nose. Or perhaps “rhinoceros” was a mistake
for “dinosaurus” on a bad telephone line? Certainly the animal de-
scribed is no more like a Brontosaurus than a hedgehog is like a horse.
But the news that so important a scientific body as the Smithsonian
Institution had sent an expedition on the beast’s track would perhaps
have allayed the sceptics’ doubts. And there was no doubt that this
Institution had in fact sent an expedition led by Harry C. Raven to ex-
plore this little-known corner of Africa, and that on 28 November the
news had come that three of its members—Lendeman, Armstrong and
Howell Farr—had been killed in a railway accident in the Katanga area
of the Belgian Congo.


Soon the Press was buzzing with the tale that as this disaster had
brought the expedition to an end so prematurely, the Smithsonian
Institution had offered a reward of a million pounds to anyone who
brought the mysterious monster back dead or alive. No more encour-
agement was needed, especially for men like Captain Stevens, to take up
Brontosaurus-hunting, which did not seem so crazy now that various


letters were turning up in the Press from old colonials who had also

But the gallant captain did not alter his plans or his armoury.
Meanwhile the world’s Press was adding embellishments to the

These tales have been current for so long that now they are some-
times repeated by perfectly serious authors concerned with the problem
of unknown animals. Everyone seems to have overlooked or forgotten

Sir, I am authorised to contradict the statement that the members of

came here to hunt the brontosaurus. There is no foundation for this
statement.

Expedition in the Katanga.
Elisabethville, Jan. 21.


This was enough to discourage the most earnest of dinosaur-hunters
and to make a permanent laughing-stock of any naturalist who dared to

note them down, but few dared to report them except under their breath.
Even the practical jokers thought it wisest to wait until the affair was
forgotten before trying to repeat the trick. It was twelve years before a
dinosaur-hunt found its way into the Press again.

Germany not long ago, after spending a year filming big-game in

of taking some sensational shots of the chepekwe, but they did not man-
age to see the beast.


Grobler’s good faith seemed indisputable, and in fact Major Schom-
burgk had said during a lecture in Germany the previous February that
there was a native tradition that a huge reptile existed in Central Africa,
adding that the prospect of finding this animal was the one thing that
might tempt him to return to this inhospitable wilderness.


Since he made this pronouncement [the Rhodesia Herald goes on] a
Swede, J. C. Johanson, who is an overseer in a Belgian rubber planta-
tion in the Congo, wrote to the “Cologne Gazette” from Mai Muene,
Kassai district; enclosing photographs purporting to establish the
existence of the animal in question.


The photos, so the journal says, were anything but clear, yet they
revealed a discovery of great importance.
Johanson stumbled on a
unique specimen of a dinosaur family that must have lived milleniums
ago.

I have not so far managed to find Johanson’s letter in the Kélnische
Zeitung (where it may not even have appeared) so I will quote the extract
published in the Rhodesia Herald:


On February 16 last I went on a shooting trip, accompanied by my
gun-bearer.
I only had a Winchester for small game, not expecting
anything big. At 2 p.m. I reached the Kassai valley.


No game was in sight. As we were going down to the water, the boy
suddenly called out “‘elephants.’’ It appeared that two giant bulls were
almost hidden by the jungle. About 50 yards away from them I saw
something incredible—a monster, about 16 yards in length, with a
lizard’s head and tail. I closed my eyes and reopened them. There
could be no doubt about it, the animal was still there. My boy cowered
in the grass whimpering.


I was shaken by the hunting-fever. My teeth rattled with fear. Three
times I snapped; only one attempt came out well. Suddenly the mon-
ster vanished, with a remarkably rapid movement.
It took me some
time to recover. Alongside me the boy prayed and cried. I lifted him
up, pushed him along and made him follow me home. On the way we
had to traverse a big swamp. Progress was slow, for my limbs were still
half-paralysed with fear. There in the swamp, the huge lizard appeared
once more, tearing lumps from a dead rhino. It was covered in ooze. I
was only about 25 yards away.


It was simply terrifying. The boy had taken French leave, carrying
the rifle with him. At first I was careful not to stir, then I thought of
my camera.
I could plainly hear the crunching of rhino bones in the
lizard’s mouth. Just as I clicked, it jumped into deep water.


The experience was too much for my nervous system. Completely
exhausted, I sank down behind the bush that had given me shelter.
Blackness reigned before my eyes. The animal’s phenomenally rapid
motion was the most awe-inspiring thing I had ever seen.


I must have looked like one demented, when at last I regained camp.
Metcalfe, who is boss there, said I approached him, waving the camera
about in a silly way and emitting unintelligible sounds. I dare say I
did. For eight days I lay in a fever, unconscious nearly all the time.


Dinosaur-hunters had become better journalists since the days of
Lepage and Gapelle, not only in making the most ofa sensational story but
also in realising the value of pictures. The article in the Rhodesia Herald


is illustrated with a photograph reproduced from a German newspaper,
presumably the one taken by the Swede and referred to by Grobler,
though one says the beast it is eating is a rhinoceros and the other a
hippopotamus. The photo itself is so indistinct that one cannot possiby
recognise the monster’s prey. Indeed, there is little doubt that this pic-
ture published in several newspapers and magazines is a crude fake. A
Komodo dragon has been transplanted somewhat clumsily into an

African swamp scene, where it is perched ballerina-like on the tips of its
toes on the carcase of a hippopotamus or rhinoceros, thus making it look
enormous.
This faked evidence is enough to destroy any remaining
belief in the truth of Johanson’s story. Once again the dinosaur has
proved to be a hoax.


All the same, the hoax has brought to light a few facts which cannot
so easily be dismissed. In 1920 Walter Winans had quoted an authority


as trustworthy as Carl Hagenbeck. This time Grobler had called on the
evidence of the great animal-merchant’s faithful agent, Hans Schom-
burgk. In both cases fact and fiction were closely intermixed, the hoax-


ers were inspired by rumours founded on authentic facts. Hagenbeck
really held the beliefs he was credited with, and Schomburgk had cer-
tainly been the first to talk to Grobler about the chepekwe, a beast
which he had first heard-of at the beginning of the century and had
mentioned in a book in 1910. Grobler had done no more than to con-
fuse or embroider the facts and make the mistake of thinking that
Johanson’s letter and photograph were a confirmation of them.


I shall do my best to explain what these facts are—though it will not
be easy. I cannot promise that it will be the “sober truth,” since the


facts are quite as fantastic as the sensational but disappointing stories
based upon them. For what could be more fantastic than the fact that
Captain Stevens, who set off to the heart of Africa as a result of a double
hoax in the hope of winning a quite imaginary fortune, might well have
succeeded in capturing a dinosaur and winning immortal fame? At all
events the animals we are concerned with in this chapter are, if not
actual dinosaurs, large unknown reptiles extraordinarily like them.


Rumours about creatures of this kind have been reported in a ring of
country 2,000 miles in diameter encircling the whole basin of the Bel-
gian Congo, the Cameroons, Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, Uganda, Rhodesia
and thence to Angola, that is to say in the upper reaches of the Congo,
the Nile and the Zambezi.


Before we go into the question of the beast’s identity, let us consider
the facts, such as they are, without drawing any conclusions and taking
care not to mix up reports from widely separated areas nor to assume
that all the tales of an ‘“‘African dragon” necessarily refer to the same


animal.


Let us begin a tour of the Belgian Congo, arranging the evidence by


place rather than time. We shall start with Alfred Aloysius Horn, whose


stilted Victorian narrative of his adventures Miss Ethelreda Lewis

When Trader Horn was published it was enthusiastically received as
literature, but hardly as scientific fact. Those who knew Africa and its
fauna better realised that he was a keen and truthful observer of nature.
“Apart from a few unimportant slips the statements made by Trader
Horn about the country are generally accurate,” writes Dr Albert
Schweitzer.


In 1902 Sir Harry Johnston drew attention in his great work on
Uganda to the mysterious creature in Lake Victoria, the third largest


lake in the world, a vast stretch of water as big as the whole of Eire.
It could hardly have come into the world with a more propitious god-
father than the man to whom we owe the discovery of the okapi.


There are also persistent stories amongst the natives that the waters
of the’Victoria Nyanza are inhabited by a monster (known to the Bag-

Mr. W. Grant, late Provincial Governor, Jinja, once had his attention

In 1910 an American sportsman called Edgar Beecher Bronson told
an odd story in his book In Closed Territory. He was hunting in the
country west of Sotik when he met another hunter called Jordan, who
told him of an encounter with a terrible monster called the dingonek.
This took place on the Gori River, which runs into Lake Victoria on the
eastern shore near what was then the Anglo-German frontier. Jordan
said the beast was 14 or 15 feet long, with a head the size of a lioness’s,
but marked like a leopard’s, with two long, straight, white fangs in the
upper jaw. It was covered with scales like an armadillo, as broad as a
hippopotamus and spotted like a leopard. It had a long and broad tail.


Its footprints were as big as a hippo’s, but had claws like a reptile’s.


At the time this story appeared [observes C. W. Hobley] it was con-
sidered that this was probably a traveller’s tale, told to entertain a new-
comer, but I have since met a man who a few years back was wandering


about the Mara River or Ngare Dubash which rises in Sotik, crosses the
Anglo-German boundary, and runs into Lake Victoria in German
territory. He emphatically asserts that he saw this beast. He was at
the time about where the Mara River crosses the frontier, and the river
was in high flood. The beast came floating down the river on a big log,

It turned out that tales about an unknown amphibious creature were
found not only in Lake Victoria, but also in some of the rivers that ran
into it. Hobley thought that there was a sensational new zoological dis-
covery to be made, and bearing in mind the creature’s scales, added: “A
survival of some extinct race of saurians is a thing to thrill the imagina-
tion of the scientific world.” This phrase—and in a scientific journal,
too—stuck, and it was no longer a question of a large cetacean or gigan-
tic fish, but “‘some extinct race of saurians.”” There were rumours that
the officers of a steamer on Lake Victoria had seen a strange prehistoric
animal with a long neck in the lake. And Arnold Drummond-Hay
claimed to have met a “‘sea-serpent”” on Lake Nyasa.


This only tended to discredit the previous reports, for the experts had
no difficulty in showing that what he had seen was merely a large python;
for pythons may be more than 20 feet long. Sir Frederick Jackson saw
the skin of a specimen 22 feet long killed in the Mabira forest. It must
have been almost a foot in diameter. A snake as thick as a man’s body
would be a most impressive sight. Moreover the python is a good swim-
mer and seems able to cross wide stretches of water. Colonel C. R. S.
Pitman writes:


I have come across this great serpent on Nkosi Island, the southern-
most of the Sese group, in the open lake. Unless it had been deliberately
placed there by man—which seems unlikely—it must have made
numerous water journeys from island to island before arriving so far
south,

All the same, the first reports quoted above hardly remind one of a
python—especially when they refer to the monster’s feet! And fuller
information came to light to show that this explanation was untenable.
In the 1930s Dr E. G. Wayland, Director of the Geological Survey of
Uganda, stated that he had been shown a piece of the Jukwata’s bone.
The natives of the Kavirondo country told him that they firmly believed
in the Jukwata; it fought with crocodiles and during the Homeric
struggle lost pieces of its skin, which were much prized as amulets. They
said that the monster’s bellowing voice could be heard a long way off;
indeed, Wayland said he had heard it himself. He could not explain
these roars unless they were made by the Jukwata—whatever this beast
might be.


Here I should mention that snakes have no vocal cords at all, are quite
dumb and can make no noise but a “hiss,” which in a large specimen
sounds like a jet of steam at high pressure. A bellowing reptile is much
more likely to be a large saurian than an ophidian.


In 1923 a study of the Nuer people of the Upper Nile Province was
published by the British Deputy Governor, H. C. Jackson. He speaks


at some length about an enormous snake, the /au, which the Nuer told
him lived in all the swampy area of the sources of the White Nile.


Various fantastic attributes attach to it, which may be mere embel-
lishments on the part of the Nuer without necessarily disproving the
existence of some hitherto unknown serpent of exceptional size.


Thus some say that it has a short crest of hair on the back of its head
not unlike that of a crowned crane: others that it has long hairs,
reminiscent of some of the mud-fish of the Nile, with which it entangles
its unwilling victims and drags them into the river. In certain years,
particularly during the rainy season, its belly is said to gurgle like the
rumbling of an elephant. This noise was heard in the year 1918 in the
Bahr-el-Arab.


The Nuer state that it inhabits holes in the banks of rivers or swamps,
and spends most of its time in swamps. They are in mortal dread of it,
and if they see the furrow in the ground that announces its presence,
they run as fast as they can in the opposite direction.
If a Nuer sees
this serpent before it sees him, all is well, but if the serpent happens to
sight even a large party of them first, all are expected to die.


The Addar swamps extend for some 1800 square miles: those of the
Bahr-el-Ghazal and its tributaries must cover an area of many thou-
sands of square miles. Neither of these vast morasses has ever yet been
explored, and many parts of them have never even been visited.
It is
therefore not improbable that some addition to our zoological know-
ledge may ultimately come from these places.

black like the python. On its vicious-looking, snake-like head it has
large tentacles, or thick, wiry hairs, with which it reaches out and seizes
its victims. If a man sees a Lau first, the creature at once expires, but
if the Lau is the first observer the human dies on the spot.

At the beginning of 1912, when he was a lieutenant in the Belgian
Congo Police, Godart was going up-river on the Aruwimi in order to set

when he was surprised to feel a violent earthquake. He was even more
surprised when the one soldier who formed his escort rushed off to the
riverside with his Albini rifle in his hand.


Some time later the negro came back rather sheepishly and said as if

“Tt had already gone back into the water.”
“What? What do you mean?” asked Godart.
“The beast [nyama] which makes the earth shake when it comes out
of the water—it has to be killed, but I didn’t see it.”


The lieutenant was amused at this charmingly naive explanation, but
he did not want to humiliate the negro, who had shown nothing but
courage, so he asked him several questions.

The reader will have recognised the “short crest of hair . . . not un-
