In later years Colonel Godart would tell this story as an instance of
the native soldier’s courage. When my father told him about my book,
the French edition of which had just been published, he saw the story
in a new light, and he agreed to write down the conversation which
I have here reported word for word. I must point out that Colonel
Godart could not have been influenced by the descriptions quoted in
my book, because he wrote his note before he had read it. Since then
his admiration for the native soldier’s courage has increased, and he
wishes that he had never laughed at him, even though he only did so
inwardly.


Naturally this story does not prove that in the Ituri itself there is a
beast related to the Jau of the Upper Nile and perhaps to the /ukwata of
Lake Victoria. It may just be that echoes of their existence have reached
this area. At all events the tradition refers to a fairly heavy and powerful
animal if it is to make the earth shake—as elephants, rhinoceroses and
hippopotami do—and be popularly credited with seismic earth-tremors.
Incidentally only an animal with feet can make the earth vibrate as it
moves.


But can we truthfully call these monsters dinosaurs? No, there is
nothing in the reports I have so far quoted to justify the name, for while
it is often hard to dispute their existence, their various descriptions
might variously apply to a stumpy and heavy snake, a giant monitor


lizard, an unknown species of crocodile, or even some very odd kind of


fish.


It is only the rumours that have come from other parts of Africa over
the last fifty years which have gradually suggested the notion that dino-


saurs, or rather some dinosaurs with characteristically long necks, may

In 1909 a German traveller, Lieutenant Paul Gritz, succeeded in
crossing Africa from the Indian Ocean to the mouth of the Congo in a
motor-boat. This remarkable feat led him to visit Lake Bangweulu, in
Northern Rhodesia, where he noted:


The crocodile is found only in very isolated specimens in Lake
Bangweulu, except in the mouths of the large rivers at the north; but in
the swamp lives the msanga, much feared by the natives, a degenerate
saurian which one might well confuse with the crocodile, were it not
that its skin has no scales and its toes are armed with claws. I did not
succeed in shooting a msanga, but on the island of Mbawala, I came by
some strips of its skin.


When Hans Schomburgk also crossed Central Africa at the beginning
of the century, he was surprised to find when he reached this same Lake
Bangweulu that, although this huge lake, 78 miles by 22, seemed an ideal
habitat for hippopotami, there was not a trace of one on its banks. When
he expressed his astonishment to his native guides, they told him that
there was an animal in the lake which killed and ate the hippopotami,
although it was smaller than they were. It was an amphibious creature,
but apparently it never came ashore, for its footprints were never seen.


When he reached the Dilolo marshes, 500 miles farther west, where
the Congo, Northern Rhodesia and Angola meet, ponomuaies heard
similar tales about a beast called the chimpekwe.


Unfortunately [wrote Schomburgk in 1910] I thought this story was
a fable and did not pursue my inquiries further. Later I talked about it
to Carl Hagenbeck, and I am now convinced that it is some kind of
saurian.
Hagenbeck has received from other sources reports which
entirely agree with my own observations and with what I was told by
the natives I questioned.


This is confirmed by Hagenbeck himself in his book Beasts and Men:


Some years ago I received reports from two quite distinct sources of
the existence of an immense and wholly unknown animal, said to in-
habit the interior of Rhodesia.
Almost identical stories reached me,
firstly, through one of my own travellers, and, secondly, through an

In the winter of 1912 a friend who had long lived in Dar es Salaam
(German East Africa) introduced me to a Frenchman who had adopted
the tough and dangerous profession of natural history collector, wan-

The name nzefu-loi meant “‘water-elephant,” but did not necessarily
refer to a true elephant of semi-aquatic habits, as the pygmy is supposed

hunt the nzefu-lot. He didn’t come back.”


The nzefu-loi used to inhabit the whole of the Kamolondo, the area of
lakes on the Lualaba between Bukama and Ankoro. There are more
than a dozen lakes between Bukama (9° S.) and Kaniamba (7° 30’ S.);
the largest being Upemba with its substantial fisheries, and Kisale, a


sea of papyrus similar to the swamps of the Upper Nile, where the Jau
dwells. Today much of the Kamolondo is included in the Upemba
National Park.

Examined objectively, none of the trustworthy reports that I have
mentioned so far justifies us in using the word “dinosaur.” So far the
animal has never been a large reptile that stands on its hind-legs or an
animal with both a long neck and a long tail, which would be reasons for

reptile: it is more like a mammal. Hagenbeck talks of “a huge monster,
half elephant, half dragon,” using the word “dragon” in the same sense


as the Komodo dragon. Unscientific reasons seem to have caused the
elephant half to be deliberately forgotten.

The late King Lewanika, who was much interested in the study of
the animals of his kingdom, Barotsiland, frequently heard from his
people of some great aquatic reptile, possessing a body larger than that
of an elephant, and which lived in the great swamps near his town. He

told, and he would at once go himself and visit the place. In the follow-

of excitement, and said they had just seen the monster lying on the edge
of the marsh, and that on viewing them it had retreated on its belly, and
slid into the deep water. The beast was said to be of colossal size, with
legs like a gigantic lizard, and possessing a long neck. It was also said
to be taller than a man, and had a head like a snake.


Lewanika at once rode to the spot and saw a large space where the
reeds had been flattened down, and a broad path, with water flowing
into the recently disturbed mud, made to the water’s edge. He de-

The Boers’ wagons were about 4 feet 6 inches wide. Millais does not

Continuing clockwise around the Belgian Congo, we come to eastern
Angola, by following up the Zambezi—the middle reaches of which are
haunted by the tsiguqumadevu—towards the Dilolo marshes, where the
chipekwe lives. It is not surprising to find tales of similar amphibious
monsters there.


In 1932 a Swiss scientific expedition set about exploring Angola, its
aim being partly zoological. This project was announced in the Lisbon
newspapers in the previous December, whereupon A. da Paz Colaca, a
former agent of the Diamang, who had lived in this part of Africa for a
long time, wrote to the expedition’s zoologist, Dr A. Monard, about a
problem which had long interested him. He said that in that country
there was a large unknown reptile, compared to which “‘the common croc


is amere baby.” He had at first doubted whether the rumours he heard
were founded on fact, but little inquiry was needed to convince him
that there was something at the bottom of them. In the correspondence
that followed he gave so much detailed information that Dr Monard
eventually decided to go and see what it was all about. He said that the
libata, as he called it, was


amphibious, of huge size, and very voracious; it is extremely rare and
is seen only in the Chiumbe area. It is larger, much larger than a croco-
dile or a hippopotamus; there are none in the Luaximo, but only up in

the Chiumbe and in the Cuilo; it appears only at the beginning of the
rainy season or at the end of the cacimbo (July, August and September).


Fortunately Dr Monard. was one of that fairly rare breed of scien-
tists who keep an open mind:


The existence [he writes] of a large saurian descended from the rep-
tiles of the Mesozoic era is by no means theoretically impossible.
Though every continent has been crossed and recrossed, most travel-
lers follow much the same track, and there are still holes in the net to
be explored.
There have been several reports that some kind of
“Brontosaurus” survives, and several expeditions have even gone to
look for it; the fact that they failed may merely prove that this prehis-
toric beast is very rare or that it lives in country as inaccessible as the
great swamps still are.


There are some reasons, based on the history of the continents and
of the great reptiles, for thinking that they could survive only in those
continents which had already been formed at the end of the Mesozoic
era, in Gondwana, which consisted of southern and central Africa,
Madagascar, South America (chiefly Brazil), India and Australia.
India seems to be too populous and Australia too dry to be included—
which leaves Africa and Brazil. While it is not scientific to be too credu-
lous, it is no better to be incredulous; and there is no reason for saying
that the survival of some types of Mesozoic saurians is impossible.


In this admirably unpreiudiced frame of mind Dr Monard set off
into north-eastern Angola with C. E. Thiébaud as his companion, and

We questioned the soma [chief] of Tyipukungu [Dr Monard reports]
and all the more intelligent natives; whenever we could we went to the

The soma set two natives to watch the river when we could not do so.

The rains began to threaten, so the two explorers, who had come to

1. Its name is pata, and not libata as my correspondent wrote. All
the natives pronounce it in the same way.

2. It exists only in the upper Tyihumbwe and in the Kasai; I have

Around Tyipukungu there are only two, one some 6 miles upstream
from the other. Some natives say that there are three, others that there

the bait for) had left its favourite haunt to settle even further upstream.


3. It is almost always hidden in the water; it does not appear on the

On 1 September 1932 a man from Tyipukungu saw it sleeping on dry

The women on the Tyihumbwe who are in the habit of fishing on the

of shouting before going into the water and this drives the beast away.


As soon as it hears or is aware of man it dives and disappears.
4. It attacks animals of all kinds: goats, pigs, cattle and even men

It will also eat crocodiles. The

This year it had taken nothing so far. Our correspondent knew of its

5. Several lipatas have been killed. When the soma was a boy (which

A white man who had shot a hippopotamus one evening came back

But which? From the Africans’ sense of zoology, it may well be that

1. The [ipata consists merely of large and old specimens of C.

2. The /ipata is one of the other African species, in a new habitat to

3. The lipata is an as yet unknown species of crocodile, either related

It

All the crocodiles are prehistoric animals: the existing genera have re-

the Ankylosaurs, actually looked like crocodiles.

If Dr Monard really wanted to find an unusual type of animal in
Angola he may have been looking in the wrong place. In the Upper
Cuango and Upper Cuanza we shall find detailed rumours about a much
more extraordinary creature than the /ipata. Ilse von Nolde, who spent

that there was an amphibious monster known in Kimbundu as coje ya

They often drew her attention to distant rumbling sounds they said
were made by this beast, which generally lived in the water but quite
often climbed out on to the bank. During the rainy season, when the
Cuanza was usually in flood, the coje ya menia moved to smaller rivers
and swamps, and it was at this time that one had the best chance of
seeing one. Thus the Angola “‘water-lion” roars like the Jukwata and
lau of the Nile marshes; it also slaughters all the hippopotami, even
though it is smaller than they are, like the chipekwe of the sources of the
Congo. And like the nzefu-loi of the Lualaba it is said to have tusks or
large canine teeth which it uses for killing.

coje ya menia. A Portuguese lorry-driver who ran a service along the

The animal is said to be of a brownish-grey colour with a smooth
skin, its size approximating that of an elephant; at least that of a hippo-

It is said to have a long and very flexible neck and only one
tooth but a very long one; some say it is a horn. A few spoke about a
long muscular tail like that of an alligator. Canoes coming near it are
said to be doomed; the animal is said to attack the vessels at once and
to kill the crews but without eating the bodies. The creature is said to
live in the caves that have been washed out by the river in the clay of
its shores at sharp bends. It is said to climb the shore even at daytime
in search of food; its diet is said to be entirely vegetable. This feature
disagrees with a possible explanation as a myth. The preferred plant
was shown to me; it is a kind of liana with large white blossoms, with a
milky sap and apple-like fruits.


The information collected by Freiherr von Stein was confirmed in
every detail in 1938 by Dr Leo von Boxberger, another German who had
been a magistrate in Africa for a long time when Germany still had


colonies in that continent. He adds,


My own contribution to the subject is unfortunately very small. At

The belief in a gigantic water-animal, described as a reptile with a
long thin neck, exists among the natives throughout the Southern
Cameroons, wherever they form part of the Congo basin and also to the
west of this area, doubtless wherever the great rivers are broad and deep
and are flanked by virgin forest.

Let us proceed to the second unknown animal in the Ubangi-Shari,
the snake-like badigui, also known as ngakoula-ngou.


In 1930 or thereabouts it was described to Lucien Blancou by the
Linda Banda of Ippy as a gigantic snake that killed hippos without leav-
ing any sign of a wound and browsed on branches of trees without leav-
ing the water. This would of course be a very odd diet for a snake,
which in any case would not be able to lift its head out of the water
unless it was resting on the bottom, so one may well suspect that there
might be a bulkier body behind the snake-like head and neck. Like the
isiququmadevu and the mokéle-mbémbe, it really does remind one of a
dinosaur.


The chief of the Yetomane division, a great hunter thoroughly at

hippopotamus at about the same time in the River Brouchouchou near
Chief Mapouka’s village. The villagers had no qualms about eating the
“water-devil’s” prey.


The Baya gave Blancou a similar description of the monster, which

So much for the reports. Do they all refer to the same animal?
Hardly. In fact there is only one respect in which all agree. They are


all amphibious. Indeed, this has been my criterion in including them in


this chapter. They are also not so very different in size. The /ukwata is
the size of a small porpoise or a large manatee, the dingonek’s back is as
broad as a hippo, the /au is as thick as a donkey or horse, the chipekwe
and the coje ya menia a little smaller than a hippo, the mokéle-mbémbe,
the nzefu-loi and the “‘beast-that-makes-the-earth-shake” as big as a
hippo, the isigugumadevu and the lipata bigger than a hippo, and the
mourou-ngou bigger than a lion—the differences are not great—no more
than might be due to the animal’s age and sex and the narrator’s degree
of exaggeration. Where figures are given the only real discrepancy is in
the size of the Jau. The negroes’ estimates varied between 40 and 100


feet. As they were all referring to the same carcase, someone must


obviously have been exaggerating considerably, especially as Jackson


says the Jau is usually smaller than the python. Old Moussa’s reckoning


that the badigui’s neck alone was 25 feet long, may well be a mistake, as


I have suggested above. Moreover half a century had passed since he


8 feet long. If the badigui’s neck was really 25 or even 15 feet long Moussa would
surely have said “‘two or three times as long as a giraffe’s.” I think a length of 10
or 12 feet is a reasonable interpretation of Moussa’s evidence.

saw the beast, and it is common knowledge that dimensions increase
with time.


We can therefore say that all the reports refer to an amphibious animal
with a body roughly as thick as a hippopotamus’s—rather less according


to most of them. This has led some authors into thinking all the animals
are the same. Yet in other respects they are very different. Here are
some of the more glaring discrepancies:


The skin is sometimes said to be covered with scales, sometimes bare


or smooth. In some the neck is short; in others it is long, even very long
and flexible. The tail is at one time compared to a crocodile’s, at another


to a horse’s or to a panther’s. Finally it is surprising to find that some
have tusks or fangs like a walrus’s, while others have a little horn on the
nose and one even has a crest and barbels. While these features do not
mutually exclude one another, they are too conspicuous to have been
noticed in some animals and not in others. They might all of them be
features peculiar to the male as a result of sexual dimorphism; but it is
most unusual to find a female with a feature absent in the male. For
instance, it is hard to imagine a species in which only the male had large
tusks and only the female had a horn on the nose. Nature is not chival-
rous, the males get all the finery.


In short, the various descriptions of African “dragons” obviously


refer to at least three quite different types of animal—so it is not sur-
prising that a mixture of these creatures has produced an absurd and
fantastic beast, which it is difficult to believe in, let alone identify.


The thorough inquiry that Lucien Blancou was able to make when
he was game-warden in French Equatorial Africa has shown that in a
particular area the natives believe in two distinct amphibious animals,
both unknown to science. One is a beast of prey, with large fangs and
hooked claws, which swallows its victims leaving nothing behind, the
other is a long-necked vegetarian which kills hippos but does not eat
them.


Two more different animals can hardly be imagined, yet even among


the natives there is some confusion between the two, doubtless because
they are so rare and because their names, which are similar, have been
misunderstood. Thus the Baya, who say that the diJali or “‘water-lion”
has a horse’s body and a lion’s claws, claim that it eats nothing but


leaves. A Zandé who was present when this information was elicited
believed that it had large tusks and lived on fish. The name dilali there-
fore seems to have been applied to two different animals.


The converse is equally true. Blancou, like Naumann, thought that

different peoples used the names, “‘water-panther” and “‘water-lion” to

the elephants and men it attacks, which hardly agrees with the second
being supposedly a vegetarian.


Sometimes known animals have similar names, which only confuses
descriptions which are vague enough already. Thus the Banda do not
use the term mourou-ngou (water-panther) only for a savage monster; it


is likewise the name for the giant water-shrew (Potamogale velox), which


is also called kovoro. This animal is a giant for an insectivore, but it is
barely 2 feet long and feeds chiefly on fresh-water snails, clams, frogs
and fish. Moreover the panther itself may have added to the legend of
the mourou-ngou: for it is not afraid of water, swims well and catches fish
in shallow water.


The whole question is extremely muddled, and if we are to make any
sense of it we must try to eliminate the various animals which have no
business here.


Let us deal first with the animals which seem to have short necks: the
dingonek (or ol-umaina) of Kenya, Lieutenant Gritz’s “degenerate
saurian,”’ the nsanga of Lake Bangweulu, and the voracious ipata which
Dr Monard searched for in Angola. The mourou-ngou with its spots and
projecting fangs is probably similar to the dingonek and should therefore
be included in this first group.


Now all these are rather heavily-built quadrupeds, between 12 and
16 feet long, reminiscent in shape of a crocodile, giant lizard or theore-


tically even an ultra-gigantic otter.


There seems little doubt that the /ipata is some kind of crocodile: the
saw-like ridge of scales on the tail, and particularly the eyes close to-
gether on the top of the head, are very characteristic.


One cannot be so positive about the others, though the dingonek or
ol-umaina has several of a crocodile’s features. It is covered with con-
spicuous scales and has a broad, long tail. It is spotted like a leopard,


as crocodiles not infrequently are. But only with a great deal of exag-
geration can a crocodile’s largest teeth, like canines, be compared to a
walrus’s tusks. Moreover, the dingonek’s head has been compared to an


otter’s, a dog’s and lioness’s, and this hardly agrees with the Nile croco-


dile’s characteristically long skull and jaws. And what are we to make of
the sort of ears it is alleged to have, which may be like the horns of a
horned viper?


It is only among prehistoric reptiles that we find true tusks. Without


469


THE TERRORS OF AFRICA


going so far as to maintain that it must be one of them, we can safely say
that the dingonek belongs to a very special genus. In the jungle rivers of
West Africa there lives the little black crocodile (Osteolaemus), which


differs from the other African crocodiles, all of which belong to the
genus Crocodylus, in being darker, smaller (not much over 6 feet long),
and especially in having a shorter rounder head like a cayman’s. Per-
haps, unknown to us, there may be a giant species, slightly larger than
the Nile crocodile, and doubtless on the road to extinction.
If small
colonies of such a species survived in Kenya, Ubangi-Shari and Angola,


it might explain the legends of the dingonek (or ol-umaina), the mourou-
ngou and the lipata.


The nsanga alone of this first group cannot possibly be classed among
the crocodiles, from which it differs in its smooth skin and in having
claws; for, while the crocodiles do have claws, they are short and more


like nails, and cannot be compared with the hooked claws on some toes
of most lizards. As lizards’ scales are sometimes so small and incon-
spicuous that the skin seems smooth, it is more than likely that the
nsanga is a large lizard. A smooth-skinned crocodile with claws reminds
one irresistibly of a giant monitor like the Komodo dragon.


As the monitors have fairly long necks—at all events longer and more


flexible than those of crocodiles—the msanga will serve as a link with the
next group of African “dragons,” those which, in part at least, are shaped


like snakes: the Jau of the Upper Nile swamps, the nzefu-loi of southern
Belgian Congo, the isigugumadevu of the Upper Zambezi, the mokéle-
mbémbe of the Cameroons and the badigui of Ubangi-Shari.


We can set the /au quite apart from the rest of this group, from all of
which it differs in so many peculiar features that its identity seems to me
quite transparent. It is described as a thick, short water-snake, with a


crest of “hair” and barbels on its head; it makes a loud, rumbling noise,
comes out of the water and leaves a broad track on land and lives in holes
burrowed in the banks.


Apart from the beast’s size, this description perfectly fits a fish of the
catfish family (Siluridae), of which there are many species in all the
muddy waters of tropical Africa. The catfishes may be recognised by
the long barbels around the very wide mouth, some of which sprout
from the nose itself. Some catfishes have a dorsal fin which might be
mistaken for a crest. They all tend to have long bodies, the extreme
being Gymnallabes and Channallabes, which have no pelvic or pectoral


fins and look exactly like eels—or snakes. Those of the genera Clarias
and Heterobranchus have complex organs inside their gill-cavities,


470


THE DRAGON ST GEORGE DID NOT KILL


thus allowing them to breathe air on the surface. At night they come
out of the water and crawl on land in search of animal food. Clarias
lazera of the Sudan even spends the dry season in burrows, from which


it also emerges on the prowl at night. And Ewurropius has long air-


sacs as further aid to respiration. Although they have no vocal


cords, these fish can still make a growling noise which can be heard a


long way off. Finally, in front of some of their fins, certain catfishes


have poisonous spines which can cause appalling wounds, and there is


one, the electric catfish (Malopterurus), called raad or “thunder-fish” by


106. African catfish of the genus Clarias.


the Arabs, which produces violent electric shocks. It is hardly surpris-
ing that such fish should be much feared and surrounded with all sorts
of superstitions. Indeed, it would be natural enough if it was eventually
believed that you could be thunderstruck if some of them so much as
looked at you.


There remains the Jau’s alleged size. In Africa none of the known cat-


fishes is very large: the electric catfish is the biggest at 5 feet long. But


the giant catfish or wels of European rivers is sometimes more than 10


feet long and weighs more than 400 pounds. Professor Osmond P.


Breland writes with his usual caution: “This fish is said to attain a


length of fifteen feet and a weight of over 700 pounds, but I have not


471


THE TERRORS OF AFRICA


been able to confirm these figures.” It seems to be the largest known
freshwater fish. It is enormously voracious, attacking not only other


fish, but also small land animals like birds and mammals.


Thus it would not be so strange if there were an unknown and per-
haps formidable giant catfish in Africa. My friend André Capart,
Assistant Director of the Laboratory of the Belgian Royal Institute of
Natural History, who led the Lakes Kivu, Edward and Albert Expedi-
tion in 1953-4, tells me that they discovered a large unknown catfish
(genus Heterobranchus) about 3 feet long in Lake Edward. The native
fishermen used to believe it was an evil spirit called giricho, and that to
catch it or even to see it brought bad luck. Naturally nobody took any
notice of them.


The lukwata of Lake Victoria, which Sir Harry Johnston thought was


“more probably a gigantic fish,” is also very likely a huge catfish. Sir
-


Clement Hill, who saw one, said that it had a rounded, fish-like head.
The head of a catfish 4 feet long may be as much as 16 inches wide, so


it is easy to see how terrifying the gaping maw of a similar fish would be


if it were two or three times the size.


The nzefu-loi or ““water-elephant” is a particularly thorny question,
but it may give a clue to part of the problem. Since it is alleged to have


a hairy tail like a horse’s, it cannot very well be a reptile. But why on
earth should it be one? The reference to a “‘very long neck” has sug-
gested the notion of some sort of Brontosaurus. May it not really be an
elephant, as its name implies, one of those little “‘water-elephants”’ that
I have already discussed? The “‘water-elephant’s” neck is longer than
that of the ordinary elephants, and it certainly has hair like horsehair on


its tail, as all the elephants do. Moreover, may not the tales of amphi-
bious monsters as much like an elephant as a hippopotamus or “‘half-
elephant, half-dragon” be founded on the same kind of animal?


Here it may help if I quote the first circumstantial account ever pub-
lished about elephants of aquatic habits. We owe it to one Le Petit; and

gave a British naturalist called R. J. Cuninghame a much more detailed
report about them. During the five years he spent travelling. in the
French and Belgian Congo, Le Petit twice saw water-elephants. The


first time was in 1907, and they were swimming in the Congo River
near its junction with the Kasai. He saw them a second time in the
swampy area between Lake Tumba and Lake Leopold II, “‘near to
where the M’fini River finds its exit from Lake Leopold II.”

in E. africanus. Tail not observed. Neck about twice the length of E.
africanus with ears similar in shape to those of that species, but rela-
tively smaller. Head most distinctly long and ovoid in form, with trunk
only about 2 feet in length. The shape of the feet was seen in the spoor
on sand and showed four toes distinctly separated as in the hippopota-
mus, but the weight of the body seemed to be carried by the toes
largely, while the plantar impression of the sole was not very pro-
nounced. The ground was level where this spoor was seen.
All the
animals observed had no traces of tusks. Skin is apparently hairless,
smooth and shiny resembling that of a hippopotamus, only darker. The
gait was elephantine, and the last seen of those five water-elephants was
their disappearance into the water, which was deep.


In habit they are nocturnal, coming out to feed on strong rank grass
after sundown. They spend the day in the water much as hippopotami
do. The Babumas (fishing natives) know this animal well and have a
name for it, ‘Ndgoko na Maiji’, meaning the water-elephant, and they
fear it greatly as it is known to rise from the water and with its short
trunk capsize canoes.
It is also very destructive to the nets and reed
fishtraps of the natives. Its locality is apparently very restricted, and the
natives maintain they are not very numerous.


Cuninghame goes on to remark that the primitive forms of the Pro-
boscidea had a “long-shaped, ovoid type of skull” like modern tapirs and
that “the cervical vertebrae were antero-posteriorly much longer than


is now the case in modern elephants.” He concludes: “These two
characteristics are very marked in the water-elephants, and M. Le Petit


is most emphatic that the heads reminded him more of enormous tapirs
than of any other existing animal.”


Le Petit’s strange Proboscidea are so much more like certain primi-
tive and supposedly-extinct elephants than any modern species that one
cannot help wondering whether the pygmy elephants so far reported,
Lieutenant Franssen’s, for instance, really belong to the same species.
None of the published photographs and descriptions showed the odd


features noticed by Le Petit, the short trunk, long neck and thinner toes.


Some fossil elephants have survived until very recently in Africa,
where they were certainly contemporary with man. The huge Dino-
therium, with tusks curving downwards like a walrus’s, was one of them.
The largest species (D. giganteum) was 16 feet high at the shoulder. The

Now that we have eliminated a short-nosed crocodile, a giant catfish
and water-elephant (which nonetheless deserve attention from the zoo-

Belgian Congo and tsiguqumadevu (perhaps also chipekwe and nsanga) to

alone are relevant to any discussion of the possible survival of a dinosaur
in Africa,


First let us consider the msanga and chipekwe, which can be included
in the long-necked group only on the slenderest evidence.


Lieutenant Paul Gratz spoke of a “degenerate saurian” in Lake
Bangweulu.
It was a sort of smooth-skinned crocodile with curved
claws called nsanga. Meanwhile Schomburgk, C. G. James and J. E.
Hughes said that an animal called chipekwe lived there.
It also had
smooth skin, but bore a single ivory horn on its forehead. Of course it
is quite usual for the same animal to have several names in different


dialects, or even in the same dialect. But we do not know enough about
the appearance and habits of the msanga and chipekwe to say for certain


that they are the same.


The nsanga, as I have already mentioned, might be a large monitor


lizard. Now, although the monitors may be compared to crocodiles in

The chipekwe also seems to have several points in common with them.
Not only is its skin smooth, but it has the odd reputation of killing
hippos but not eating them. Only Schomburgk reports that it devours
them, but this may be his own opinion, since all the other legends and
reports unanimously contradict it. The chipekwe and mokéle-mbémbe


are, moreover, linked by a secondary anatomical feature: the single horn
which they both have on the nose.


Yet if the chipekwe really belongs with the mokéle-mbémbe, isiqguquma-
devu and badigui, it is odd that no one has mentioned that it has a long
neck. Perhaps their necks may not be so conspicuously long after all.


The isiququmadevw’s “long neck” and the mokéle-mbémbe’s “long and
very flexible neck” might indeed be only relatively long, like a monitor’s
compared with a crocodile’s. A giant monitor whose body was 8 feet
long from shoulder to rump would have a neck half that length—that is,
4 feet. But in this case how are we to explain old Moussa’s description
of the badigui? A neck longer than a giraffe’s, that is to say I0 or 12 feet
long at least, could hardly be said to be relatively long. And it is cer-
tainly not a feature that could be overlooked, especially if it was as thick


as a man’s thigh.


In short, we must isolate one or the other from the long-necked
group: the chipekwe because its neck seems too short or the badigui be-
cause its neck is too long. The chipekwe is the better choice, as all the
others have more points in common. But it need only be provisionally


isolated; if it is shown in the future that the chipekwe also has a long
neck, but our authorities have merely omitted to mention the fact, then


its quarantine will be over. Actually we know so little about this animal’s
appearance that it is impossible to say what it may be. Denis Lyall may
have had good reasons for calling it a “water-rhinoceros,” so may
Schomburgk for thinking it was “‘a sort of saurian,” but neither of them
has told us what they were.


So let us concentrate on the mokéle-mbémbe, badigui and isiguquma-
devu. The badigui is the least known of the three, but it may well be


identical with the mokéle-mbémbe, since they both have a snake’s head, a
long neck and smooth skin. Moreover they both eat leaves, and though
they attack and kill anything which annoys them, whether it be
hippopotami or men in canoes, they do not eat them. They also live

in neighbouring areas, the Ubangi-Shari and the Cameroons, both

The mokéle-mbémbe and isiququmadevu are no less alike, though one


lives in the Cameroons and the other in Northern Rhodesia, at least
1,200 miles apart. They both have a body almost the size of an ele-
phant’s, a long neck and long powerful tail like a crocodile’s or a


lizard’s. The isiguqumadevu has a snake’s head, and both it and the
badigui leave a track about 5 feet wide. The isiququmadevu is the only
one of the three whose legs have been described: they are said to be like


a lizard’s. No doubt this means that they are rather to the side of the
body, with the knees and elbows well away from it. This would seem to
be confirmed by the evidence that the beast sometimes slides on its belly
with its feet off the ground.


The mokéle-mbémbe’s skin is said to be brownish-grey. The badigui’s,
on the neck at least, is marked with pattern like a python’s but bigger.
The only adornment on the three is the mokéle-mbémbe’s single tooth,
which is presumably a horn. It may well be an inconspicuous bump or
a feature peculiar to the male, and might thus have been missed by some
of the witnesses.


We now have a fairly detailed picture of the African “dragon,” pro-
vided we assume as a working hypothesis that the three amphibious
animals are of the same kind. This is reasonable enough, for while the
various information we have about them is sometimes complementary,


it is never contradictory. This gives us a picture of a large quadruped
with a small, rather triangular head adorned with a little inconspicuous
horn on the end, a long and flexible neck, a thick thorax a little bigger
than a hippopotamus’s, legs on the sides of its body and a long and
powerful tail.
Its skin is smooth, brownish-grey and marked with a
large dark pattern. From the bulk of its body let us say that it is roughly
25 to 28 feet long or even more than 30 feet if its tail tapers very
gradually.


It is amphibious and spends most of its time in the water, making its


lair in a hole in the bank. It also ventures on land in search of its food,
which is basically vegetable. Although it is not carnivorous, its terri-


torial instinct impels it to kill its rivals the hippopotamus and probably
the manatee too. No doubt the same instinct impels it to capsize canoes
stupidly mistaking them for rivals too.


What, then, is its zoological identity? The first step is to assume that


it is a reptile. But it need not necessarily be one. Denis Lyall thought

case, but a long-necked monster, even if it has a horn on its nose like the

may look like a rhinoceros without being one. In North America there
were once horned dinosaurs, the Ceratopsia, which looked like early
versions of a rhinoceros. A Swiss scientist, Dr Martin Wilfarth, has
attempted to show that the African “dragon” may be a single-horned
Ceratopsian called the Monoclonius. This theory could apply only to
the chipekwe, and it still remains to be proved that any of the Ceratopsia
ever lived in Africa.


Other scientists, feeling that surviving dinosaurs are too strong meat,
have recalled that there were once large herbivorous mammals with fairly
long necks and formidable claws, which were probably amphibious into
the bargain, and that the “dragon” might be one of them. As Hichens
remarks, “‘According to some it may be a Chalicotherium, that remark-


abie beast from the end of the Miocene which had a horse’s head, ‘feet
with toes, and looked like a cross between a horse and a sloth.”


Some of the Chalicotheria survived in Africa until the Pleistocene, so


this is not too daring a theory. But the likeness is only partial, for the
beast lacks the long tail and legs sticking out from the sides of the body.
Moreover, it has been shown that the Chalicotheria were not amphibi-


ous, as was at first thought. One of them would make a much better
Nandi bear than a “‘water-dragon.”


No doubt it is the “dragon’s” smooth skin that has led people to
think it is a mammal rather than a reptile. But some living lizards have
such small close scales that the skin merely seems to have a very fine
grain; and there is no reason why large aquatic reptiles should not have


lost their scaly skin. Moreover, those who have seen the beast, while
comparing it in size to an elephant or a hippopotamus, generally describe


it as a snake, a lizard or a crocodile. A reptile’s stiff, jerky and hesitant
movements can be told at first glance from the more graceful and
continuous action of a mammal.


Assuming it is a reptile, what kind is it? In outline it is certainly like


a dinosaur; that one can hardly deny. But it could be a giant species of
monitor. These reptiles are found in all the hot countries in the Old
World. The Australian monitor has a relatively long and slender neck;


its cousin, the Komodo dragon, stands upon very substantial legs; and
until very recently there was a giant monitor (Varanus priscus) 25 feet
long in Australia.


Those naturalists who do admit that there is probably a large reptile


478


THE DRAGON ST GEORGE DID NOT KILL


unknown to science in Africa much prefer to think it a large monitor
than a little dinosaur. This is not because the monitors belong to a more
recent group than the dinosaurs. There are, as I have already remarked,
two main groups of dinosaurs: the Sauripelvians, which include the


most enormous species, and the generally smaller Avipelvians. The


latter group gradually ousted the first during the Jurassic and Cretaceous


periods. The monitors also derive from the Jurassic period. The zoo-


logists’ objection to the “dragon” being one of the dinosaurs is that they


all seem to have been extinct since the Cretaceous period. This, of


coursé, is negative evidence, based on the absence of any trace of dino-


saurs’ remains in Tertiary and Quaternary deposits, and is far from


conclusive. The latest traces of the Rhynchocephalians, which preceded


the dinosaurs, belong to the very beginning of the Mesozoic era, yet there


is a living Rhynchocephalian in New Zealand. It is the tuatara.


There are two more trivial objections to surviving dinosaurs. Firstly,
they are far too large to remain hidden even in African swamps—this
overlooks the fact that some dinosaurs were not much larger than a
pigeon. Secondly, the idea of a dinosaur is far too “sensational” to be
admitted by serious zoologists—this, apart from its irrelevance, could
hardly be more absurd, for what is there “‘sensational” about a medium-
sized vegetarian dinosaur, when the world still produces man-eating
crocodiles more than 20 feet long?


All we can really say is that there seems to be a large and unknown
reptile in Central Africa. Its identity remains to be determined, and in
view of its size it is probably, like the crocodiles, the Komodo dragon
and the giant tortoise, a relic of the great reptile empire that flourished
in the Jurassic period. I have already mentioned the remarkable geo-
logical and climatic stability in Africa, which could hardly be better
suited for preserving such an ancient type.


The most surprising aspect of the Congo “dragon” has been bril-
liantly expounded by Willy Ley. He shows that pictures of the beast


are found not only in Central Africa but even on one of the most re-
markable of ancient Babylonian monuments, the Ishtar Gate.


In 1902, after three years of excavation, when Professor Robert
Koldewey brought to light the splendid arch raised by King Nebuchad-


nezzar to the glory of Marduk, supreme god of the Babylonians, he


found that walls were decorated with glazed brick bas-reliefs represent-


ing alternate bulls and dragons. The king had proudly stated in a Cunei-


form inscription:

The “‘fierce rim” (plural of rim), often referred to in the Bible by the
Hebrew word re’em, have been shown to be the aurochs (Bos primi-—
genius), the terrible wild bulls which survived in Europe until the Middle
Ages, the last survivor dying near Jaktorova in Lithuania in 1627. The
sirrush (singular of sirrushu) is much more of a problem. It is a scaly
quadruped with the front-legs of a lion and the back-legs of an eagle, —
with a snake’s head on the end of a long neck. A forked tongue darts —
from its mouth, and it bears on its head a single horn, various wattle-like.
ornaments and even ashort mane.
_


Bizarre though this animal is, it seems to be intended to be a real
beast, since it has been alternated with very realistic bulls, and in the
passage leading to the gate there is a double row of no less realistic


lions. The three beasts seem to have been chosen as the three most
powerful and savage creatures known. What can the dragon be?


If the Ishtar Gate had been excavated a century earlier [Willy Ley

would have been sufficient proof that the “Glamour Snake”’ was no whit
more credible than the winged bulls and man-headed birds of Assyrian
and Babylonian mythology.
During these hundred years, however,
Georges Cuvier had become the “‘Father of Paleontology,’’ Professor
O. C. Marsh in America had earned the title of ‘‘Father of Dinosaurs,’’
and our conceptions of what was biologically possible had changed
greatly.
Paleontologists “had discovered fossil animals that sported
endless necks and endless tails, big bodies and small heads, serpent
heads with horns on them—and possibly even forked tongues (although

had even found a special group of dinosaurs, the ornithischians, or
“‘bird-footed ones,” + that walked upright on their birdlike hind legs,

Whether or not this living “dragon” in Babylon is anything more
than apocryphal, it does not seem to have served as a direct model for
the one on the Ishtar Gate and on many other Babylonian monuments;
for the sirrush is certainly not an accurate picture of the Iguanodon or
Ceratosaurus. But it is a good stylised likeness. Willy Ley thinks that


the faults and absurdities in the sirrush’s picture, like those in the
aurochs’s, arose because the Babylonians thought both animals were
‘monsters of a far country,” for he adds that the rim was then extinct in
Mesopotamia.


The sirrush could have lived in Central Africa, where it has been
proved that the Chaldeans went, and where they could have seen a giant
lizard. When Hans Schomburgk came back from Europe with native


tales about the chipekwe, he also brought several glazed bricks of the
same type as those on the Ishtar Gate. Naturally he had no idea that the
beast and the bricks could have any connection—which Willy Ley was
the first to recognise. It is therefore possible that one of the amphibious
species of Congo “dragon,” whether tsiququmadevu, mokéle-mbémbe or
badigui, was known to the Chaldeans 5,000 years ago from travellers’


tales, and that this beast was the origin of the strrush on the Ishtar Gate.


This can be demonstrated by a simple experiment. Ask someone
who has never seen a picture of a dinosaur—a child, for example—to
make a drawing from your own verbal description of the Congo
“dragon.” They will begin by drawing a quadruped, similar in outline
to some well-known beast (horse or cow, dog or cat), and then go on to
give it the long tail and snake’s neck and head. When you mention that


it has large claws on its feet they will give it a lion’s or a cat’s paws.
They will add the required ornament to its head, and when you say that
it is a reptile, they will cover it with scales. There is every chance that
the result will look very like a sirrush apart from the hind-legs. Repeat
the experiment with another naive and amenable artist, this time draw-
ing a picture of a dinosaur, such as Charles Knight’s Ceratosaurus facing
page 480, from a dictated description, and the result will probably be a
sirrush again, even down to the bird-like hind-feet.

I need hardly say that despite all the evidence, many zoologists are as

This article brought a thundering reply from Dr Edwin H. Colbert,

This digs up all the old specious arguments on whether dinosaurs still
exist and hashes them over again. This is the type of stuff one might
expect in a Sunday supplement of one of the less reputable newspapers.
But why does it have to be brought into a magazine that is trying to
represent itself as an authoritative and carefully written journal devoted
to animals?


The race of Cuviers and Owens is not extinct. So much the better.
Heraclitus of Ephesus used to aver that Polemos, strife, was the father
of everything, and that without opposition and competition nothing
could grow and prosper. Modern biology maintains that life is a conflict
between a conservative stabilising principle of heredity and a dynamic
and creative force of evolution. Without the stabilising effect of heredity


it would have fallen into chaos, offspring being unable to succeed their
parents; an< without the adaptability that evolution gives it, it would
have been at the mercy of the smallest change of climate. So long as
zoology is to be a living science it must have a conservative element of
rigorous, positive and dogmatic minds and also a revolutionary element
of adventurous, ardent and imaginative spirits.
It needs both Cuvier

A large packing-case was brought on to the platform, while the horri-

The face of the creature was like the wildest gargoyle that the imagi-

It was mali-

coal. Its long, savage mouth, which was held half-open, was full of a

them were draped what appeared to be a faded grey shawl. It was the

Thus it is not impossible that flying lizards might have survived until
today in places inland without leaving the least trace of a fossil.


There is in fact a sort of aerial lizard living today, the “flying dragon”
(Draco volans) of the Malay archipelago. But it hardly deserves the
name, for it does not really fly, but merely glides from tree to tree on
folds of loose skin supported by movable extensions of its ribs, like the


ribs of an umbrella. It is barely 4? inches long and may glide as much


as 15 feet, losing about 5 feet of height in doing so. The more modest
name of “butterfly-lizard,” sometimes given it because it looks like a
huge butterfly, certainly suits it better than “dragon.”


This little beast has nothing in common with the Pterosaurians of
the Mesozoic era which probably flew like bats, though actually we
know very little about them. A flying reptile seems a contradiction in
terms, a creature that both flies and crawls; and the result is naturally
bizarre. When Cuvier reconstructed the Pterodactyl from its fossil
remains he described it in language no less romantic than Conan
Doyle’s:


From this data one can draw the Pterodactyl in its living state; but
the picture will be so extraordinary that it seems the result of a diseased
imagination rather than the normal forces of nature.


112. The “flying dragon”’ or “‘butterfly-lizard.”’


KONGAMATO, THE LAST FLYING DRAGON


To complete the confusion, these reptiles very likely did not share the
most typical features of the class to which they certainly belonged. True
flight needs powerful wing-beats involving a great expenditure of energy.
To avoid a fatal loss of heat the Pterosaurians must have had a fairly


efficient system for regulating their body temperature, like that of the
birds and bats. Now, for an organism to remain at constant temperature


it must have fur or feathers to prevent it from losing too much heat on


its surface. The flying reptiles do not seem to have had feathers, the


imprints of their bodies show that they had wings of membrane. Some


of them may have had fur. On the Rhamphorhynchus’s enormous tail


113. Reconstruction of the Rhamphorhynchus.


traces have been found of hairs and of the sebaceous glands that secrete


an oily fluid to keep the fur in good order.


Most of the Pterosaurians ranged from the size of a sparrow to that of


an eagle, but there was also a vast American species, the Pteranodon,


with a wing-span of 24 feet—double that of the largest living flying ani-


mal, the wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans), which reaches 12 feet.


The Pteranodon was an incredible beast. Its head was flattened in such


an extraordinary way and extended behind in such a long bony crest


that it must have been used as a rudder and performed the normal func-


tion of a tail.


But the rumoured flying lizard in Africa is a much smaller beast—no
more than 7 feet in wing-span. If it is a Pterosaurian it is most like the

Professor C. Wiman of Uppsala University attempted to answer this

It is certainly remarkable, as Dr Wiman says, that in Africa, where

But the most convincing disproof of Dr Wiman’s explanation is that
a similar report comes from the opposite corner of Africa, the British
Cameroons, and here the beast was seen by a naturalist sent out by the
British Museum.


Ivan T. Sanderson, the well-known zoologist and writer, led the
Percy Sladen Expedition to West Africa in 1932-3. When they were in
the Assumbo mountains in the Cameroons, Sanderson and one of his
companions pitched their camp on a little tongue of grass surrounded
by wooded mountains. A very steep-banked river ran near by, and they
were obliged to wade along it or leap from boulder to boulder when they
wanted to go hunting. It was while working along the river in this way
that Sanderson shot a large fruit-eating bat, which fell into the river. He
went into the water to fish it out, but stepped on something which
moved—probably a turtle—lost his balance and was nearly carried away
by the current. He was floundering back towards his rock when sud-
denly his companion, George, shouted, “Look out!”


And I looked. Then I let out a shout also and instantly bobbed down
under the water, because, coming straight at me only a few feet above
the water was a black thing the size of an eagle. I had only a glimpse of
its face, yet that was quite sufficient, for its lower jaw hung open and
bore a semicircle of pointed white teeth set about their own width
apart from each other.


When I emerged, it was gone. George was facing the other way blaz-
ing off his second barrel. I arrived dripping on my rock and we looked


at each other.


‘Will it come back?” we chorused.
And just before it became too dark to see, it came again, hurtling back
down the river, its teeth chattering, the air ‘“‘shss-shssing”’ as it was cleft
by the great, black, dracula-like wings. We were both off-guard, my
gun was unloaded, and the brute made straight for George. He ducked.
The animal soared over him and was at once swallowed up in the night.

This evidence comes from a first-rate naturalist whose works are
authorities all over the world. He has refrained from making any com-
ment about the strange animal in this book, but as it happens this is
evidence of his good faith. He speaks of it as a sort of bat, but we may
be certain that it is no known species. Indeed, it is so obvious to a zoo-
logist that he did not think it worth mentioning. For the general reader
I will explain why.


The bats, which form the order of Chiroptera, are divided into two
very distinct groups: the Megachiroptera or greater bats and the Micro-
chiroptera or lesser bats. They differ not only in size but also in diet.
The Megachiroptera are called “fruit-eating bats.” The most typical
of this sub-order is the flying-fox (Preropus), the largest known bat.
The edible Malayan species (P. edulis) may have a wing-span of


as much as 5 feet 6 inches. By comparison eagles are often more


114. Head of the flying-fox.


KONGAMATO, THE LAST FLYING DRAGON


than 6 feet 6 inches in wing-span and sometimes reach as much as
8 feet,


The flying-fox, which does indeed have an attractive fox-like head, is
a shy and timid animal; in captivity it is easily tamed and makes an
affectionate and lovable pet. There are several species of Megachirop-
tera in Africa, but their wing-span never exceeds 4 feet. One of the
largest is the hammer-headed bat, which well deserves its Latin name of
Hypsignathus monstrosus, though only for its appearance, since it is a
perfectly harmless beast, the last creature in the world that one would
expect to dive and attack a man.


It is true that Sanderson’s story may make one wonder whether the
creature that attacked him was not a parent or mate of the bat he had


115. Head of the hammer-headed bat.


just shot. In grief and despair, even the most peaceable of animals are
sometimes capable of acts of unusual bravery to revenge a dead mate or
young. Moreover, the Megachiroptera do have the very widely-spaced
teeth that Sanderson noticed.
The hammer-headed bat belongs to
West Africa, and as Sanderson himself pointed out in his Living Mam-
mals of the World, these bats “for reasons unknown do a lot of dipping


into water,” so one might be tempted to suggest that it was one of these
monstrous animals which had innocently attacked the naturalists wading
in the river. But there are two objections to this identification. The
unknown beast was black all over, while all the African flying-foxes


are a brownish, or even a yellowish mahogany colour. Moreover the


negroes’ terror implies that the animal was habitually aggressive, which


a beast that fed only on fruit would hardly be.

CHAPTER TWENTY-TWO


Tratratratra, Vorompatra, etcetera


Madagascar is another land of promise. Here,
too, mountair and forest prevail; situation is
favourable; and we know almost nothing of the
interior.


P. H. Gossz, The Romance of Natural History.


ONCE upon a time there was a famous doctor who cured all his patients


(this is a fable, of course); his one fault was that he was very incredulous.
One day a little girl came running to him, quite distracted, and begged
him to leave everything and hurry to her mother’s sick-bed.


“Your mother is all right, my child,” he replied with a smile, “she
imagines she is ill, but actually she’s as sound as a bell. Don’t worry,
she will get well by herself.”


“But, doctor, she is in terrible pain!”
“Never mind. Run along now, I have other things to do.”
The little girl went. The mother died. And the doctor proved that


it was not enough to have complete mastery of his art. His first duty
was to examine his patients.


Many zoologists have this doctor’s fault, with equally tragic results in
a different sphere. While they remain obstinately deaf to rumours about
unknown or supposedly fossil animals, these animals die out, some are
already extinct, and we have lost the opportunity of studying them ex-
cept as wretched remains. Their intellectual deafness may well have
prevented the zoologists from finding the solutions to some problems
they are concerned with. This thesis is amply borne out by the history
of our knowledge of the animals of Madagascar.


When Admiral Etienne de Flacourt published his Histoire de la
Grande Isle de Madagascar in 1658 after a long stay in that country he
gave a great deal of very exact information about the fauna which was
so different from that of the African continent.
But some of it was


499


THE LESSON OF THE MALAGASY GHOSTS


disbelieved as mere travellers’ tales and was only proved to be true after
several centuries. Among the woodland birds he mentioned:


Vouroupatra, a large bird which haunts the Ampatres and lays eggs
;
like the ostrich’s; so that the people of these places may not take it, it
_
seeks the most lonely places.?


Subsequent travellers told more detailed but also more fantastic tales
about the bird’s size, saying that its eggs were enormous, eight times as
large as an ostrich’s, big enough for the natives to use as tanks for drink-
ing-water. Needless to say, hardly anyone believed these tales. The
ostrich was already a monstrously large bird at 8 feet high. A bird that


laid eggs eight times as large would have to be impossibly huge. Orien-


talists suggested that these tales were just another version of the legend
of the roc which Arab seamen believed could carry off a whole ship and
her crew. Sinbad the Sailor ran across one in his second voyage after he
found a roc’s egg, which at first he mistook for a white dome of prodi-
gious height and bulk: “I drew near it and walked around it, but per-
ceived no door to it . .
. I made a mark where I stood, and went round
the dome measuring its circumference, and, lo, it was full fifty paces.”
This is a long way from the two-gallon shells reported in Madagascar.


Herodotus was told by Egyptian priests about a race of gigantic birds
“‘beyond the sources of the Nile” which were strong enough to carry off
aman. As the most powerful eagle cannot lift more than a rabbit or a
small lamb, this would be a staggering feat, though nothing to that of
the Arabian roc.
.


In the thirteenth century Marco Polo claimed that Kublai Khan had
shown him a bird’s feathers 90 spans (about 60 feet) long and two eggs
of prodigious size.? He said that he thought the roc came from some
islands to the south of Madagascar. But the roc and the huge bird of
Madagascar were assumed tu be equally fabulous.


Nevertheless in 1832 the French naturalist Victor Sganzin actually
saw an enormous half-eggshell in Madagascar. The natives were using
it as a bowl. They would not sell it to him, so he drew a sketch of it, and
in 1840 sent it to a renowned ornithologist from Paris, Jules Verreaux,
then in Cape Town. In the meantime a traveller called Goudot found
remains of similar eggs in Madagascar and showed them to Professor

It is a singular circumstance, if nothing more, that Marco Polo refers
the Roc, of Arabian Nights celebrity, to the island of Madagascar; but
as the Roc, however gigantic, was decidedly not brevipennate [since its
feathers were 90 spans long!] a discussion of its history would be
irrelevant to our present subject.


Other naturalists concluded that both birds were equally fabulous, for
nobody took much notice of these reports; they were not much pub-
licised and seemed too fantastic to be true.


In 1851 the existence of a giant bird in Madagascar was at last officially
admitted when a merchant captain called Abadie found three eggs and
some fragmentary bones on the south-west coast of the island. They
were presented to the Académie des Sciences at Paris by a certain M.
Malavois. The two largest eggs were 13§ inches by 8} inches and
12% inches by 15% inches, one being more elongated than the other.
Their capacity was nearly 2 gallons. Each egg would have held six


ostrich’s eggs or 148 hen’s eggs—enough to make an omelette for 70
people.


On the strength of these éggs and bones and with the precedent of
Owen’s Dinornis, described in 1839, Isidore Geoffroy-Saint-Hilaire
christened the Madagascar bird, naming it Aepyornis maximus, or “the


tallest of the high birds.” This name was not entirely deserved. The


tallest of the birds was not the Aepyornis but the moa, or rather one
of the moa tribe, which reached a height of over 11 feet. Geoffroy-
Saint-Hilaire deduced that the Aepyornis must be 16 feet high partly
because its egg was double the dimensions of an ostrich’s. Actually the
Aepyornis very rarely reaches 10 feet: it is a bulky rather than a tall
bird.


In 1866 the explorer Alfred Grandidier fished out of pools at Ambo-


lisatra some huge bones in a perfect state of preservation. At first sight
they seemed to belong to some large pachyderm, but when examined
they proved to belong to the mysterious Aepyornis which was at once
nicknamed “elephant-bird.”” Soon enough other bones were disinterred


502


TRATRATRATRA, VOROMPATRA, ETCETERA


for the huge bird’s whole skeleton to be deduced. The complete skeleton
of Aepyornis maximus reconstructed at the Paris Museum is 8 feet 9
inches high—a very respectable size for this bird.1 There is no constant
ratio between the size of a bird and the eggs it lays. The kiwi’s eggs are


as big as a medium-sized ostrich’s, 5 inches by 23 inches, although the
bird itself is hardly any larger than a hen. Its body is only three times


as heavy as its egg.


All the same, even if Aepyornis maximus is not the tallest known bird,
it is the largest and weightiest. Dean Amadon, an ornithologist of the
American Museum of Natural History, has measured the principal
Aepyornis and moa bones and compared them with those of the most
similar living birds, the ostrich, rhea and emu, and has deduced that the
Aepyornis maximus weighed 965 pounds, while a 10-foot moa weighed
only 520 pounds. The smaller, dumpier moas were no doubt propor-
tionately heavier and more like the Aepyornis.


Gian-Giuseppe Bianconi, a zoologist from Bologna, was so convinced
that the Aepyornis and the roc were quite identical, that he published no


less than 18 notes between 1862 and 1865 in his attempts to prove that
the remains of birds found in Madagascar belonged to a giant bird of
prey related to the Andean condor. But in due course a more thorough
study of the Aepyornis’s bones made it clear enough that, unlike the
legendary roc, it could no more fly than the ostrich, cassowary, emu and
other running birds. Like them, it had no breastbone, and its wings
were useless stumps. All the same, there is little doubt that it was the
bird that de Flacourt described by the name of Vouroupatra. Does this
mean that it was still alive then? There is no doubt that the eggs found
in the sand-dunes and mud around the great pools in the south and
south-west were sometimes so fresh that they seemed to have been laid
quite recently. The bones were equally fresh. And the natives said that
the giant birds lived in the thickest forests of the island but were very


rarely seen.


Unfortunately most naturalists were still so soaked in Cuvier’s ideas
that they refused to believe that such a monstrous bird could survive
and, instead of looking for the bird itself, racked their brains to find out
why it was extinct. Man could not be directly responsible. Unlike the


moa, the vorompatra had not been slaughtered for its meat. There is no


local legend to this effect, and the natives were not thought to be well

enough armed to hunt it—though, since the Maoris killed moas with

Some have even gone as far as to allege that noxious natural gases 3
escaping from the ground killed off the Aepyornis. But to find the most
likely explanation we should consider the bird’s habits. It is generally
thought to be a bird of the bush, like the ostrich, though the natives
insist that it lives in the forest. Certainly it is more likely that a slow and
heavy bird would take refuge in the forest. On the other hand, the con-
—
ditions in which its eggs are found lead one to believe that it laid them
on the rushes like a moorhen. From its anatomy it might well have been
largely aquatic and spent its time paddling in wooded swamps.


The fairly recent and drastic change of climate, when the rains
dwindled, dried up the immense lakes in the high plateaux and the
swampy areas of Antsirabé and Betafo. Forced to huddle in ever more
wretched little pools, the Aepyornis would have eventually become ex-
tinct for lack of food and suitable shelter. The heaps of their remains in
peat-bogs support this theory.


No doubt the thoughtless deforestation perpetrated by Bantu, Malay
and Arab invaders had a decisive effect on the change of climate, and
thus man indirectly hastened the vorompatra’s end. Since he has only
arrived in the island fairly recently—for no prehistoric human remains
have ever been found on Madagascar—it is very possible that the great
bird survived until not at all long ago. The consequences of the gradual
destruction of the virgin forest would have taken quite a long time to
make themselves felt, and until 1867, if not later, the natives maintained
that the voromparra still lived in some remote areas. Today there is no
hope of finding a living specimen, because the swampy forest that was


its peculiar habitat has decreased so dramatically.


If the naturalists in the last century had not been so incredulous of
Malagasy legends and travellers’ tales, but had searched systematically
for de Flacourt’s Vouroupatra, we might know much more about this
extraordinary bird which may have aped the hippopotamus in its habits,
as it did in its structure.

The change in climate exterminated other Malagasy birds, among
them the Muillerornis, a large cassowary from the Ankaratra area, and
the Centrornis, a relative of the spur-winged goose of the African main-
land. It was also said to be the death-knell for several giants of very
different groups; so that today Madagascar’s fauna consists only of
small or medium-sized species. But is this necessarily true? The


504


TRATRATRATRA, VOROMPATRA, ETCETERA


change in climate was not sudden and was so recent there is still a faint
hope of finding some survivors of these giants of the past.


Like the neighbouring Mascarene and Seychelle islands, Madagascar
once boasted a giant tortoise (Testudo grandidieri), which was consider-
ably more than 3 feet long and weighed more than a ton. It liked to bask
in the sun, half-submerged in shallow water, and seems also to have
been a victim of the same drought. But Raymond Decary, former head
of the colonial service associated with the Paris Museum and author of
the authoritative work on Madagascar’s fauna, writes:


It has been established that a mysterious animal which may be a large
tortoise lives in certain lakes in the caves in the south-west: is it a last
survivor of Testudo grandidieri?


Besides the species of crocodile known today (Crocodylus madagas-


cariensis) which is identical with the Nile crocodile, there was until
recently also a giant species (C. robustus), with a skull 2 feet 6 inches
long. Specialists have long debated whether there are one or two species
of crocodile on the island, and the question is still far from settled. So


it would not be at all surprising if C. robustus, found in a sub-fossil state
by Alfred Grandidier, proved to be surviving today. In any case there
seem to have been giant crocodiles in Madagascar until recently, for in
1802 the French naturalist Pierre Denys de Montfort, speaking of the
incredible length that some crocodiles were alleged to be, said that “new
and trustworthy accounts say that there are some in Madagascar which
reach 60 feet.” Even allowing for obvious exaggeration, this is a long
way from the maximum length of present African crocodiles which is
20 feet.


Another victim of the disastrous drought is the hippopotamus. There
was once a small species in Madagascar related to the Pleistocene fossil
hippopotami found in Africa. Its extinction is usually thought to have
occurred several thousand years ago. Yet it is odd that the great naviga-


tor Dumont d’Urville mentioned in that fictitious omnibus of facts
about the world, his Voyage Autour du Monde, published in 1829, that
there were hippopotami in the rivers of Madagascar. Moreover the
hippopotamus, or a distorted traditional picture of it, is said to be the
origin of the legend of the rsomgomby, a fabulous monster described as a
humpless water-buffalo or as an animal not unlike a horse or a mule. If
the tsomgomby really derives from a memory of the hippopotamus,
which may have abounded in ancient times but must have become very
rare after the Europeans’ arrival, it has certainly been much altered on

Madagascar is the land of sub-fossil creatures. No other place in the
world gives so strong an impression of having just emerged from Pre-
history. The excavated remains of huge animals, whether they be


birds, reptiles or mammals, are sometimes so fresh that one cannot help
wondering whether the species they come from are really extinct. The
native traditions often make it perfectly clear that they were known by

man until quite recently, for, according to van Gennep’s principle, which
I have already quoted, the memory of an event dies out in two centuries
when there are no written traditions. This makes the old accounts


of voyages so valuable to our knowledge of recently extinct animals.


Admiral Etienne de Flacourt did not only speak of the Aepyornis as a
living bird. He also mentioned another animal which no zoologist has
yet been able to trace:


Trétrétrétré or Tratratratra is an animal as big as a two-year-old calf,
with a round head and a man’s face; the forefeet are like an ape’s, and
so are the hindfeet. It has frizzy hair, a short tail and ears like a man’s.
It is like the tanacht described by Ambroise Paré.! One has been seen
near the Lipomani lagoon in the neighbourhood of which it lives. It is
a very solitary animal, the people of the country are very frightened of
it and run from it as it does from them.


Most naturalists, of course, took this animal to be mythical. No such
grotesque beast could have lived in Madagascar, where there are no true
monkeys and therefore no man-faced beasts with ape’s feet. De Fla-
court’s tale was no more to be trusted than his repetition, in the middle
of the seventeenth century, of the fable about dog-headed men that had
been told by Ctesias, Marco Polo and many others. The sceptics re-
ceived their first blow when the indris (Indris brevicaudatus) was found


to exist. It is the largest of the lemurs known today and is extraordi-
narily like a little man with a dog’s head. Three feet high and with no


tail but an inconspicuous stump, the indris is astonishingly like a man
in outline.
Like the other lemurs, or half-monkeys, it has a fine and
pointed muzzle, which makes its head more like a fox’s or a dog’s.
When you have seen one it is easy to understand why the Betsimaraka

Madagascar’s fauna reached that country through the ages and how it

One might reasonably expect to find the same fauna in Madagascar as
in Africa except for a few insular differences. Actually the animals on

119. The indris, the largest known living lemur.


the island are sometimes quite original and sometimes related to crea-
tures from as far afield as South America and South-East Asia. The most
typical of Madagascar’s fauna are the lemurs, which, like the monkeys,


are primates, but have many distinctive features in their anatomy: the
longer muzzle with a “wet nose” like a dog’s, the claw on the second toe,
the large ears and even more highly-developed eyeballs. It was because


599


THE LESSON OF THE MALAGASY GHOSTS


of their wide, staring sleep-walkers’ eyes that the old naturalists called
them Jemures, the Roman name for the ghosts of the dead.
The lemurs are so closely connected with Madagascar that few people


realise that at the beginning of the Tertiary era they were found all over
—
the world. They are often found in Eocene strata in North America and
—


even in Europe. From Madagascar’s size and position one might think
that it had been the last refuge of these defenceless beasts, just as New
Zealand was for the last rhynchocephalous reptile and Australia was
for all the marsupials. But here the situation is a little different. The
lemurs were not driven to Madagascar; it was the home from which
they spread over the world, where they were almost all eventually ousted
by the monkeys. Just then Madagascar was cut off from Africa and the
island which had been their cradle remained their undisputed empire.
—


Although three-quarters of the species of lemurs are found in Mada-
gascar, there are galagos, pottos and angwantibos in Africa and the
slender and slow loris in Asia, which have managed to survive by all
becoming nocturnal.
In Madagascar itself there are almost as many
species which are active by day or at dusk as there are which are
thoroughly nocturnal.


Madagascar is also the home of some small carnivores of quite a
special type, the Galidia and Galidictis, genets with longitudinal stripes,
the fanaloka (Fossa fossa), the odd anteater-civet (Eupleres), which has
become insectivorous, and the strange fossa (Cryptoprocta ferox), a sort
of cat with plantigrade feet. Madagascar is also the original home of the
chameleons and boasts no less than 35 different species.


So much for originality. What is much more extraordinary is to find
quite un-African forms of animals in this island off the African’ coast.
All the insectivores there except the shrews belong to the family, ex-
clusive to Madagascar, of tenrecs, whose nearest relatives are the almi-
quis (Solenodon) of the West Indies. The truly indigenous rodents also
reveal secret links with America, the various species of Malagasy voles
(the sub-family Nesomysinae) are closer to the American Cricetinae than


to any in the Old World. There are also two kinds of iguana, though all
the rest of this large family of lizards are found in South America.


On the other hand, the fauna of Madagascar, as I have remarked, is
related to that of India and the Malay peninsula, where there are two
nocturnal lemurs, the slow loris (Nycticebus) and the slender loris (Loris).
This relationship is confirmed by the typically Asian frogs (Racophorus,
Dyscophorus and Calophrynus) which are found in Madagascar.


This strange assortment of animals derives from very ancient geo-


510


TRATRATRATRA, VOROMPATRA, ETCETERA


graphic links. In the Palaeozoic era, the whole of the southern Atlantic
and Pacific was filled by the vast continent of Gondwana, which em-
braced South America, Africa, South-East Asia and Australia. Mada-
gascar lay almost in the middle, which explains how it came to be the
centre from which various groups spread. It was the heart of the oldest
continent.


During the Mesozoic and Tertiary eras this continent of Gondwana,
upon which the sun never set, was gradually disintegrated and whittled
away. First the eastern arm submerged into the ocean in the Jurassic,
leaving nothing but Australia and the neighbouring islands. Gondwana
was then merely a South Atlantic continent, but a huge promontory
stretched right across the Indian Ocean and remained there until the
Cretaceous period. This spit of land has been called Lemuria, for it is
the centre from which the lemurs spread. The fact that it reached from
East Africa to the middle of India helps to explain their present dis-
tribution.


Not until the Cretaceous period was the bridge broken between South
America and Africa. The almiquis in the West Indies and the odd
iguanas in Madagascar are the only living evidence of it that remains.
Madagascar remained attached to India for a little longer, allowing a
few lemurs to be exchanged for the frogs it had already received. Dur-
ing the Tertiary era it was only occasionally attached to Africa, to be
finally cut off for ever in the Pliocene. These connections can only have
been tenuous, for Madagascar has never had any of the ungulates that
are the pride of Africa—with two exceptions: the hippopotamus, which


is recently extinct, and the Malagasy wild pig (Potamochoerus larvatus),
closely related to the bush pigs and the red river-hog of the African
mainland. Both these are semi-aquatic species, leading one to believe
that during the ungulates’ period of expansion Madagascar must
have been already cut off from Africa, but only by a narrow strip of
water.


There is also a breed of wild oxen on the island, but they seem to be
descended from tame cattle imported by the Bantus and returned to a


state of nature. Some people connect them with a sub-fossil ox (Bos


madagascariensis), but this does not disprove the theory that Madagascar


was cut off only by a narrow strip of water. Cattle are not afraid to swim


across quite wide rivers.


Safe from the large beasts of prey, almost without herbivores, and
innocent of any monkeys, Madagascar was a perfect place in which the

lemurs could expand and flourish and become almost as varied as the
marsupials in Australia.

that are still extant. Apart from the aye-aye (Daubentonia), which, be- —

fairly similar. All the same, it is a mistake to think that they are all
small, long-tailed, nocturnal, arboreal and vegetarian quadrumanes of
social habits: Some are tailless, others live in rocks, some are quite di-
urnal, many are insectivorous or even omnivorous, and according to the
natives eat birds. And there are some which live alone or in pairs.

What of the other Malagasy tales of animals unknown to science?
