Surely it is not pure chance that this barely credible legend of a large
arboreal quadruped should be found in the only country where such an
animal—the Megaladapis—has ever lived?


And what are we to make of the kalanoro, the Madagascan gnomes
that Raymond Decary speaks of ?


All the tribes believe in the existence of little creatures similar to our
gnomes and elves. Their name varies with the district: Biby olona,
Kokolampo, Kotokely, and so on. The Kalanoro is, if I may say so, a
sort of amphibious variety. In Lake Aloatra, the Kalanoro are women
like naiads or mermaids, with hair that falls to their waists; they live at
the bottom of the water in watertight palaces, seducing canoers and
fishermen and luring away children. The Betsileo, on the other hand,
believe that Kalanoro is a little land dwarf, which is not more than two
feet high, entirely covered with long hair and is the wife of another
dwarf called Kotokely; Kalanoro lives in caves where she lies on a fairy’s
bed made of silkworm cocoons.
She is interested in the children of
men, stealing them and substituting her own young; she makes the
babies she has stolen drink special potions which prevent them
from growing.
Ill-favoured new-born children are sometimes called
“sons of Kalanoro,’”’ and in the country the parents still keep careful
watch at a birth to see that Kalanoro does not succeed in making an
exchange.


Around Lake Kinkony the Sakalava have a very different notion of
the Kalanoro. This rather more masculine creature lives in the thickets
and reeds on the edges of lagoons. It is less than three feet high; it has
long hair and only three toes on its feet. It has a sweet woman’s voice,
lives on fish and raw food, and walks in the country in the evening. If
you meet one, it will accost you and hold you in conversation while it
gradually leads you away until you disappear into the lake. Farther
north, on the other hand, the Kalanoro lives in woods and caves, and
does not try to lead human beings astray, but it has hooked nails with
which it can give cruel wounds to anyone who tries to capture it; it lives
on milk, which it sometimes comes and steals even from the natives’

car, and it would be odd if they were utterly without foundation. —

The freshness of the bones found in the south-east, as well as the
state of the deposits, seems to show that the Hadropithecus must have
lived until quite recently, at least in the Bara country, and one may well

All this agrees well enough with what we might expect of the Hadro-
pithecus, and it is not impossible that the natives who lived in this area
only a few centuries ago saw these animals, the memory of which has
been handed down from generation to generation, gradually being
altered to become more and more mysterious, as is the rule among
primitive peoples.


But as some areas of Madagascar are still almost unexplored, such as
the Ambongo reserve and the lonely Isalo mountains, and there are still
some 8 or 9 million acres of virgin forest, it would be rash to assert
categorically that not a single giant lemur survives. After all, the okapi,
which is as big as a horse, remained unknown for a long time because of


its nocturnal habits.


Raymond Decary, who has written about the mysterious beasts of
Malagasy legend at some length, thinks that most of them are mythical,
though they derive in part from the sub-fossil hippopotami and lemurs
“which haunted the forests and waters only a few centuries ago, and the
memory of which has been confused, giving rise to legendary beliefs.”
But there are others which he thinks look more real—the habéby, for


instance, which the Betsileo call fotsiaondré, or white sheep.
It is a
purely nocturnal beast, which is said to be sometimes seen by moonlight
in the uninhabited wastes of the Isalo range. It is as large as a sheep and


is also supposed to have a cloven hoof and a white coat, somewhat
spotted with buff or black. It has a long muzzle, long furry ears and
large staring eyes. Some say that it is a beast of prey, but another ver-
sion, according to which it is vegetarian, is more likely to be correct.
Little-known animals are commonly assumed to be more savage than
they really are.

Personally I very much doubt whether the habéby is really a sort of
sheep, for sheep are not in the least nocturnal. Besides, no one seems to
have ever seen a habéby ram, at all events they have never mentioned
horns.


On the other hand, some of the lemurs are curiously specialised.
Perhaps there are some types we have never dreamt of, and perhaps a
branch has developed parallel to the Megaladapis and has chosen to live
on the ground because of its great weight. This would not be odd.
Even among the monkeys there are the baboons, which have completely
given up living in trees. The habéby’s large and staring eyes, which all
witnesses insist upon, are not at all like an ungulate’s, though they are
a striking feature of the lemurs, especially the nocturnal species, which
are the most ghostlike of all.


Admiral de Flacourt reports yet another puzzling Malagasy animal:


Mangarsahoc is a very large beast, which has a round foot like a
horse’s and very long ears; when it comes down a mountain it can hardly
see before it, because its ears hide its eyes; it makes a loud cry in the
manner of an ass. I think it may be a wild ass.


Ten years later, in 1770, the Comte de Modave said that the animal
lived some 10 leagues from Fort Dauphin, describing it as follows in his
correspondence (hitherto unpublished):


This animal is much feared by the negroes, who give terrifying
descriptions of it; at bottom it is but a wild ass; many are found in this
part of the island, but you must look for them in the woods, for they
never leave these lonely places and are hard to approach.


Decary says that in Anosy they still speak of an animal called man-
garisaoka (literally “‘whose ears hide its chin”), which is of course the
same as de Flacourt’s Mangarsahoc, and thinks that the tokatongotra
from the lonely south may be a similar animal. Its name means “single-
footed,” in the sense that a horse or a donkey is a “‘soliped,” and it is not
unlike these animals.
Decary thinks it may derive from an ancient
tradition that wild horses used to live in the south.


A wild ass has several times been reported in the Ankaizinana forests
and the Bealanana and Manirenjy districts. Tracks of its hooves have


been found. This harmless beast (if it really is an ass) has a vile reputa-


tion among the natives, who think that the mere sight of it will bring


bad luck. It was the subject of a manuscript report by the administrator


Bollon in 1936.


It is significant that several naturalists are almost ready to admit that


515


THE LESSON OF THE MALAGASY GHOSTS


in Madagascar there is a wild ass or horse which no white man has ever
seen and of which not the slightest remains have been found, yet they


flatly refuse to consider the possibility that any large lemurs can have
survived. These nimble, intelligent creatures which live in forests and


are nocturnal in habits would have a much better chance than a horse or


ass of eluding our searches. And their ghostlike, owlish eyes would be
able to arouse the greatest superstitious terror among the natives. The
survival of sub-fossil animals in Madagascar is denied out of the same
obstinate prejudice that I have attacked throughout this book. It all
stems from an obsolete scientific doctrine, Cuvier’s Revolutions of the
Globe.


Madagascar seems to have its own variety of many of the unknown
animals that belong elsewhere.
The railalomena echoes the Congo
dragon, the kalanoro is a pendant to the tales of the mittaewo, orang
pendek, agogwe and other African dwarfs. It has a version of the konga-
mato (or olitiau) in its fangalabolo, “that-which-seizes-the-hair,” a giant
bat which dives upon belated travellers and tears their faces and hair.


Madagascar even has its own version of the Australian bunyip or the
Patagonian temisch: it is the kavay of the Ankaizinana mountains, the
terror of the Tsimihety. This aquatic animal is supposed to creep
craftily out of the water to tear the eyes out of incautious travellers.


The Malagasy also believe in a gigantic hydra, a three-coloured ser-
pent with seven heads called fanampitoloho, which is rather like the
Australian bushmen’s rainbow snake and other similar myths. When it


rises above the water its heads touch the sky, and the wash that it makes
can destroy a whole village.


This fantastic monster turns out to be a poetic personification of the
waterspouts that sometimes arise on large lakes like Alaotra and Itasy.
Surely there is some truth behind the more prosaic legends of the fanga-


labolo, the kRavay and the other mysterious animals described in this
chapter, and surely the simplest solution is that they derive from a tradi-


tional memory, distorted in the handing down, of sub-fossil animals.
Are we to believe that during the last few centuries we have let them all
die out without having so much as a glimpse of one of them: the giant
birds, giant tortoises, giant crocodiles and giant lemurs—the Brob-
dingnagian inhabitants of this Lilliputian continent?
It would be a
remarkably bad run of ill-luck. If there is the faintest hope of finding a
single one of these creatures alive, we should be mad to neglect it.


Some of them have certainly vanished. They have been lost to zoo-


516


TRATRATRATRA, VOROMPATRA, ETCETERA


logy forever because modern zoologists have been too incredulous or too
incurious. We must not repeat their mistake.


Most of the giant forms of all the zoological branches disappeared all
over the world before man had even arrived. Those evolutionary bursts
of activity, when forms diversified, always tending to giant types in the
end, belong to the past.
I have already remarked that the Tertiary
era did not see the birth of any really new type of animal. Our own
era is hardly likely to witness anything sensational in evolutionary
enterprise.


This does not necessarily mean that the animal world is in decline.
But the period of life’s great experiments and multiple attempts, which
©
were often extravagant and destined to failure, certainly seems to be
past.
Palaeontological collections are like museums of early flying
machines or the first locomotives: mines of inspired discoveries, but
how many clumsy failures!


Constantly weeded out by the merciless forces of natural selection,
only the most flexible, the most adaptable to changing conditions have
survived today: at least they are the only ones to show real vitality. Mice
and men, swallows and flies are the most characteristic examples. The
battle has been won by simplicity of line, balance and harmony of form,
medium size, light weight and sober colours; economy of weight and
strength, economy of means.
The age of giants is past. The giant
amphibians, reptiles and birds have all disappeared with only a few
exceptions. In 50 or I00 years the last of the very large mammals—
rhinoceroses, elephants, hippopotami, buffalo, antelopes, deer, zebras,
bears, lions and apes—will have vanished, except in those museums of
obsolete zoology, the nature reserves and national parks.


In Madagascar fortunate circumstances have almost enabled us to
watch the extinction of the giant fauna of the past, but we have missed
our opportunity. We should take the lesson to heart, for there are still
numbers of strange or giant forms of animals hiding in the more remote
corners of the world, as is shown by the persistent and often exact re-


ports that I have recorded here. Are we to let these monsters die out


without attempting to know them? Surely the inquiring spirit of Aris-


totle and Pliny, Gesner and Aldrovandus, Buffon and Darwin is not


dead?


In a sense I hope that it may be. Now that I have reached the end of


this book I feel a vague sense of regret—regret that I have revealed the
still-undisturbed retreat of so many unknown animals. When I think


517


THE LESSON OF THE MALAGASY GHOSTS


of what man has done with a rifle, I am horrified that I should offer him
new targets.


The most dreadful of the monsters I have mentioned attacks man
—
only in self-defence or to provide himself with food. Only man kills for
pleasure. I hope that the International Union for the Conservation
of Nature and Natural Resources, which has already begun to do such
good work, lays down an absolute prohibition to protect the creatures
which are still unknown to science and are obviously interesting to all.


No sooner is one of them discovered than the hunt for trophies be-
gins. These maniacs must be stopped at once. History shows how
alarmingly quickly man can exterminate a whole species. We have
hardly known our noble cousin the gorilla for more than a century, yet,
despite the tireless efforts of those institutions set up to protect him,
he has been ignominiously slaughtered, and perhaps will soon vanish
without our having learnt anything about his habits, so full of signifi-
cance from our own point of view.


Tomorrow we may know one of our other relatives: the abominable
snowman, for instance, who is surely a shy and gentle great ape; or
perhaps an even more human primate like the tiny agogwe or the elusive
orang pendek. 1 hope with all my heart that when he is captured there
will be no needless murder.


Have pity on them all, for it is we who are the real monsters.


Paris, 1958.

THE AUTHOR


with his woolly monkey Belinda


Bernard Heuvelmans was born in Le Havre in 1916 of
Belgian parents in exile. From the first he was fascinated
by animals and has kept all sorts of them, being now
particularly devoted to monkeys. At school he shocked
his Jesuit teachers by an unholy interest in evolution
and jazz, and at the Université Libre of Brussels he
received a doctorate of zoology with a thesis on the
aardvark’s dentition (hitherto thought to be unclassi-
fiable) as well as winning first prize for small bands at
an International Congress of Amateur Jazz. He had
no sooner been called up for military service in Belgium
than war broke out. Captured by the Germans he
escaped four times before he was able to eke out a living
as a professional jazz singer until he was given the
chance of writing a regular column on the history of
scientific humanism.
This entailed
a study of all
branches of science, in the spirit of the humanist
thinkers of the Renaissance, for he was already con-
vinced that many problems could not be solved by a
single scientific method. Although the Germans were
so offended by his writings that they arrested him, the
Belgians did likewise after the Liberation because he had
written at all. Despite this discouragement he continued
to publish articles on all kinds of scientific matters until
he was able to migrate to Paris, where he became more
and more interested in the subject of unknown animals.
He is at present working on a book about unknown
marine animals, the first volume of which has recently
been published in France. But the subject which has
